When I first heard that praise and rewards could be damaging I scoffed at the idea! I considered myself and extremely positive parent and I always wanted to encourage my kid. So the idea that something that seemed so positive could actually have a negative effect was very hard for me to understand. In fact it took quite a while before I was able to grasp the concept and really accept it. Now that I understand, It seems as clear as day! Rewards used as motivation are very problematic. Even the most seemingly innocuous ones, like for example we might tell a kid" After you do the thing, we can do this activity together". Like if you brush your teeth now we'll have time for an extra story. If you do your homework for half an hour, we'll go to the park and play. The main problem with the reward is not the idea of looking forward to an activity (or candy or extra time on the tablet or whatever it is), it's the withholding of the activity if they do not do the thing to the adult's satisfaction. That means they have failed, they have not performed well enough to be worthy of acceptance and connection. There is an implicit punishment in every conditional reward. If they get to do the activity regardless of whether or not they do the thing, then it's just an activity, it's not a reward, and that's great. Instead of a condition, it's a celebration. It's wonderful to connect with our kids that way. Remember, the other side of the reward is withholding the reward, and that is always a punishment. Regardless of our intent, it feels like a punishment to the young mind. There's no way around it. It hurts not to get the reward, it feels bad to not get the reward, and the kids know they didn't get it because they didn't fulfill the expectations of the authority figure who has all the power in the situation. They end up carrying the message of conditional worth and acceptance with them all their lives. I certainly have those patterns in me. People pleasing, conditional self-love, perfectionism, harsh self-talk, self-judgment, fear of judgment from others. Let's endeavour to treat our kids with unconditional acceptance and love so that they don't develop these negative thinking patterns. That way they will know that they are unconditionally worthy and won't spend a lifetime seeking those things from external sources.

If you are overwhelmed and under resourced, even if you know the thing, you may not be able to do the thing. Too often people suggest surface level simple solutions to a complex problem. In fact most problems are much more complex than people recognize. There are many influences that contribute to our struggles. A truly integrated and effective solution will take into account the myriad of obstacles, layers and levels of what people are dealing with. There are physical, emotional, mental, neurological, sensory, environmental, systemic and relational influences in just about every situation. When we take an approach that doesn't factor all this into account we are much less effective. This is why it doesn't help when you just tell someone to think differently! It doesn't help when you tell someone to just act differently. It doesn't mean there aren't solutions, it means that they need to be more thoughtful, compassionate and holistic. This is why the more I work with parents the more I understand how complex thinking is needed to navigate the challenges of life. When my suggestions were less complex, parents often felt unmet, unseen. They felt a sense of pressure and maybe even some shame. The more I have been able to integrate all the different aspects of our humanity into the work I do, the more parents feel deeply supported and accepted. Even hopeful in the midst of the most difficult situations.

My kid is Gay. They came out to me a few years ago. I was ready for it because I had suspected for a little while. When they came out to me, I was super conscious to make sure my reaction was empowering, embracing and accepting. I've heard too many horror stories of young people coming out to their families and being rejected, criticized and ostracized. This is in addition to the pain of societal judgement, peer pressure and the stress of hiding who they are. Far too many 2SLGBTQ+ youth self-harm and even take their lives as a result. People in the 2sLGBTQ+ community are at risk of being beaten and even killed just for walking down the street. For holding hands or showing affection. Even just for appearing not to be heterosexual and CIS gendered. I drew this (colour pencil) picture of a Pride Resistance Fist because existing outside of the dominant demographic and being yourself, loving yourself and honoring yourself is a profound act of resistance. When my kid saw this drawing, she felt so seen and supported. She saw the validation and celebration. Validation of her struggles, Celebration of her beingness. Pride month has always been important to me. It is important to me because I care about humanity, I care that all people are treated with dignity. Because I know how the community has faced oppression and violence throughout history. It also seems like these days there is a dramatic rise in the prejudice and hatred towards this community. I support Pride because of my values and my activism. I also support Pride because of how personal it is to me. My child and some of the people I love most in the world are in the 2SLGBTQ+ community. When they are hated and discriminated against, when people support passing laws that discriminate against them, it becomes entirely personal. It is the combination of both the philosophical and the personal that makes social justice activism such an important part of my life. This is why the personal and the political are linked. If you tell me you voted for someone who hates my child because of who they are, or a party that discriminates against my friends because of who they are, or if you personally hold the opinion that they are less valid and worthy humans because of who they are, there's no way for you and I to be friends. There's no way for you and I to work together. There's no way for you and I to see eye to eye, unless you change. This is important. The change is never towards more hate, the change is always towards less hate. So it's the one with more hate that needs to change. It's not two equal sides. Social Justice is about bringing balance, peace and love to the world. Less hate. The personal, political and philosophical are one.

The way many parenting professionals talk about kids is so disheartening to me. So much power, control, and even violence. We often think of violence as just hitting, but violence comes in many forms. There's emotional violence, relational violence, access to resources violence, as well as physical violence. It doesn't always have to be hitting. For example, I recently saw a video where one prominent parenting person was advocating for setting boundaries with kids. They said that a boundary is not what you expect the other person to do, the boundary is what YOU choose to do. This is a common idea being shared around about boundaries these days. And I think there is some validity to it with adults, where we might need to set a boundary when someone is not treating us well. But when we're working with kids, the power imbalance and the role of guiding them through their development is so important to keep in mind. This is why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting, we treat boundaries very differently So this person said if your kid is wanting to push all the buttons in the elevator, you set a boundary. She tells the kids "If you're going to push all the buttons, I'm going to stand in between you and the buttons and I'm not going to let you push the buttons." Then she physically blocks the kid from pushing the buttons. When one is operating from the non-coercive mindset, when one understands the mind of the child, this is such a painful approach. It causes disconnection between parent and child, and doesn't help the kid understand the context of what's happening or learn new skills. Some friends who are totally committed to the Non Coercive Collaborative Parenting Mindset, saw the video and asked me how I would respond instead? So as I was walking yesterday I recorded an audio and I'm sharing it with you now. It's all about what I call GO WITH. Going with our children's direction, instead of resisting it, opens up so many doors to profound relationship and opportunities for deep guidance.

Power, Domination, and Violence are the three cornerstones of mainstream parenting. And also a lot of so-called gentle parenting! We have a choice to place ourselves above them, and be our children's authority, or walk alongside them as a trusted guide. When we use our power to stop our kids from doing something they want to do, or make them do something they don't want to do, instead of that trusted guide, we become the adversary. Problem Mindset vs. Solution Mindset When we approach our children as a problem to be fixed, we give them the message that they are broken. This is one of the main problems with focusing on behavior. When we try and modify behavior, our kids know we do not accept them as they are. Having a solution mindset instead of a problem mindset means we recognize that our kids need support, and we are here to help them. This is when we switch from a behaviorism approach to a relational approach based in helping kids meet their needs and dealing with their feelings. This helps our empathy come online, our creative imagination, and our kids feel we are their support rather than a critic. The problem mindset makes kids turn away from us when they are struggling. The solution mindset inspires them to turn towards us. Instead of an adversary, we are a trusted guide.

A number of years ago I gave a workshop on how to foster our children's intuition. After the workshop was over I was hanging around answering questions from some of the parents. As I was talking to this one mom, her two year old had found some sidewalk chalk and was playing with it. She was finding it incredibly fascinating to put it in her mouth and taste it. Immediately her mom noticed and asked her not to do it. She explained that the chalk was for drawing, not for putting in your mouth. Of course that inspired the kid to want to taste that chalk more than anything in the world. The more the mom tried to explain and ask her to not eat the chalk, the more she wanted to do so. At one point she kind of looked at me helplessly. I said to her, "You've just listened to me talk for an hour about going with our children's direction, why don't you give it a try?" She said she wasn't sure what to say, so I suggested she start validating the kid's experience with the chalk. For example, "Oh I see that you really enjoy the taste of that chalk. It must be very interesting to put it in your mouth. The way it feels, the way it tastes. It's all grainy, and you can feel the texture in your mouth. How interesting, how wonderful that you're experimenting with it. I think it's so fascinating. I really love the way you think and the way you explore the world." She turned to her kid with a bit of scepticism, and tried it. She wasn't very convincing so I nudged her a little and encouraged her to really put some enthusiasm in it. I was impressed that she rose to the challenge. She put real feeling into her voice. As soon as she did her kid looked at her very strangely as if she wasn't sure what was going on. She put the chalk in her mouth one more time, testing to see what would happen. Mom held firm and said "Wonderful. How does it taste?" As soon as she did that the kid took the chalk out of her mouth. went to the chalkboard and started drawing with it and never put it in her mouth again. Mom turned to me somewhat in shock and said, "I have no idea how that worked, or why that worked, but oh my goodness I'm going to keep practicing." Lately I've been sharing a lot of stories like this with you because I have tons and tons of them. I know it seems counterintuitive to encourage them to do the very thing you want to set a boundary around. It's a weird feeling to validate their impulse when it's something you want to teach your kids not to do. I know the common approach is to want to set appropriate boundaries and limits and tell our kids what to do or what not to do. However, over and over again I have seen with all sorts of kids, in all sorts of situations and different family dynamics, that when we GO WITH their direction, when we validate their impulse and their feelings, they are much more willing to follow our guidance. Their resistance decreases dramatically when they feel we see them as beautiful beings of light just for who they are. Any hint of criticism or wrongness gives them the opposite message. If we want our kids to trust our guidance, we have to make it palatable for them to do so. In a lot of interactions with their parents kids experience what I call "Reliable Unpleasantness". Kids live in an ocean of No. When this is their consistent reality it is not surprising, they turn away from and resist, our guidance. Learning becomes a drag. It becomes something to resist and avoid. Because the kids feel that our guidance is going to be an imposition on their happiness and their exploration of life. We become an obstacle to them getting their needs met rather than a trusted partner. This is why it's important for us to pay attention not only to what we want to teach our kids, but also to the feeling they have in receiving our guidance. As you interact with your kids try and see how many ways you can validate their impulses, their mindset, their perspective. Look first for what you can appreciate in the moment, rather than looking for what to correct. Especially when you feel the need to correct. Changing this mindset is not easy because the patterns are deeply ingrained in us. But as you develop this capacity, you will find dramatic shifts in the way your kids respond to you and the overall harmony in your relationship. Mmmmmm... That chalk must taste yummy?! (PS I'm going to put the YouTube link to the intuition workshop in the comments on the original post. If you are reading this somewhere other than @meaningfulideas please click through and watch the video. It was a great workshop with lots of really helpful information) Peace, Vivek Edit to add: Folks will often ask what about situations where we absolutely need to intervene for safety? Of course we need to keep our kids safe. We don't want them to get hit by a car, we don't want them to touch the hot stove, we don't want them to eat the poison, or stick the fork in the electric socket! In moments where we have to intervene for immediate safety, I want to make sure that my verbal and emotional expression is still positive and connecting. If I come at them with Wrongness, aggression, and fear, it's going to make things more intense and also probably make them want to explore the thing further in the future. Sometimes the fear does stop them, but doesn't actually teach them the discernment. The needs they are trying to meet aren't satisfied so the exploration ends up with something else dangerous. Approaching them quickly and decisively, but with a connection and validation still has the best effect. It also prevents the relationship of trust, leaving the door open for us to explain why some things are actually dangerous. These conversations are best to happen after the intensity of the moment has passed and connection has been re-established . The key is to explain it in such a way that it relates to their needs and priorities. Usually the need for play, exploration, and expression. Like "If you eat bird poop you probably won't be able to play for a few days and I really want to help you play because when you play it's my favorite thing. "There are lots of really interesting things that we can put in our mouths that normally people don't, we should try and see what they are. Like maybe rocks and sticks and grass?" I call it WIIFM? - What's In It For Me? Kids respond so well when they sense we're trying to help them meet THEIR needs. When they feel we are trying to control them, resistance arises (and rightly so). The kid who was eating the chalk didn't really feel the desire to continue, and was easily snow to accept the request, once she had the validation she needed. In the end it's really about caring for the relationship and the feeling experience that the kids have. Often kids just need to feel seen and accepted. Redirection is always best when it comes with connection. Ps, I will put the link to the intuition parenting workshop in the comments.

Whenever kids roll their eyes at me I always thank them. It is such clear communication that there's something for me to shift. I consider it a gift. "Thank you for the feedback. Edit to add I try and tune in to where the kid is at in the moment and express this in different ways depending on what I feel from them. Traditional Parenting sets a Terrible Model for our Children Forcing someone to do something against their will, using the power you have over them, is a terrible model to set for our children. This is why I consistently advocate for not using our power to control our children's behavior. This includes not using punishments, consequences, limits, boundaries, taking away "privileges", as well as emotional manipulation. As parents we have systemic power over our children. We have Physical, Emotional, Relational, and Access to Resources Power. There are so many ways we knowingly and unknowingly exert power over our children. Instead of ignoring that fact, or defending its use, let us make an active, and meaningful search for those moments of Coercion, and then rewire them. I used to call it my SHAME RADAR back in the early days. I would always say "I have my Shame Radar turned up to 11!" I was eagerly on the lookout for the slightest bit of coercion, the slightest bit of manipulation. When I would notice one, I would jump all over it! The reason for this is, I valued the integrity of our relationship so highly that I didn't want to let a single one slide by. It doesn't mean I was perfect, it meant I tried to be aware, and then I would repair. Aware and Repair! This is the path of Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. We keep stretching ourselves towards the ideal. We may never be perfect, but we will always be striving. This is a much better model to set for our children. Instead of being based on hierarchy and control, it's based on connection, respect, and collaboration.

2024 04 03

Non-Coercion does not mean Not Guiding, it's a Deeper Guiding One of the most common objections I receive when sharing the idea that it's not a good idea to control our kids is that, if we don't control them, we're not guiding them, and they're going to run wild. This is one of the most important points about the philosophy that I teach. This is not a hands-off parenting philosophy where the kids figure out life on their own. That is not what I do, that is not what I teach. Non-Coercion does not mean Not Guiding, it's a Deeper Guiding Hierarchical, Authoritative, Coercive guidance is less effective, and disconnecting. I prefer that parents and their kids become co-explorers of life. Learning, Guiding, and Teaching each other side by side. The thing is, in order to have the deepest guiding role with our children, we have to give up using our power and authority to control them, because that does damage to the deep trust required to have a true guiding relationship. It's a big leap. It's not the customary way that parenting is done. Most of the world cannot fathom working with kids without control, force, and authority. And yet there's something profoundly beautiful about this Mutual Learning Relationship. I say "The Magic Is In The Mutuality." When my kid was in grade one, she had an assignment about responsibility with three questions. 1) Who is a responsible person in your life? 2) What are they responsible to you for? 3) What are you responsible to them for? Her answers were: 1) My dad is a responsible person in my life. 2) He is responsible for teaching me what's right. 3) I am responsible for teaching him the same thing. She felt the mutuality of our knowledge exchange even back then. I make sure when I'm working with kids, that they always feel the mutuality in our exchange. This way they feel truly valued. What can you do to help your kid feel that you are a trusted guide? What do you need to do more of? and what do you need to do less of? Remember Non-Coercion is not Not Guiding! It is Deeper Guiding.

Transition Philosophies are parenting philosophies with one foot in the old mindset and one in the new. The old, being a hierarchical power relationship, authoritative control, consequences, firm boundaries and limits. The new, being a collaborative power sharing relationship, based in communication and connection. Transition Philosophies will tell you on one hand to respect your child as a whole human being, then will tell you it's ok to enforce a limit (against your child's wishes and consent) as long as you empathize. My saying about this is ""You cannot be the Perpetrator and the Empathizer at the same time." One foot in the old, one foot in the new. Empathizing is great because we help our kids learn their feelings are valid. But if we are the ones causing Avoidable Pain to our kids, we are the perpetrator, and this is a pattern that we are working to change. As Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parents we strive to step all the way into the new mindset, stretch towards the ideal. And stretching towards an ideal is always inconvenient. It asks more of us, because we stay engaged in life process, rather than interrupt it. Authority interrupts the life process. Transition philosophies are important stepping stones for many people who are trying to move from coercion to more collaboration. They help people give up spanking, punishments, consequences, etc as parenting strategies. Loving limits are certainly better than shaming limits! However they still have the hierarchical, power over structure which causes disconnection. Disconnection between parent and child, and disconnection between the child's relationship with themselves. It also causes a disconnection in our relationship with ourselves, because when we exert power over another human being, we lose a piece of our inner connection. This is why we dedicate ourselves to the path of non-coercion, we are preserving all three relationships. The relationship of parent and child, the relationship of the child with themselves, and the relationship of the parent with themselves. So whatever parenting information you consume, including mine, evaluate it carefully to see if there is coercion embedded into it. The Coercion can be overt or covert. Sometimes it's subtle, sometimes it's dressed up to look really gentle! And also keep digging into your own mindset and choices, and see where you might be defaulting to the old ways. Then keep the parts that are based in non-coercion and collaboration, and release or transform the rest. . .

Tell your kid not to Obey you! I told my kid when they were just 2 years old that I never wanted them to obey me. I wanted them to think deeply about life and follow their heart, and I would support them regardless. When they first went to school I informed them about the oppressive structures they were going to face. Consequences, punishments, rewards, grades, comparison, conformity, and the imposition of adult values, etc. I let them know that no adult in that building has any authority over them, even though they think they do. Don't be fooled. Your power is your own. This is Empowerment. Part of learning to manage coercive and oppressive structures is to be clear about our own values. That is the other side of this exploration. We think about how we want to treat other people? What kinds of people do we want to be? What kind of relationships do we want to have? What kind of world do we want to contribute to? If our children are treated with respect for their humanity at home, they can recognize disrespect in the world. The opposite of this is also true, which is why so many adults have no clue what real respect is! We explore different ways to respond to coercion, both personal and systemic. How to balance caring for the community, with caring for one's own values and boundaries. We discussed the nature of imposed consequences, why adults give them, and when a choice might be worth the risk. Even at kindergarten age, kids are able to understand these concepts. Exploring these concepts over many years is preparing kids for the real world. Giving them consequences is not preparing them for the real world. That's why I always say we didn't have Expectations, we had Explorations. Once we make this mindset shift, obedience feels shallow and empty.

One of the most empowering gifts we can give our children is in fostering their relationship to their intuition. Most parenting info out there is about tantrums, sleep, hitting, food, screens, defiance, respect, siblings, and setting limits.

There isn't a lot of parenting information about deep things like Intuition and Relationship with Self. When I think about my child going out into the world, and facing inevitable difficulties, obstacles and struggles, having a strong connection to their intuition can be one of the most powerful things we can offer our children. I go into detail about what intuition is. why it's important, and how we can best support our kids in forming that deep trusting relationship with themselves. Our children's relationship with themselves is one of the primary things that we have the opportunity to help them with. As adults there are so many aspects of life that are challenging. We often struggle to make decisions, or we make them based on fear, social pressure, insecurities, and trauma. So much of that comes from not having a deep relationship with ourselves nurtured in our early years. We weren't taught to listen to and trust our deep wisdom. Let's give our kids something we didn't receive.

We need a revolution in parenting. We need to treat our kids with profound respect. It's not enough to do traditional parenting more gently. We need a radical departure from the authoritative ways of the past. I want us to operate from a completely different mindset. A different set of consciously chosen values. Let us put our efforts towards a true Non-Coercive, Collaborative relationship with our children. The old patterns of the past have been handed down to us through 10,000 years of Coercive history, and Hierarchical, Violent Power structures. We have inherited some pretty terrible patterns. The entire world is falling apart because of it. I shake my head when people try to defend the old mindset. All throughout history, we've had oppression, marginalized and vulnerable people have been oppressed and dehumanized. If we want to work towards a world where we bring everybody together, where we support each other because we care about each other. Where no one has to go hungry, and no one dies because of violence, oppression, power, and greed. If we want to create that world together, (and not everybody does), but for those of us that do, if we want to create that world together, it is foundational to start with our children. One of the first places to start dismantling oppression is in our homes. We cannot create a world free of oppression if we are mirroring those same patterns in our home. It doesn't mean we don't teach our kids about oppression. Informing our kids about how the world works is important. One of my sayings is, "We can teach kids about oppressive systems, without replicating those systems in our homes. So when you're with your kids, think to yourself, Am I oppressing them in this moment? Are they feeling oppressed? Am I Repeating the same patterns? For example, if your kid wants Ice Cream Before Breakfast, and you say NO, (or even No, because&), what power allows you to say no in this circumstance? It is because we have a lot of power over our children that we can enforce such a No. Access to Resources is a major power difference between adults and children. For many years they are completely dependent on us. We have power that they don't. We have physical power, emotional power, relational power, and access to resources power. When we use that power to deny their freedom. That's oppression. I have been doing this a long time, so believe me when I say, I know how extreme this sounds. It feels extreme, until it doesn't, and then it sounds natural, and necessary. From the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset, even something as small as ice cream is important to consider deeply. If we use our power to control our kids, to deny them ice cream, they experience this as a micro-oppressions. The repeated experience of this, over and over and over again, for years and years has a deep effect. It affects their mindset. Their self-image, how they see/feel about themselves. How they treat others. These are deep and foundational parts of our humanity. That's why we pay so much attention to these concepts when we are practicing Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. Let's Always ask The Questions: 1) Am I oppressing or empowering? 2) Am I imposing my values or supporting their self-knowledge? 3) Am I violating their consent or respecting their autonomy? 4) Am I controlling or collaborating? 5) Does this make me feel less safe or more safe to them? When we let these questions guide our thinking and our decisions, we soon find many things we need to change. As challenging as that can be, it is also something to celebrate. I want to encourage you to consider shifting away from any use of power to control your kids. What would it mean to not impose a hierarchy? To share power? Ideas worth exploring.

2023 10 17 Micro Meditation The Micro-Meditation is one of a series of micro-practices I share with parents. The main three are: 1) Micro-Meditation 2) Micro-Compassion 3) Micro-Self-Observation A Micro-Meditation is taking One Conscious Breath. Do your best to block out the world and just take one breath. Let your shoulders relax. Feel the ground under your feet. Feel the infinite sky above your head. Just for one breath. Then go on about your day. When stress and overwhelm try and get their grips on you, that's a good time to connect with your centre. Much of life as a conscious parent is a search for balance amidst the chaos. This is where the Micro-Meditation is so powerful. People who practice it are finding greater awareness and calm in difficult moments. I try to practice Micro-Meditations throughout the day. Even when I watch my own video of the Micro-Meditation, I do it with myself as I watch! Sometimes people ask me for help when they have trouble meditating. I share the Micro-Meditation. The two main areas of struggle people have about meditation are either that they don't have time, or they cannot concentrate. The Micro-Meditation addresses both of these. With it being one breath, it's almost always the ideal time and place to meditate. We can even connect with our deep Selves on the toilet! When I'm in there, I try to take a break from playing with my phone and use a moment of my toilet time to reach out to the spirit of the universe. (Then go right back to my phone!) You can take that one breath pause when you are picking up a toy off the floor, when you are brushing your teeth, when you are putting your shoes on, or even tying your kid's shoes. Take that one breath Micro-Meditation and value it, honour it and Oh, believe that you are worth it. There is an accessibility to meditation when you are not having to carve out blocks of time from your day. Take That Slow Conscious Breath In and out That's All. In and out. The goal is not to have a quiet mind while you do it. The goal is simply to take the slow conscious breath. I suggest practicing the Micro Meditation whenever it occurs to you throughout the day. Sometimes I will even set an alarm on my phone every hour to remind myself to take that breath. Over time you will build some pretty powerful layers of self-awareness and self-compassion

One in which your kids will respect, and even seek out your wisdom and perspective on things. One of the main ingredients in creating the safety is not expecting your kids to follow your guidance. Especially in the teen years when traditionally kids turn away from their parents. Free Thinking and Microwaves I'm 15 years old, I'm removing my lunch from the microwave. My uncle stops me and tells me to leave it in there for one more minute. He said "that's when a microwave does it's real cooking." I remember it clearly to this day. I said, but there's no power, how is it cooking? He said it just is. He had so much Authority in his tone. And I knew he didn't know. At 15 I could see through him. He was yet another adult acting as if he knew, and I possibly couldn't because I'm just a kid. I also knew I didn't know if this was true, but I certainly wasn't taking his word for it. I could tell he had read it somewhere and just believed it. I didn't quite have the words for all of this at the time, but I perceived it very clearly. I knew at that moment that I never wanted to believe something just because I read it. It was a defining moment for me in learning about how to think. Even though he was a goof, I kind of have my uncle to thank for that. Since then it's been very important for me not to be satisfied operating from a script. To believe what I believe based on my thinking, to choose my values based on my own exploration, to be open to learning and continuous growth. I also wanted to pass these values on to my kid. I didn't want her growing up being forced to believe what other people believe. I didn't want her having adult thoughts and values imposed upon her. I wanted her to discover her own thinking and her own values through her experience. Of course the experience included me, because we did the exploration together. But it still was not an imposition. One of the most beautiful parenting priorities we can adopt is caring for our kids' thinking process, for the relationship to their own thinking. This is something so profound. That moment with that uncle influenced my parenting quite a bit over the years. I never wanted to come across as the authoritative adult. Because I know that puts a separation between parent and child. So I fought against the tendency with all my might. And it really is a fight. Because pretty much all the messages of society tell you that Authority is necessary. That the hierarchies. That the control is necessary. It is a rebellious act to reject it, and choose a relationship of equals instead. Where you are learning partners, where you are each other's guides, where you create a true collaborative relationship. It's still such a rare thing, but it is growing in popularity, which makes me very excited. I think more and more people are starting to recognize that by embracing the non-coercive, collaborative mindset, we can have much more profound relationships with our kids, and we are giving them a more powerful foundation to face a very difficult world.

Gentle Authoritarianism There are lots of parenting philosophies out there that seem gentle at first glance, but are still based in authority, coercion, hierarchy, and control. When we give up spanking, punishments, and consequences, it's a big step forward from the parenting mindset of the past. Just making that change is a huge leap and takes a lot of effort and courage. However the journey doesn't stop there. This is important to understand. That is a first step. The journey to treat our kids with respect continues to unfold. We need to continuously dig deeper into what it means to treat our kids non-violently. I want my kids to be able to rely on my non-violence. One of the biggest areas of presently acceptable coercion and violence, is what is commonly called "Loving Limits". The concept is that you set a limit, and then empathize with the kid if they don't like it. And of course it's very likely the kid is not going to like it! The problem with this method is it is still rooted in the old relationship of hierarchy, control, and power. If you try and set a limit, like around screen time, or bedtime, or food, and the kid just says no and that's what they want anyways, the only way to enforce the limit at that point is with power. This is the problem with gentle authoritarianism, with imposed hierarchy, it leads to using power to control the other person. If you take the option to control completely off the table, what you're left with is figuring out how to work with your kids collaboratively! This is the wonderful challenge we face as people who are creating A New Path. We don't have all the answers, but we know the principles and values we hold dear. Non-Coercion, Collaboration, Connection, Safety, Trust, Consent and Autonomy, Kindness, and Compassion. I encourage you to use your discernment when consuming parenting information. Keep a gentle authoritarianism lens on, so that you can notice when someone is trying to convince you it's okay to coerce your kids. Please even keep that lens on when checking out my material. If you are a parent coach or educator reading this, I encourage you to delve deeper into these ideas. Where might you be teaching some gentle authoritarianism? How can you transform that into something deeper and more collaborative? This way we can keep moving closer to being in alignment with treating children with respect for our shared humanity. If you have been teaching a particular philosophy for a long time, it can be really hard to change, especially if you have a lot of people following you and you're really popular because of it. But I still encourage you to push yourself in that direction. Become even more non coercive than you are now. If as a parent coach or a parent educator, you're unsure about this, I invite you to reach out to me and we can chat about it. The Gratitude Response Gratitude is one of the most powerful secrets to increasing harmony and cooperation in your home. So many parents struggle with how to work with their kids in such a way that they learn proper values, and their homes are places of harmony and cooperation. The mainstream parenting strategies that we employ end up bringing us the opposite results. The old system of thinking handed down to us is that strong boundaries and clear expectations, combined with rewards for positive behavior, and consequences for undesirable behavior, will produce the kind of environment that we want in our homes. The thing is, that is not how it works. Rewards and punishment are not effective strategies in producing long term harmony, cooperation, or deep relationships, where people care about each other's needs. In fact, when we engage with someone regularly from the coercive mindset, it degrades the relationship they have with us, and degrades the relationship they have with themselves. The gratitude response is a way of responding to our children in difficult moments, and even in positive moments, so that they have a different experience of us. The gratitude response, when practiced regularly, creates for children an environment and relationship in which they can relax into us, trust our guidance and be open to learning from/with us. The gratitude response is about having that energy of really accepting and embracing our children. We're not just thankful for them behaving "well". We're thankful for them all the time. We're thankful for their struggles, we're thankful for their tendencies and patterns, we're thankful for their awkward learning processes, because they're no less awkward than ours. We accept them, we love them and we're grateful for them. It's amazing to me that when we offer kids appreciation and gratitude for who they are, how powerfully they respond.

The Gift of NO! When my kid would say NO to me I would always thank them. I would receive their NO as a gift. This is because I genuinely wanted their truth. I didn't want them to stifle their NO out of any sense of obligation, fear, or pressure. You can imagine the long-term effects of doing so throughout our formative years! So Empowering. I always want my kids to know that I honor their NO, and I want them to honor their NO, because very often the world will not honor it. A beautiful effect of honoring kid's NO, is the more they know we honor their NO, the less they need to use it as a self-protective mechanism. If kids are not using no as a defense mechanism, then what's left over is their organic no. This leads to a deeper level of trust between parent and child. It also leads to children trusting themselves more as they develop throughout their lives. There is a common idea that honoring a child's NO, by honoring their consent and autonomy as human beings, they will somehow become entitled and not be able to take it when someone else says no. In fact the opposite of this is true. When a person is raised knowing themselves, and honoring themselves, their relationship with themselves is solid. They do not have to compensate for their insecurities by taking things out on other people. This is why receiving our children's NO as a gift, and thanking them for it, is so profound. It helps them develop a powerful relationship with their inner self. How do you help your kid feel empowered to say NO?

Punishment Produces Selfishness When we use punishment, consequences, or any form of wrongness to alter our children's behavior, we actually inspire a selfish motivation. If the kids get a consequence because they didn't clean up, they might clean up next time to avoid the consequence. But they're not cleaning up because they care about the family community, they're not cleaning up with a sense of joy or even a sense of genuine responsibility. They are not cleaning up feeling connected to their parents, they're cleaning up to avoid experiencing the pain that they've been promised by their parents. The focus is on how they can avoid feeling pain, and experiencing the disconnection that comes with it. Their focus is not on caring about their impact, or on working together in a cooperative spirit with the family community. And I want to be very clear about this, you can't have both. If you are punishing and giving consequences to your kids, it is not creating a sense of family community. It is creating a division of hierarchy. A relationship of power over. Necessarily. This is why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting we don't use any of those techniques, including enforcing limits and boundaries. We try to do everything collaboratively, through connection, collaboration, exploration, learning, play, and the understanding that this process takes time. The difference in result however, is that the kids really own their values. They make their decisions based on an exploration of the kind of person they want to be, the kind of relationships they want to have, the impact they want to have on those relationships, the impact they want to have on their communities, etc. They are not making their decisions based on a fear of consequences. Doesn't that seem like a much more shallow motivation now? Let's teach our kids a deeper and broader understanding of decision making. Will you join me in leaving behind the old ways of hierarchy and control?

The Empty Boat There's a Zen story that I love. There once was a person who took their boat to work every day. They rowed down the river to the factory. Everyday someone would bump their boat, they would get angry, turn around and yell at the other person. "Why don't you look where you're going? You better watch yourself." For years and years this happened every day. And every day he got angry. One day as they were rowing to work, a boat bumped them and like always they turned around to yell, but noticed the boat was empty. There was no one to be angry at. And they started to laugh. I had an experience very much like that once. This guy behind me was honking at me, honking at me, and honking at me! I got very angry, I was like; "What's your F&$ problem?" Eventually I chased him down, I got out of my car to confront him. I was very heated by this time. When I asked him why he was honking at me, he said that he actually wasn't, but his horn is broken, and it won't stop honking. It was the Empty Boat. I immediately started to laugh, probably the exact same laugh! And then suddenly the memory of that story came back to me and I laughed even more. I apologized to the poor fellow and shook my head as I walked back to my car. That moment created a significant shift in my relationship to my anger. I was able to perceive it more clearly, to have a bit of distance from it. That was more than a decade ago, and I have, thankfully, worked through a lot of it. When I noticed myself getting angry, I think about the empty boat. I wonder if there is an empty boat here that can help me have some perspective? The Empty Boat The Honking Horn

ACBOD - Anger Caused By Obstructed Desire This is one of my favorite acronyms - ACBOD. So often in life our desires, our needs, our plans are obstructed. Our kids are excellent sources of that obstruction. When it happens anger can flash through our system. It can be easy to respond from that place. Also not helpful! If we can recognize that the anger is coming from ACBOD, and not the child's actions, we can take a pause, breathe through it, and choose a different reaction. It takes time and practice, but you can get better at this. Noticing the Obstructed Desire, Pausing, Breathing, Choosing. ACBOD!

My Ideology is Clashing with my Reality When my kid was born I knew I wanted to parent differently than the mainstream. I had a lot of ideas about what I was going to do. Turns out I had no idea how hard it was going to be. I was a mess of triggers, trauma, emotional reactions that I had no idea were there. I knew the kind of parent I wanted to be, I knew how I wanted to act, but it was like this other person kept showing up and taking over. In those early years I used to tell people that my ideology was clashing with my reality. Not for all of my intentions, things weren't going quite how I wanted them to! This is when two important lessons presented themselves to me. The first was anti-perfectionism. I realized early on that there was no way for me to get through even one day without making some kind of mistake. Often many, sometimes dozens! Depending on the day of course. You know what I mean. I needed to accept myself as a fallible and evolving human being. The more I worked on accepting myself as a being in process, the less pressure I put on myself to be perfect. I found this actually accelerated my growth because I didn't have the same amount of Shame holding me back. The second lesson was a clear realization of how important it is to be on a conscious healing path. Those triggers and patterns aren't going to go away by themselves. They need conscious intervention, they need our loving attention, our loving consistent attention. In a way I'm glad that my ideology clashed with my reality so intensely in those first few years. Because I learned those two lessons, the first of self-acceptance, the second of continuous growth. Think about how you might be able to deepen those two ideas in your own process. Can you deepen your self-acceptance? Can you accept that you're an evolving being and that you're going to make mistakes, and love yourself through it? And can you commit to a lifetime of growth and learning? Can you keep stretching towards the ideal? It's a great combo!

Preserving our children's relationship to their original self is a primary priority in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. The message of all punishments, consequences, and rewards is; I love you MORE when you act like this. I love you LESS when you act like that. I accept you more when you act like this, and I accept you less when you act like that. I offer you more of myself when you act like this, and less of myself when you act like that. You are more deserving of love, kindness, and respect when you act like this& Kids soon get the message of conditional acceptance, conditional love, conditional relationship, conditional worth. Then they have to navigate that conditional worth as an obstacle. We become the obstacle. Because of that, they're not engaging in a deep human relationship with us. They're not going within and discovering their relationship with themselves. And painfully, they're not relying on us as a guide as they're exploring their relationship with themselves. This is why I'm so adamant that in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting, we don't use any consequences, or punishments, or rewards to try to get our kids to do something. From a behavior focused mindset, it's hard to understand because you're trying to modify behavior. I'm not. I'm helping a human to explore themselves, to explore the world, and to nourish a deep relationship with them. That's what I'm trying to do. It's a much more profound way to guide a child because it's a co-learning relationship built on safety and trust, rather than imposing our values and ideas on the kid. If we have expectations, and hold them in place with consequences, punishments, and rewards, then the kids have to contort themselves in order to fit the shape that we've demanded of them. Then they can't be themselves, and discover themselves. What a loss. I don't want to participate in that loss. I want to be the one who empowers my kid to know themselves, not disempowers them and takes them away from their self-knowledge. When my kid was young, I kept that phrase in my mind to warn me about conditional acceptance. It was kind of like an anti-mantra; "I love you MORE when you act like this, and I love you LESS when you act like that."

BITE YOUR TONGUE Tongue biting is an essential Parenting skill. I often say I only have 7% of my tongue left. Every time we punish our children (including giving them consequences) they trust us a little bit less. They believe in our love a little bit less. They believe in our good intentions a little bit less. Punishment forces kids to lie to us. We become an obstacle for them to find their way around. They may not even know they are lying at times because it's self-preservation. They put up an armor around their hearts and keep us at a distance. It is a natural reaction to protect oneself in a situation like this. This is the mindset that punishment forces upon them. Our kids learn that they cannot be themselves if they want to be loved and accepted by their parents. They have to contort to the shape of our expectations. They end up wearing a mask over their essence to achieve a semblance of belonging. To avoid the pain of their parents judging them, punishing them and controlling them. This is why one of my one-liners is - "Parents Are Not Mask Designers"! I recently got into a heated discussion with some guy on my post called "The 4 Problems with Punishment." Which are: 1) Punishment gives kids the message that we love them conditionally and not unconditionally. 2) Punishment teaches kids that the reason to do good is to avoid pain, as opposed to living our values. 3) Punishment erodes the bond of trust and love between parent and child. 4) Punishment teaches kids to treat others oppressively when they have power over them. He was making the case that if we don't control our kids they'll just do whatever they want and chaos would ensue. This is such a common concept. We were going back and forth a bit when he writes this line: "We are not good at heart, we are evil" That is the assumption he makes about humanity, about himself, about his kids. This prevents him from seeing a Non-Coercive, Collaborative possibility. I know many religions teach this, I know many people believe this. It is a concept that is embedded into society as well. This is why so many people say they deserved to be punished, they deserved to be spanked, believe it's the only way they would have learned. They believe they are fundamentally bad and need to be forced to be good. That they are broken and need to be fixed. I responded to him: "This is where we differ my friend. As long as you believe that humanity is evil, you'll never understand this philosophy. I prefer to operate from the assumption that our essence is Kindness, Compassion, and Love. This is the truth of our being and we're taken away from it by the very systems of thought you are defending. The philosophy I share points children to their inherent goodness. We guide through relationship, not fear." I am struck by the assumption of evil. It's the direct effect of the punishment and reward, control-based, hierarchical power, relationship of traditional parenting. We are punished and made to feel wrong when we make mistakes. Our parents cause us pain when we act out of alignment with the expectations they hold for us. This gives us the repeated message that we're broken and need to be fixed. That we cannot be trusted. That we are not fundamentally good. This information gets wired into our nervous system, it becomes part of our sense of self. The child feels "There must be something wrong with me if my parent, who is my guide, intentionally causes me pain, in order to modify my behaviour." This creates adults who carry the belief that human beings, including themselves, are fundamentally bad, that we are broken. This is one of the reasons we see so much coercion, shaming and violence in adult relationships as well. In order to counter this devastating long-term effect, let's focus our efforts on doing everything we can so our children know they're unconditionally worthy of love, acceptance and connection. When children grow up feeling deeply valued and respected they will naturally reflect that mindset in all their relationships. Offering an experience of love and acceptance when our children act "badly", is one of the hardest and most important things for us to do. (Check out a video on my YouTube channel @Meaningful Ideas called "When One Kid Hits Another Respond with Kindness Instead of Wrongness) It is the opposite to traditional thinking of how to respond to these types of situations. Problematic behaviors are usually dealt with using lectures, boundaries, and consequences. When children act in ways that seem rude, disrespectful, or disobedient, these are opportunities for giving deeper love. I acknowledge that this is very challenging when we have our own triggers to deal with, when we are overwhelmed and under-resourced. There is so much for us to overcome in order to not react and demand respect or obedience. This is why Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting takes great courage. The times we can offer love and acceptance, rather than criticism, consequences, and punishment, will stay in their hearts forever. It will transform them at the deepest level.

They were explaining, convincing, bribing, trying to set a boundary, distracting, etc. This kid was not to be fooled however, and held on to that book! You can see it on the comment sections of pretty much any of my posts, everyone saying that it's an impractical philosophy. I imagine the folks there were curious about what I was going to do. In typical Vivek fashion I went to the kid and told them that I wanted them to keep the book as long as possible. I wanted them to keep it as long as they wanted it. And I didn't want them to give it to anyone no matter what, as long as they wanted to play with it. I said the most important thing to me was that they kept that book as long as they felt good about it. And then when they were done, I would love to read the book because I'm so curious about what my card is. But even if I have to wait till tomorrow or next week I don't even care, I want you to keep it as long as you need. In the middle of all of this the kid just reaches out and hands me the book. I met those needs and the resistance vanished. One of the reasons I share this philosophy is because my life is full of hundreds and hundreds of these stories. The Power of Empathy This kid was throwing chairs and tables around, he was that angry! His mom called me over not having any idea what to do. We were both at a dance camp together a few years ago, and her kid got really upset. She knew I do this parenting stuff, so she called me over and asked me if I could help. Kind of challenged me in a way. Because she never knows what to do when her kid gets like that. I could see that the kid was upset about something, and needed to express his feelings. He just didn't know how. So I called him over and I asked him what the heck was going on? I started by telling him that I appreciated he was throwing chairs and tables around, because it really helped me to know very clearly that he was angry. I said you look really angry. Are you angry about something? He then told me he was angry that the other kids didn't play with him. He felt excluded. With just a little bit of connection, he opened up something quite deep. Note I didn't tell him "it was okay for him to be angry, but he can't throw chairs". I avoid that approach at all costs. I even thanked him for throwing the chairs. And I also explained why. Because it helped me to know what he was feeling, so that I could help him. I told him it was really painful when kids didn't want to play with you. I remember how that felt. I asked him if he would like some help with it? He said that in fact he would like some help and we did a little creative brainstorming together. Then he just felt so relaxed that he went off and started playing on his own. His mom looked at me quite astonished and said - is that really it? I said not always of course, but sometimes. However connecting to feelings is always going to be more effective than trying to control behaviors. That's The Power of empathy. I tell the story in more detail in the video, and it's a bit of a long video so I split it into three parts that I'm going to post over 3 days. This is part 1 of 3.

Exploding Watermelons There are these videos on YouTube where people put elastic bands around watermelons. 1 or 2 elastic bands don't really do anything. But when it gets up to 200 or 300, the pressure builds up so great, the watermelon EXPLODES! You can see a clip of an exploding watermelon in the video about halfway along. Our emotional nature is very much like these watermelons. We build up residue all throughout the day, every day. Sometimes the residue is years old. When our emotional elastic bands build up and the pressure gets too much, we explode, our kids explode! It seems disproportionate if we are unaware of the elastic bands. When we ARE aware of the elastic bands, instead of being surprised by a seemingly disproportionate response, we can say to ourselves; "This is an Elastic Band moment." Another thing that helps is something I call Elastic Band Management. Knowing that they are building up throughout the day, we can find regular times to release them. And when we notice a particular elastic band in ourselves or our kids, instead of ignoring it, we find a way to express it, or work through it, so that there isn't the same residue. Less elastic bands leads to less explosions. Can you imagine how you can apply the elastic band-watermelon phenomena in your own life, with your kids, and your family system? And of course to yourself? x0x0x0

You don't have to Change Anything to be Worthy of Infinite Love Kids are so much deeper than we usually give them credit for. They can understand profound truths, often in ways adults struggle with. Adults might be quite good at intellectualizing and putting lots of words to things, but somehow kids can grasp deep Truths in a natural and embodied way. I often perceive kids as little spiritual Masters here to teach us and guide us about our own humanity. A few years ago I was doing a conflict resolution workshop at a youth conference. I'm fortunate to have had the opportunity to volunteer with a lot of different youth organisations over the years. I have worked with kids in lots of difficult situations. This particular workshop ended a little early, and the kids were hanging out. I decided to show them my meme with my saying: "You don't have to Change Anything to be Worthy of Infinite Love". It was a bit of an experiment. I wanted to see how they would react to such a serious sentiment. There were about 30 kids scattered about the room. I went to one after the other and told them that I made memes and asked them if they wanted to see one? And then I would show them without saying anything. I didn't want to influence their reaction. If you watch the video I include an image of the original meme about halfway through. Every single kid, 30 out of 30, every single one of those kids paused, took a deep breath, and considered it really deeply. Every single one of them nodded as if they understood the truth of it. It might sound like I'm exaggerating, but I'm really not. 30 out of 30 kids nodded with some kind of recognition with this message of infinite love, of unconditional worthiness, like they haven't lost it yet. It really touched me to see that reaction. I think one of the reasons this happened was they had already spent a couple of hours with me during the workshop. They knew that I was not authoritative. That I was not like most adults who believe they're in control, and that they have power over the kids, even if they wield it mostly benevolently, the hierarchy is still there. It doesn't take long for kids to sense that I don't consider myself above them in a hierarchy. If you go to my YouTube channel I have story after story of interactions with young people, where treating them with an unorthodox amount of respect completely changes how they perceive me, and therefore engage with me. Especially check out the earlier videos, there's some really helpful sense inspiring stuff there. I share this about the kids because so often we miss how deep they can be. It's probably a decade later and I still feel deeply moved, to be honest. It makes me want to keep refining my mindset so that I don't perceive kids as less. It's so tempting. You would think that me, I release a video every day, I release a piece of writing with the video every day. You would think I wouldn't be so paranoid about it, or perhaps vigilant! But I still don't relax my mindset. Childism is everywhere. Hierarchy with kids is everywhere. It takes active work not to engage from that perspective. It's also worth noting, that if the kids saw the truth, it might also apply to you. That in fact, You don't have to Change Anything to be Worthy of Infinite Love. I need to work on believing that more and more every day. Perhaps you'll join me? And let's raise our kids so that they believe that from their nose to their toes.

Protect your Child's Freedom of Choice Choice is one of the fundamental capacities that humans have. Something precious that we need to nurture and care for, especially in our kids. Helping them have the experience of being able to really exercise their freedom of choice, and to help them have a relationship with it. So many of us don't have a clear sense of our choice because so much of our choices were taken away from us. We were told how to think, we were told how to behave, we were told what to do, we were told what's right and wrong. And if you disagree with the authority figures idea of what's wrong? If you exercise your choice and think differently? You get smacked down for it. So it's hard for us to really embody our sense of choice and to use it wisely, and with real care. Let us think deeply about how we can help our kids develop an empowered relationship with their sense of choice? and what do we do that gets in the way of it? When your kid is about to make a choice, or has a hard choice to make you can offer them guidance on how to think about it, without thinking for them. Give them information, different ways of looking at r situation, different ways of getting information, different types of information to seek out. Suggest to them that they pay attention to their mindset and their thinking. Listen to their body and what the body feels. Feel your emotions and what they are telling you. Listen to your heart, the intuitive, the deep inner wisdom that they have. Put all that together and decide what makes sense to them. Once they make the decision, regardless of what happens, support them, let them feel your love, and you can learn from it together. Learning together in a way that feels comfortable, safe, and not filled with wrongness. This helps them create a conscious relationship with choice. It's very empowering. It also feels very respectful. I respect your wisdom. I respect your self-knowledge. Part of protecting our children's freedom of choice is untangling the knots from our own programming in our formative years. Don't assume that right now, you're thinking for yourself. I'm fact I suggest just assuming that you're not. I try and always assume that I'm thinking from patterns. And then I wonder; How can I move beyond those patterns? How can I help my kid not develop patterns, or more accurately, develop consciously chosen patterns, that are in alignment with who she really is, and not who I want her to be? Freedom of choice is a powerful thing. How can you take back your choice and how can you protect your child's freedom of choice?

Don't Impose Your Values This is a primary focus of Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. We don't impose our values on our children. We support them in discovering their own values. We guide them towards their conscience, to listen to their ethical sense. What is your inner compass saying? We explore values together, without telling them what they SHOULD think, what their values should be. We don't want our kids to form a value system based on trying to gain acceptance from us. Or trying to avoid punishment or judgement. Then the values will be only surface level. Externally motivated. Trust in your child's journey, join them in their exploration, don't try and force your child into a box. Let them discover themselves through their own process. We are there to guide, support, and model, along the way.

Self-Empathy is so important. Like, so important. Having a strong self-empathy practice means you allow yourself to feel your emotions. Rather than repress them, or judge yourself for them, you hold space for them, and allow yourself to feel them. This is how we build a strong relationship with our emotions. Another benefit of feeling and empathizing with our own challenging emotions, is we do not project them onto our kids unconsciously. Or at least we do it less so! It's probably never zero, and that's okay. Another thing to give ourselves empathy over! Self-Empathy isn't weak. It helps us build inner strength. Self-Empathy isn't selfish. It helps us build reserves so that we can be of more service. Self-Empathy isn't easy. Many generations before have programmed us not to be kind to ourselves. It takes great effort to write a new pattern.

Boundaries can be Fun! Boundaries are a part of life. I don't have a problem with boundaries. I know that might be surprising, given the fact that I'm always complaining about adults imposing boundaries on kids. It's not the boundaries I have a problem with, it's the imposing I have a problem with. It's the unpleasantness of the experience that I have a problem with. It's the power dynamics at play that I have a problem with. Thankfully it is not a choice between having no boundaries and imposing boundaries. There is always another option. A non-violent, non-hierarchical, collaborative option. A couple of days ago I had the great opportunity of interacting with an 8 month old. What a joy! I came over to say hi, and within a couple of minutes of interacting with me the kid jumped into my arms. He wanted to grab my mask, and his mom said "No honey, that stays on." I wanted to respect the mom's boundary, so instead of letting him grab the mask, I playfully kept it just out of reach. We made it into a game, we were laughing and enjoying each other. We moved on to something else shortly after. During the experience I was suddenly realizing, "Hey Vivek, you're holding a boundary!" And I laughed because I'm always talking about not setting boundaries with kids. But the fact is, with little ones we're always setting boundaries. At one point he wanted to jump out of my arms, clearly I couldn't let him just fly to the floor and land on his face! LOL. So I redirected that energy and gave him something to jump off and he enjoyed it very much. In both of those cases the setting of the boundary was something that the kid ended up feeling good about, he didn't feel it was an imposition, he didn't feel it was a power play, he didn't feel it was unfair. When I say don't impose boundaries on kids, I am not talking about the natural flow of life where we keep them safe. I'm talking about imposing boundaries that they don't agree with, that they don't like, that they're resisting, and we're using our power to keep in place. This is what we're told is normal and acceptable. It's called firm, but kind boundaries, empathetic limits, loving limits, etc. Working with boundaries with kids is important. However when we make the experience a drag, when we make it feel disconnecting, we are setting them up to have a negative association with boundaries. This works directly against the goals that we have in mind when we're trying to teach them boundaries! That's why my saying is; "I didn't want to teach my kids to respect boundaries, I wanted to inspire them to WANT to respect boundaries." How can you reframe boundaries and limits in your house in a way that makes your kids feel good about them? Where they feel included in the process? Where they feel that the limits are for their benefit, and not imposed by an authority figure? Where they are enthusiastically joining in? Those kind of boundaries I can get behind. They help kids learn about themselves, they help kids learn about the world. Imposed boundaries just don't do that.

Who am I? (Part 1) I was being spanked by my father when I was just 3 years old. I can still see the scene so clearly in my mind. I was on the landing on the way to the basement. I had done something that 3-year-olds do, I have no idea what it was now, but the message was clear; What I did was wrong, I was bad, I needed to be punished. And yet something in me rebelled against this idea. I could see the indignity in it. I could see the dehumanization in it. I knew that humans did not deserve to be treated this way. At that moment, at just 3 years old, in the midst of that pain, these words came to me; "One day I'm going to be a Dad, and I'm going to do it differently." That phrase stayed with me all throughout my life. It was the inspiration for so many of my radical parenting choices. When I was 13 I made a commitment to myself, that when I grew up I wouldn't treat 13 year olds the way adults treated me and my peers. I decided I never wanted to forget what it felt like to be 13. I scrunched up my fists, squeezed my eyes shut, and I screamed out "I'm THIRTEEN I'm THIRTEEN I'm THIRTEEN!" This is why when I'm with kids I don't place myself above them. I just can't do it. I know 90% of society tells me I should, but I just can't do it. I remember too clearly. And the kids feel it from me too. This is why even in the most chaotic of environments, the kids always love to follow me. They trust my guidance. We find an easy flow because they don't feel the need to protect themselves, in the way that they do for the majority of adults in their lives. This is why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting we place such a high emphasis on respecting the Humanity of our children. Even when it makes life highly inconvenient. Because we perceive clearly the strong foundation of self-love, self-respect, and self-knowledge, that we are nourishing with this choice. This video is part 1 of me introducing myself and talking a bit about how I came to develop this philosophy. Please check out part 2 tomorrow.

What is Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting? This is the name I coined for the parenting style that I share. It's a little bit different from the mainstream gentle parenting stuff out there. I tend more towards non-coercion. In fact non-coercion is one of the primary values we operate from in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. It's even in the name! This means we put great effort into not using our power to control our kids. We don't use punishments, consequences, rewards, boundaries, and limits, to control and modify our children's behavior. Instead we look for more collaborative ways to work with life's many challenges. We explore life together, through play, through inquiry, through conversation, through observation, through practise, and a hundred other ways. Behavior is always an effect, and we are more interested in the cause. This is why we operate from a mindset of No-Wrongness. Instead of making someone feel wrong for what happened, we learn from it together as a community. We don't hold power over our kids, instead we choose to share power with them. We want them to feel we value their whole humanity. In traditional parenting we put parents above children. In Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting, we are walking alongside them. We are learning, exploring, growing, making mistakes, and being human right alongside them. Trust me when I say, I understand the logistical challenges when imagining parenting in this fashion. All of my posts are full of people telling me this is impossible! And it very well may be. Still I think it is something worth chasing after. I have certainly made a million mistakes myself, I really didn't know what the heck I was doing. But I did have a sense of what I wanted, and what I didn't want. I had a direction, and I stumbled towards it. What I wanted was, to be my child's safest place. What I didn't want was, to place myself above them in any way. That's why after many trial names, I settled on Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. The non-coercive is what we don't do, the collaborative is what we do do. That's the Don't Do and the Doo Doo. Will you join me on this grand adventure of turning the traditional parenting paradigm upside down, on its head, and inside out?

When we do come upon a big moment, big feelings, a big obstacle, a big challenge, we will have built a foundation through our conscious relating that will carry us through it. When we have expectations, there are certain things our kids do whether you receive more acceptance, and certain things where they receive less acceptance. This by definition is conditional acceptance. Around here we do our best to operate from a mindset of unconditional acceptance. I don't want my kid to contort themselves to fit my expectations, to gain acceptance from me. This is what expectations do. Kids end up creating a mask to present the face they have been told is acceptable. Either that or they resist the mask, rebel, and distance themselves from us. In both cases our kids do not feel safe to be themselves around us. It's a terrible loss. This is why I say; "Parents are not Mask Designers". Let us offer them unconditional acceptance so they are free to be their full, human selves with us. This doesn't mean we don't explore values, and learn about life together. In fact this kind of relationship fosters a much deeper exploration of life. This is how real values are formed. Only in Freedom can a person examine their own values. Conforming or resisting the expectations of parents, takes the child's attention off the their own value system, and places it on trying to please, or protect oneself from, the adult. This is why I always said, we don't have expectations, we have explorations. And now my kid is 26, we are still exploring life together to this day. Learning about values, about human nature, about communication, about the way the world works, this is something that we do enthusiastically together. You will find an amazing result happens when your kid no longer feels they have to conform. The Feedback Sandwich I love The Feedback Sandwich and use it all the time. Especially with kids, but really with just about anyone, it makes offering feedback much smoother. It helps to maintain the relationship, it helps to have the feedback received more easily. It's a wonderful communication tool. (You're a tool! x&) Simply put when we have to give constructive feedback to someone it is useful to introduce the feedback with some sort of positive statement. This is the first slice of bread in the sandwich. The next step is to give the actual feedback that you want to share with the person. The cheese, the meat, or the tofu depending on your particular diet. Finally we conclude with another positive statement in order to leave on a good note. The sandwich is a very effective tool for offering someone constructive feedback Like any skill it takes some time to do this naturally and gracefully. In the beginning it can feel artificial and forced. What a Poorly Executed Sandwich Looks Like Unartfully done it can go something like this: You have nice hair. Your writing sucks. I like your shoes. We can safely call this a bad sandwich. Planting The Seed of Change When I think of the positive-negative-positive format I see it like planting a seed. I'm most effective at planting the seed, if I nourish the soil first. I must dig a little hole in the ground so there is space for the seed to be received. Then I can plant the seed. Of course it makes sense for me to plant the right kind of seed. If I want a plum tree it will not benefit me to plant a cherry seed. Finally it is time to cover the seed with soil and perhaps even spread some fertilizer on top. Be There To Support the Process If you want to take the analogy further we can say that even after planting the seed it might be useful to water it and also be there as a source of sunlight as it begins to sprout. It is quite a responsibility to offer somebody constructive feedback. If we can do it in a way that makes it easier for them to assimilate and act on it we are doing a much greater service to them. If we can remember that the reason we're offering the feedback is not just to vent, but to actually create some sort of change that will improve the quality of life for everyone involved, then it makes sense to do it consciously and compassionately. I have found that taking that extra moment to connect with kids before sharing my thoughts with them makes all the difference in how I am received. We wire our kids' nervous system with every interaction. If those interactions feel good to them, if they feel safe and nurturing, they are more likely to be open, and even enthusiastic about learning with us. d
