Good Authority - I always talk about rejecting parental authority. When we approach our kids from an authoritative standpoint, they automatically have to protect themselves from us. The hierarchical power structure creates a disconnection between parent and child. Kids cannot bring their vulnerable selves to us when we hold power over them because they never know when we will use that power to cause them pain, or to judge them. However there is a good kind of authority. This comes about when children feel deep trust in our guidance. It's not something we impose, but rather we inspire. It's a natural outcome of operating from the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset. When we DON'T impose authority, kids will grant it to us willingly, and spontaneously. So often we read parenting posts where we're told we should be The confident leader. This usually means imposing consequences, boundaries, and limits, and then empathizing with kids when they disagree or resist. x Not doing so is labeled as permissive. However when we take this approach children can NOT trust our leadership. No one can trust the leadership of someone who causes them avoidable pain. Of course there are situations where we have no choice, but 90% of the time when adults are imposing consequences, boundaries, and limits, it's a choice. Kids know this, they know we are choosing to hold the limit. They know we could simply choose not to hold the limit. So how do we create a relationship where our kids trust our guidance? We treat them with respect for their humanity, we refuse to use our power to control that, we include their needs and feelings in all of our decisions. We empower them, we validate them, we hold space for their feelings. We put the effort into finding collaborative, mutually agreeable solutions to life's many challenges. When our guidance feels consistently good to their nervous system, when their experience of us is safe and nurturing, when our guidance regularly makes their lives better, helps them get more of what they want out of life, out of their relationships, out of their play. When learning with us is a joy and not a drag. Can you look at your parenting and find the areas where you make your guidance less trustable, and where you make it more trustable? Listening Without an Agenda Being deeply present and listening to our kids with an open heart is one of the most profound gifts we can offer them as parents. When your kid is sharing something with you, especially if it's challenging for you, especially if you think you need to teach them something, or correct them in some way, put your thoughts and pre-conceptions away. Listen without preparing a response. Listen with your full being. Listen with genuine curiosity and love. There will be plenty of time for other stuff later. In this moment, be here, be fully here with your kid. Watch your mind, watch your thoughts, and when they start to intrude, take a pause, take a breath, feel the ground under your feet, feel the air on your face, do something to bring yourself back to the moment. Listening without judgment, listening without an agenda, listening without preparing an answer, this is something magical. Do you notice the thoughts in your head while you're listening? It's a great exercise to practise.

Connection through Communication Creating stable, trusting, positive, and safe communication dynamics in your home is one of the most important things you can do to Foster deep connection. When your kids know they can come to you with anything it opens up space to work through all of life's problems together. One of the unfortunate effects of the traditional parenting mindset is that kids have to guard themselves from their parents. Authority, rules, consequences, limits, and boundaries, imposed upon the child all create a condition in which children cannot feel safe expressing themselves vulnerably to their parents. This is why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting we place great emphasis on creating that safe space for kids to communicate with us. This doesn't only happen when we're talking to them, the safe space is created with all of our interactions. What do you do with your kids, and in your family, to encourage them to communicate openly with you? And What do you do that might inhibit them, and how can you change it? I asked myself these questions on a daily basis. It helped me to continuously refine our communication and it has deepened and evolved throughout the years.

Obedience and Respect are Opposites! We earn the respect of our kids so much more by modeling it rather than demanding obedience. The traditional mindset thinks we have to demand respect, demand obedience, and then use punishment and reward to create those conditions. It really is a dehumanizing way to treat other people. Especially our children. To respect is formed from a deep, trusting, connected relationship. It comes from going through hard times together, good times together, and developing trust over the long term. There is a realization that occurs where we recognize that control and authority do not create a respectful relationship, that punishment, consequences, and rewards, actually work against our interests as parents. When you're on this side of that realization, it seems obvious that when you demand obedience from your kids, you actually lose respect. But before you have the realization, it seems impossible to let go of control and authority. Because if you release that grip, the kids are going to run wild and you won't be able to control them. This is a very stressful thought. This thought makes us force and push our kids, then they resist, and power struggles are not far behind. You slowly grow apart and they're off with their friends, they don't listen to your advice, they roll their eyes at you, and eventually we lose the relationship. It doesn't have to be this way though. If we parent from a mindset of respect and deep connection, the relationship is preserved. The other benefit of this is our kids learn to trust our guidance and wisdom. No one wants to trust the wisdom of someone who punishes them, criticizes them, and controls them. But it's easy to trust the guidance of someone whom we feel has our best interests at heart. And when I say feel, I mean in our nervous system, and our subconscious. So the next time you are tempted to demand obedience, or when you feel frustrated that your kids aren't listening, take a breath, step back, and try a different approach.

EmpathyButt is when we offer empathy to our kids, and then we interrupt it with a lesson or an instruction. EmpathyButt sounds like this: "I see that you're upset they took your toy. That's a natural feeling, BUT you can't swear at your sibling when you're upset. You have to find a different way to express your feelings." This is EmpathyButt. Or "I understand that your friend made you mad and it hurt your feelings that they took your stuff. But it really hurt their feelings when you said mean things to them. You can have your feelings, but you have to learn to express them without hurting anyone." The empathy is interrupted as soon as we say "But". In this interaction the kid really gets about 10 seconds of empathy. There is no opportunity for that emotional connection to do its work, to sink into the nervous system, to help the kid feel seen and safe. When it is cut short too quickly, kids learn not to trust it. They can't lean into it because they're never sure when it will disappear. The opposite of EmpathyButt is what I call "Sustained Empathy". Imagine instead saying something like: "Hey sweetie I see that you're mad they took your toy." (Or whatever) "Yes I'm mad. They're so mean." "Ya, it's so hard when someone wrecks our hard work. Of course you're upset about it. I can totally understand that. I get upset too when my friends aren't nice to me. Thank you for sharing your feelings with me. I love you." And that's it. No lesson. No Butt. I know it might feel like we're letting them get away with something if we don't add the lesson or boundary. The thing is that this sustained empathy helps kids be open to learning and exploring the issue together. This openness is more important than anything else. In fact they often end up coming to us to help them learn because we become such a safe place. Offering empathy is often more important than offering solutions, instructions, and especially corrections. It's important to keep in mind that empathy isn't a quick fix. It isn't actually a fix or a strategy. It is a sincere human connection. Another of my one-liners is "Our Acceptance must be greater than their Resistance." Sustained empathy has transformational magic in it and I invite you to work with it in your family and see what unfolds.

Disguising a NO as a Yes Many times when kids ask for things, the thing itself is not what they want, they are trying to meet a need, they are trying to deal with the feeling. When we say no to the thing, we are saying no to their needs and feelings. We are often not aware of it, and they are not aware of it, but that is what is going on. This is why iceberg Consciousness is so important. When we perceive beneath the surface, we can address the real needs and feelings the kid is trying to meet, without necessarily having to say yes to the specific request. Of course I always encourage saying yes as much as possible, but life is life and sometimes we just can't. Saying a hard no, or even a soft no, still produces defensiveness and a feeling of loss in the child. There's a sense of not being met, not being cared for, even a sense of being oppressed. When we help a kid feel deeply mad, cared for, and supported, they're much more likely to go with the flow and trust our guidance. In this video I tell a wonderful story of a time where I interrupted a friend who was about to set a boundary with a kid, and shifted that dynamic to needs and feelings. The young human opened their heart so profoundly, that it still touches me to think about it to this day. I call this a experience, "The Sketchbook Story". Watch the video to find out why. I would love for you to watch and let me know what you think.

In a world full of NO, home should be a Haven of YES for a child. Adults don't realize how often kids experience NO on a daily basis. So many of their needs and wants are restricted. There's so much they can't do, either because of safety, ability, development, access to resources, access to transportation, access to finances, rules in school, adult authority, etc. This is why it's important for parents to put a lot of effort into saying yes as often as possible. Especially at home, we want our kids to feel like the home is a safe place for them to be themselves. A safe place for them to express their needs and desires. So often parents say things like "As long as you're in my house, blah blah blah&" with the implication being that it is not the child's house. And if we don't see it explicitly, often the way we arrange things, the way we structure things has this message embedded in it. I always wanted my kid to feel like this was equally their home. One of the ways that helps them feel it is if we put a lot of effort into giving them yes experiences. Even the times we have to say no to a particular thing, we can tune into the emotional, relational, beneath the surface, needs and help them meet those. That way they feel it's less of a no, and more of a yes to something else. And tomorrow's video I tell an astonishing story of doing this with a young person. I know I talk a lot about saying yes, but it's one of the most important things on this path. It changes the relationship between parent and child, and changes the relationship they have to themselves, and their environment. Where can you stretch yourself to say more of a yes? How can you notice the moments where your kid experiences a no and turn it upside down?

Saying YES Inspires Cooperation Saying a really BIG yes opens the heart If your kids can trust that your effort is towards the YES, it makes it so much easier for them to accept when you need to say no. Because they know you don't say no unless you absolutely have to. They feel that you are always working towards turning a no into a yes. If your kids feel your efforts are more towards the NO, you become the adversary. They have to protect themselves from you. You are the obstacle they have to work around in order to get their needs met. They can't relax and be there vulnerable cells around you because they know a NO is just around the corner. Check out the video for a wonderful example of how I used this principle to inspire a kid to clean up some water they spilled with joy and connection. Just after their parents had tried for like 5 minutes using gentle, but really traditional methods. It will make a huge difference in your dynamic with your kid.

Anti-Behaviorism Behaviorism is the study of how to get people to alter their behavior. Primarily using positive and negative reinforcement, and the withdrawal of positive reinforcement. Most of the conventional parenting philosophies operate from a behaviorist standpoint. How can we modify our kids behavior,? How can we control their behavior? How can we mold their behavior to fit our expectations? How do we fix bad behavior? How do we encourage more good behavior? Behavior Behavior Behavior! But children are not a collection of behaviors to be controlled! They are deep human beings with thoughts and feelings. When we focus on behavior, we miss the iceberg of feelings, needs, and other causes underneath the surface. Behavior always has a cause. When we focus on the cause we are so much more effective in dealing with the effects. So the next time you're feeling like changing your kid's behavior, take a pause and respond with curiosity instead of correction.

Honoring the Consent and Autonomy of children. In Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting, we treat kids as equal human beings, giving them respect for their autonomy and consent. When young people know they have a right to their bodily consent, it's natural for them to see other people's consent as worthy and important. This is the foundation of respect. When we take care not to impose our will on our children, but to honour their essential right to their bodies and their freedom, we are setting the deepest model. It's important to remember honoring consent doesn't mean doing nothing. It means we find ways to work with every situation that respects each person involved. That's why the parenting style I teach I call non coercive collaborative parenting. The collaboration part is how we work together to manage all of life's many situations, challenges, schedules etc.

Systemic power is power you didn't choose, and power you can't refuse. As parents we have systemic power over our children. Access to resources, food and housing, financial, emotional, relational, and physical power. We can legally lock them in their rooms, take away their stuff, and deny them food. If they don't act within our expectations, we can intentionally cause them pain to force them to behave. We can even hit them! As conscious parents wanting to honour our children's humanity, we are very intentional about how we relate to this systemic power. We avoid using it to control them at all costs. Of course it's not easy, but the key is that we are always stretching ourselves. We are always questioning ourselves. Can I release some more control here? Can I introduce more collaboration there? What are my true intentions? Is there any inner child stuff interfering in my perception? It is an ever-evolving path. There are many layers, it's a lifelong process. I call it 'The Infinite Onion', the layers never end. So the next time your kid asks for something that seems unreasonable, instead of saying no and explaining why, take a pause, take a breath, and ask them a question about it. "That sounds interesting, tell me more about why you want that?" And then you can get into a discussion about needs, feelings, and what all of your capacity are, and make a collaborative decision. That question has actually saved me from a lot of authoritarian moments. I might make a whole video just based on the question. "That's interesting, tell me more?" It's a much gentler, more connecting, and deeper approach than approaching things authoritatively and with our power.

Resistance, Compliance, and Distance These are the three responses to coercion. When we impose our power or authority onto our kids, they will do one of three things. 1) Resistance: they will resist us. In the fight for their autonomy, their sense of self. They resist, they push back, 2) Compliance: This is not cooperation. Cooperation is when we choose to work together. Compliance is when we are forced into a particular action. 3) Distance: In both of the above cases, the kid has to put a shield around their heart. The distance is created. The parent is no longer the safest place. The goal of Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting is to avoid all three of these reactions. The opposite of all three is collaboration and connection. That's where the real work gets done! That's where deep relationships are forged. That's where family patterns are created that last a lifetime.

a terrible model Forcing someone to do something against their will, using the power you have over them, is a terrible model to set for our children. This is why I consistently advocate for not using our power to control our children's behavior. This includes not using punishments, consequences, limits, boundaries, taking away "privileges", as well as emotional manipulation. There are so many ways we knowingly and unknowingly hold power over our children. Instead of resisting that, or defending it, let us make an active, enthusiastic, and meaningful search for those moments, and then rewire them. I used to call it my SHAME RADAR back in the early days. and i would always say "I have my Shame Radar turned up to 11!" I was always on the lookout for the slightest bit of coercion, the slightest bit of manipulation. The reason for this is that I valued the integrity of our relationship so highly that I didn't want to let a single one slide by. It doesn't mean I was perfect, it meant I tried to be aware. And then I would repair. Aware and repair! This is the path of Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. We keep stretching ourselves towards the ideal. We may never be perfect, but we will always be stretching.

Transition Philosophies Transition Philosophies are parenting philosophies with one foot in the old mindset and one in the new. The old, being a hierarchical power relationship, authoritative control, consequences, firm boundaries and limits. The new, being a collaborative power sharing relationship, based in communication and connection. As Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parents we strive to step all the way into the new mindset, stretch all the way to the ideal. And stretching towards an ideal is always inconvenient. It asks more of us, because we stay engaged in life process, rather than interrupt it. Authority interrupts the life process. Transition philosophies are important, because we are moving from less coercion to more collaboration. But it is a process. In a sense we are always in that transition. So whatever parenting information you consume, including mine, evaluate it carefully to see if there is coercion embedded into it. The Coercion can be overt or covert. Prioritize your child's relationship with themselves When my kid was growing up one of my most cherished parenting priorities was preserving and nourishing her relationship to herself. I wanted her to think deeply, feel fully, and know herself profoundly. I wanted her to know her values and to explore them using her own ethical sense, her intuition, her reasoning, her observations, and exploring values with me over many years. I would pass almost any parenting decision through this filter, "Is this nourishing her relationship to herself?" This is why I could never punish, why I didn't hold any kind of hierarchical authority or power. I once asked my kid about how it would feel if I said no to her? Because I so rarely do. On principle. She said that because I never say no, she would know that if I did say no, it was for a good reason. Edit to add: When I say that I rarely ever said no, I really mean it literally. I know it's so common for people to think you have to say no to kids, but that hasn't been my experience. I have found cooperation and ease of flow increase dramatically when we resist the urge to say NO, from an authoritative place. Exerting authority and power, however gently, always ruptures relationship. There's no way around it. By avoiding the word no, by avoiding imposing my will, instead I focus on becoming a safe and trusted guide. Someone that my kid turns to for wisdom, rather than having to impose it. This is one of the places authoritative parenting falls short. It still puts parents as the authority. Yes they attempt to handle that authority more gently, but the wall separating human to human relationship is still there. This is why I avoid saying no at all costs. Edit 2: Someone asked what about kids that want to eat ice cream and candy? It's kind of hard to understand without seeing it in the broader picture of the whole philosophy. What I teach is called Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. Non coercive means we don't use force, power, or authority to control our kids. Collaborative means that we make decisions together as a family, we do a lot of communication, a lot of listening and processing. Part of the philosophy is not we don't hold authority or power over our kids, as I said. Therefore it's not so much that I say yes or no to ice cream, it's that I've removed myself as an authority that CAN say yes or no to ice cream. only somebody with more power can say yes or no. but if i share power with my kid equally, then Im not giving myself that option. From the mainstream mindset this seems like it would create other chaos, but in fact the opposite is true. Kids are so much more willing to cooperate when they don't feel like they are being oppressed. I know oppressed is a big word, but kids often feel that way when they are punished, given consequences, given limits, and controlled in so many ways. Non coercive collaborative parenting creates the deepest relationship of safety. It creates a deep co-learning relationship. From this place we can explore things like how the body works, how nutrition works, how sleep works, how money works, how communication works, and all the wonderful things that we want to impart to our kid. We explore it because there's no resistance. There are of course nuances to this because life is life, and human relationships are very complex. But my nuances are always in the direction of creating a positive and trusting relationship with my kid, and not exerting authority.

As I mention in the video, when somebody says ""what about if they run into the street?", what they're really saying is, What if I don't want them to have a second cookie before dinner? If it's okay for me to coerce them because I'm protecting them when they are going to get hit by a car, it's okay for me to coerce them over the cookie, because I'm also protecting them. And people wouldn't necessarily say that out loud, but we know the subtext, otherwise why even bother writing the comment? It's because the implication is, if we think it's good for them, it's okay for us to violate our kids" autonomy, consent, and humanity. That's why when we become Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parents, what's happening is we are committing ourselves to a principle, to a value. It's a choice, and a pretty deep one. I say deep because it's very much the less tidy option most of the time. Inconvenient a lot of the time. So we are committing to the mess and chaos of authentic human relationships. It also comes with a relationship where your kids feel no need to protect themselves from you. So you become their safest place. You become co-explorers of life. There's nothing better! It's a big deal to deal with kids from this mindset because we avoid using our power at all costs. Even though it's totally normal, we resist it. So then we think "Well, if I'm not punishing, using consequences, or limits, then what the heck do I do now? How do I manage everyday life now? and the thing is, the principle is so important to us that we figure it out. Always imperfectly, but consistently. And now that we have more communities doing this work, we're figuring it out together. Will you join me in taking the leap and parenting from the deep? Committing to the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset? By facing that question ""Well, what the heck do I do now?" How do I manage everyday life now? you are changing the world. Don't give up. Are you a Safe parent? Are you a safe parent? I asked myself that question all the time. When life gets busy, when we are overwhelmed and under-resourced, we can forget to ask ourselves this question. Many of the things we do with our kids make us feel less safe to them. When you're making a decision around how to handle something, think about your kid's perspective. What choice will make them feel the most safe with you. This thinking is one of the reasons I never had rules, I never imposed limits, or consequences, avoided wrongness, blame, and shame at all costs. Because I knew those things would make my kid feel I am less safe. And so they should! There are a lot of things we have to give up from the traditional parenting, and even the common gentle parenting toolbox if we are going to place safety as a priority. A lot of people think that giving up control means our kids are going to run wild. Or they won't be good people. However I have found that by releasing control, my kid trusts me more, and we are able to explore life, values, communication and relationships more. Let us work at shifting those old patterns and focus on being their safest place.

Caught Stealing! Caught Stealing I was caught stealing from the mall when I was 7 or 8 years old. My parents marched me back to the store, made me apologize, and return the item. I didn't learn not to steal that day. I felt terrible as I walked into the store, but not because I had stolen, because of the shame. I stole for years and years after that. This is one of the reasons why I am so committed to the path of no wrongness. Only when we are free to really choose for ourselves can we discover our own value system. If our parents tell us we're wrong, the only thing we learn is that they think it's wrong. We don't get to discover it for ourselves. If you want your kids to discover their own value system so that they know themselves and have real personal integrity, we cannot impose our value systems or our judgment on them. I know that many people will think, if we don't tell them they're wrong how will they know right from wrong. Or, it's a parent's job to teach a kid right from wrong. Or, if we don't tell them what's right from wrong, we're not preparing them for the real world. And my favorite of course is that they will end up in jail or some other extreme outcome. However I believe the best gift we can offer them, and the deepest preparation we can give them, is self-knowledge. What could be more powerful than that? So I recommend deeply considering your reaction to your kids when they do something and you're tempted to tell them they're wrong. Approach it with curiosity and true acceptance. No Wrongness! Two important things will happen. 1) Your kid will trust you more, you will become their safest space to process and learn. 2) Your kid will learn to tune into their own wisdom and form a deep relationship with themselves. I know it's challenging to change old patterns, but it's worth the effort.

REFUSE to use your Power and Authority on your kids. Refuse it at All Costs. Even if it would make it so much easier to control your kids in that moment, bite your tongue, sit on your hands, run from the room. I know this is hard, because we're programmed to see parents as an authority. Dismantling that mindset is challenging. Even for those who are working actively at doing so, it's a continuous struggle. It's a mindset wired into us from thousands of years of history. Handed down throughout the generations. Breaking that ancient cycle is no small thing. It requires courage, dedication, persistence, self-awareness, a learning mindset, and lots of patience and self-compassion. Even now that my kid is 26 I still remind myself all the time. Even with the best of intentions the tendency to control can linger for years. I want my kid to feel that we're equals, that we're both humans, walking the path side by side. I call it a "Whole Being, Co-Learning, Relationship of Equals" Our kids cannot trust us with their vulnerability if we are holding authority over them. They will protect themselves. The benefit of choosing to walk side by side with our children is it creates a deeply trusting, connected relationship. More than a hierarchical relationship can ever hope to achieve.

Apologize to your kids! If you are not apologizing to your kids at least once a week you are not paying attention. This concept was one of my guiding principles when I was raising my kid. One of the reasons we are so close now that she's 26 is because we had a consistent and reliable repair process. I made tons of mistakes when she was growing up, but I always acknowledged them and made the effort to learn and change. Apologizing on a regular basis was one of the ways I modelled accountability. I never asked my kid to apologize for anything ever. I never suggested it or hinted at it. But I did give her the regular experience of what it felt like when someone took responsibility for their impact and did their best to make amends. Another important part of apologizing that I didn't mention in the video is forgiving ourselves first. If I still feel blame and shame, then my apology is partially trying to get Absolution from her. I never asked my kid to forgive me, because that means I'm trying to get something from her rather than give something to her. And an apology is an offering. What kind of repair process do you have with your kids? How do you take accountability for when you are out of alignment and cause a harmful impact?

IceBerg Consciousness Ice Berg Consciousness is when we look past the behaviours of our children and see the deeper causes underneath. Trying to modify behaviors is dealing with the effects instead of the cause. We're always going to be more effective in supporting and guiding our kids if we go deeper. The causes are feelings they don't know how to manage, needs they don't know how to meet, the desire for autonomy. They could be reacting to struggles at school, with other kids, with other adults. Sometimes it's sensory or other processing challenges. We humans are very complex, and kids are too. When we use Iceberg consciousness we are honouring their complexity. A complex system often needs complex thinking and problem solving. How can you remind yourself to look deeper?

One of the most important ways we help our children have a positive relationship with themselves, is how we model our relationship with ourselves. *How do you treat yourself? Do your kids witness you being kind to yourself? Do they witness you doing nourishing things for yourself? I know a lot of the time in a busy chaotic life, it can seem like there's no opportunity for these things. However even a little bit of intentionality around it can be an important message for our kids. The message is "We are worth the effort." *How do you talk to yourself? What kind of self-talk happens in your mind? Are you gentle with yourself or harsh? How often does that come out of your lips? Let your kids hear you saying kind things to yourself, showing yourself appreciation, lifting yourself up. They absorb this example and start to reflect it in how they talk to themselves. *How do you respond when you make mistakes? Can you be more compassionate with yourself when you make mistakes? Forgive yourself, and at the same time be willing to learn something from them. When kids see you responding gently to your mistakes, and taking accountability and learning at the same time, it helps them develop a positive relationship with their own mistakes. They learn to be kind to themselves, and also always be evolving. What a great combination. *How do you acknowledge yourself when you do something well? Let your kids hear you celebrate your successes. Even the smallest ones. "I tried for 3 minutes to open that jar, and I did it! Woohoo!" "I finally got that email sent. Three cheers for me!" When this becomes part of their everyday experience, they will start noticing those things for themselves. *Modelling Out Loud Tell your kids stories about your inner process. Share with them the times that you struggle and overcome. Share with them experiences where you made a mistake and how you responded kindly, and learned from it. Revealing our inner processes helps kids recognize their own inner processes. This increases their self-knowledge, which is deeply tied to Self-Love. ----------

After I do a few drawings I like to do a practice page. The practice page is where I don't focus on what it looks like, I just practice a similar line or shape. In this one I'm practicing long straight lines. Over and over and over again I draw the same kind of line. I pay attention to the small muscles in my fingers, relaxing my wrist, I watch how the line changes when I'm breathing in, breathing out, holding my breath in, holding my breath out. You can see that these lines aren't perfectly straight, there's a lot of wiggling. And yet there's quite a bit of fine control at the same time. I can see where I need to keep working. I will probably do another long straight line practice page before I do another drawing. I find practice to be something so empowering. I can choose to do something over and over again and get a little better at it. How amazing! As a martial artist, and a dancer, and a dad, and a partner, and a friend, as well as with my drawing, practice helps me grow. My former martial arts teacher Kacem Zoughari said that it's important to practice, and it's important to practice the right thing, and it's important to practice the right way. So I also practice how I practice! Deepening the practice of my practice. Or if I consider my art the practice I could say: deepening the practice of my practice of my practice! LoL. I love words. What do you practice? What would you like to practice?

Children are much more willing to cooperate when they feel valued and connected. They resist us much less when they have a sense of belonging and acceptance. When kids feel their contributions are meaningful, and they have a positive impact on our lives, their enthusiasm for engaging increases. They want to be part of a connected and harmonious family system. I know it doesn't always look that way, but it's important for us to keep that in mind. A parent once came to me stressing out because their kid was not wanting to engage with them. The parent was organizing a fundraising fair with lots of fun games and events. Their 10 year old was constantly complaining about it, saying they wanted no part of it. They would criticize it, call it stupid, and talk about it being a waste of time. The parent kept saying they wanted the kid to join in and help, but they didn't even want to attend. In fact, they refused to attend. People were suggesting that they hold a boundary around it, that they ask the kid "How would you feel if someone talked to you that way?" (I call that the - How Would You Feel school of empathy), and also to let them know how their words hurt them. Of course, none of these things actually shifted the dynamic, because they weren't meeting the very real and valid needs that the kid was expressing. They are also rooted in wrongness which creates distance, not connection. That's why one of the foundational principles of Non-Coercive Collaborative Parenting is No-Wrongness. If you search my Facebook page for no wrongness, you'll find a video called No Wrongness No Wrongness No Wrongness! I go into more detail about the philosophy there. When the parent came to me, I suggested that they change the whole approach. Start by letting the kid know that they truly accept their feelings. If they didn't want to come to the event, that was perfectly okay. In fact, the parents PREFERENCE was that the kid honour themselves, because they really want them to always trust their feelings, and they will stand behind them no matter what they decide. I suggested they acknowledge they had been pressuring them before and they wish they hadn't done so. That It never feels good to be pressured, and that is not how they want to treat their beloved child. Then to tell the kid that the real reason that they wanted them there was because they really enjoy their company. They love being with them because they're such close friends and they feel great joy whenever they have a chance to spend time together. They enjoy working with them and co-creating with them. They also wanted them involved because they value their input. Their insights are so creative and interesting that their ideas would probably make the event a much better experience for everybody. So the parent went to their kid and told them this, in their own words of course. I always suggest that parents find their own words for the message. I share Vivek words, but they need to make the expression their own, while keeping the same principle. They came back to me the next day and told me that it was like a light switch turned on in their kid. They did a complete 180 from complaining about the event to being full of ideas and support. They not only decided to attend the event, they actually wanted to co-create and run it with their parent. The enthusiasm was thick in the room. They spent an hour brainstorming and exploring all of their ideas and implemented a number of them. I found out later that the event was a great success and they were deeply connected throughout the whole thing. In this example, the parent honored their child's feelings and at the same time looked for the relational/emotional needs that were not being met. Oftentimes when we try and work with our kids without tuning in like this we push them farther away. The mindset we hold and the approach we take is so important. This is why I don't advise the idea of saying "when you do that it hurts me." I don't advise saying "I won't let you..." or anything that has judgment and coercion as part of it. Coercion makes learning a drag, makes Co-Creating drag, make Exploring Values a drag. Anytime kids feel this, they naturally will distance themselves and resist us. They are protecting and honoring themselves. If we can see it this way as opposed to seeing it as a problem, it can lead to beautiful things. Letting go of the judgment and force we can instead merge with them and help them feel how much we value them. Natural enthusiasm and connection arise. The next time you are struggling with your kid, take a moment to slow down and think of things that you really appreciate about them. Tune into the bright light that they are beneath whatever behavior they might be exhibiting. Then let them know how much they mean to you. Let them know you see them and you value them. Making this change of mindset and approach can help you shift directions and create new relational dynamics. It can interrupt old patterns and set you on a new and more positive path. Peace, @[593266790:2048:Vivek Patel]

Let go of Control and Embrace Collaboration. Collaboration centers around the concept of horizontal power-sharing. This means abandoning the idea that we have power over our kids. Or rather acknowledging that we DO have power over our kids, and choosing not to use it in a coercive way. There's a lot to consider about how to approach our relationship with our children once we've decided to give up controlling. We have to break so many old patterns and establish new ones. This is hard work! The problem with imposing our will on our kids is that it degrades the trust and connection between parent and child. Even when we believe we're doing it for "their own good", we are making things worse for everyone. When we work collaboratively with our kids no one is holding power over the other, the parent does not enforce anything, it is a mutual exploration aimed at creating the best outcome for everybody. However this is not a simple process. Especially when we have ten thousand years of coercive history on our shoulders. Re-wiring those old patters takes work and dedication.

Teens are just aching to be met where they are and to be accepted for who they are. They want their struggles to be seen. It is an intense challenge being at that stage of life. In my experience when we take ONE step towards a teenager, they take TEN steps towards us. Especially since, most of the time there are no other adults in their lives who take them seriously. I remember that feeling as a teen so clearly, that there were few adults I could trust. Back then I swore I would not grow up and become one of those adults. I knew it from that age. Recently I saw a picture of my dad in our old house from when I was a teenager. He passed on a couple of years ago. When I looked at the date on the picture, he would have been exactly as old as I am now. I really took in that moment in time. I was with my mom when I found the picture and I said to her that he looks like an adult. I felt very grateful in that moment that I never became an adult. That rebellious teenage Vivek was, in many ways, the basis for my entire Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting journey. Pushing back against the mainstream narrative of how we're supposed to treat young people. I could feel myself heal a little bit, little Vivek heal a little bit, every time I made a radical choice. It is a rebellious path. It is a courageous path. If you walk the conscious parenting path you know what I mean. People looking in from the outside think it's weak, but they don't know the daily struggle it is to rewire ancient patterns. Ancient in our family lines, ancient in our culture, ancient in global history. Hierarchical, coercive patterns are deep in us. However I believe beneath that is a more ancient pattern, something even deeper. Something that we recognize when we see a baby, the innocence, the pure consciousness. When we can remember that pure Consciousness within ourselves, and see it in the other, that's when young people feel we truly see them. We see their humanity. It doesn't mean we're exactly the same, it means that we are equal, even though we're different. This is where true respect comes from. This connection is the basis of collaboration. In all my years working with young people, I have never failed to connect and collaborate with them. We take ONE step towards them, they'll take TEN steps towards us. That thing is real. Like this one time, I was volunteering at a youth conference. The @Future Aces conference took youth from all over the city, from challenging and disadvantaged areas. Lots of kids with really hard lives for whom, in many ways, survival was a daily fight. We offered them four days of empowering workshops and experiential learning. Lives were changed. It was an amazing thing to be a part of. I facilitated a Leadership Through Movement workshop that combined Martial Arts and Dance. The kids love it. Towards the end of the conference, I had to deliver a lecture that was kind of boring, as part of my volunteer duties. I tried to make it more exciting, but really, there was only so much I could do and I knew the kids were going to tune me out. So I thought to myself, How can I set the right tone in this room? So we can have an experience of mutual respect? I believe that when young people feel deeply respected, they naturally let that respect flow back. We adults set the stage for mutual respect. So at the beginning of class these kids were all shoving each other and talking. They weren't listening. Their teachers were at the back of the room trying to shush them. I could see the familiar patterns playing out. I'm standing at the front, letting them do their thing for a little while, because who am I to interrupt? I'm just some guy. At one point when the teachers were shushing, I asked them to please not interfere and let me handle things. When I felt like the young people had some space to get their feelings out, communicate with each other, and settle into being in the room, I jumped up, spread my arms out wide and said, "Hey, everyone, I have something very important to tell you. This is a somewhat boring presentation, but it's important information, and I have to get through it. Here's the thing, I'm going to be standing up at the front talking and sharing this information, and while I'm up here, if you're talking to your neighbor at the same time, and you can't hear me... That's OKAY! Because I'm sure whatever you have to say is as important, or probably more important than what I have to say. You're a human being deserving of respect. If you want to talk you have every right to. Who am I to tell you not to talk to someone? Then when you're done, just let me have your attention back again, please. They said, "Are you serious?" And I said, "Yes. I mean it." Immediately one of the kids who was being the loudest prior to my saying that, got up and turned to his teachers and said, "Miss, can this guy come and teach at our school?" and everybody laughed and clapped. At one point after about 10 minutes a couple of young people were chatting a bit loud. I saw another opportunity to use humor to reinforce the connection and my sincerity. I stopped my presentation and I walked slowly over to them. The whole room went quiet and ominous, wondering what I was going to do. They certainly know what every other adult does in those moments. I stood in front of them with my hands on my hips and said "Hey, you know at the beginning I said that if you have something to say you should just go ahead and say it, even if I'm talking...?" After a brief pause I said, "Well I want you to know I meant it and I'm glad you did, that you trusted me. That was awesome." Again everybody laughed and the two of them relaxed. People felt this sense of community in the room. All this happened within the first 10 minutes and already the human connection was buzzing. Barriers were being torn down. Masks were being removed. ONE step - TEN steps. I swear it's real. One of the slides I had in my presentation was about Pink Day. Here in Toronto the schools have something called Pink day as a day of LGBTQ+ youth awareness and support. There was a young gay teen who wore pink to school one day and was bullied so intensely, he took his own life. Pink Day was started in his honor. When I was talking about this issue, one of the tough guys in the audience, let out a snort. It was a sound of derision. PPPPFFFFFTTTTT! The teachers at the back of the room got on their feet, ready to intervene. I made eye contact and held out a hand for them to stop. I didn't want the typical adult wrongness and moral superiority to infect the situation. You know what I'm talking about. "That's disrespectful. That's uncalled for. This is a serious issue. Please take this seriously. Keep your thoughts to yourself." Normally, he might have got a bunch of laughs from his peers, but because of the connection the group felt with me, they were less willing to laugh at this. They respected me, and if I was taking pink day seriously, there must be something to it. So I walked over to this young man with genuine curiosity, believing the best about him, and I said that I really wanted to know why he made that sound? What were his thoughts? His friends were elbowing him, telling him he shouldn't have said that, but I said "No, no. I want to know the truth. I really want to know what you're thinking, because I believe you have very deep thoughts about things and I want to know them." He said to me "I think the whole thing is stupid." I could feel him challenging me to get defensive. I said, "Yeah, maybe so, maybe so. Tell me why." Disarmed by my openness he replied, "Because how could anybody be in that much pain that they would take their own life? I just can't understand it, I just can't understand it." I said to him, "Yeah, just think, with all the struggles, all the pain you've been through, and all the crap that you've had to face, all the abuse you've taken in your life, and you can't imagine how much pain that is? Imagine how deep that pain that young man felt that he would do that." This was not shame, because I was going with what he gave me. I would have flowed with whatever his response was. I have faith in this approach because I believe there is goodness in him, in every teen. He just stared at me, and for a moment we had silent eye contact. He felt the space of no judgment. We got through the surface layers to something deeper underneath. We had a human moment. I asked him "What do you think about Pink Day now?" He said "I get it." and the whole room was quiet for a moment, then I went on with the presentation. This kind of depth is always available to us when working with young people. This is one of the reasons I love working with teens, they have so much to offer. They are so often deeply under listened to. Can you remember back to your own teenage years? Think about the adults that you could trust, and the ones that you knew you couldn't. Think about the ones that really saw you, and the ones that you knew had stories about you. Think about the ones that treated you with respect, and the ones that thought they were better than you, and abused their power. Every one of us has this experience. Instead of repeating that cycle over again, instead of being the perpetrator, when at that age when you so clearly knew it was wrong. Let's make a change, let's do things differently, let's make some radical choices and treat young people with the respect they deserve. We can do it. It's not easy, but we're doing it together.

Preparing Kids for the Real World One of the core elements of the parenting philosophy that I teach is a focus on preparing kids for the real world. It's ironic because that's usually the criticism I receive, that treating kids non-coercively doesn't prepare them for the real world. But these folks aren't thinking of what skills, knowledge, mindsets, and relationship with self, that will be relevant to the constant obstacles, challenges, relationships, and systems that they're going to have to face in life. These are the kind of things that are important to think about if we want to help our kids prepare. Like I always say, we can teach our kids about consequences without actually giving them consequences. There are certainly enough examples of it in the world, we don't have to be yet another perpetrator. In fact, when we drop the role of rule maker, judge, and enforcer, and instead embrace the role of Learning Partner, we become a much safer space for our kids. When we let go of using consequences, Wrongness, and all coercion, we have more potential to guide them towards these deeper life skills. It is through building this deep relationship that we have the most influence with our kids. Like my saying goes: "Coercive influence Decreases over time. Relational influence Increases over time." I want to help my kid learn how to navigate the obstacles of life. I do not want to be yet another obstacles. Empowering my kid with skills, knowledge, mindsets, and relationship-with-self, has been the focus of my role as guide. Exploring how the world works, and how to work the world, was integrated into every part of our journey. For example we love to study systems. We have always been fascinated by systems, how they interact and affect each other, and the individuals that interface with them. The awareness how these systems work is one of the most empowering skills to have when facing the world. Something so important is not a one-time conversation. We weave it into our everyday experience. When we see systems at work we will name them. Walking downtown I'll say "Look at this building. It supports a banking system that serves a political system. Or is it the political system that supports the banking system?" We look at how different systems intersect. The economic system and the education system. The justice and correctional system. Systems of morality, ethics, religion/belief/spirituality, systems of government, systems of parenting, systems of thinking. We analyze and look at the pros and cons of each. We think about how to navigate different systems. And then suddenly we're having a conversation about how humans interact with each other. This can happen with the kid as young as 2 years old! There's no age limit to thinking about life. When my kid went into kindergarten I talked to her about the different systems that she would be engaging with. I especially wanted her to understand the system of rules, authority, consequences, and rewards, that the whole School model is based on. We didn't do those things at home, so I wanted her informed about what she was going to face. I did not have to replicate those systems in our home in order to help her learn to navigate them. In fact if I did, I would lose the trust that we had, and then why would she believe me anyways! I wanted her to know how adults think about kids. The power they believe they have over children. I didn't want her surprised by it. Once she had all this information, she was empowered to make her own choices. Whatever choices she made, she would share with us and we would learn from them together. Even though we talked about it, it still was a bit of a shock to her system of course. As well it should be. Every day when she would come home from school we would process different things that happened. We would talk about how the kids view the teachers because of how they treat them. When she was in school and received a consequence, like detention, or points or even a "talking to", she was able to endure it with equanimity, it wouldn't touch her heart. She knew what was real. She knew love was real, and all this was error. Knowing how the system works she was able to make conscious choices. Checking in with her desires, her values, and evaluating the risks. From this we would be learning about power structures, decision making, values, communication, priorities, intuition and more. I have never met a kid who isn't a philosopher. Being able to discuss deep things in the absence of judgment, or any unpleasant consequence, feels empowering, safe, and even joyous. I take a similar approach with all the different things I want to explore/impart/guide. I take the role of guide as a parent very seriously. I try and put a lot of thought into it. The different values, ideas, skills, explorations that I want to engage in, I would weave into our everyday life. I would infuse them with a sense of connection, joy, importance, tradition, wonder, etc. This is the beauty of the Non-Coercive, Collaborative, Learning Partner, relationship. The guidance is consistent. Force not necessary. I titled this piece "How To Prepare Kids For The Real World" as a rebuttal to 25 years of being told this philosophy is not preparing kids for the real world. For example, I often talk about never giving my kid consequences to modify their behavior, (not even using natural consequences) to modify their behavior in the direction that I think it should go. Invariably there is a slew of comments from people telling me that the real world has consequences, and I'm not preparing them for the real world by not giving them consequences. I will often ask people, how then DO you deal with consequences? How do you evaluate them? How do you decide which consequences are worth it, and which ones aren't? How do you decide if they're fair? How do you evaluate the system that they're a part of? Do you include values? And then once you have all that information, how do you impart that information to your child in a way that empowers them so that when they actually have to deal with the consequences they feel somewhat prepared? LoL Of course people saying you have to give them consequences aren't actually thinking about what are the skills necessary to deal with systems that have consequences. They are largely reacting from unexamined biases, implanted by their upbringing, and the ubiquitous messages of society, that coercion is necessary, that kids need to be controlled etc. I understand it, but it still frustrates me. Partly because I know that parents are making things so much harder for themselves. Partly because I know the impact it has on the relationship the child has with themselves, and relationships they form with others. AND it does nothing to prepare them for the real world! Especially comparing it to the idea of building skills, in a deep and conscious way, over a couple of decades, with a foundation of a trusting, non-coercive relationship, the punishment and reward model seems ineffective and shallow. This is why being a conscious parent is hard. Bloody hard. We are constantly learning and growing, constantly evaluating ourselves and doing the work to make changes. Always evolving. So, if you really want to prepare your kid for the real world, think about what are the most important, most empowering skills, awareness, values etc. What do you think makes a person successful? What do you think are your deepest values? Your deepest priorities? As you gain more clarity around these things you can't be more intentional with how you bring them into your life, how you bring them into your relationship with your kid. Every time we interact with our children we are influencing them. We are modeling life and relationships to them. We model in three main areas, how we treat THEM, how we treat OURSELVES, and how we treat OTHERS and the environment. We affect our kids with every move we make. The influence is inevitable. That we can't avoid. We can however make the effort to choose what kind of influence that is. Let us make that influence kind, compassionate, and based in deep thinking and feeling. Then we really will be preparing kids for the real world!

Empower and Inspire A Different Vision of Leadership . My 25 year old daughter went for a job interview a few months back. It was for a company she really wanted to work for. . At one point they asked her "Who is a leader she admires?" . She named me as her inspiration. She told them that her dad is an example of someone who leads using inspiration, connection, and communication, and not coercion. . After the interview she called her mom and I to tell us about it. She was so excited to share this particular response. . Personally I love this because how often do 25 year olds reference their parents as inspirations on important job interviews? She could have chosen someone else, she did have other ideas in mind. Artists, athletes, political personalities, historical personalities. She chose me because it felt the most authentic and organic for her. . Another great thing about this is she knows my flaws. She's had to live with them for 25 years! She knows I am a fallible human being. I always included my fallibility in our relationship. That made space for her fallibility. This way of relating is more deeply human. . I share this with you because I want to emphasize that I raised my daughter without using punishments, without having any rules, without using authority. We never used consequences, or enforced any limits (Explored? Yes. Enforced? No.)... All the traditional parenting mindsets and methodologies we threw out the window. . We didn't even ever tell her she was wrong, for any decision she made. Everything was a learning opportunity, and we learned side by side. . 25 years ago when I started parenting this way, and talking about it, everyone told me I had to be a leader in the home, or my kid would run wild. I had to prepare her for the real world! What they meant by 'leader' was I had to use coercion and wrongness, I had to exert my power. But I never saw that as leadership. . Leadership feels good to the people who are following. Leadership uplifts the whole system. Leadership Empowers and Inspires. . Leadership is based in deep respect. In honoring our shared humanity. In balancing form and function, product and process. . Our children can relax into our leadership when it makes sense to them, and feels good to them. If it doesn't make sense, and it doesn't feel good, it is an imposition. This is not leadership. . I want to acknowledge that the traditional mindset says, "If we don't take control, they will run all over us. They aren't smart enough, developed enough, prefrontal cortex grown enough, life experience enough, to make their own decisions. So we have to make decisions for them. If they don't like it, their feelings are welcome, and we empathize with their frustration. However we hold firm on the limit. Boundaries and limits make a kid feel safe." . And . "What if they run into the street and get hit by a car?" . I'm writing that out because that is how we've been taught to think. You can see it in any comment section. People will fight ardently for coercion, swearing it is necessary. . So let me get ahead of it and say that I know this is how we have always thought about kids, how we've always thought about parenting. Myself and people who teach a similar philosophy, we are here to change that whole mindset. It's not just making the old mindset a little more gentle, it's an entirely new way of looking at this relationship. There is a leap here. . This is why I am emphasizing, that we can treat our kids entirely non-coercively, we can respect their consent and autonomy, we can include them in all the decisions, we can work collaboratively with them, . AND . We can be leaders. . In fact it is the path to being the most effective leader. . We can teach them values and help them learn the attitudes, skills and knowledge they will need to manage life. Helping them prepare for the "real world" does not automatically have to mean exerting power and using coercion. We can still hold true to our values of non-coercion, and collaboration. . Martial Arts story time: . I've been studying and teaching Martial Arts for a few decades. Back in 2012 I was invited to a martial arts and combatives conference in the UK. There were people there from all over the world, only two from Canada. I was honored to be chosen as one of the two. . This entire experience was put on by my friend and mentor, Luke Holloway. My whole life changed after I met Luke. My understanding of self-defense and martial arts was completely transformed. So it was a big deal to me to be invited to this conference! . At one point there was an outdoor survival element. We were split into four teams and we had a competition to see who could build a shelter out of branches and leaves. The goal was to have the quickest shelter put up, but it also had to be sturdy and weatherproof. . I ended up being leader for one of the teams. Because my personality tends to be a bit softer, I often get underestimated in martial arts spaces. It was no different at this conference. I was constantly having to prove myself. That's not a complaint, that's just the nature of the culture. . On this particular day I wanted to show how my leadership style plays out under real life, stressful situations. So when the leader of this competition ask for volunteer leaders I jumped up and raised my hand! LOL I must have seemed a little too eager . This guy was a wilderness and survival expert that Luke had brought in to put us through the paces in the forest. He split the group randomly into four teams and we all went for it. The other teams immediately started running about putting up their shelters gathering branches and yelling orders at each other. . I gathered my group in a huddle. We all slowed down and looked at each other. I told them that each person here is important, that we're trying to achieve a goal together, and if we put our best into every moment we can beat all the teams. I said we have amazing expertise in this group and if we use that wisely nothing can stop us. . By the end of this talk everybody was jumping out of their seats to get going. We started about 5 minutes later than everybody else, and we finished a half hour before anyone else! . We were sitting around and laughing after we were done, adjusting little details. The wilderness guy came over and asked us what was going on, and we told him we were done. He was so surprised! He checked over our shelter and it was Rock solid. It ended up being the best shelter even though it was done the quickest! We were all glowing with pride to be on this team. . Each person in that group felt inspired and empowered. That's why they gave their all. We achieved an amazing result, but honestly the other teams could have done that as well. They were just missing that human element! That's leadership! . I want to add that, while there was an acknowledgment that the way I led the group clearly produced this result, also everybody kind of forgot that because I included myself in the work, I worked just as hard. I never really gave anyone an order, or criticism, so I didn't set myself up as a traditional leader. It ended up being about the group. . We can parent the same way - Empower and Inspire! We can be the leader of this team, this community, this family system and still stay true to values of Non-Coercion and Collaboration. . Then when your kid is older, they will fearlessly use you as an example on a job interview. Ok maybe not that exactly , but in the Spirit of that. You know! . When things get stressful, remind yourself: . Empower and Inspire. . P.s. By the way - She got the job!

Nourishing Empathy without Wrongness or Shame Empathy is something to NOURISH and INSPIRE, not something to TEACH, and certainly not something that can be FORCED. It's a common idea that asking "How would you feel if someone did that to you?" is a good way to help kids develop empathy. We imagine we are encouraging them to think about another's experience. This approach rests on the idea that when the kid thinks about it, they will feel bad. The desire to avoid feeling bad, will lead them to making better choices. This is the same basic philosophy as punishment. If we make them feel bad, they will want to avoid feeling bad in the future and make a different choice. We are also hoping that by making them feel bad they will somehow be inspired to not want to make other people feel bad, even though the lesson was taught to them by making them feel bad. There is a serious logic feedback loop there. It's not enough for kids to know that their actions had an impact on someone, they have to care about it. It's the caring that makes a difference. You cannot force someone to care. You cannot punish someone enough that they will care. Shaming someone will never make them care. The only way to inspire care, is to help people touch their own hearts, and feel a sense of their shared humanity. In the prison workshops that my mother does, she uses the same mindset. She doesn't tell the guys they are wrong. She doesn't tell them what is right or wrong. She helps them find a connection to their deep wisdom, to their inner light and love, to their conscience. All of a sudden what is right, kind, compassionate and loving becomes obvious to them, when it never was before. This is why unconditional acceptance is the deepest route to empathy. When a kid isn't facing a judgement of how they should act, they don't have an external pressure to compare themselves against. At this point the only place they have to look is within. Looking into their own selves, empathy arises. From the inside out. This requires us believing that our children already have empathy, compassion and kindness within. We don't have to force them, or guilt them into having empathy. That doesn't work anyway! Instead we help them tune in to their own sense of empathy. We point them to their own conscience rather than insist that they use our conscience as their guide. That's what's happening when we tell the kid what's right and wrong. We are making them follow our conscience. This inhibits them from learning to listen to their own. Once kids start to feel their own sense of connection to other humans, which is where empathy arises from, their value of wanting to care for their impact on other people will arise naturally. I have seen this happen countless times. You can go through my YouTube channel and my videos and articles here where I tell many many stories of examples in my own work with young people. I witnessed this kind of spontaneous empathy with a kid recently. I tell the story in a video I'll be posting soon. Please keep an eye out for it. How do you nourish empathy in your children without wrongness or shame? It's a whole new way of thinking! We can learn together about it.

Accountability doesn't come from FEAR of consequences. Accountability comes from CARING about other people. If accountability came from consequences, recidivism would not be such a big problem in prisons! But it is. They talk about revolving door prisons for a reason. Because the fear of consequences, even going back to prison, is not enough to stop people from repeating their behaviors. True accountability comes from our feeling of caring about other people, caring about our impact on other people. You cannot force someone to care. You can never punish someone enough to make them care. When we think deeply about what real accountability is we realize it is not a fear based value. I'm sure if you think about your own self, you don't treat other people well because you're afraid of what will happen if you don't, you treat other people well because you care about your impact on them. Because it's the kind of person you want to be. Consequences and Punishment can never teach this. The times I have taken true accountability for causing harm to another person, it's never come from fear of consequences. It came from genuinely wanting to take accountability because I regretted what happened. The times that I have apologized because of fear of consequences, of being judged, of being abandoned, of being punished, it has been to protect myself. To be clear, punishment is not only physical, it is also emotional and relational. This is why it's so important to create a safe relationship for kids to explore their decisions, their actions, their thinking, their explorations of the world. Because only in freedom can they learn the importance of taking accountability from the inside out. Something that punishment can never do. Something that wrongness can never do. If you truly care about teaching your kids accountability, you will commit to never punishing them again.

Transforming School Culture with Empathy and Respect . When my (now 25 year old) kid was in elementary and middle school, I volunteered a lot. All the kids knew me. . I treated them with an uncommon amount of respect. I saw something special in each one and reflected their light back to them. . This was something they did not receive from adults very often, if ever. . The effect this had on their Consciousness was not subtle. These kids came alive and opened up in a whole new way when I treated them this way. . I was careful to treat the 'bullies' with the same respect. When you spend a lot of time with kids you learn to read their social structures. I made sure to hold them in the same spirit of compassionate, No Wrongness. I looked past the surface of their behavior and reflected their light back to them also. . When they were around me they would always soften. In fact it was very hard for them to be unkind to others, not because they were afraid of any consequence, but because they felt deeply valued. . Perhaps that filled a need of theirs to be seen, to matter. I listened to them and took them seriously. . Perhaps they were able to drop their defenses and be their truest self around me, because they knew I would accept it, even celebrate it. . Even a decade later when I talk to my kid about those days, they remember how the social structure of her entire class was affected by my presence as a volunteer. . We CAN change the choices of kids who regularly engage in bullying behavior. We need to implement a connected, relational, empathy based approach. . No amount of wrongness or consequences will ever achieve the kind of systemic shift that we're looking for. . The intensely humanizing way I treated those kids affected an entire class, from kindergarten up to grade eight. . I was the most radical adult they had met. Someone who held no authority over them, someone who always respected them, and at the same time saw through any manipulation attempt. . When I called them out, it was always in a spirit of acceptance and understanding. I would say: . "I understand that you have to do that with most adults. I did the same when I was a kid. It's no different. I know you have to survive. . But with me you don't have to do that. I'm with you and I'm listening." . And they knew I meant it. . This is how we can point things out to kids without it being a criticism. In fact I was encouraging them. I validated their defense mechanisms. I acknowledged there's a real threat, and it makes sense to protect yourself from it. . We ended up on the same side. Once this connection was made they would open up and we could look at the situation together, fearlessly. Defences dropped. . The kids got used to being treated with respect, as well as being encouraged to treat others the same way. I helped them see the benefit of doing so, especially because of how good it felt to be treated like that by me. . The modeling, the relationship, the philosophy, the stories, and the consistent integrity were all very inspirational to the kids. They started to open up and take on those behaviors themselves. . Feeling like this adult was on the same side as the kids, they began to see each other the way as well. Their lenses were changing. Gradually the bullies, the victims, the marginalized kids, everybody seemed to come together. . In fact there was an active effort to include the people who were usually excluded. I noted a distinct difference between the grade levels I had less interaction with. Even so the entire school was profoundly affected by this whole experiment. . By the way I was also school council chair. I coached or assistant coached pretty much all the sports teams all the way up through middle school. I also had the opportunity to teach a number of classes. I taught math, science, English. In grade 8 they couldn't get a music teacher so I taught the entire grade 8 music program as a volunteer, including putting on a music night! . I spent a lot of time with these kids, with the teachers, the admin, and the parents. Deeply embedded in the school culture. . When I recently went live with my kid, who is now a young adult, she was talking about some of the classes I would teach back in middle school. She said even then she and her friends knew it was about more than the math, science, or English that I was teaching. They all had a sense something deeper was going on. . I was constantly trying to expand their minds. I would try and help them believe in themselves, their capacity, their dreams. I wanted them to know that despite so many of the messages they receive, they are not bad people. . I also wanted them to believe that they had power. So often young people feel they are powerless. I showed them their power at every opportunity. As well as to care for how they wield it . I was grateful to hear that my intentions were clear, and came across positively. My goal was always to help kids see the bright light that they are. To know their worth. I used my time with them to share values however I could. . For example: In science class I would tell them that our bodies are made of atoms. I would say there's no difference between us except the difference in arrangement of those atoms. We're different arrangements of the same stuff and so we are all one. Whatever we do to each other we do to ourselves. . However I wouldn't word it as if I was the moral superior authority telling them what they need to do. It was more that I was admiring the power they have. . You have the power through your arrangements of electrons to affect the experience of another arrangement of electrons. How you use that power will always be up to you. . Adults will try and tell you what you should do and what's right or wrong. You can take that in as information, but always know that the truth is in your heart. Each of you knows what's right and wrong for you in the moment. The most important thing for you to honor that. . Adults are guessing most of the time anyway. x . We would start out talking about physics and end up talking about life. . This is the same approach my mother, @Shivani, takes in her work in self-empowerment workshops in prison. She has designed a six week course that helps those guys see themselves. See the light that they are. See their No Wrongness, the Pure Love they have in their heart, and then want to express it to the world. . In the same way that those kids wanted to be their truest self around me. (Note I'm intentionally not saying best self) the prisoners wanted to be their true selves for my mom. . We are operating from the same principles in both environments. Connection, No Wrongness, Empathy, Validation, Exploring Values etc. . The same principles will work in your family. . In implementing this mindset you can start with a practice. Every time you think of expressing a complaint to your kids, bite your tongue. . I know that might not sound very spiritual, but it is extremely practical! I often say I only have 7% of my tongue left. . Take a deep breath and be pleased you averted a disconnecting moment. Now you can look for a way to connect instead. . Every time you want to criticize or correct, stop for a moment, and breathe. Think about what you really want to achieve. Think about the deeper experience. Think about nourishing the relationship of trust and connection. . Choose your responses from that mindset. You will see the same kind of effects that I did in those school years. It shifts dramatically how kids relate to us when they feel our deep respect for who they are. . Can you reflect your child's light back to them, even when they are at their most difficult? Can you do the same for yourself? . d
