If someone were to ask your kid, "What could you do to get in trouble with your parents?", if they can come up with an answer, You Need to Change Your Parenting. When kids adopt a morality based on whether or not they're going to get in trouble, they aren't actually developing values. They're learning how to navigate a coercive system for their benefit, for survival. This is a whole different thing than teaching them how to care for other people! When their decisions are based around not getting in trouble, they are trying to figure out what WE think is right and wrong, rather than learning what THEY think (and feel) is right and wrong, they never get to develop their own value system. They haven't had the chance to find what makes sense for them, from their own experience, and their own inner journey. They couldn't make a personal choice because they never had the option of choosing the opposite in Freedom. Without the free choice we can't look within clearly and listen to our inner guidance. To discover what our own values are, what is our conscience say? What kind of person do we want to be? How do we want to treat people? What kind of impact do we want to have on the world? These are the Self-Reflective Questions. Young people are at the stage of development where they are discovering values for the first time. These questions are very important for them to explore. It's how they form a sense of who they are. If they are focused on not getting in trouble, they are NOT focused on exploring their own sense of values. Then we end up with adults who don't have a clear sense of what is right and wrong. The focus of their values has always been external. I know for myself, as I began to realize this in my early twenties, I felt like I had to rewrite and reclaim my entire value structure, my thinking, my relationship with myself, and the world. I could feel that much of it was imposed. It meant I wasn't really me, I wasn't in control of myself. I wasn't being true to myself. When I would have a thought, I would ask "Is This Chose Or Imposed?" Most of the time it was imposed. I realized a lot of my values and beliefs weren't truly arising from my own thinking and feeling. I do not want to impose that programming on my own child. I wanted them to know themselves through their own exploration from the beginning. To be clear I was an integrated and important part of that exploration. Even to this day she regularly tells me of the things that she's learned from me. My 25-year-old is not shy to share many examples, and we celebrate it together. I mention this because many people continue to make the mistake of thinking that, by refusing to impose my authority on my kid, no consequences, no limits, no boundaries, honoring their yes and no, that I am not guiding them. The exact opposite is true. It is this relationship that allows for deep and consistent Co-Guidance without resistance. This is not something that would exist if my kid grew up relating to me as someone she could get in trouble with. Having to navigate around those expectations. Creating a mask of acceptability. One of my early one-liners is "Parents are not Mask Designers." This is why I write: If someone were to ask your kid, "What could you do to get in trouble with your parents?", if they can come up with an answer, You Need to Change Your Parenting. I know it's a bit harsh, but I want to be clear. If you have a relationship with your kid where they feel they can get in trouble with you, even just a look, it's going to degrade over time. They're going to continue to withdraw their trust and not be vulnerable around you. Therefore it's worth to be continuously examining your interactions with your kid and making adjustments. Always trying to create more safety and Trust in the relationship. My kiddo is 25 and I still am actively working on it. Just this evening I was going over a phone call I had with her and discussing it with my wife. I was noticing some of the patterns that I was playing out and thinking about what I could change the next time the two of us had a call. There's great power in the path of continuous evaluation and change. And this change is a big change. Moving towards No-Wrongness, towards Radical Acceptance. It's powerful and courageous work. I admire every parent sweating with the effort of breaking old cycles and creating new patterns. It's no picnic! Thank you for making the world a better place. Keep at it, don't give up. Tomorrow is always another opportunity to practice!

He has seen how much his brother has struggled, how much oppression he faces on a regular basis and it breaks his heart. The other thing he shared was that he deeply regrets the years that he misgendered his brother. He wishes he could take back every time he called him his sister instead of brother. He now knows now how painful that was for his brother. He said that experience has made him a passionate ally for the LGBTQ+ community. He holds the regret, AND is doing something about it. I appreciate that. At one point, his brother came on screen and watching the two of them interact was so touching. I could feel the love and support between them. Yesterday was National Coming Out Day and I wanted to write a post in honor of that. I'm a day late sorry about that. This story touches me deeply because homophobia and transphobia are such deadly diseases. Literally deadly. The prejudice that the LGBTQ+ community faces contributes to a high number of suicides and a whole host of mental health issues. Recently I read an account by a friend about going to a school district meeting in her area where they were removing the anti-discrimination policy from the district because teachers didn't want to call trans kids by their chosen pronouns. They wanted to impose the teachers own choice of pronoun on them. There were 400 people in attendance at this school meeting. Only six of them were there to speak up for the rights of these children. Children wanting to be called what they want to be called. Just imagine the hate in these people's hearts, screaming, yelling, and accusing in the meeting. Over children wanting to be called what they want to be called. To be filled with so much hate and prejudice is to be deeply disconnected from one's humanity. I have to believe that a person who is connected to their sense of their shared humanity with others would not want to hurt them. But hatred is a great motivator. It gets people up out of their seats. It gets us riled up and even violent. It helps us dehumanize other people so we can justify oppressing them. When we are hyped up on hate, we can easily forget our values, the kind of person we really want to be. This is why I do not speak lightly about prejudice. I have faced it all my life (as racism). I have witnessed it all my life. It is one of the most damaging parts of our human nature. I don't pretend to be free from it myself. I consciously evaluate my biases, keeping an eye out for them, counteracting them when I notice them come up. It's a lifelong practice. LIMITS! Non-consensual, imposed limits was something I avoided as much as possible as my kid was growing up. Sometimes these limits are called Loving Limits. "Loving", because we empathize with their feelings of sadness, frustration, anger, or disappointment, as we hold the limit. Except it doesn't feel loving to the kid. I did not want to go down this path of using my authority to create negative experiences and associations. So instead, each of the areas I was tempted to control, we transformed into co-explorations. This had the effect of making exploring limits a joyful and connecting experience. Limits were not a heavy, disconnecting thing, laced with power and control. They were one of the tools in our kit of taking care of ourselves, loving ourselves, creating the best quality of life for ourselves. When framed and explored this way, limits cease to be such a struggle between parent and child.

Power Struggles It's always the parent's responsibility to shift the dynamic from competition to collaboration. It's never the kid's responsibility. When your kid is resisting you and you feel the pressure building up, that's the time to take a step back, take a breath and re-evaluate. When it feels like there's a power struggle happening, remind yourself that your kid has valid reasons for what they're feeling. The most powerful defense against power struggles are the qualities of Listening, Curiosity and Empathy. Become genuinely interested in what they're feeling, ask them what the reasons are, tune into what needs they are expressing. Think of power struggles as an opportunity to connect and understand. Let go of the idea of being an authority that has to be in control. It is not a battle that you need to win. As soon as we think of our parenting as a battle, Nobody Wins. Whomever wins, you both lose, because your kids lose trust in you. When we allow our own programming and triggers to rule our choices, rather than our compassion and our principles, we end up pushing our kids away. Power struggles cause pain to everybody. What are the damaging effects of Power Struggles? -Decreases the trust in your relationship -Children feel our love and acceptance is conditional -Conditional acceptance creates a focus on external approval to feel acceptable -Weakens self-esteem and self-confidence, whether they win or lose -They learn about manipulation and control from us -They are more likely to lie to us -Power Struggles do not teach kids to embrace and learn from their mistakes -Inspires an attitude of self-protection (as opposed to self-awareness) This is why it's important to study how we can transform power struggles into a collaborative, problem-solving relationship with our kids. Understanding the concepts and implementing some powerful and deep strategies, you can reduce and even eliminate power struggles. Benefits of reducing power struggles: -Deepens the trust in your relationship -They feel our love and acceptance is UNconditional -Unconditional acceptance creates a focus on internal approval instead of external -Strengthens self-esteem and self-confidence -There is no "win" or lose because we're on the same side -They learn about respectful interaction and effective communication from us -They are more likely to trust us with their most difficult truths -We teach kids to embrace and learn from their mistakes -Our kids never feel they have to protect themselves from us Even though it is a lot more work, especially on ourselves, to choose connection over correction, to flow with our kids direction, to resist using our power to control with coercion, the benefits make it well worth the effort.

I have made a lot of parenting mistakes over the past 25 years. I have stumbled and struggled many times. I never gave up on the philosophy however. When things went awry, I would pick myself up, give myself some love, rededicate myself to the Non Coercive, Collaborative Mindset, and try again. I call it "Stumbling With Purpose". Even with all the mistakes, the purposeful Stumbling builds conscious layers and patterns. One thing I know, is that my child knows I don't control them. She knows this from her nose to her toes. I have never put myself in the power position that would allow me to control her. We are not the same, but we are equals. When my kid was born, I knew I wanted to do things differently. I wanted to not yell, to not use punishments and consequences, to collaborate on decisions. However that was not enough for me, I wanted more (I always want more!) Those things I considered the branches of the Conscious Parenting Tree, but I wanted the Trunk, I wanted the Roots, I wanted to go all the way into the Earth. What is the deepest relationship I can have? How can I foster a truly non-violent, consent based, deeply connected, relationship with this human? One of the prime ingredients of going into the Earth with my child was choosing not to control them. It is so normalized in society for parents to control their kids. The idea of not controlling them, of honoring their choices, of refusing to violate their consent and autonomy, is so radical that even now whenever I post about it, people defend the practice. They say adults know more, we have more experience, children's frontal lobe isn't developed, they don't think long term, they can't make decisions for themselves, therefore they need to be controlled. Whenever we want to use power and violence to control someone, we can always find a reason. However, none of those reasons necessitate that we control our children. There are other ways to care for our kids. Other ways to keep them safe, that don't involve holding power over them. After a couple of decades treating my kid this way, she knows deep inside that I do not control her, I do not want to control her, that I do not set myself up as somebody who has the right to control her. So often as parents, even when we're trying to be collaborative, we hold that control in our back pocket. When kids know that we give ourselves permission to control them, they always have to keep one eye open around us. They put up a protective barrier around their hearts. They cannot be totally vulnerable with us because they can never be sure when the collaborative parent is going to show up, or when the controlling parent is going to show up. If we take that choice off the table altogether, children are able to relax into our relationship, into our guidance. This is when a deeper trust is formed. Choosing to not control our kids is a big mindset leap. It fundamentally shifts all of our decision making, it shifts our perspective, and our priorities. It is a different way of engaging with our kids. It is a different way of looking at relationships. I know very well there are lots of seemingly reasonable reasons why we should control our children sometimes. As my kid was growing up we fought together as a family to resist using control at all costs. People witnessing our family dynamic we're often confused by it. Folks would regularly tell me how I was ruining my kid by not imposing control and boundaries. Treating my kid as an equal seemed irresponsible. To this day, 25 years later, I still get those comments on just about every post I publish! The fact that I have been hearing those comments for so many years, decades, it gives me great confidence in the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting philosophy. The trust that has developed between my kid and I over 25 years of doing this work could not exist in a relationship where she cannot rely on my non-violence. Letting go of this kind of control can be quite scary because it's a big unknown. We don't know how our kids are going to respond to having more freedom. We don't know what's going to happen to our relationship with them. We don't know how their behavior will change. This is one of the big leaps of trust we take. We trust our kid's path, their process, their wisdom. Those are the big three I always pay attention to, trusting their path, trusting their process, trusting their wisdom. When we control our children it feels much more predictable. It feels safer somehow. A relationship of freedom carries an inherent risk. Risk can be scary! This is one of the situations when it's important for us to be aware of our deep priorities. In our parenting we often face Competing Priorities. For example, I might have a priority for my kids to eat well. I also have a priority for them to learn to have a positive relationship with their bodies and with food. I also have a priority to be a safe space a trusted guide. When we face competing priorities, sometimes we have to choose one over the other. If we take the above example, my priority for my kid to eat well might make me want to control their eating. They can't just eat whatever they want. What if they want ice cream before dinner? Parents often say that because they are responsible for their kids they have to say no and stop their kids from having ice cream before dinner. Especially if they had ice cream yesterday. They feel they have to set a boundary. Even with the best of intentions, there is no way to stop your kid from having ice cream against their will, without using power and violence. If you don't exert your power over them, they could just go get the ice cream. This is the problem with non-consensual limits and boundaries. Every time we use this kind of power and control, we degrade the relationship of trust between ourselves and our kids. This is why we need to be conscious of our priorities. I call it the hierarchy of priorities. My other priorities around food are that my kid develops a deep relationship with their own body, a healthy relationship with food, and a trusting relationship with me as their guide. If I set those as my deeper priorities then it makes it easier for me to make the decision to not control their eating. It also means I have to find other ways of dealing with situations. This is an important point because a lot of people are under the impression that there are only two options, control our kids or do nothing. This is a false dichotomy. In fact there is another option, a collaborative, co-learning, co-exploring option. It takes some time and effort to learn the skill, but it is absolutely possible for us to guide our children without control, power, and force. When I have to make a decision about how I'm going to work with my kid, I tune into my deepest priorities. I also recognize my sub priorities. I don't want to ignore those, but I want to make sure I work with them in a way that honors my deepest priorities. So if we take the ice cream example, if one of my deepest priorities is to preserve the trusting relationship with my kid, I cannot use any power over methods to work with my other priority of caring about them eating well. I don't ignore the sub priority, I find ways to work with it so that I can honor the main priority. In Conscious Parenting, in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting, Gentle, Peaceful, Responsive, etc. We strive to treat our children with the utmost respect for their humanity. This means we need to engage with them in a way that is not violent and oppressive, even if we think it's good for them. Because, of course, oppressing people because we think it's good for them is an ancient practice. I want to encourage you to daily dig deeper into how you can let go of controlling your child. Look for all the ways you exert power over them. This can be hard when the power makes things convenient! However the effort you put into this will inspire your kids to know you respect their humanity, they drop their armor and open themselves to you. True Non-Coercion nourishes a profound relationship of connection and trust with your kids unlike anything else can.

My mother has been in the hospital for the last 7 weeks. I have been by her side pretty much every day. My powerful and wonderful sister and I take shifts in spending time with her. This is no ordinary woman. My mother is a Warrior Goddess of Love and Wisdom! My mother has also made many mistakes in her parenting journey, and she would be the first to tell you so. However I always credit her as the original cycle breaker! While I am doing all the writing and making videos, she is the one who planted the seeds. From early on in my development, and all throughout the 53 years of my life, she has dedicated herself to learning and growing. She has pushed the boundaries of friendship, acceptance, respect and trust in relationship with my sister and I. All of this throughout the 70s and 80s. With so many obstacles working against her she created a very special relationship with her kids. Today at the hospital we took a walk down the hallway and sat on the windowsill looking at the cars and people going by. We were talking about life, making jokes, appreciating each other, and enjoying each other. A nurse who was nearby was listening to us, and as we got up to go, she stopped us. She said "You two are just chatting like friends. No one would ever think that you were mother and son. There's no difference between the two of you." My mom said "We're best friends." The nurse went on, "I see a lot of families go through this place, and I have never seen any parent and child relate the way you two are." My mom has a way of weaving a Magic Spell of Love on people. Even throughout this hospital stay all the nurses fall in love with her. She makes each one feel important, seen, and appreciated. Usually I talk about my relationship with my kid, but right now I want to talk about my mom. Partially because she really is the source of all the radical things I did as a parent! I took her efforts and did my best to carry them forward. I'm right now writing an article about my kid and how she knows in her deepest knowing that I do not control her. It's one of the best things in our relationship because there's a profound trust between us. I could go on but I'll save that for the other article. Another nurse said to her Shivani you're so nice to people, and it makes us want to do things for you. Another nurse a few weeks ago had casually mentioned it was her birthday in a couple of days. My mom had me go and get a muffin and bring a birthday candle from home. She gave it to this nurse and the young woman broke down and cried in my mother's arms. It was really beautiful. My Love Warrior mother has also been taking her magic into the prison system. Until covid shut down all volunteer programs, my mom had been doing a weekly self-empowerment workshop at a men's prison. She has been doing this work for 10 years. In the first few years her program became the most requested, with a waiting list over 50 people long, and the most prescribed by the unit manager is, psychologists, and case workers. It takes a lot of strength to soften hearts in an environment like that, because the shields are very important. She does six two hour classes. The guys walk into her first workshop giving her the side eye, checking her out, grabbing their crotch, generally suspicious and closed. By the end of 2 hours almost every single participant is leaning on the edge of their seat, with their eyes wide open, and a sense of hope that they might not have felt in a long time. Her program is called Freedom Thinkers. She tells the guys in the first class, "You were in prison before you got here. The prison of your mind. These four walls imprison your body, but they don't have to imprison your mind. You can be a free person before you walk out of here." The same love she gives in the prison, she's giving to the nurses. The same love she gives to her family. She's also hilarious!

When exploring values with our kids, forcing behaviors does not teach a deep lesson. In fact any kind of force, criticism, consequences or any of the other coercive methods used in traditional parenting to teach values, ends up working against us. We create negative associations to the values we're hoping to pass on. One of my one-liners is: "I don't want to teach my kid to respect boundaries. I want to teach my kid to want to respect boundaries." One is a behavior and one is a value. The thing about a value is that it's self-sustaining. Even when we're alone, and no one can see us, and there's no consequence, if we know our values, if we live our values, we will still do the thing that's in alignment. Yet if we're doing it for external motivation, as soon as there's no external reason, as soon as there's no consequence, as soon as no one can see us, as soon as we think we can get away with it, we're much more likely to do the thing if we want to do the thing. There's no value holding it in place. This is why teaching through force wrongness, through behavior modification of any sort is never effective. These things only affect the surface, they never get to the core. Perhaps for a time it might see a shift in behavior, but it is short-lived. On top of that we are creating negative associations and problematic patterns that will cause issues later on in life. This is what "Iceberg Consciousness" is about. Perceiving beneath the surface. Working with deeper causes. Exploring values rather than controlling behaviors. One of the rules of a parent is a guide to our children. As a guide it's reasonable to want to help our kids learn and grow, but let's do it in a way that's aligned with how learning works, in alignment with how the mind and emotions work. Exploring values from the inside out, caring for our impact on the nervous system, nourishing a safe relationship, and modeling consciously. It's a bit of a slow burn doing things this way. It takes patience and dedication to work from the inside out, to work from cause to effects. The long game allows us to go much deeper in our process with our kids.

I just spent an unexpected 24 hours with my daughter and I'm in heaven! 2022 09 06 Conscious Parenting and Social Justice are intimately related. Social Justice is anti-oppression work, and Conscious Parenting is also anti-oppression work. Conscious parenting is not just about getting your kids to do what you want in a more peaceful way. It's not traditional parenting done more gently. It is a child liberation philosophy. Conscious parenting is based on treating kids as whole human beings. Not less deserving of respect, autonomy, or consent because they are different. Not more deserving of being controlled and having their freedom curtailed because they are different. I mention 'difference' because in almost every post or comment I see justifying coercing and oppressing children, people talk about their "brain development" and "frontal lobe" as the reason. That because kids think differently than adults it gives us the right to control them against their will. This same attitude has been used to justify oppressing many other groups in the past. Indigenous people were seen as different, black people were seen as different, women were seen as different, disabled people seen as different, neurodivergent people seen as different... all of these groups of people have been oppressed by the dominant demographic and power structures of society using the same mindset. And still are! Adults have systemic power over children. The four main areas of this systemic power are Physical, Mental, Emotional, and Access to Resources power. In the traditional mindset it's perfectly okay to use that power to control our children "for their own good". In conscious parenting we recognize children are more vulnerable than adults, they are widely oppressed in society, and we endeavor to do things differently. The things we do to kids that are normalized, would immediately be considered abusive tactics in an adult relationship. Taking away their belongings, putting them in their rooms, yelling at them, making them eat what they don't want to, sleep when they don't want to, obey without question, using fear of pain, punishment, and consequences to alter their behavior, to control their choices. When we engage in conscious parenting practices we are refusing to use our systemic power to oppress kids in this way. Sometimes, conscious parenting strategies are much less convenient than the more controlling ones. However, we do them anyways because it is the right thing to do. It's the right way to treat other humans. Social justice activists are working against the oppression of vulnerable, marginalized communities. As conscious parents, we do the same. This is why social justice activism and conscious parenting are intimately related. If you hold racist, sexist, genderist, ablest, homophobic, transphobic or classist views you are not doing Conscious Parenting, or at least you are not fully embracing the mindset. Of course we all hold biases around these things, that's part of living in an oppressive society. We are steeped in those prejudiced mindsets from the day of our birth. It's in every aspect and system of society, the education system, financial system, legal and correctional system, the media, and in our general thinking patterns. To work through our biases is a constant effort, that is part of social justice activism, just like working through our childism is a constant part of conscious parenting. Doing this work is essential because if we pass on the mindset that it's okay to oppress one group of people, we are not truly raising our kids with a liberation mindset. We cannot oppress one group of people while claiming to liberate another. This is why conscious parenting and social justice activism are intimately related.

Conscious Parenting and Social Justice Activism are intimately related.

Conscious parenting is not about getting our kids to do what we want in a more peaceful way. It is a child liberation philosophy. If you hold racist, sexist, genderist, ablest, homophobic, transphobic or classist views you are not doing Conscious Parenting. We cannot oppress one group of people while claiming to liberate another.

2022 09 05

*Teens Live In A World Of Their Own* Teens feel misunderstood and alone. Neither fully autonomous adults nor carefree children. They are expected to have the responsibility of an adult, but are given none of the freedoms or respect. It's a transition stage that can be so confusing and painful. Adults in general don't understand or appreciate the intensity of the teen experience. We don't give them enough validation for the struggles of teenage hood. *Teens Largely Feel Misunderstood And Alone* How often are they dismissed!? I see the plight of teens and feel despondent. It's very rare for young people to be treated as equals by adults. They are usually treated as if they are less than. We adults often do this without even realizing it. Looking down on young people, giving them a message that they have less wisdom, less capacity and therefore less worth is deeply embedded into the consciousness of society *They Internalize This Mindset* They carry this message into adulthood, of not being accepted who they are, of being wrong, of having to fight against power and authority. This affects their sense of self, their self-esteem, self-love and self-worth throughout their lives. This is why we have so many wounded, angry, defensive and closed off adults in the world. Just check out any comment section on the internet for evidence of this! *Teach them to Question and Evaluate* Young people are never taught to question authority. Yes teens rebel, but rebelling against authority is reacting to it, not questioning it. Instead of reacting we want our young people to learn to evaluate authority, rules and systems, based on principles and values, using discernment, critical thinking and intuition. Too often the perspective of teenagers are invalidated by the adults in their lives. This is why it's important for us to honor our kids perspective on things. To encourage them to question us. To stand behind them when they do - that's the hard part! *How can they think freely when their lives are controlled?* If we can create an environment of Freedom, of Choice, of Support, and Validation for our teens they will learn to think for themselves. Instead of trying to control their thinking and their behavior, let us nourish and support their process. I always say - I didn't teach my kid what to think, I taught them how to think. This meant being side by side with them in their process, not standing above them like an authority figure. Learning is a messy business and we will get much further ahead by getting into the mess with our young humans, rather than trying to avoid the mess. When we control we are trying to avoid the mess. It is a great work and a great joy to become your kid's learning partner in life. *Be Their Learning Partner* People always say that kids don't have the brain development to make proper decisions. I know very few adults that know how to make proper decisions! I rarely do, do you? Seriously! If we are going to teach our kids to question authority, we must be willing to be questioned ourselves. Don't insist that your perspective is the correct one, even if you believe it to be true! Fight the urge, humble yourself, and listen deeply. Let's be their learning partners so they know that they can lean on us without hesitation or fear. Let's help them learn to evaluate and question, to push back against oppression, to recognize disrespect, to set boundaries and protect themselves when necessary. This is How They will learn to Know Themselves, Love Themselves and Honor Themselves. This is possibly one of the best gifts we can give them to send them out into the world.

Cooperation rests upon the instinct to care for the experience of others. When kids feel cared for it awakens their instinct to care for others. . People often say that young kids don't experience empathy. This has not been my experience. Even the youngest of children can feel empathy for others when they feel safe to do so. . When kids feel judged, they can fear losing love and connection. It's hard for them to feel safe. This sends them into a protective mode. Their attention is now on managing the perceived threat. . When a child, or anyone, is concerned for their safety, it's hard to open our hearts and care about other people. When we feel safe, that heart opening happens naturally. . It is this opening in safety that inspires us to care about meeting other's needs. That's what cooperation is, working together to meet all our needs. . It's not only important that we get the task done. . How everyone feels before, during and after matters as well. This focus inspires caring, cooperation and collaboration. If I care about your experience I will want to take some of the load off you. . How to inspire that kind of natural, relational cooperation is a deep study. Especially since it's likely not how we were raised, and it's not reflected in most of the systems in society. . It is therefore largely creating A New Path. Perhaps it is revitalizing and renewing an old path? Let's be Trailblazers together and let go of the Force and Wrongness usually used to create cooperation. Let's explore and discover how to do so in a kind, connected and relational way. . If you go to my YouTube channel @meaningfulideas there is a 2-hour Workshop in two parts on cooperation that I gave in San Diego in 2018 that goes into more depth on how to actually implement this idea. I invite you to watch it and share it!

The problem with saying we're proud of our kids when they accomplish something is that there is an implied message of conditionality in it. Do we tell them we're proud of them when they DON'T try hard? When they don't care about the thing? When they didn't put a lot of effort into it? When they didn't study and got a bad grade? Usually no. So kids get the message early on that we are proud of them in certain circumstances and less so in other circumstances. This develops conditional self-esteem, and conditional regard from parents. I know you may not mean it that way, but that's what's happening. If you do want to offer them positive regard, make it specific. Tell them that you feel impressed by how much work they put into it. Tell them that you appreciate that they listened to their energy and chose not to put work into it. This way they don't feel like you accept them more with a particular output of energy! You honor their choice, you honor their beingness. Tell them that you enjoy the blue they put in the sky and that you can feel the clouds as if they're about to rain. This is much better than saying I'm proud of you for making this picture. Saying "I'm proud" is a judgment. I know it seems like a positive judgment, but the absence of it is the negative and that's where the problem comes in. There are lots of ways that we can show our kids positive regard without making it conditional. This is the point, not to say that our kids should never feel that we appreciate them or admire them. I always worked hard to show my kid UNconditional regard and at the age of 25 she knows very well that I am her biggest fan!

A Conscious Parenting Approach to Power Struggles - an IN PERSON workshop with Vivek Patel . Power Struggles are the worst. They sap our energy, deplete our relationships and make communication next to impossible. Everyone leaves feeling upset, drained and unsafe. . Something in us knows this is not how things are supposed to be. We feel that more harmony and connection with our kids is possible. Yet it seems like there's no way out. . So many families live this way for years. The disconnection builds over the decades and when the kids are young adults they can't wait to get away from their parents. They certainly don't accept their parents' guidance. . Practicing a conscious parenting approach to power struggles strengthens the bond between parent and child, increases trust and leads to easier collaboration. . We turn around power struggle moments to become opportunities to empower our children. To guide them into a relationship with their own power, to help them become power-full rather than power-empty. . We want to teach them that they have personal power and choice. We want to inspire them to use that power and choice as responsibly as possible. . We do this by creating a relationship that is safe, by processing the situation with them in an accepting and non-judgmental atmosphere, by helping them listen to their inner wisdom, by giving them courage to follow their wisdom and by being a powerful model with our own power. . In this Workshop we are going to explore concepts and practices that will help us transform power struggles and bring more Harmony and Ease into our relationship with our kids.

My kiddo does NOT like peanut butter. Can not even stand the smell. I LOVE peanut butter! I put it in everything. When I eat it she will cover her face with her shirt to mask the smell. The other day I said "sorry" when I saw her do this. She waved off my apology saying, "You gotta eat. I want you to enjoy your food. I don't mind doing this." I commented that we all support each other to enjoy our food. This young woman was joyfully enduring something unpleasant for my sake. She only mentioned it because I brought it up. Not entitled! This is the kid that grew up without punishments or consequences. Who didn't get in trouble no matter what she did. No rules. No authority. When she would say no to me, for anything, I thanked her for telling me her truth. I never considered it defiance! I was told over and over that she would grow up selfish if I didn't say no to her. She would grow up entitled if I followed her lead. People couldn't see the deep relationship we shared. The mutual respect. The profound co-learning partners that we were... From day one! I saw that she had things to teach me and I did my best to be a willing student. Her small act of lovingly supporting my peanut butter habit without complaint moves me so deeply because it is the opposite of selfish and entitled, the opposite of all the things the traditional parenting mindset is so sure will happen if we don't control.

Happy Father's Day! . I love being a Dad. It's the best thing in my life. It has also been the most transformative thing in my life. In order to live as the conscious parent I want to be, in order to live according to my values and principles, I have to dig deep into who I am! I have to examine all of my patterns and redesign them to be in alignment with my most profound priorities. . One of the benefits of committing to the Non-coercive, Collaborative Parenting path, is having a deep relationship with your kids. . My 25 yr old and I have a relationship of deep comfort and safety. We enjoy being in each other's company. We learn together, we laugh together, and we share wisdom with each other. . This is not me showing off (maybe a little). I am sharing this because the principles of Non-coercive, Collaborative Parenting allow for the opportunity of a deeper relationship than mainstream parenting ever can. . I apologize if that sounds harsh. It's just how things are. Coercion and Authority create disconnection and damage trust, every time. . Parenting from a different paradigm is powerful and challenging work. Letting go of control and authority with children goes against all of the ways we deal with children in society. It's not easy, yet it is available to you. . Going against the grain by treating our kids as equals is hard. It takes courage to push back against the old mindset. It is a lifelong journey that requires continuous effort and self-evaluation. . The result of 25 years of non-coercive, deeply connected, relating, has created a relationship of safety, ease, and joy in each other's lives. . It's truly one of the greatest gifts of non-coercive, collaborative parenting. . I know that there are so many things that we feel are important when we are raising kids. Sleep, food, chores, manners, obedience, homework, hygiene, social skills.... The list is never ending. . Having our attention pulled in many directions like this can make us forget our deep priorities, principles and values. . I want to encourage you to put Relationship First in all your interactions with your children. Empower your kid with every interaction. Preserve the trust and connection between you. Help them to foster a powerful relationship with themselves. You will create a foundation that will grow and deepen throughout the years. . Peace Vivek

'Conscious Parenting is an Act of Resistance". If you follow my stuff you know that's what I'm about. Pushing back against the established power dynamics. I would often reflect in the early days of my child's life that I was parenting from my rebellious 16 year old! Pushing back against the world of adults that didn't respect me for who I was. I knew very clearly I was being looked down on by most of them. Even ones who were being friendly, behind it I could still feel they saw me as "just a child". The land of my parents was colonized by the British for 200 years. Generations of my family before me was seen as sub-human. That mindset is absorbed over time and then passes down from parent to child. I was determined to break this cycle and treat my kid as the unconditionally worthy person that they are. To imbue this Self-Love/Self-Awareness/Self-Image into every cell of their being. I wanted them to know they were not "Less Than". I wanted them to know this from the inside out. This was my primary parenting priority. It often felt like a big FU to the weight and very painful residue of 10,000 years of coercive history and hierarchical power structures. Choosing to parent based on respect, relationship and empowerment. Pretty much every post on Peaceful parenting has some adult saying "Kids have to learn respect" or "Kids need boundaries and limits to feel safe" or "I am their parent, I am not their friend" or "If we let kids just do whatever they want they'll run into the street and get hit by a car!" (That one is my favorite x) Non-Coercive Collaborative Parenting is a completely different way of looking at, and engaging with power. I do not want to model a violent and oppressive use of power. I do not want to violate my child's autonomy and consent because I think I know what's good for them. I reject the Power Over model. I choose one based in connection, relationship, and horizontal power sharing. I will not replicate the oppressive structures in my home that have been used by the people who have held power for so long. Each of us has the choice and the potential to parent from this new mindset. A mindset that doesn't put one person above another. Embrace a revolutionary, anti-oppression parenting philosophy and become a powerful voice for social justice. You can do this. You can change age old patterns and create something new.

Let your kids see you and know you deeply. Be vulnerable with them and share your heart. Let them know your joys and your pains. Share your hopes, dreams and fears. Not in a way that burdens them, but in a way that lets them see you as deeply human. This is not about making them responsible for your feelings. My kid knows that they can lean on me for support. They trust in my strength, they feel the solidity of my acceptance, the safety of my No-Wrongness attitude, and my learning mindset. And at the same time they know my humanity. It is a delicate balance, but one worth working towards. Let them know you. The more you let them know you, the more they will open themselves so you can know them. My kid knows me better than almost anyone. It's something she takes great pride in. We celebrate it with Joy. She was on a walk with her partner recently and she shared with me about 20 pictures from that walk. I picked out this picture in particular and said that I'm going to meme it because it really resonated with me. She told me that of all the pictures she took that day, she was thinking of me as she took this one. I said to her kiddo, you really know me. It reminds me of the time a few years ago when we had this psychic experience. We have this 20 year, ongoing game of punch buggy. Over the decades we have developed a whole system of rules, It's very complicated. So much so that this year my wife and I made a rule booklet and gave it to her for Christmas to celebrate. One of our traditions is if we see a punch buggy at the same time, we break the tie with ROCK-PAPER-SCISSORS one day as we were driving somewhere together. I pulled over so that we could decide who would get the point. First game - Tie - rock rock Second game - Tie - scissors scissors Third game - Tie - scissors scissors 4th 5th 6th... Tie! We started to laugh because we just kept tying. We tied 12 times before she bailed and decided to just keep doing rock over and over till one of us lost. We were amazed at how similar our minds work. It was a moment of celebration for us. She values our relationship as much as I do. Just this afternoon I was telling her that I was writing this article and am planning to tell this story. She said she was recently thinking about it, and even so many years later it still makes her laugh with joy. Let your kids know you, let them know who you are, share yourself with them. This is a prime ingredient in creating a deep human relationship So often in the hubbub of a busy, stressed out life, we get focused on the tasks, the control, the behavior. We can forget about the opportunity we have before us to create and nourish a deep authentic, vulnerable, sustainable, and resilient relationship with our kids.

I believe we are all connected at the deepest part of ourselves, our Pre-Label consciousness. My Teacher showed me that we appear separate and distinct, like the waves on the Ocean, yet we all arise from the same source. Beyond all our differences, there is a common consciousness we share. When I feel into that part of myself, I can love you. But through the layers of time, indoctrination, pain and trauma, we lose sight of our Oneness. When I look into the eyes of a baby I see love and pure connection. I always ask babies to share their wisdom with me. "What is it like where you just came from?" If you listen close they will share their wisdom. When my child was first born I asked her this question and she replied: "You are limitless and free beneath all that skin" Can you feel the Ocean beneath the wave? Can you feel the depth of who you are, the part of you that connects to everyone and everything? The Ocean cannot abandon the Wave. I am more than just wave, yet I struggle to believe I am Ocean. The wave springs up and has its own existence. It has its own direction and form and shape. It has beauty, limitation, adventure and learning. It comes for a time, then disappears back from whence it came. Yet all the while it is only Ocean. While the wave exists, why should it not try and be the best wave it can? To express its full waveness, to enjoy being a wave and have meaningful relationships with other waves. What kind of wave do I want to be? How do I want to express my particular bit of ocean? What kind of wave do you want to be? When I remember I am ocean and you are too, I tend to treat you with more kindness. This is what I aspire to. The following is a poem I wrote a number of years ago. I share it with you in the hopes that we waves can all come together and create a better world.

I am not human I am the Stars and the sand and the Ocean Yes I am the Ocean

Yet at some point I forgot I am The Ocean I began to believe that I was only wave. If I don't do something about it I will hold that belief to the grave and what a grave situation that would be. I must find a way to be free from the delusion of my individuality For truly I am Universal This is a powerful reality to absorb I am not one of many I am all We are not two, you and I We are one with the Ocean and the Sky But it is a great comfort to think of myself as separate and feel limitation My true emancipation can only come when I embrace the truth of my being I have to lift my sight beyond seeing only what is in front of me and peer deeply inside Where there is no past, no present, no future for that is where Infinity resides It is the timeless Truth that I seek I peer under every rock I look around every corner gaze at the endless sky and ask the stars the ancient question: Who am I? So that I can reclaim my original identity As Ocean And wave goodbye to the wave Peace, Vivek Patel

2022 05 22

Today I honour my daughter as she turns 25 years old. She is a young woman who knows herself. She knows she is worthy, she knows she is loved, she knows she is a bright light. She sees the world through limitless eyes and I learn that from her daily. Being her parent has been the most powerful, transformative experience of my life. It has made me go deep into the core of who I was and change myself into who I needed to be. To be worthy of this awesome responsibility to guide this spirit into the world. To help her decipher the puzzle of life, to navigate the maze that is this plane of existence. To be a conscious parent means not letting a day go by where I don't work to learn and grow. From the time I was three years old I knew I wanted to be a father. I remember being over my dad's knee and he was spanking me for something. I had a kind of out-of-body experience where I was viewing the scene from above. I could see the indignity, the inhumanity of the moment. The phrase came to me ""One day I'm going to be a dad and I'm going to do it different". I knew I wanted to break a generations-old cycle and do things in a new way. That feeling never left me. 25 years ago when my kiddo arrived I felt like the central purpose of my life was revealed. I celebrate my childs appearance in the world because it's a better place for having her in it. Her excellent, cool, awesomeness continues to enrich my life beyond words. Today is their 25th birthday. I remember the moment she popped out (Thank you mom!). I looked her in the eyes and repeated over and over... I love you I love you I love you I love you for 30 seconds before the doctors shooed me away! I wanted that to be her first experience of this world and I have done my best to continue being a foundation of love for her in her life. I remember we looked into each other's souls. Deeper than language, deeper than ideas, maybe deeper than love itself? She spoke to me so clearly. Gave me a warning: "If you treat me like most parents treat their kids I'm going to hate you when I'm a teenager!" I heard this as clear as day, I'm not even kidding. I just said "Noted. Thank you." Thus began my conscious parenting journey. I recognized early on that friction and tension in our relationship was not my kid's fault. I have many old patterns that come from my past, my pain and trauma. Every time I would see myself react harshly or lack patience with my kiddo I knew I found another spot in myself to love and heal. I remember when she was just a couple years old someone asked me "What is the hardest part of your kid's development? I replied ""The hardest part of her development is MY" development! My wife and I decided our priority was "Relationship First. Therefore we would never punish or use consequences to modify her behaviour. She has never being in a timeout. We did our best to never hold authority over her. We have been equals from day one. We had no rules. The problem with rules is the enforcement. To enforce rules one needs to use power, and that's a relationship killer. We have guidelines and principles that we try to live by. When any of us were not in alignment with these guidelines, we would learn from it together. We never told her we were disappointed in her for "this choice" or that she was wrong for making "that choice". We did not operate from a Right Wrong mindset. Every choice had its effects and we learned from them together. This atmosphere of acceptance Acceptance of mistakes, of process, of the messy job of learning. She knew when she did something "wrong" she was not going to be in trouble, she was never in trouble. She knew I would not judge her, but embrace and accept her unconditionally. I celebrate her humanness I celebrate her vulnerability I celebrate her messy learning process Parenting is deep stuff. Growing up is deep stuff. Deep stuff is messy. When we try to avoid the mess, when we judge it rather than work with it, we can never get into the deep stuff. When people would ask my kid what it was like growing up with radical parents like us, she would say It's normal and nice. I loved that simple answer. Being treated with that kind of respect was just life. It wasn't until she started to see other families interact that she noticed something different. When her friends would come over they would often stand in the doorway in shock at first because of how we all treat each other. There was no authority, no expectations, no adult centerd control, and no fight for freedom. The moment they walked in we would celebrate! It's a strange land! Eventually they relaxed and join in. They would often open up about the struggles they faced at home with parents who criticised and controlled them. It didn't take long for them to know that we were a safe space to share their vulnerable feelings and experiences. --------

This young woman is so amazing. She inspires me daily. The natural way that she Knows Herself, Loves Herself And Honours Herself is an example that I myself try to follow.

She's comfortable in her own skin, she feels a sense of her personal power, and she knows that she is unconditionally worthy of Love and Acceptance. She understands the deep importance of play. Play is sustenance, it is life breath, it is essential to growth and discovery& and joy. She's a ninja, a comedian, a philosopher and powerful in every sense of the word. With this inner Foundation she does not need to steal energy from other people. She is exceptionally generous and at the same time she knows and honours her boundaries. She is strong, kind and funny. Being her father has been a great joy, a great challenge and a great adventure. It's also been a grand experiment. When she was young I was often told that parenting her without control or authority, without consequences or rules, without at least saying no to her, was going to backfire on me. She was going to grow up entitled, rude, unable to get along in the world, and never hold down a job. People were so upset at how we were doing things, that I lost friends and family, and even had one of my closest friends publicly call me disgusting for experimenting on my child rather than using the established parenting formula. I had to work hard to trust in this way of seeing things and doing things. If you're on this journey I'm sure you know what I mean. Of course I have made many mistakes, still do. The one thing I haven't done is give up on this path. The relationship I share with my kid is quite special. There is a profound trust and acceptance between us. Connection like this cannot be created in a hierarchical system of consequences, punishments, and rewards. It arises naturally in an atmosphere of freedom and respect. Our relationship is one of the primary motivations to Share the radical message of non-coercive collaborative parenting that I do. I want to help other parents experience the joy of this kind of connection. Today I am filled with gratitude for the opportunity of walking the path of life alongside this special being, a fountain of wisdom, my learning partner, my teacher, my best friend.

Stop Spanking Kids! Kids Need Guidance, Not Violence Spanking children is an act of violence. It does damage every time. It doesn't teach values. It only inspires fear-based obedience and perpetuates the cycle of violence. There is no difference between hitting and a 'swat', a 'pop', or a 'tap'. Spanking is always violence. It is never discipline. Discipline means to guide, not harm. Spanking teaches kids that they deserve violence, that it's ok for those who love them to hit them. This is an attitude they internalize and then are more accepting of mistreatment and abuse in their adult relationships. Not just romantic relationships, but also friendships, family and work relationships. Kids learn more from what we model than anything that we say. If we use violence to control them and alter their behaviour, even in the name of love, we are teaching them this is the way to behave in the world. In fact we end up building an association between love and violence. Spanking does not teach respect. That is something we hear all the time, but it just isn't so. One of my sayings is: "Respect comes from caring about other people, not from being afraid of what will happen if you don't." When we hit someone in order to teach, they do not learn WHY it makes sense to respect people. They don't learn to CARE about the impact of their actions on other people. They learn to be afraid of the violence or they learn to tune it out. They may stop the behaviour because they are spanked, but not because they learned to have more love, empathy, compassion, or responsibility. It is impossible to teach a child love and compassion by hitting them. The simple truth is, you cannot force someone to care. Spanking is a damaging model of relationships and communication to set for our children. When parents hit their kids for "misbehaving" they model the opposite of kindness and respect, then our kids follow in our footsteps. We teach them that violence is an acceptable problem solving method. We teach them that it's appropriate to use violence to control those who are weaker and more vulnerable (that's bullying). The lesson is, when people aren't behaving how we want them to, we should use our power to bend to our will. They learn to use fear and pain to control those we love. Now a word to the objection that "Kids have to learn that there are consequences in life". I first want to acknowledge that this is actually a valid concern. We want our kids to be prepared to face the challenges of life. However most of the time when people say this the only approach they have is to give kids consequences to toughen them up. This is not the most effective way to teach kids to deal with the systems of rewards and punishments that they will face in many different ways of life. Giving kids consequences to teach them how to deal with consequences is like punching somebody in the face hoping they'll learn to block the punch. I taught martial arts and self-defence for 30 years and I can tell you that's not a very effective approach! We are better off helping our kids understand the systems, and give them the tools to navigate them. Discernment, self-confidence, empathy, awareness of psychology and how the mind works, a positive relationship with their emotions and body, communication and collaboration skills, the ability to make well considered decisions. If you take a little time to think about it you could probably add 20 more things to that list. You have great wisdom in you. Every time you use a consequence or spank it is a waste of your own wisdom. It's also untrue that the primary reason we do good things is to avoid the consequences. Most folks would not suddenly start hitting people, stealing and being terrible to others if there were no consequences. The lesson we want to teach our kids is not that they should only avoid doing bad things if there's a consequence attached to it. That they should only do good things if there's a reward? This is conditional morality, conditional values. They are only on the surface. Or do you want to teach them that they should do good simply because it's the right thing to do? To treat people with respect because it aligns with their values? To have love and compassion because that's the kind of person they want to be? When kids feel safe with us, we can explore the self-reflective questions with them. What kind of person do you want to be? What kind of relationships do you want to have? What kind of impact do you want to have on others? What kind of world do you want to contribute to creating? It's much more effective to guide kids to be self-reflective and self-aware, to operate from deep values and principles. We explore these values together as learning partners. Forcing kids into a behaviour pattern is not teaching them from the inside out, it is only on the surface. Another common objection we hear is "They'll end up in prison if they don't learn about consequences". In response I will add that I have been doing self-empowerment workshops with my brilliant mother in prisons for a decade. It's her workshop and I assist. We have worked with hundreds of men over the years, and not a single one of them has changed their choices and behaviour from a fear of the consequences. This is why the vast majority of them end up back in prison over and over again. They only change when they feel a deep sense of love and respect for themselves. If you are a parent who is presently spanking and punishing your kids, please know this is not an attack on you. I say this with the utmost compassion, it is never too late to change. It's never too late to heal from being hit and punished yourself and change your way of looking at the world. The path of peace is always available to you. We absolutely can teach our children compassion through compassion. We cannot teach compassion through violence. I hope this makes sense to you and you will open your heart and mind enough to take it in. There is no power stronger than love. There is no teacher greater than kindness. There is no motivator stronger than empathy and compassion. Why don't we all work together to end the generational cycles of violence and put our efforts towards creating a world of peace and harmony? Something that we desperately need. Peace, Vivek

https://youtu.be/IFpaOLT2tZo When my kid was growing up we had no rules in our house. Radical, I know! The problem with rules is the enforcement! How do you enforce a rule? The only way to do so is with power and violence. Check out my YouTube channel @meaningfulideas for the video I made called: "Enforcement Suuuuuucks!" There is significant damage done to the relationship between parent and child every time the parent needs to enforce a rule. Even for the people who say their only rule is "to be kind", how do you enforce that? Can you really enforce kindness? Isn't kindness an attitude, a value? Isn't it a relationship, a mindset? Like I always say, "You cannot force someone to care." That's why I love the idea of guidelines, because guidelines are collaborative and rooted in relationship. They are not created from the top down, but rather collaboratively in discussion with each other. We recognize that the process is as important as the product. In fact, when we have a solid process, we are more likely to have a solid product. There is no imposed consequence for not adhering to a guideline because our process is rooted in relationship. We don't want to make anyone in the community feel wrong when a guideline doesn't work for them or when they have trouble engaging with it. Rather we want everyone to feel supported. Instead of Wrongness, we go back to the process. We all gather and support each other, we think it through, we look at the needs, feelings and preferences of each person. Then we rework the situation and try again. Rules are static, rigid and based in hierarchical power. Guidelines are an evolving community process. Caring deeply about each member of the family/community. Instead of disconnection and a break in trust, this process fosters a deeper connection. It creates more effective, stable, sustainable, and resilient, relational and communication patterns. I encourage you to re-examine any rules you have in your house and see how you can transform them into guidelines. Consensual, Collaborative Guidelines. Think about why you have the rules and share those reasons with your kids. Bring them into the process. Make it clear you are also bringing their needs deeply into it. You might even acknowledge that you hadn't considered their needs as much as you would like to in the past, and this is something you are trying to change. Then you can all do some creative brainstorming and try different approaches. There is great potential to create a sense of belonging, teamwork and being on the same side. Resistance decreases when kids feel that their perspectives matter. Transforming rules into guidelines, (as well as the related mindsets), will transform your relationship, and the whole dynamic in your family.

Raising Kids Is Like Growing Watermelons Have you ever seen one of those cubed shaped watermelons? The way they make them is to grow the fruit in a cube shaped container. As it grows it is confined to the limitations of its surroundings. After the fruit has grown and taken the shape of the container, they open it and the fruit maintains that form. Raising Kids Is Like Growing Watermelons When I first learned about this it struck me how similar this process is to parenting. Regardless of our best intentions we shape our kids according to our personality. Both our joys and our pains get passed along to them. These are the walls of the container that we surround them with as they are in their formative years. Every word we say, every time we interact with them and even every thought we think has an effect upon them. It affects how they think of themselves, what they learn about relationships, what they understand about communication, intimacy, authenticity, their own capacity and more. We are the Primary Source of Their Self-Image We are, of course, not their only influence. Our kids are exposed to many influences and environmental factors throughout their lives. We are, however, their first and primary container. They quickly learn to take the shape of our expectations, fears, and judgements. This is why it is so important for us to operate from a learning mindset. It takes effort to become more and more self-aware. Effort that is necessary if we want to consciously choose the kind of shape that we surround our kids with as they grow. It is not possible for Us to avoid influencing and shaping our children with our personalities. Mutual influence is a natural part of living in community with each other, and having a deep relationship with another human. Therefore, it makes sense to have that influence be as conscious as possible. In alignment with our values, our principles, and priorities. It makes sense to put effort into minimizing imposing a shape on our kids. Rather, let our influence be one of self-discovery and freedom. Reclaiming our Original Shape I have also heard that if the cube shaped watermelon is freed from the container while still attached to the vine it will eventually reclaim its original shape. This is important to know because we ourselves continue to carry the shape of our own past. When the patterns of our past remain unexamined, the generational cycle continues. Yet this is also where a great opportunity lies. We can be their Vine, we can release the container. This is something we do continuously over the years, not a one-time thing. It is a process, a lifelong process. My kid is 25 and I am still deep in that process. I grew up with a particular environment and it shaped who I am. The expectations, judgments and fears of my parents translated into a whole host of patterns. I had to form Survival Strategies to manage the coercive, oppressive and violent system I was facing every day at home. It was not a safe and collaborative experience growing up. That led to a pretty strong shape. I knew early on that without conscious attention I would pass that shape along to my kids, because that's all I knew. We Carry The Shape Of Our Childhood For Many Years In many ways we live our whole lives with that container surrounding us. It can feel like we will never break free to reclaim our original shape. It is not hopeless however. We can shift patterns and we can find our way back to ourselves. Recognizing the pain and fear based patterns we hold in our mental, emotional and physical systems and working with them to heal and bring them into more alignment with who we want to be. This is powerful work to engage in. Inside each of us is core of love, compassion, empathy and understanding. That same essence is in your child. Part of the watermelon is seeing that essence, even when their behaviour seems to be indicating otherwise! As we practice this, we help them grow into their own shape and we can reclaim more and more of our own original shape. The more we reclaim our inner Truth, the more we are able to pass that along to our kids. This is how we shift to a positive cycle. This is how we create Generational Family Evolution. Be conscious about the shape you hold for your kids. Conscious shaping is a two-fold process. The first being the self-development work that we do. To clean out the wounds of our past. To notice our patterns, our imposed values, opinions, biases etc. To ask ourselves, what the kind of person do we want to be? How do I want to impact my relationships? How can I work consciously with my thoughts and feelings. The second is paying deep attention to how we interact with our children. Early Regrets or "The Watermelon Within When I think back to the early years of my daughters life I feel many regrets about things I did, choices I made and glaring omissions in my understanding. For all of my good intentions I know I caused her a lot of damage. Recently I have seen a few videos of us interacting from when she was young and I cringe every time! Of course it's 20 years later and my capacity has grown a lot, but still... Ouch! At the same time I can recognize that I did this because of my own cube shaped watermelon within. Breaking The Mold Over the years I have worked very hard at breaking the mold and allowing more of my original shape to emerge. It is something that I continue to work at daily. I do so for myself. It benefits me in the day to day quality of my life, it allows me to have deeper and more connected relationships. Of course it also benefits my kid. The more I am liberated from my imposed shape and reclaim my own shape, the less I'm inclined to force a shape on my kid. As you go through your day with your kids, try and notice the container of your expectations, judgments, and fears. Every time you become aware of imposing a shape on your kid, take a pause and re-evaluate. See if you can point your kid to their own authentic shape rather than imposing one of your design upon them. One of the greatest gifts we can offer to our children is a deeply authentic relationship to themselves. We do not want them growing up as cube shaped watermelons! Be their vine, be their freedom.

2022 04 10

It is not the point of Conscious Parenting to try to achieve the same Hierarchical, Power and Control Dynamic as mainstream parenting, using Gentler Methods. Gentle parenting is a different paradigm, a different mindset. It cannot be easily understood from the old mindset. Looking from that vantage point, it is easy to think conscious parenting is permissive. It's not. (at least the system that I share is not). It's actually much more involved. Just because we aren't controlling our kids, doesn't mean we aren't guiding them. In taking away the Power Over and the Threat of Control, the guidance feels good and it feels trustable. Gentle Parenting respects the autonomy, consent, and human rights of a child. Gentle Parenting is based in relationship not in control. Gentle Parenting does not try and modify behavior. Rather we look at the iceberg of influences that lead to behavior. Feelings, needs, relationship, environment, mental health, physical health, sensory sensitivities, neurology etc. We guide by tuning into and working with these underlying causes. As soon as we allow ourselves to control our kids there is an automatic dehumanization that occurs. We are no longer two human beings walking the path together. We become an obstacle to navigate. To the mainstream mindset, the adversarial nature of the parent-child relationship is just normal. Even natural! That's why we hear things like "Pick Your Battles"! I was very aware when my kid was young that if I followed the normal path, I would also be in a battle with them throughout our lives. Instead I wanted a deep relationship with my kid. I wanted them to know I was their most trusted place. That safety is not something that can occur from the old mindset, because the threat of punishment, consequences or control of some kind is always there. When kids interact with me, (and I worked with hundreds of kids over the years in many different capacities) after a very short time they know in their nervous systems they are safe with me. They know there is no possibility of them getting punished, there is no possibility of them getting a consequence or even getting in trouble. They will only receive acceptance. They also know that I offer them deep respect. I see their inherent worth. Inherent meaning it is not affected by their behavior. We often hear people talk about consistency in parenting. They usually mean be consistent with your consequences, be consistent with your boundaries etc. These things only serve to push kids further away. When we are consistent in seeing their worth, when we are consistent in responding with Kindness instead of Wrongness, when our guidance feels good and trustable to them, we create the most stable and profound relationship possible. From this place of deep honoring, respect flows naturally from young people. Collaboration and Cooperation has always been possible. The relationship becomes important, they care about their impact on me. Like I always say, you cannot force someone to care. We can however nurture and inspire it. This is why I suggest being on a continuous journey of digging into the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset (NCCM). Every time you notice yourself being even slightly coercive, pause and ask yourself, "What mindset am I operating from?" Then see if you can shift to a more collaborative perspective, based in horizontal power sharing, rather than a top-down model. I call it the Micro Mindset Check. Very useful for those of us who are shifting from old paradigms. Letting go of the familiar, even if it's greatly limiting, can be very challenging. Deep change doesn't happen as easy as turning on a light switch, it is a lifelong process. Very often folks doing conscious parenting feel alone, because a lot of people in their environment don't follow the same ideology. That was certainly the case with me! So be kind and compassionate with yourself as you engage in this challenging work. You are courageous for shifting age old patterns. You are engaging in conscious generational family evolution. It's a glorious thing and it is something that requires blood, sweat and guts effort. I wish it weren't so, I really really wish it weren't so! That's why things like boundaries and limits seem so tempting. We can just say No more cookies, empathize with their feelings, and we don't have to do the blood and guts work. Finding solutions that honor each person, their Consent, Autonomy, and Humanity, and that are rooted in Collaboration, is a lot harder. Working WITH humans is a lot harder! What a wonderful model we are setting though! Being willing to go through that effort in service of our shared humanity. Our troubled world needs more of that. Thank you for walking alongside me on this path. I'd love for you to follow me on social media on Facebook Instagram, Twitter YouTube, all @meaningfulideas Peace, Vivek "x"

When one kid hits another, respond with Kindness not Wrongness When I see one kid hit another, I don't see a victim and an aggressor. I see two struggling, suffering kids that need the guidance of an emotionally centered, wise adult. In that moment of dysregulation, chaos and violence we have the most profound opportunity to guide them. When we respond with kindness instead of wrongness in those moments, it touches the heart in a way that nothing else can. There's an experiential guidance that happens that you can't get any other way. But Oh, it takes a lot of discipline and effort to do so. When we respond with anger, punishments, criticism or even ignoring, we are setting a model of the exact opposite of what want from them. Kids are quick to pick up on this contradiction. Wrongness also damages their self-image, their the relationship with themselves. When kids feel it is unsafe make mistakes and be vulnerable, it's not possible for them to self-reflect and learn with you. They put up a shield, run away, or laugh at us. They are protecting themselves from the wrongness.

It can be a real struggle to stay calm with our kids. We know we want to, but the stress of life catches up with us and we act out of alignment. If we are on the conscious parenting path we will take responsibility, repair and reconnect with our kids. Even so we would like to have to do this less! This is where learning some strategies to process our challenging emotions can be really helpful. Unprocessed emotions leave a residue in our system. In our bodies, brains and nervous systems. I want to share with you some concepts and processes that can help you work with your emotions right in the midst of the challenges of daily life. Doing some of this work on a regular basis can greatly reduce the likelihood of us yelling at, spanking, or threatening our kids. The less we repress the more choice we have in the moment. The more we're able to act in alignment with our values, principles, and priorities. In other words, we're able to choose curiosity over control and compassion over criticism so that our kids stay open with us and our relationship is preserved. The more we practice the more of these moments we have and that's what I want to support you with. This is why I am giving this FREE 2-hour Workshop as part of the No Spank Challenge event put on by the wonderful Amy Bryant and @[100064624992227:2048:Stop Spanking] The workshop is called: Processing Challenging Emotions with Vivek Patel April 29 at 6pm Eastern/3pm Pacific I will be going live right on the event page so please join the event to attend the workshop.
