Go FECK Yourself! Forgiveness, Empathy, Compassion, Kindness. I tell the parents that I work with all the time, Go FECK Yourself. Or sometimes I say FECK You! It's honestly one of the primary tools in Conscious Parenting because we have so much working against us so much of the time. We're trying to change age old patterns about how we treat children. Patterns in our family lines, our culture, and global history. An integral part of the process changing how we treat children, is learning to reframe how we treat ourselves. That Self-Compassion model is one of the primary things that we can offer our kids. Not the model of our perfection, but the model of our effort. FECK is an important element in how to recover from parenting mistakes. A solid FECK Yourself practice can help us find more equanimity, and therefore more choice in our parenting path. What is your relationship with Self-Forgiveness? Do you have any strategies you use to convince yourself that you're doing okay? I do a lot of mirror talk myself. I stand in front of the mirror, look into my eyes and tell myself "It's okay if you make mistakes Vivek. It's gonna happen because you're human. You're trying your best to live according to your values and that's what really counts." Then I sigh and I go on with my day. Maybe you can try something like that? I encourage you to FECK yourself daily. FECK yourself in every room of your house. You deserve it.

Make Room for Mistakes When working on collaborative solutions with your kids, make sure to leave room for mistakes. Recognize that learning is a process and that you are together in that process. I always tell the parents I work with to expect the first plan to fall apart. Knowing that's going to happen we're not surprised and we can flow with the moment. Consciously leaving room for a mistakes, even building an awareness of that into the process, leads to a better result. Even as we are making a plan, and a strategy, the kid agrees and says they're not going to pull the dog's tail anymore, they're not going to spill water, jump on the couch or throw near the TV. Or that they are going to brush their teeth, flush the toilet, to turn off the tap, do their homework, or whatever it is. As we're having the conversation, make room for mistakes. Say to the kid, "We have this whole plan in place and I'm really excited to work on it with you. But you might forget sometimes and that's ok. You might still forget to flush the toilet, because it's been a bit of a habit. We just started talking about this. You don't have to worry." So the kid knows leaving the conversation, even if they go straight to the washroom and forget to flush, or if they go play with the dog, lose control and pull the tail. They know that they're not going to get in trouble for it. They don't have to hide from us. When they do forget, because we are prepared, we do not react with frustration or complaint. Instead we respond with understanding and support. "It's natural, I'm here to help, it takes time to learn new things and develop new patterns. We're in it together." Make room for mistakes and the learning process. Make it explicit through your words, your actions, and the systems you create in your home, that your kids cannot get in trouble. Not only won't get in trouble, they CANNOT get into trouble. When kids feel this from us we become very trustable. They are not afraid to share their messy learning process with us which allows us to guide them. If they have to protect against us, they put up a shield and we cannot reach them. Please listen to this 2 minute video and let me know your thoughts.

The following article and video are slightly different, but related. Please read/watch and let me know what you think x"xd When I say don't control your kids I am not saying don't guide your kids. I'm saying create a relationship such that there is so much safety that they trust your guidance. Then they will be more willing to collaborate. Non-Coercive doesn't mean Not Guiding I call the parenting style I practice and teach Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. The Non-Coercive is what we don't do. We don't punish, control, criticise and shame. The Collaborative is what we do do! Empathize, connect, respect, guide and learn. I call it the Don't Do and the Doo Doo! When we treat them in ways that make them trust our guidance less, they resist us more. When this happens we are often at a loss for what to do and end up resorting to coercion. This makes them resent us more. The cycle keeps amplifying. When we damage trust, kids are less enthusiastic about collaborating with us because collaboration, real collaboration, requires a feeling of safety, especially with vulnerable children. When making decisions together, everyone involved has to feel that their needs are going to be tended to. We may not get all of our needs met, but if we feel that they are taken seriously, and real effort is made towards each person, we are much more likely to be engaged in the process. If a kid doesn't feel confident in this, it's likely they're going to resist or disengage. Neither of those options is desirable. What we want is enthusiastic, connected engagement! When I interact with kids I treat them as whole human beings. I respect them and I honour their autonomy. With this as our starting point we have always been able to collaborate with each other. Regardless of how rough and defiant their exterior is. It's hard, but it's possible. It takes time to develop the capacity to manage our emotions and hold space for our kids' process! It's something we will be working on throughout our lives. I can attest to this as a parent of a young adult who's almost 25 and I still feel like I'm on my learning edge every day. Working at adopting a new mindset. When we radically trust our kids, they radically trust us back. This is what I want to focus on. It's the Iceberg Consciousness, perceiving beneath the surface. When we do that, we have so much more influence WITH our kids because it's not influence OVER our kids. It takes patience because it takes time to set new patterns. That's why it's hard. That's why it's not always immediate results. A lot of the time switching from a more controlling parenting style, to a more collaborative style comes with a transition period. There's a time of chaos first. I call it the "Test, Treat and Tornado" Phase. Test When kids experience more freedom from us, first of all they're going to test us to see if it's real, or are we going to revert back to our old ways as soon as it's challenging? This dynamian last for a while because, of course, we do slip back sometimes, we're human and learning too. Then we repair and keep building the relationship. Treat When kids have more freedom and agency in their lives, there is an excitement and joy that comes with it. This is the treat. They want to revel in the treat of it after being previously denied. They are stretching new freedom muscles. Absolutely reasonable, of course. Tornado Then what we have is the Tornado. This takes some patience. Meditate! Breathe! Under the old structure kids don't feel free to express themselves. When we start to change our mindset and hold more space for their feelings, a lot of the repressed emotion comes to the surface. It may be more than we expect. It might be more than they themselves expect. This is where we become the calm in their storm. Recognizing these are natural parts of the process we can support our kids through them rather than fight them. It's like my saying: "Guide your kids like the banks of a river, guiding the flow. Not like a dam blocking the flow." This is an ongoing process. The Tornado sometimes reappears. As we develop our capacity to hold space for our kids, they feel more confident to be vulnerable with us. As this confidence grows they relax into our relationship. They also develop a deeper trust in our guidance. They feel we're supporting them in learning together about their emotions. We're no longer complaining and disciplining them for expressing themselves. It's very much like the martial arts. When someone attacks, you don't want to meet force on force. Instead you want to guide the force and use it to your advantage. It's related to the point above to guide your kids like the banks of a river. The banks of the river aren't separate from the river. That's what's beautiful about it. It's not like we're a completely separate being, we're connected. Kids crave this deeper connection. It feels safe and trustable to them. Their inner voice says "Oh, my parent is a wise guide. I can trust them to care for me. I trust their intention is to make my life better." This sense of being a trustable guide has been one of my top priorities throughout my parenting journey. You know, my kid is going to be 25 yrs old soon and they still trust my guidance and we still have that deep learning relationship. It's a beautiful thing. It's taken decades of consistent hard work. Making tons of mistakes, growing and operating from a learning mindset. Working to align my principles, priorities, values and actions into an integrated whole. This is what it is to be in a conscious, non-coercive, collaborative relationship with somebody. Over the long term we create stable and resilient relationship and communication patterns, based on deep trust and connection. This is something no amount of punishments, consequences, limits, boundaries and rewards can ever produce. It's hard, but it is possible and I want it for you. Every time you resist the urge to force, every time you resist the urge to control you add another layer to your capacity and you build another layer of trust with your kid. This is the daily work, take that extra breath, go scream into your pillow or break out into spontaneous interpretive dance. Call a friend, do some yoga, write in your journal, pray, meditate, talk to your ancestors. However you do it, be in a conscious process with your body/mind/emotions. Do whatever you can and whatever works for you, but do it! This way we can pause and ask, "Can I make a different choice here? How can I preserve the relationship?" It's important to note this doesn't mean you completely ignore your own needs either. It does mean that how we chose to work with our kids doesn't feel like a punishment. I say it doesn't FEEL like a punishment because our intent is secondary to their experience. When we set traditional boundaries, it feels punitive to the kid. It has to because the boundaries are held in place with a hierarchical power relationship. It doesn't feel collaborative, the kids don't feel included. We want the kids to feel authentically part of the process. That's how we inspire cooperation. Another thing that happens when we are transitioning from coercion to collaboration, is it can bring up the worry that we're not preparing them for the real world. It's an important part of parenting to empower our kids to manage the many challenges they will face in life. It's reasonable to want to equip them with the strongest foundation and most effective tools we can. We want them to not only survive, but thrive in this very challenging world. The question is, what is that foundation and what are those tools? These are the questions I gave a lot of thought to in the early days of my parenting. I realised I could empower my child the most by working on and nourishing things like them having a strong sense of themselves and their own values. Knowing their own boundaries and caring about other people's boundaries. The capacity to say yes and no when it's real for them, and not from any kind of pressure. To know how to communicate effectively with people and not just "don't talk rudely". Communication is deep listening. Listening to not only the content, but also the needs and feelings present. How to collaborate and work with others in a team. To have a solid learning mindset so they can learn whatever they need. The list goes on and on when we think about it deeply. None of these things can be imposed with rules, consequences and structure. These are things that can be inspired through relationship, modelling and co-exploration. This kind of ongoing, whole-being, co-learning relationship cannot be achieved in the mainstream hierarchical power structure. Kids have to protect themselves because it's not safe to be vulnerable. Real learning is done through the mistakes, not by avoiding them. This is why I feel deeply that Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting is the most effective way for us to guide our kids, and to give them the strongest foundation to go out into the world. It also nourishes a relationship that is alive, responsive, resilient, deeply connected and trusting. So I really want to encourage you to pause every time you're tempted to control your kid, even if it seems reasonable, ESPECIALLY if it seems reasonable! Just pause for a moment and ask: Can I make a different choice? How can I preserve the relationship? Will this make them trust my guidance more or less? Because that moment of reflection will always increase trust, because if they feel our guidance is safe and nourishing, they will be less inclined to resist us and even enthusiastic about receiving our input. I hope this is helpful for you. Please share this around and follow me on all the spaces @Meaningful Ideas. Peace out, Vivek

When I impose my priorities and values on my kid, I'm programming a computer, rather than having a deep relationship with a human being. Edit to add There seems to be some confusion between the idea of imparting and imposing. They are different experiences, different relationships, different methodologies and strategies. In order to impart without imposing, we honor our children's freedom to think differently than us. We can share ideas with them, we can think through issues with them, we can share our own values with them, but when we insist our values are more valid than theirs, we are forcing. We are imposing. That is the specific difference. I hope that makes this more clear. Personally I think sharing our values and exploring ethics and morals is a big part of parenting. It's a big part of any deep relationship. I do that with my partner, I do that with my close friends, I do that in my close communities. As soon as we think our values and perspectives are right and our kids are wrong if they're different, then we are inclined to use coercion and manipulation to force them into thinking like we do. That is the point. Like I said to my friend Chris, I recognize that we are always demonstrating our values by how we live our lives and how we relate to our kids. Modelling is a powerful influence in our relationship. Therefore I want to have great integrity when I engage with that power. I'm very careful not to have a preference that they DO follow my model. I want them to feel the same acceptance and celebration from me even if they choose the opposite. It is this Freedom for them to think for themselves and choose for themselves that prevents me from being that authoritative computer programmer! And rather a co-explorer of life.

I am full of rage. I am angry at the violence committed towards black people. I'm angry about the violence committed towards BIPOC. I'm angry about the violence committed towards women. I'm angry at the violence committed towards the LGBTQ+ community. I'm angry at the violence committed towards disabled people. I am full of rage. I posted this a year ago and am resharing with some updates including my protest dance video! This is as relevant today as it was a year ago, as it was 30 years ago. Content Warning - I speak very plainly about social justice and oppression issues in this post. Some of it might be triggering for people. My anger isn't new. I have been angry for 30 years every day without a break. It was 1990 when I became a social justice activist. I have seen racism, sexism, ableism, and homophobia flourish all throughout the decades. I believe there is more general awareness of it now than there was back then, but I don't think there is less of it. It is in every part of society, in every system we engage with, in every age group, except the youngest children. Unfortunately it doesn't take long for kids to adopt some prejudice as well because it is taught to them pretty early. I was beaten on a regular basis for being one of the only Indian kids in the school when I was in grade 7,8,9. I just assumed wh1t3 people were worth more and I was an outsider, not fully human. These kids were programmed with this attitude. Programmed by their parents, programmed by their families, programmed by every bit of media they consumed. It wasn't subtle back then and it's not subtle now. I see it in the nicest and kindest of people. Oblivious to their prejudice because it is the very air they breathe. I see it more brazen and bold today than I have in a long time. The previous 'president' of the United States had a lot to do with making it cool to be cruel. He emboldened the hateful mindset that we see in our world. He did not create it, but he certainly brought it into the forefront. The day after the 2016 US election I was on the street doing a dance protest with my powerful activist friend @Kathleen of @reason the cascade of events that have happened since we're not subtle to us. (Video posted below) Myself and all my activist friends could see it clearly. The constant stream of hatred, fear and prejudice that came from his mouth amplified that mindset in millions of people. The day after that a friend of mine posted that they were in a parking lot somewhere in the states and a stranger came up to them out of the blue and grabbed their crotch yelling "I can grab them by the pussy all I want now." And I cannot even tell you the number of friends of colour that have been told over the last 5 years to go back to their country. Never mind the harassment and violence that they have faced. Years ago I shared a video of this guy taunting some black people and calling them all sorts of horrific names. So many of my friends were trying to assure me that this was a rare case and people weren't really like this, that it was an exception. I assured them right back that they were living in a fantasy world if they thought that was true. Black people risk their lives every time they leaves the house. (All BIPOC of course, but I acknowledge the specifiontext of Black folks) If they perchance get stopped for making a wrong turn, getting a speeding ticket or nothing at all, it could be the last thing they ever do. This is simply not the case for wh1t3 people. I recently read that in 1970, only 2 years after I was born, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld the plan to close a local public park in Macon, Georgia rather than to integrate it. This is not ancient history. It is naive to imagine this mindset is not alive and well today. Not only in the states, but here in my beloved Canada as well. I know it might be difficult to read these words if you are used to me writing about peace and love all the time. If you have been following my comments around Facebook lately, they might seem more aggressive than you're used to. I am sorry if this is disturbing to you. This aggression is part of me. My rage against injustice is part of my peace and love, not separate from it. It comes from a lifetime of experiencing and fighting against the violence of the dominant power structures. I know that calling out racism, prejudice and hatred directly can be triggering for those of us that are in demographics that hold power and privilege. It can make us defensive and feel a lot of discomfort. I've been saying this for 30 years, unless we willing to sit in that discomfort and not run from it, to face our power and privilege and not shy away from the impact it has on marginalized communities, we will never be effective agents of change. All the love and good wishes in the world, all the good intentions are wasted if we ignore the violence, the prejudice and hatred, that go along with systemic power and privilege. It's no longer enough to just say I'm a good person and I'm not racist. The folks who are suddenly full of passion to fight for their freedom, I wonder if I went to their pages and went back in the history if I would find a whole lot of support for black lives matter protests? For indigenous rights and environment protests? For LGBTQ+ rights, disabled rights? Because if oppression only matters to you when it inconveniences you personally, you are not actually fighting for freedom. So please don't pretend you're fighting for the freedom of anybody but yourself. I know this post is likely to make me lose some followers. I'm okay with that and I wish you well. There's no point in me hiding who I am. I cannot fight for children's rights and ignore all the rest. This is what intersectionality is all about. I do think protesting against oppression is a vital part of how we progress as a society. However in order to do so with integrity and consistency we need to trace ourselves and our own prejudice in the process. We need to stand up for vulnerable and marginalized demographics, especially when their issues don't affect us directly. This is what being an activist and an ally is about. If you are doing this work, welcome! I'm happy to fight alongside you. It will take effort and courage to do so. I believe in you.

There's a lot of talk in mainstream parenting about preparing children for the "real world. What is often meant by that is that children must not appear weak, vulnerable, or sensitive. Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting is Anti-Oppression Activism Mainstream parenting principles are based on oppressive power structures. We have inherited systems that are Coercive, Violent, Unequal and Unjust. These systems are being questioned more and more these days, but it seems less so when it comes to children. The oppression of young people is so normalized that people will fight to defend it. As Conscious Parents we reject the mindset that has been handed down to us from the very systems created by oppressors. It's time to liberate ourselves and our Children! Instead let's create Systems and Structures that are Empowering, Collaborative, Safe, Equitable and based on Just Values and Principles. Marginalized demographics have been denied their autonomy by those in power for millennia. Refusing to use our systemic parental power to do the same to our kids is a radical re-writing of the past. We are changing ancient patterns of re-writing the future history of our children. When they look back in a few decades theyll recall how deeply they were respected. They won't recall every little mistake, they will remember the years of effort to treat them as a human being. I told my kiddo when they were as young as 2 yrs that I didn't ever want them to obey me or do what I say. I wanted them to Know themselves, Honour themselves and Love themselves. Systems of power do not want us to be fully ourselves. It is essential to break our spirits and damage our sense of self. We are compared, contrasted and judged. We are dehumanized to the point that we forget our own brilliance. There is a deep essence we all have. The light that we see in a newborn. I call it the Unchanging self. Mainstream parenting does not nourish the preservation of this essential self. In fact breaking the childs connection to their deep selves is at the core of the control through power mindset. This is why empowering our children is an act of resistance. Clear Self-Knowledge and Deep Self-Relationship make one very hard to control. When you interact with your kids ask yourself: Am I empowering or oppressing? Am I supporting their self-knowledge? Am I respecting their autonomy? Am I controlling or collaborating? Shifting those old habits is hard. HARD. I honour the effort of every parent who is fighting daily to break the cycles of the past and create new patterns. You are liberating your children and changing the world at the same time.

Non-Coercive Parenting Principle Just because you identify a problem does not mean coercion is the solution. Coercion is NOT the Solution. For example: Problem: My kid is watching too much screen time. The answer is not coercion. You don't have to enforce a limit. You don't have to take the tablet from their hands. You don't have to give them a consequence if they overstep the agreed boundary. There is always a Non-Coercive, Collaborative solution. Problem: Kid wants 2nd bowl of ice cream before dinner The answer is not coercion. You don't have to say no. Because that NO can only be enforced with hierarchical power. There is another way. A relational, play based, connected, exploratory, long term approach has a much more profound effect. Problem: My kid won't brush their teeth. Even though dental hygiene is important, holding them down and forcing the brush into their mouth is not the solution. I know that we can become desperate at times. Especially when the dentist puts fear in us the way few other professionals can! This is when we must separate the issue from the strategy. This is the main point here. Yes we want to help our kids with their teeth. NO we don't have to violate their consent and autonomy to do so. We don't have to damage the connection and trust in our relationship to do so. Instead of force, yelling, consequences, if/then ultimatums - there are other ways. We can start by trying to ease the previously acquired unpleasant and even fear based associations to teeth brushing time. Then foster a positive association with teeth. We can also inspire them to love and care for their bodies so they'll make self-motivated choices. I've dedicated a whole podcast to helping kids brush their teeth in a connected way. You can find the link below. This is why I always try and remember that when I identify a problem, it does not mean coercion is the solution. Coercion is NOT the solution.

Having said all that I know it's not easy to put into practice. Really I know. I support many parents on a weekly basis and we work HARD to put this mindset into practice.

It's blood and sweat work. Inward and Outward. It pushes us to our limit. I hear you when you share your pain and struggle. I hear you when you feel helpless and hopeless. Parenting in general presents so many challenges, and then when we do it from this radical paradigm, it adds an extra dimension to the struggle.

As you watch/listen/read the resources, make some notes as you go along, jot down whatever stands out to you. Pick one thing every day that you can try practicing and see if it has any kind of impact on your experience.

You can even keep a journal of your process, your insights as you go. Maybe you prefer to express that through art, poetry, movement or song? I like to write and speak so that's why I make so many videos and write so many articles. It's largely me doing my own processing and then sharing it with you! I encourage you to daily dig deeper into the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset (NCCM). Look for the subtle coercions we allow ourselves with our kids. Sometimes they're just so damn convenient. I mean really and honestly. There is a hidden cost to letting these go unaddressed. Connection, trust, influence. That's why my one-liner says "Coercive Influence Decreases Over Time, Relational Influence Increases Over Time" Once we see the cost clearly, it's worth the inconvenience. That is why we dig deeper daily (I used a different order that time. Which sounds better?) Speaking of digging, do dig into all the resources above. Absorbing material about the mindset and practice can help so much. Don't give up my friends, the road is hard, but you are not alone. We are here on the path together. You have great power, wisdom and love inside of you. You also have pain, fear and trauma. This is the human condition. This is why we can have great compassion for ourselves, each other and our children.

Whenever I have a chance to interact with kids I focus on empowering them. I inspire them to feel validated and celebrated. What we reflect to our children informs them about the world. It informs them about relationships, values, power and compassion. This is why I say we are Sacred-Mirrors for our children. A while back I facilitated this anti-racism workshop for kids and it was really profound. The kids are so wise, I learned a lot from them. I also took the opportunity to share some empowering messages with these amazing young people. Whatever the context, whether it's anti-racism, martial arts, dance, conflict resolution, anti-bullying, leadership, math, science or music (I've taught a lot of kids!) whatever it is, the message is the same. "You are powerful You are free You deserve respect. Anyone (adults) who thinks they are more valid than you and that you're less worthy? They are wrong. It's a lie they tell you so they can control you. You are powerful beyond measure. Powerful beyond measure means the power to be oneself. There is a lot of pressure to be what other people think you should be. I want you to know that who you are as a person, the real you, is amazing." One of the kids in the workshop was telling us that there's been a long history of racism in the US. They said it's amazing how things that happened a long time ago are still having an effect today. I thanked them for their wisdom and said to the group, everything we do has long lasting ripples. As individuals the decisions we make have ripples. Even now in this very moment it's happening. Every one of you is a ripple maker, and you have the choice what kind of ripples you want to make. It makes sense then to decide what kind of ripples do YOU want to make? in thinking about this we can ask, what kind of person do I want to be? What kind of relationships do I want? What kind of world do I want to contribute to? What are my values? What do I care about? What am I passionate about? What am I interested in? How do I think people should treat each other? I call these the self-reflective questions. Exploring these questions helps us clarify our own values and priorities. This is one of the seeds of self-knowledge. Then we work towards creating ripples in the world that align with those values. This approach is powerful because it allows us to examine values with kids without imposing our own on them. I'm not telling them what the answer should be. It's important to ask the question in an open way so there isn't a feeling that if they give the wrong answer they will not be accepted. These questions are always with me in my daily life. As the answers evolve and deepen, the way I live changes. My choices change, my relationships change, my inspiration changes, I feel more a sense of myself. My Self! One of the most important ripples is how we treat ourselves. Are we kind to ourselves when we make mistakes? Do we recognize that we are on a learning Journey? Can we give compassion to ourselves when we make mistakes? This self-compassion is an important thing for both parents and kids. We are all on this learning Journey together. When we have compassion for ourselves we model such an important skill for them. I told the kids one of my favorite lines is "I didn't teach my kid what to think. I taught them how to think." One of the kids responded saying it was odd to hear an adult encouraging us to think for ourselves. It's not what they were used to. Every single time I give a kid that message, they respond. They want to open up. They want to be vulnerable. They want to be trusting, helpful, and caring. They want to be valued and involved. It all comes from that radical, mindset of deeply accepting, respecting and connecting. It helps to avoid complaining or criticizing. When we choose non-coercive and collaborative methods we find it easier to flow with them and feel with them. This makes it easier for them to hear us as well. It's like my other one liner (I have a lot of one-liners) "The more willing we are to visit our children's universe, the more willing they will be to visit ours." The next time you are in front of a child think of it as an opportunity to empower them. Take a moment to breathe and then think of something connecting, accepting, loving, empathetic and understanding to say. We are Sacred Mirrors for our children. Let them know you see them and you believe in them. How we see them has a significant effect on how they see themselves.

What do you know that no one else quite knows? . What perspective do you have because of your unique experience, that no one else has? . What do you understand about life in a deep way? Even if nobody else knows about it. . Identify these things as clearly as you can and then share them with your kids. This is one of the greatest gifts you can offer them, the wisdom that is uniquely yours. . Every one of us has something like this in us. Throughout all of the billions of years of the universe's existence, spanning from the very beginning to its end, there will never be a consciousness exactly like yours. You are unique in all of time and space. . This is why I say that parenting asks us to touch the very deepest part of ourselves. . I see Life in a very particular way. My perspective has come from my life experience, combined with my temperament, combined with my genetics, (combined with my karma, if you believe that kind of thing). . My understanding of Life, Relationships, Communication, Parenting, Trust, Learning, Joy etc. is very specific. It has its own style and perspective. I wanted share that uniqueness with my kid. . I encourage you to turn inwards and value your own uniqueness. The particular journey of your life has created something special in you. The pain and loss as well as the joy and successes, they all combine to create the particular spark that is you. . That is where your unique wisdom lies and is one of the greatest gifts you can offer to your child. . It's not that they will become exactly like you, it's that your uniqueness will add to their own (sounds like the Borg!) . If you'd like to hear how all of this plays out over a decades, join me and my daughter this Saturday October 9th at 2:00 p.m. Eastern on my @[100063717370269:2048:Meaningful Ideas] Facebook page. We are going to have a father-daughter discussion about what it was like to grow up in this radical fashion. . Please join us on Saturday for what will definitely be a very interesting discussion.

No! Kids do not have to learn respect! This is one of the most common things I have heard in my 25 years practicing Non-coercive Collaborative Parenting. It is spoken as if it is Law, "Kids have to learn respect." They HAVE to! No They don't Fuck you! There is such a deep disrespect embedded in this statement that it's impossible to actually teach respect through that lens. "Have To" implies a lack of choice. This is something that has been chosen for them. This isn't, and can never be respect. They don't Have To. However we can inspire the feelings of respect in our relationship and model how we demonstrate it. Kindness, collaboration, connection, communication, empathy and play. Caring about our impact on each other. If we want to pass on values of respect to our children we need to let go of thinking they have to learn. Instead let's embrace nurturing a relationship of respect. Peace, d Vivek

Celebrate Every Success Appreciate the good moments. . Appreciate moments where there's a success, moments where there's a connection, when there's collaboration. . We can get caught up into the challenges of life, because there are no shortages of challenges in life to navigate. . Add to that our own inner stuff, our kid's stuff, and then there's the practical stuff... There's a lot of Stuff. . As you know, I do not recommend repressing our feelings. It's important for us to feel them and not to run from them. To have an effective working relationship with our painful emotions. . I also think it's worthwhile to tune into when we have moments that are joyous, connected, and easeful. Interactions that are beautiful, playful, and where our kids do something that's connected and playful and we feel the flow. . Celebrating big moments of success is wonderful. It can really give us hope for carrying on. . Let's take that from the macro to the micro as well and notice little moments of connection. . Like if I'm texting my kid. And we just have like a particularly easy banter, I will jump up and down with joy. Not because there's a shortage of of good moments necessarily, but because I like to celebrate those things! . When we celebrate, it amplifies it, it makes us notice it more, it helps us tune into it catch those moments and opportunities. And it feels good too! . It can be something as simple as, you were getting a glass of water, and instead of just handing it to your kid, you handed it a little bit playfully and they got a smile on their face. . Celelbrate! . Let's make the effort to really notice those small moments and acknowledge them. . "I was playful for a second there and my kid had a smile that they wouldn't have had, if I hadn't been playful." . Acknowledge that. Feel it in your body, remember how it felt. Allow yourself to feel good about it. Thank yourself for it. Really have that little moment to celebrate it. . It can be a really powerful when we practice doing that. It helps us recognize that a lot of good moments are happening that we might have missed. . If we yell once twice in the day, but we have 10 moments that are connected and kind, we can easily focus on the yell and we can forget those moments of beauty. . I'm not saying we don't have to work on the yelling. I'm not saying to push difficult feelings away. . I am saying let's also look at moments that go well. Once we start looking at them and looking for them, we can also start creating and cultivating more of them. This can really help us in our journey.

2021 10 03

Fostering a deep and safe relationship to our inner child is as important as creating a connected, safe relationship to our (physical) children. . It's not something many of us think about on a daily basis, and yet that inner relationship affects us in every moment. The quality of that relationship certainly affects how we treat our kids. It's an inside out kind of thing. . The way we regularly talk to our inner child, consciously and unconsciously, influences how we react/respond to them. Those reactions are often automatic and just happen in the moment. . But they're not random. They are based on the patterns wired into our brains and nervous systems. Many of these patterns were created in our formative years. . They were not curated based on well thought out values and principles, for the most part. They were the effect of our parents and caregivers passing on the patterns that they themselves had imposed upon them. Thus the cycle continues. This is why we say conscious parenting is cycle breaking. . It is therefore important and helpful to rewrite those patterns consciously and bring them into alignment with the values that we have chosen. A large part of this of course is to think deeply and study to figure out what are our own values. . Have you deconstructed and chosen your own values? Or are you still operating on the values that were imposed upon you in your childhood? . That can be a very hard question to answer, because we often identify with our values. The fact that we acquired them without our consent or reasoning means that the values we operate from aren't entirely our own. . This is why it is important, powerful, and I would say necessary, for us to go through this process of examining our values in order to support our kids to find their true values. I have found this to be a continuously evolving process. . I recently made a video where I explore how to talk to our own inner child in a way that helps it feel safe, seen, understood, free, and... Loved. . I recommend going to my YouTube channel @meaningfulideas and watching. It will be an excellent companion to this article. . I know many (most) of my less than ideal reactions come from fear and trauma responses. I'm trying to feel safe in a situation that feels unsafe. . The problem is, most of the time, those reactions do not create real safety, nor even the feeling of safety. . My subconscious and my nervous system are responding to an entirely different situation. Even though on the outside I am an adult interacting with a four year old who's screaming, in my subconscious, and in my body it can feel like I am myself a child under attack. . Many of the survival strategies we developed as children are no longer helpful. They were necessary at the time and I honor them. Little Vivek was trying to survive in a world that seemed in many ways built to go against him. Every coercive moment, every Power Over/Power Under relationship came with it the need for another strategy. . This is why the self-compassion aspect is so important, because we start by honoring where we're at. We also choose to learn new and more effective strategies as we work on healing the wounds of our past. . Here are some of the things I say to my inner child: . "Little Vivek, I love you. You are always safe with me. You are free to play, free to explore, free to be who you are. . I believe in you. I will listen to you. I LOVE to listen to you. Your feelings are valid. Your experience is important to me. . When you fall, I will pick you up. When you cry, I will comfort you. When you're afraid or sad. I will hold you. . I'm here for you. You can relax into me. I am safe. You are safe." . The more our little selves believe this, the less they react. They trust us to care for them. . It's also the case that when the inner child has a big feeling come up, (because it will happen) we are more self-aware. . The result of this is less of those feelings leak out onto our children, and other people in our lives. We find ourselves more present when our kids are bringing the chaos, as happens in every family! . It is surprising how practical presence can be. Kids can feel more safe in our guidance when we are tuned into them. . I encourage you to read back over the script of how I talk to my inner self and use it to make your own. Have little sayings that remind you of your worth, of your No Wrongness, of your values. You can do it in small moments. I call this Micro Self-Compassion. . Or if you're really hurting, you can slow down and take a little more time with it. I do this on a semi-regular basis because it allows the compassion to go deeper into my system. Often I end up moving or making sounds when this happens. . You will find your own approach in a way that helps your inner child feel seen and this will have a profound effect on your relationship with your kids. . Wherever you are on your journey keep digging. Let's keep digging together. Peace, Vivek

Beware of anyone who uses science to justify coercion. So often we see people talk about children's brain development and what the science says. And then they use that info to go directly to coercion. There's no logical reason to go from brain development to forcing a kid to do something they don't want to do or stopping them from doing something they want to do. Every time we do this we are acting from an authoritative, power over, non-consensual relationship. The model this sets and the relationship damage that's done is profound. There's always a non-violent way to work with our kids. Not using coercion does not mean we are not guiding. Or to put it in the positive-we can guide our kids very well and still respect their consent and autonomy, their humanity. This relates to my previous post about consent. You cannot respect the consent of your child and take the tablet out of their hands. The two are fundamentally incompatible. There is a distinct difference between knowing about brain development and the choices we make because of it. You do not have to control your child. You can work with them. Remember that learning is a messy process. Let's get into the mess with our kids rather than use our power to avoid the mess. ddd

It's never too late to start. Start right now. Right now make the decision that from this moment forward you will never punish your kids again. You'll never give them a consequence. You'll never use your power to control them. This is the truly humane (and most effective) way to guide children. We dehumanize them when we use our power to control them and take away their autonomy and choice. (Please don't be the one who comments about kids running into the street and getting hit by a car. I know you weren't gonna do that, but I'm mentioning it just in case!) We dehumanize our children when we take away their autonomy and choice. We justify using force to violate their consent by saying "It's our job to take care of them." Or "We have to control them because we know better." When children are treated this way for years, they predictably turn away from their parents as they grow older. They put up a shield of self-protection. It's become so normalized people just expect their kids to pull away. Conscious/Gentle Parenting rooted in the Non-coercive Collaborative Mindset (NCCM) offers us a way to relate to our children so that break doesn't happen. We don't relate to each other from a power over dynamic so kids don't feel they have to protect himself from us. They don't need that shield. It's not that they don't gain their independence. Independence arises out of interdependence. It's not a break, it's a blossoming. My 24 year old is hardly around these days. She's got a job, a girlfriend and a life. Yet we text each other every day, all throughout the day. We share our thoughts and feelings. We send pictures of random things to each other. For example, I made a smoothie and I sent her a picture of my process. She sent me back a picture of the UFC fight she was watching with her friends. We are a part of each other's lives. It is not a common thing for 24 year olds to feel comfortable and relaxed with their parents, to feel they can be themselves around them. How beautiful it is that when we treat our kids with profound respect they carry us with them as they as find their way in the world. The relationship of friends and trusted guides we have nourished over the years is part of who they are. No break needed. It's a natural outgrowth of a non-coercive relationship over the long term. It's never too late to start. Even if you've been punishing up until now, you can decide to stop this moment. You are free, and you have that power. It might be a little bit chaotic for a while that's the old patterns fade away and you create new ones. Better to have some chaos based in deep human relationship, than order and obedience where the distance builds day by day. Wake up tomorrow morning and make the decision that no matter what your kids do, you're not going to punish them, you're not going to give them a consequence. You don't even have to tell them. Just don't do it! Commit to responding with acceptance and empathy. Work with collaboration and discussion. Instead of trying to control behavior, support the underlying causes. Focus on connecting together, playing together, breathing together, and exploring together. If you're unsure how to do this, please check out the vast resources I've made available. There are over 100 articles and many videos on my Facebook page and on Instagram. There are over 75 videos on my meaningful ideas YouTube channel (and more added all the time), my blog meaningfulideas.com has 400 articles. There are a lot of tools, strategies, concepts and examples in that body of work. This decision is one that will completely transform your relationship with your kids. It will bring a kind of peace and harmony to your home that's not possible when punishment exists. I believe in you and I know you can do it. You have deep love in your heart. It's never too late to start. (That last bit rhymes, which means it has to be true.)

As Conscious Parents we reject the mindset that has been handed down to us from the very systems created by oppressors. Marginalized demographics have been denied their autonomy by those in power for millennia. Refusing to use our systemic parental power to do the same to our kids is a radical re-writing of the patterns of the past. We are re-writing the future history of our children. When they look back in a few decades theyll recall how deeply they were respected. They won't recall every little mistake, they will remember the years of effort to treat them as a human being. I told my daughter when she was as young as 2 yrs that I didn't ever want her to obey me or do what I say. I wanted them to Know themselves, Honour themselves and Love themselves. Systems of power do not want us to be fully ourselves. We are compared, contrasted and judged There is a deep essence we all have. I call it the Unchanging self. Mainstream parenting that is based on the hierarchical and violent structures of the past, does not nourish the preservation of that essential self. In fact breaking the childs connection to their deep selves is at the core of the control through power mindset. This is why empowering our children is an act of resistance. Clear Self-knowledge and Deep Self-Relationship make one very hard to control. Also makes one much easier to collaborate with.

How to Guide Your Kids Around Food (and everything) Guiding our kids around food - Part 1 In this video I give tips on how to guide our kids around food (and everything). I offer ways of thinking about food and helping kids form a deep relationship with their bodies. Food is a multi-dimensional experience. It has many aspects to explore, Nutrition is the obvious one, but there is also the Social experience, the sensory enjoyment, taste, smell, feel, appearance. We can make Preparation something connecting and collaborative. There are lots of ways to engage with food that creates a holistic relationship. This way kids learn to have a conscious relationship with food, based on caring for themselves and having positive associations with food.

My session is 'Conscious Parenting as an Act of Resistance". If you follow my stuff you know that's what I'm about. Pushing back against the established power dynamics. I would often reflect in the early days of my child's life that I was parenting from my rebellious 16 year old! Pushing back against the world of adults that didn't respect me for who I was. I knew very clearly I was being looked down on by most of them. Even ones who were being friendly, behind it I could still feel they saw me as just a child. The land of my parents was colonized by the British for 200 years. Generations of my family before me was seen as sub-human. That mindset is absorbed over time and then passes down from parent to child. I was determined to break this cycle and treat my kid as the unconditionally worthy person that she is. To imbue this Self-Love/Self-Awareness/Self-Image into every cell of her being. I wanted her to know she was not "Less Than" from the inside out. This was my primary parenting priority. It often felt like a big FU to the weight and very painful residue of 10,000 years of coercive history and hierarchical power structures. Choosing to parent based on respect, relationship and empowerment. It is a completely different way of looking at and engaging with power. I do not want to model the use of power to kids in the way that has been taught to me by the people who have held power for so long. I reject that Power Over model. I choose one based in connection, in relationship and horizontal power sharing. Each of us has the choice and the potential to parent from this new mindset. A mindset that doesn't put one person above another. You can do this. You can change age old patterns and create something new.

My wife just caught me talking to myself as I often do. She asked me what was up. I said I was coaching myself. She replied, You're the best coach Vivek. I said, Yes that may be true, the problem is I am NOT the best client! . LOL . I was talking myself through some unhelpful habits that I struggle with. Feeling my feelings, noticing stories, fighting shame's stranglehold, forgiving Vivek and encouraging him to love himself. . It's a constant practice, deepening my relationship with myself, my thoughts, my emotions, my body. Being engaged in this self-reflection process is what helps me stay grounded in myself. It's also a big part of why I'm able to help parents the way I do. . I don't coach from some far off place of knowing everything. I'm deep in my sh-t on a daily basis. I walk side by side with the parents I support, whether it's one on one, a workshop or speaking to an audience. . I don't really think I'm not a good client. Being a human with the desire to grow and learn is enough. Perfection not required. This was me using humour to remind myself of my vulnerable humanity. It was also a moment of connection and understanding between my wife and I. . This is also how I approach my relationship with my kid. I am NOT above her. I do not expect perfection from her. I accept her vulnerable humanity as I am working to accept my own. . I make mistakes every day. I call myself a mistake making making. Every time it's a reminder that my kiddo and I are learning partners, also walking side by side on the path. This is why I often say we grew up together. . It's a primary reason why we made the decision to parent from the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset (NCCM). We wanted to foster a relationship of equals. . My kid is now 24 years old. Not a kid anymore :) The cumulative effect of more than 2 decades of working this way is so clear in our relationship. There is so much trust, comfort, safety and joy between us. It's been worth all the blood, sweat and tears that we shed over the years. . I recognize it requires a lot of effort to parent in this way. It's a radical departure from the mainstream. It's not traditional parenting done more gently, it's a true parenting paradigm shift. A new lens that acknowledges our shared humanity and puts Relationship First. (You can check out my video on parenting from Relationship First here https://www.facebook.com/meaningfulideas/posts/2323646727916111 ) . The next time your kid does something that you wish they didn't, take a moment to reflect on your own mistakes. Remind yourself that you're all human and learning together. . This will help you engage with them as a wise guide rather than an authority figure. Your decisions will be based on building trust and helping them learn about life. . And remember what I said above, Perfection not required. Being a human with the desire to grow and learn is enough. Keep walking the path, dig deeper into the NCCM and don't give up. I believe in you. <3 Peace, Vivek

Conscious Parenting is a radical act of Social Justice. Children are the most widely oppressed demographic. It doesn't matter where you come from, what your socioeconomic situation is, if you are a child you are a less valid human being. Children's marginalization is also intersectional. A child who is BIPOC, disabled, neurodiverse, LGBTQ+ or any number of other marginalized identities, the systemic oppression they face is that much more intense. When we teach children the truth about Injustice, hierarchies, power dynamics and prejudice we are not robbing them of their innocence, we are not doing them a disservice. We are giving them the awareness and tools to engage with oppressive systems from a place of wisdom and empowerment. Conscious parenting is a radical act of social justice because we are modeling and living the integrity, courage, values and love that are the enemies of oppression. In mainstream parenting the adults have a position of authority over the children. They also have systemic power over them. (My saying for systemic power is: "It's power you didn't Choose and cannot Refuse." Power like access to food, entertainment, resources and housing, financial power, emotional and physical power. When parents use this systemic power to get their way and control their kids, the children learn their place. This is what I call "the Hierarchy of Human Worth". It is clear that they are lower and the parents are higher in this hierarchy. The thing about someone being above you is that it also means someone is below you. This is the seed of oppression sown into the developing mind from the very environment they are being steeped in. When we follow the non-coercive, collaborative path we still have the same systemic power over our children, that's the nature of systemic! The difference is we acknowledge it and put great efforts into not using it to control them. When we do use it we try to use it with integrity and an awareness of its impact. The social-justice minded parent does not treat their child like they have less rights because of who they are. They don't place themselves above their children. We step outside of the hierarchy in how we relate to our children. It is a radically different form of steeping. It creates a radically different result. Children who don't feel they are below anyone, don't feel they are above anyone. If you are raising a child that has any form of marginalization. You are aware that teaching them they are equal, that they are equally worthy, has its challenges. That message is not reflected in most aspects of society. The more layers of marginalization, the more challenging it is. If you are reading this and have a relatively privileged existence, you may not understand how many obstacles and prejudices people who are in marginalized demographics face every day. It is an extra layer of effort to instil in these children that they are equally worthy. There are two main benefits. One is that they will know themselves, and they will know when they are not being treated with respect. We can over the years, teach them to stand up for themselves and others, and do so with strength and dignity. The second is that they will contribute to a new culture, where we do not look up and down at each other. This is not a weakness. It is a strength. This is why I say conscious parenting is a radical act of social justice, because we are sowing seeds that have the potential to transform the world. Our children are going to be running things in just a few years. They will be running the stores, they will be doctors, they will be cab drivers, they will own donut shops, they will be cops and security guards, they will be checking people out at the grocery, they will be CEOs and politicians. Sending a generation out into the world who do not see themselves above or below anyone, and at the same time are highly aware of the injustices in society, will produce profound change. I very much believe it is our best chance for thriving as a species. Peace, Vivek

On an article I wrote about limits, someone asked, "What about if my child doesn't want to wear warm clothes and it's really cold. Shouldn't I set a limit?" Here is my response. The way I look at it is, sometimes I have a choice to make. Prioritize the relationship or the practical concern. This is when we have "Competing Parenting Priorities". The choice is in our face. I try my best to choose relationship 99% of the time. I reserve the 1% practical concerns for when they're really necessary. The reason I do this is, when parents set a limit that the kid doesn't like, the damage that's done to the relationship is so clear to me. We use our power to control their choices and a break in trust is created. I see it and feel it. In the mainstream mindset it's nothing really. They're just kids, they're upset for a couple minutes, then they're over it. That is not what is happening. Kids are very aware of how we treat them. They know when they're being forced and when they're being collaborated with. They may not have the words for it, but they know. When they feel that force they pull away from us. I call it Protective Distance. This is why I minimize any force moments. I don't want to push them away. However it doesn't mean we don't guide. We can still try to get them to wear the clothes if we think it's important. 3 main differences between authoritative and collaborative limit setting First: We do our best to make it fun. If things are fun they have a tendency to go over really well. Second: We do our best to make it make sense. If our request makes sense to our kids they'll have much less resistance. If we can show them how it will actually benefit them and meet their needs, they might even join in. Third: At the point where relationship is going to be sacrificed, we soften. Relationship First. It's not worth the rift. Of course there are exceptions. Life has certain realities and demands. Each of us has to decide what limit is worth a layer of relationship damage. No one else can tell us that. We can explore it together, but in the end it's ours to decide. I know it can seem harsh to word it that way, but I find it helps keep me honest. That way when I do make the decision I am sure it's the least damaging option. My personal journey, my work, is to always stretch towards less force and more collaboration. That is one of my mantras: "Less Force, More Collaboration" along with "No Wrongness! No Wrongness!" and "Relationship First" I like affirmations :) Can you say them? If this was a workshop I'd have everyone repeat them and then again louder! "Less Force, More Collaboration" along with "No Wrongness! No Wrongness!" and "Relationship First" Say them in your mind, say them out loud. Keep Stretching Towards. I want to draw attention to the fact that I added "No Wrongness" to the Mantra list. This is because it's easy to think we're failing and doing everything wrong if we're not peaceful and collaborative 100% of the time. No one is 100% peaceful. No one knows what they're doing all the time. You are not broken, you are not failing. You are Evolving. When you act out of alignment with how you want to act, pause for a moment, take a breath and say "No Wrongness, No Wrongness". Remind yourself that you're learning, just like your kids are learning. As you absorb this lens you'll also see your kids differently. Less like they're broken needing to be fixed. You'll see they're not failing. They're Evolving. This is the seed of much patience and humility on the parenting path. I am offering a FREE Power Struggles workshop where we'll go into these concepts in more depth. The date is Wednesday May 19, 2021, from 7-9pm eastern. I would love for you to join me. Please register at: www.meaningfulideas.com

2021 05 17

Power Struggles are the worst. They sap our energy, deplete our relationships and make communication next to impossible. Everyone leaves feeling upset, drained and unsafe. Something in us knows this is not how things were supposed to be. We feel that more harmony and connection with our kids is possible. Yet it seems like there's no way out. So many families live this way for years. The disconnection builds over the decades and when the kids are young adults they can't wait to get away from their parents. They certainly don't accept their parents' guidance. One of my daughters friends told me a power struggle story from when he was 17. If he was getting out of the shower and his parents told him to get out, he would climb back in for 10 minutes just so that he wasn't getting out when they told him to. This isn't unusual. There is an urge in us that wants to protect our autonomy when it is threatened. When this happens we put kids in a position where not cooperating is an act of self-empowerment. Even a 2 year old experiences this. Most parents of 2 year olds will agree. We aren't teaching them the lessons we think we are; Responsibility, Accountability, Honesty. What we are doing is pushing them to rebel or comply. Neither one is true cooperation nor education. This is why it's worth the effort to operate from a mindset that builds trust instead. Power struggles, like much of life, are largely a matter of perspective. We can shift our awareness from their behavior to what is underneath. This is what I call having "Ice Berg Consciousness". There is always a need being expressed, there is always a growth and learning opportunity and there is always a way to increase the trust and connection you have with your child. When you are getting frustrated and the power struggle is beginning, Pause Take a breath Listen Focus on what will actually reach your child. Engaging in the struggle never does. Even when we KNOW we're right. ESPECIALLY when we know we're right. That's when the greatest disconnection can occur. We can also frame it as a moment of deepening the relationship. That's why we pause. Interrupt the pattern, disrupt the flow. It requires some humility, but we can always soften and connect. Soften and Connect What gets in the way? Often we have a pre-conceived idea of exactly HOW our kids should behave, how they should talk, how they should feel, eat, work, play, apologize, sleep and learn. Oh those expectations. We're bound to be disappointed! Letting go of the power struggle doesn't mean we give in. It means we shift away from those expectations and focus on the person we have in front of us in the moment. We change the power relationship from a power over (hierarchical) structure, to one that feels more shared (horizontal). Taking this approach the whole concept of "giving in" disappears. It means we listen deeper and validate more authentically. Communicate with our children. Let them know we see their feelings and needs. We have to make sure they feel seen, heard. When I reflect back to a kid I do it with this open and connected mindset. They usually say Yes, that's exactly what I'm feeling. Sometimes theyll say It's a little more like this&. Then I repeat until they say the first response. Once kids feel heard like this they open up their hearts. Even the hardest exterior can be melted. When working to reduce power struggles we also have to be honest in our self-evaluation. What are WE holding on to that we could let go of? Do I feel a need to be in control? Do I feel that giving in is a weakness? Those old ideas don't belong here. That's the mindset we're here to change. So every time you find yourself in a power struggle with your child, Pause Breathe Listen Interrupt the pattern, shift your mindset, and you will be much more effective. Your child will learn to trust you more and soften into your guidance. You will reduce the adversarial relationship between you. In the traditional parenting path this adversarial relationship reliably develops throughout the years. We lose our influence with them over time. Reducing power struggles by choosing collaboration and relationship first changes all of that. We trust the learning path of our kids, no longer adversaries, we partner with them on their journey.
