Please do not hold the limit firm if your child is resisting, angry and crying. The emotional-relational impact is more damaging than the benefit of holding the limit in that moment. It is always okay to soften and connect. I know it's very challenging when I write about asking parents to not use limits and boundaries with their kids. It can activate quite a defensive response in many people. There is a deeply held belief about how important limits are, how they make children feel safe. While I understand the philosophy, this is not the actual experience of the child. From the kids perspective receiving the consequence or having the limit enforced, it feels like an obstruction to their freedom and autonomy. It feels like an imposition by someone who thinks they know better and has more power. When I say limits I am talking about coercive limits. Coercive means forced. This is a limit in which the kid has no choice. For example we set a limit on food and kids have no choice in the matter. We set a limit on bedtime and kids have no choice in the matter. Take away the screen, shut off the TV, the kids have no choice. If the kids can simply say No and do what they want, I would consider that a suggestion and not a limit. This is honoring their autonomy. What is commonly called a loving limit, or an empathetic limit is when we enforce a coercive limit and then empathize with the resulting distress. ie "I know it's frustrating that you can't have 4 cookies before dinner." I am not suggesting that we should never help our kids set limits for themselves. When I'm working with kids I'm often engaging with limits because it's a natural part of being a guide. In fact it's a natural part of any relationship. What I am suggesting is that we do not remove their freedom of choice in the process. I want them to feel they are part of the process rather than feel it as an imposition. They trust the limit, they feel in their nervous system that it's in their best interests. There are ways of working with limits that preserve choice and don't require force or power. It's the difference between collaborative versus coercive limits. In a collaborative limit we are all working together as equals to figure out how to best work with a situation. Children feel very included in the process. They have a lot of input into how it plays out. If the collaboratively agreed upon limit doesn't work for everyone we can sit down and adjust it. At no point is there power or force involved. When going through these processes with kids, I focus on tending to our relationship and their emotional state more than the limit itself. This is what makes it feel deeply connecting rather than disconnecting. This connection and trust inspires a higher degree of willingness to cooperate. Just yesterday I was talking to a parent who had been trying to set loving, empathetic limits with their kid around candy. They didn't want them eating too much before dinner. At least not the whole bag! They were reasonably trying to keep their kids healthy. After setting the limit and empathizing with their upset, she later found them hiding in the bedroom eating a bag of sweets. Trying to set a more firm limit or even giving them a consequence for doing so, the only lesson they're going to learn is how not to get caught next time. This is what I'm trying to avoid. That feeling that we are an obstacle to navigate around. I know parents are operating from a loving intent in setting limits. To try and keep kids safe from something that might be harming them. Perhaps we feel they are too young and cannot self-regulate. While the intent may be honorable, the way we go about it doesn't usually encourage our kids to join us in the process. All sorts of power struggles result, no one is learning, no one is happy about the situation. To them we are the obstacle. This is where it's important for us to look beyond our intent and acknowledge the impact that we are actually having. Moving in the direction of force is never going to work out well. It causes damage emotionally and relationally. It certainly doesn't teach children to care for their bodies and minds. We mostly teach them to resist us. If we want to create that lifelong guiding relationship we have to always be stretching ourselves towards Less Force and More Collaboration. This is why I say ""My Parenting Mantra Is Relationship First". This priority is firmly set. It guides my decisions. There are times I will work with my kid on setting limits, but I always keep in mind that it's about her process and her learning. I focus on respecting her personhood, her choice, her consent, her self-knowledge. I will not hold a limit firm if it comes to a point where the kid is resisting and crying about it. The emotional-relational impact is more damaging than the benefit of holding the limit in that moment. It is always okay to soften and connect. It's related to a concept I teach called NSP which stands for "Nervous System Programming. NSP states that "In every interaction with our kids we are informing them about Who we are, Who they are, Their place in the world and How the world works. This informing doesn't only happen intellectually, but also emotionally, relationally, physically, in the nervous system and the neural pathway patterns that get developed in the brain. If you are reading this you are probably already committed to the idea of conscious, gentle parenting. In this mindset we know it's neither effective nor kind to control our kids using punishment and consequences. Things like taking away a 'privilege' or putting them in their room. As we move towards a more non-coercive, collaborative approach we focus on treating them with respect as humans. The emotional experience of being punished leaves a significant residue on our emotions and our bodies. It's something we carry with us all our lives. Every time we use force with our kids there is an impact on their (and our) nervous systems. Another layer of memory is created. The cost is too high. It damages their relationship to themselves and their relationship to us. They feel like an authority figure with power is stopping them from doing something that they enjoy. Forced against their will. Even when we empathize with them, they know we are empathizing for something that we ourselves did. This is why it's important for us to parent with an understanding of the impact we're having on our children's system with our choices. I recently spoke for an hour on NSP and published the video. Please watch it for an in depth exploration on how to use Nervous System Programming in parenting. In my experience it's a much more effective strategy to collaborate on ideas to meet everyone's needs around limits. Create an environment where everyone's voice is heard and taken into consideration. This helps kids feel deeply seen and valued in the process. When we can inject a spirit of fun into the process it can make a big difference as well. So often we make looking at limits with kids such a heavy thing. We know we're restricting them and they feel imposed upon. We can however approach things with a lighter heart. Try and hold a different perspective. Genuinely wanting to keep them safe, and deeply respecting them at the same time. Let's play with this. Here's a video where I tell a story of a time that I set a limit around a campfire with a whole group of kids in a way that inspired them to want to follow my guidance. I give an example of how I used a very connecting and fun way of communicating to get them excited and engage in a collaborative limit setting experience with me. The other adults were scrambling around trying to control the kids, chaos ensued! Then I jumped in Vivek style and within a couple of minutes had them all following me and doing things in a safe way that still felt so much fun. Setting Limits With Joy (p.s. please follow my YouTube while you're there d) It's an amazing thing to witness when kids become involved in, and even enthusiastic about setting their own limits because they start to learn how it is a benefit to them. I call it "WIIFM - What's In It For Me". (Pronounced wi-fum) Helping young people understand in an experiential way, not just intellectual, the benefit to them. This makes the whole process of collaborating on a limit much easier. It also forces us to think a bit deeper about why we are setting the limit and how to explain it to them. Can we actually show them how thinking about these things makes a difference to their lives? It's also important for us to recognize what needs of ours are being met or not met. How much of that are we projecting on our kids? There is a lot of introspection required to relate to our children with integrity, given the power we have over them. You can check out my video on WIIFM-What's In It For Me It is a messier and more long-term process to work with our kids, to gain their trust and agreement. It also leads to the deepest relationships, both of guide and friend. This is why I have put out so many hundreds of articles and videos talking about how to implement these ideas in a way that is workable for parents. Trying to nudge our mindset towards interacting with our kids in a non-coercive, collaborative fashion. True collaboration requires that same integrity. Without integrity we have collaboration on the surface only and this has a limited shelf life. If the person on the bottom of the power structure knows that their input can be overridden at any moment by the person with more power, they cannot trust the process. Kids learn early on that their autonomy is conditional. It lasts only as long as the adults deem it appropriate. This sense of self-determination is something very deep for young people and they will go through a lot to preserve it. In the mainstream parenting paradigm it is not one of the main focuses. We rarely see articles about how to encourage a fierce self-determination with children. We usually see articles about how to get them to cooperate. The fact is though that an increase in cooperation accompanies an increase in choice. We miss out on a big opportunity to understand and connect with our kids depending on where we place our attention. Attending to this sense of self is so fundamental to safety in relationships that we lose our kids when we don't pay attention to it. Our young people end up in a situation where they have to protect their autonomy. They do this in three primary ways that I call the responses to coercion - Resistance, Compliance and Distance. The resistance is when kids become very defiant or when they start hiding the candy in the bedroom. The compliance is when they are following along, but they do it from a place of having given up on their own sense of self and autonomy. They are operating from fear or resignation, but not from caring or connection. Distance is something that accompanies both of the above. Kids put up that armor, the shield because they know they aren't free to be themselves. When we resist holding firm limits with our kids they don't need to resist us. They don't need to put up that shield. Then they can relax into our guidance and trust our wisdom. This is when we have the most stable, sustainable and resilient positive influence in our kids lives. I encourage you to keep moving a little further along the non-coercive, collaborative path. It takes an effort to keep stretching ourselves in this direction. Consider taking another step. Wherever you are on your journey you can take one more step. Peace, Vivek

Edit to add: Yes I know there are exceptions. I know.

I also know it's really hard. Trust me I know. I have the scars to prove it. Exceptions will always be there. Let the article inspire us to minimize the exceptions as much as possible. Don't think of it as judgment for the times that we have to set limits we'd rather not. Life is like that sometimes, I understand, we all really truly understand. This article is intended to stretch us. Stretch a little bit every day. It's the stretching that really matters. Edit to add 2: Someone asked, if we're not going to set a limit how do we work with our kids around the candy? This of course is a very reasonable and important question. Some people suggested making it fun, some people suggested exploring ideas around the body and nutrition. This is what I added to the conversation. I agree with what others have shared here. For me I paid close attention to what my kid ate. I was a very involved guide in her learning about her body, food and its effects. This was not a case of leaving them alone hoping that they figure it out. It's a continuous exploration of looking at what the body is telling us. Of experimenting with different foods and understanding them. Exploring the joys of eating as well as some things to be cautious of. The key to all of it is the relationship between parent and child. If it is stable and connected the child will be open to learning and exploring. If there is a break in that trust it would have to be rebuilt first to a reasonable degree before the child will be more open to that collaboration. By this I mean if the kid feels the parent is going to control them, they aren't going to be interested. I do think however humans are capable of guiding each other and working together in harmony, with great efficiency and powerful effectiveness, without using any kind of force. I believe that we can work together in such a way that everybody feels like their needs are being met and we all feel cared for. I believe in this. I believe that part of Gentle Parenting is putting in the work to discover this with our family systems. They are complex, with diverse people at diverse stages of development. As parents we are in many ways leaders of establishing the non-coercive, collaborative mindset in our homes. It's a great responsibility and a worthy one. It requires us to be thinking and learning and stretching ourselves all the time. I might also buy less candy, but if I felt that my kid felt a sense of shame because I wasn't buying candy, I would go out of my way to make sure I brought home some extra candy. I want to be really clear that the shame is always my first priority. Our relationship is always my first priority. This is precisely why kids are so open to my guidance. They feel my deep honoring of them. I know it can seem like we're going to lose all control over them, and for a time it can feel that way because control feels different when it turns into influence. Influence is very different however. Influence is relational. Influence is flexible and connected to the growth mindset. When I set limits with a kid I want it to be from that perspective. I have a very diverse experience working with young people. I have volunteered in school, all the way from kindergarten to grade 8. I have taught English math science and music. In grade 8 there was no music teacher and so I volunteered to take on the music program. I taught the entire band program, two classes a week including testing and grading. We even put on a music night for the community! I have also taught children's martial arts for many years. I have worked with at risk youth in a local youth organization. My experience with young people is quite extensive. I have always used these principles in each of these different circumstances. Helping kids feel like we are on the same side has the most profound effect on our working relationship. This has been consistently true. I hope that answers your questions. I think I'm going to have to add this to the article. x

Nervous System Programming - NSP Nervous System Programming - NSP With every interaction we inform our kids about: Who we are Who they are Their place in the world How the world works This information isn't only absorbed by the intellect, it's a holistic experience. We impact our children on many levels in addition to the content alone. They are affected on Emotional, Relational, Environmental, Developmental, Physical and Spiritual levels as well. Whether or not a rule, limit or boundary is a punishment is determined by the impact and feelings of the child, not the intent of the parent. This is an important distinction that we often miss. This is why the saying "impact over intent" exists. . If my child feels that I am using my power to make them unhappy, then it is a punishment regardless of my goal or intent. . It is however possible to work with our kids in a way that makes them feel consistently empowered and loved. Where they engage with us willingly because they trust us. . As soon as they don't want to follow our limit and we use our power to enforce it, it is no longer consensual and becomes punishment.

I heard that voice and recognized it immediately. I was in the grocery store this afternoon. I was looking at the almond milk when I heard someone speaking in a very tense, harsh tone. I turned around and there was a woman speaking to somebody I couldn't see, just behind a display case. From her tone and demeanor I knew right away she was talking to a child. Only then did I realize she wasn't even speaking English and I had no idea what she was actually saying. I just knew that pretty much no one other than children gets talked to that way in public. That particular dehumanizing, 'power over' voice is reserved for the kiddos. I decided to stand around to wait and see if I was right. Sure enough within another few seconds a four year old comes walking around the corner, head hanging low. He looked dejected, unseen and unmet. I know the look well. I remember how that feels. Do you? Anytime that kids are talked down to by adults, it's so painful for a young person. Most of society just thinks it's normal, but to me it's heartbreaking. Even as I'm sitting here editing this and the memory comes back to me my heart feels heavy. Kids learn from an early age they are not on the same plane of the human hierarchy as adults are. I call it the hierarchy of human worth. They are most definitely on a lower rung. Of course if one has any sort of marginalization the whole thing is amplified. When they noticed the disrespect with which they are talked to an armor goes up. They see us as other. Kids always act different around adults. They learn to keep one eye open around us. I don't mean to make anyone feel bad although that's very possibly going to happen. I am sorry that I come across harshly sometimes. I've had a chance to spend some time interacting with young people recently and have been having very deep experiences with them. Lots of deep conversations and explorations of life. Realizations of self, of values, of priorities. It doesn't matter what age the kid is or what they're into I can always turn things deep, because I honor where they're at with no resistance or obstruction. I remember when I was volunteering at a youth conference, (Held by the @[100066388039139:2048:Future Aces] Foundation) and I had the opportunity to talk to some young people about how adults viewed them. I wanted to share with them what I knew about how adults viewed them and I wanted to find out how they felt adults viewed them. It was very challenging for those kids to believe me at first when I started talking to them about being their equal and not being above them. I was so damn insistent that they finally were starting to see it. I told them I am not better than them because I'm an adult. I told them I don't deserve more respect than them, because I'm an adult. I told them I don't have the power to tell them what to do just because I'm an adult. I encouraged them not to listen to me. I encouraged them to do whatever they felt was right in the moment. Part of my task with these kids was to get them to fill out these forms. After all that freedom talk they challenged me and said, "Do you mean we don't have to fill out these forms?" I said no. There's no such thing as have to. "Have To" is a lie you've been told. You always have a choice. You still have to deal with your choices and whatever happens because of them, but it's always your choice. You never have to obey an at all if you don't want to. Even if I insisted as the adult, you could just put your pen down and sit back. What can I do pick up the pen and try and force it in your hand? If I was that kind of person I might try punishing you? As long as you could take whatever the punishment was you could just do whatever you wanted. I DO NOT have more power than you do in this situation. Even though everything in your life has told you the opposite of that. You are a free human being, and you have power. There was a moment of slightly stunned silence. Then I added "However, I would really like you to fill out these forms because as an organization we actually do use them. It helps us to make better choices around the youth conference in the future. But my priority is always your freedom and your choice. If you choose not to do it because that's what you really feel then I will be very happy that you honored yourself Because if you don't want to fill it out, I don't want you to fill it out. That's what's most important to me. Every single kid out of the 12 or so that were there filled it out, except maybe a couple. They were very enthusiastic to do so. I was also true to my word and the kids who didn't fill them out received the same level of validation from me as the kids who did. That way there was no external motivation for them to fill it out or not fill it out. This is freedom. This is deep human connection. This is modeling respect and consent. This is the exact opposite of behaviorism. The opposite of trying to give them positive reinforcement to make them behave in a certain way. We cannot do positive reinforcement without implied negative reinforcement if it's conditional. I saw them as whole and complete people, with control over their agency and autonomy. I related to them from a deep place. I talked to them about how they felt adults viewed them. The idea that an adult could treat them as an equal, or admit they were wrong... Seemed like science fiction to these kids. They knew when it came down to it, adults would insist on their way of doing things They knew their choice was only an illusion. It existed only as long as their parents, and other adults to a degree, let them have that illusion. They also felt with me that I wasn't holding that power over them. I explicitly and firmly rejected it. I named it and drew attention to it. Then I gave it back to them with no conditions. I refused to control them and their respect for me was palpable. You can watch the video. I will link below. It's called Treating Kids As Equals. By the way I'd love it if you followed my YouTube channel. You'll see me have a conversation with these kids. We spent about an hour together and then suddenly I had the idea to get their reactions on video and they were so happy to do it. It's one of my favorite videos ever. Ah and that event today, seeing that adult talk to the child that way. It makes me remember back to talking to these kids. It feels connected. I want us to raise our kids so that they know their inherent worth. This does not produce arrogance or entitlement. Arrogance and entitlement are protective responses to feelings of inadequacy and lack of worth. They do not come from believing in oneself too much. They come from not believing in oneself enough. When kids know themselves and know their inherent value. They do not need to prove it to anyone else. They do not need to defend it. This is the opposite of entitlement. The more they know their selves, the more want to help others feel the same. The desire to contribute to others wellbeing is nurtured. When you're interacting with your kids listen for that tone in your voice, even the slightest bit of it. Change it if you can. Continuously humanize them as deeply as you can. Notice for the slightest othering or hierarchicazenating (yes I made up that word.). Once you notice it work towards shifting it. Try and notice the lens that you're looking at your kids through. What is mindset with which you're perceiving their actions? None of us are perfect at this of course. That is why we practice. The more that we practice, the better we get. We may slip and fall sometimes, but we can get up and keep going. I often say even if we make a million mistakes it's getting back on the path that counts. We have been programmed by many generations that children are not equal to adults. That we do have power over them, and that's how it should be. I do not believe this. It is not what I practice. It is not what I teach. That mindset always creates disconnection. That is the typical thing that happens with teenagers and their parents. They are wary of them. They lie to them. Many parents don't know their kids. But it doesn't have to be that way. We can make different choices and choose a different lens. Keep getting back on the path towards the non-coercive, collaborative mindset and practice. I hope that woman in the grocery store has some kind of epiphany and changes the way she talks to her kiddo. That little one is going to keep withdrawing farther and farther away from her and she may never know that something else is possible. Something else is possible. Please know that I know this is not easy, none of this is easy. Oh, and it's exhausting. That's something I can't do anything about. What we can do is hold it together. As community of people who are working towards increasing children's rights and changing the way they are treated in the world, we can all support each other. This is why I have a mountain of free resources for you to absorb the conscious parenting mindset and practice. Take some time and go through my YouTube channel (link below) or read my articles and watch my lives here on Facebook. The more you read about it, listen to it and think about it, the more it becomes natural and is reflected in your demeanor and your choices. If you would like to work with me more personally I have a membership based support site where I do live classes, coaching calls and meditations on a weekly basis. It's a great way for us to get to know each other and have a close working relationship around your parenting. I will put a link to it in the comments. I believe in you, and I care about you. You are doing deep work. Thank you Vivek

I'm writing a LONG article on coercive Limits and Boundaries. In it I discuss how they degrade the parent child relationship. A coercive boundary is one in which the child has no input and has no choice. It violates their autonomy and consent. It is held in place with a 'Power Over' model of relationship. The more work I do with parents and kids, the more convinced I am of the power of collaboration. Working with young people in a 'Horizontal Power Sharing' relationship creates stable, sustainable and resilient patterns early on. Coercive limits do not inspire profound collaboration, communication and cooperation. The deeper we go into the non-coercive mindset, the deeper our kids let us into their hearts and minds. I explain this in a lot more detail in the piece I'm writing. Keep an eye out for the full article coming soon. <3 Vivek

One of my saying is: The question isn't "How do I get my kids to brush their teeth?". The question is "How do I get my kids to LOVE their teeth." When children, and really all of us, feel there is a real benefit we will choose those things ourselves. When it feels like an imposition on our autonomy (which is what all manipulation techniques feel like) resistance is a natural, and appropriate response. This what I call SMSR vs FMSR - Self-Motivated Self-Regulation vs. Fear-Motivated Self-Regulation. I'm 52 and to this day I struggle with brushing my teeth because of how it was framed for me. My kiddo who's almost 24, she really does not enjoy brushing her teeth, but she does it every day and often reminds me. We never focused on the behaviour, we focused on inspiring the inner landscape that leads to the behaviour. My other saying is, "Inspire the Desire and the Behaviour will follow." It's the magic of intrinsic motivation. Having said all that I think I'll go brush my teeth.

Tickling and Consent - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel . Honoring each other's consent is one of the most vital aspects of a connected relationship. . In this video I talk about how important it is to validate our kid's consent. We teach consent by modelling it in all our interactions. . When I was a kid people with tickle me to the point of desperation. I hate being tickled to this day because of my childhood. Even when I said "No. Stop!" they would find it funny and continue. Unwelcome tickling is violating consent. There are 100 other ways that we do this to kids and dismiss their very real feelings. . Let's inspire our kids to know that they are worthy of having their consent respected. The more they do, the more they'll naturally want to respect the consent of others as well. . Trying to teach respect for consent through rules, lectures, talking and "how would you feel?" questions are largely ineffective. Especially when we don't reflect the message in our own actions. It's an unfortunate part of kid's lives that their consent is denied on a regular basis. . We often don't realize how many times a day we violate their consent because we think it's just normal. However every time we say no to them we are doing it. . No you can't have ice cream for breakfast. No you can't have ice cream for breakfast again! No you can't watch tv all evening. No you can't sleep whenever you want. No you can't eat that. No you can't eat in that room. You can't keep your toys like that. You can't talk like that, climb this or jump on the other. No no no no no. . On and on and on it goes. The message is clear. Your consent doesn't matter. . Instead the message that we need to send to our children is, "Yes. I honour your consent". . Adults often defend these NO choices as necessary for a variety of reasons. Regardless of how valid we believe those reasons to be, the effect on the kid's experience of consent is the same. . Their experiential message is always stronger than the lectures. The impact teaches more than the intent. This is why words are ineffective in creating deep change if the message is in opposition to their lived experience. . Can you go through the list above and challenge yourself to say yes to all those things? I know it's super hard to even imagine it. All sorts of good reasons come up to deny their consent. . Even if you don't have any of these particular restrictions, it is worthwhile to look closely at where you might be denying your children's consent. This requires a high level of self-awareness and self-honesty. . We have to keep them healthy. We have to respect the common space. They need sleep to function well. They have a right to their feelings, but not to talk disrespectfully when they express them. I can't afford new furniture. They can't take food into their rooms because of bugs and mice. They aren't yet developed enough to make decisions. We know more than they do. We have to prepare them for the real world. . Feels like all good reasons to say no. We have the best of intentions when we "set limits" like this. There is a difference between intention and impact. If we look at the cumulative impact of these constant consent denying restrictions we can see that it creates an unhealthy relationship with consent far beyond anything we can tell them or try to teach them. . Once we recognize these patterns we can start to change them. We can start to look for more ways to collaborate rather than control. We can guide our kids to learn intelligent decision making rather than decide for them. We can help kids feel their consent is IMPORTANT and RESPECTED. The key word is FEEL. It's important to remember that telling them their consent matters doesn't matter if their experience doesn't match up. . Watch the video and then if you feel brave share a way you have noticed you deny your kid's consent and how you might change it.

Thinking about apologies again. There is a type of apology where we are hoping to receive forgiveness and repair the relationship. We might do this because we feel bad and we don't want to be alone or we don't want to lose the person. It could also be because we feel their pain and we don't want to be the cause of it. The problem with this kind of apology is that it is asking something of the person that we have already hurt. We are asking for their effort and attention to forgive us. This can actually feel like a burden to the person who is hurt. There is another kind of apology in which we are not asking anything of the other person. It is entirely the recognition of what we did, a recognition of the impact that had, an expression of regret and an expression of wanting to do better. Underneath this apology is a freedom to accept it or not, to accept it on their timeline if at all. The first kind of apology is like offering someone a gift, but having a few conditions on how they are to use it. The second is offering the gift in complete freedom. In my experience the second kind of apology has a more profound effect. This of course requires us to get clear inside. We have to actually forgive ourselves and love ourselves so that we are not consciously or subconsciously demanding forgiveness from them when we apologize. It's interesting isn't it? - An effective apology requires self-forgiveness! When someone apologizes to me I will often ask them to forgive themselves and not hold self-blame or shame in their hearts. I do this because I'm Selfish. I want a really good apology!!

Saying "No" (or even "No", because) vs Yes, and& As you may know if you've been following my parenting posts and videos, I'm not a big fan of saying No to kids. I will put great effort into turning a no into a yes. I think NO inhibits independence and creates a separation (an unnecessary separation) between parent and child. I know this is a controversial point of view and bugs a lot of people! x" **I Don't Understand the Question** When my kid was 17 she wanted to get a tattoo. I remember I was talking to a friend about how she wanted one going down her arm and that she had wanted me to design it for her. They said "Did her asking you to design it make it easier for you to say Yes? At first I honestly didn't understand the question. Say yes to what? I was wondering. I was genuinely confused. Then suddenly I realized that they were thinking my kid was trying to make it easier to say yes to her getting a tattoo! I laughed and said "I would never say no to her. I just don't do that!" Then it was my friends turn to be a bit confused. I just don't get that. they said. I wrote the story of my daughters tattoo back when this happened (she's almost 24 now). It illustrates the point very well so I am sharing it with you. **You Want to do WHAT to Your Body?!** My kiddo is now 17. When she was 15 she asked me if she could get a tattoo. (now that in itself should be interesting to note. Why would a kid that always gets told yes think of asking for permission?) I told her Of Course she could get a tattoo. It is her body and she has the right to decide what is done with it. No one else has that right. (isn't that a good message for a young person? I think so!) **Saying "YES" and teaches a lesson, "NO" closes down thinking** I said yes, though it wasn't a permissive and uninvolved yes. So many people are afraid that they're "permissive" if they say yes. It's like there are only two choices, control or permissive. I prefer non-coercive guidance and collaborative exploration! I said: Yes& and here's something to think about when making the decision. At 15 you're still evolving. Right now you're a young woman and growing into such an amazing person. Sometimes from the ages of 15 18 we change a lot of things about ourselves, our tastes in music, art and other preferences, our friends and lots of other things. If you choose a tattoo now and you change you won't be terribly happy. If you wait till your 18 then you'll have a few more years under your belt and youll feel more sure about your choice. Think about that and whatever you decide I'll stand behind you. She thought about it for a few days. She did her own processing. After some time she decided not to get the tattoo. It's worth noting that she thought about it for a few DAYS. That means she knows I'm not imposing my will on her. She knows I'm giving her information and guidance to include in her own decision making. It also means she took the suggestion seriously. No resistance. I don't want my kid to immediately resist nor immediately comply with me. I want them to be deeply, collaboratively involved in whatever we're exploring. **YES Encourages Self-Awareness and Self-Knowledge** Shortly after she turned 17 she came to me and asked Dad, Do I you think I have to wait till I'm 18 to get a tattoo? I'm 17 and I know myself pretty well. I want to get a happy face and I know I'll always like happy faces. (again, she knows I'm going to say yes& why does she ask me?) I said "Of course you can! You know yourself best and if that's what you want then let's do it." She responded saying that she also wants a longer one on her arm and a band on the other arm, but she feels like "itll be a good idea to wait till I'm 18 to make those decisions." (The long one on the arm is the one she wants me to design!) Clearly she had been thinking about the suggestion I offered 2 years ago. She has been self-evaluating and assessing the situation intelligently and independently. **YES Gives Kids Ownership Over Their Thinking and Their Lives** If I had told her "No" or even "No", because& instead of Yes, and& she would not have done the same level of self-evaluation. She would not have made the decision her own. She would not have felt the same level of ownership and autonomy over her body. And I am quite sure she would not have involved me in the process to the extent she has. It's likely she would have felt pressure and that leads to protective distance. Instead of being a source of guidance and wisdom in her processing I would have been an obstacle in her achieving her desires. NO closes doors while YES and opens them, it allows for more possibilities! **Teaching deep life skills from the inside out** The other benefit of this approach is that I know she will apply this decision making model to other areas of her life. It is now hers. It is her wisdom, her understanding and her self-knowledge. The model will evolve and adapt as she grows. Developing this kind of capacity is far more important to me as a parent than laying down the law. **YES Helps Kids to Feel Safe With Us** This uncommon level of acceptance that I have always worked to offer her has inspired her know that I am a safe place to express herself. That she can count on me to validate her no matter what. Because of this she actually seeks my guidance, even when she doesn't have to. This is why she asks me when she already knows the answer is yes. She values my guidance, she trusts my wisdom. If I have anything important for her to consider I will share it. I care about her decision making process and support her once she decides. This is safe guidance. To me this is so wonderful. This is why I'm such a fan of Yes! Can you challenge yourself to deepen your relationship with YES? To trust it more? I believe you can d

I know it's my job to guide my daughter. To help her develop her the tools she will need to face the world. It's important for me to teach her what I know and encourage her to follow her heart. . Tools of love, of acceptance, of giving and receiving in the most pure way possible. The gift of joy and laughter! . I've always said that I can teach her how to sit on a chair and eat with a fork, because doing the opposite is inconvenient and painful. . However the lessons that I learn from her on a daily basis are deep and profound. . Her beauty and innocence inspires me to follow my own heart. For how can I be the best father and friend to her without being true to myself. . Now that she's 23 I often talk about how we grew up together. I don't say I raised her, I don't even say she grew up. We have been on the journey side by side. . So while I often play the part of the guide in this relationship, really we are co-guides and co-followers. I am happy to be her student and learn the wisdom she has that I can only dream of!

Biting Is Awesome! A few years ago a friend of mine and I were playing with a lovely and energetic 2 year old. At one point he was climbing all over my friend and having a great time. Suddenly he bit the guy right on the chest& Ouch! My friend, who is very gentle and loving, said no biting please in a very calm tone. There was no judgement or anger in his voice. Of course knowing what I know I realized that was not going to stop the little one from biting, but was actually going to make him want to do it more! So immediately jumped in and enthusiastically proclaimed: "Biting is AWESOME! They both stopped for a moment and just looked at me. This is not the type of thing people are used to hearing in those moments. I kind of love that it was surprising to both child and adult. **Validate the Impulse, Redirect the Behaviour** I grabbed a pillow from the couch and bit it, shaking my head and growling like a dog. The kid started laughing immediately and I gave him the pillow to bite as well. He copied me growling and shaking his head. Then I joined him and the two of us had the same pillow in our teeth and were biting the corners like dogs fighting over a piece of meat! It was quite dramatic and hilarious. The beauty of starting this way is I'm not operating from a mindset of wrongness. Wrongness, even gently expressed, causes kids to put up defenses. It's very hard to get through that shield once it's in place. **Offer a Suggestion Once Connection is Established** At some point I said to him "Biting things is awesome, it feels good. It's so much fun. Biting people isn't so great because it could hurt them. There are so many things we can bite and it's so much fun. I LOVE biting with you and I want to do more!" After another minute of competitive pillow biting he went back to climbing on my friend. I could see the urge to bite suddenly come upon him and he paused... He looked at me, grabbed a pillow and brought it to me to bite, which I did so vigorously of course! Then he grabbed it and started biting it as well. This happened four more times over the next few minutes. **A 2 year old Learns Self-Regulation** Every time he went to bite my friend he remembered how much energy I gave him for his biting and how much fun we were having doing it. I Was Myself quite amazed at how quickly and how well he took to this. Even though I teach it, it still seems so wonderful to me how effective it is when we go with our children's direction and what a difference it makes. **Going With** It can be challenging, but if you can try "going with your kids impulses and directions, rather than correcting them, you might find that things can shift in unexpected ways. We can tend to resist this idea, especially in the more difficult moments, with the more difficult behaviors. **A New Way of Relating** The hard part about this is of course it goes against so much of what we've learned and experienced over our lifetime. We are taught that if we don't maintain control, our children will control us. So many of our systems are built this way, the education system, legal system, correctional system& it's not surprising that the family system is also modeled this way. The idea that we are "condoning bad behaviour" is deeply set in mass consciousness. Few people take the time to really question it. Wrongness never teaches the deep lessons nor does it inspire self-awareness. Note how this wonderfully rambunctious 2 year old was able to operate so consciously with so little input. I know everyone says kids have little impulse control. I know this is true in a way, but what is impulse control? It means forcing ourselves to do something we don't want to do, to resist our 'impulses'. I made self-regulation appealing! I also helped him notice the impact of his biting without any wrongness. He didn't need to "control" anything. It's what I call SMSR vs FMSR Self-Motivated Self-Regulation vs Fear-Motivated Self-Regulation. I have had such amazing experiences with countless kiddos over the years using this approach. Read through my articles and watch my videos, you'll find so many examples. If we can change our way of thinking from one of control and competition to a mindset of cooperation, collaboration and connection, then we can teach our kids whole new way of relating. The next time you want to help your kiddo with something, consider this story. See how you can implement the same approach and mindset. Connect, validate, go with and guide. This creates a much deeper and closer relationship with them. It increases the trust our kids have in us and in our guidance. It nourishes their ability to think for themselves. It will take some effort for us to adopt such a different way of approaching those moments, but the results are worth it. If you have a chance to try this, let me know how it goes. Peace, Vivek

Don't be the System. Be the Wise Guide that shows your kids how to navigate the system. We all know that there are real life consequences to our actions. We can teach kids about consequences without giving them consequences. Often we hear people say if we don't give them consequences they're going to end up in prison! I have been doing weekly self-empowerment workshops in prisons with my mother for a decade. This is real life prison. I can tell you the threat of punishment never stops these guys from coming back over and over again. We think teaching kids about consequences by giving them consequences is going to help them learn right from wrong when they're adults, but the evidence doesn't bear fruit. The only thing that consistently helps these men make different choices and not end up in prison again is when they look inward and learn to love themselves. No threat of punishment, even years in jail is enough to get them to change. It's self-worth that does the trick. Let's empower our kids with that mindset from the beginning so they don't need to go through that pain. Even if they don't end up in prison, they will be in a prison of their mind. This is one of the first things my mother tells the guys, that their true prison isn't the four walls. Many people walking around out there are also in prison. As these men start to see how Worthy of Love they are they naturally want to spread that love around. The reason my kid treats other people well is because she loves herself and she knows how it feels to be loved, so she wants to do that for other people. She's not doing it out of fear, she's doing it because she cares genuinely. How do you teach someone to care without fear? Peace, Vivek

On the same post I received the same feedback from two different strangers on two different comments. They both said they agreed with my point about honoring the freedom of children, and my post sounded like I was judging parents. I first clarified that I'm not judging them, because really I don't. I couldn't support the many families I do if they felt any judgment from me. But receiving the same feedback twice like this, I'm hip enough to know there's something for me to learn. I treat it as a gift. A chance to become more Aligned with my true self. What is a true self? I have no idea :D When I re-read my comments I felt the lack of empathy and compassion. I felt the anger. Now let me be clear, I LOVE my anger. I'm angry because children aren't being treated as they should. I have been angry about this since I was 3 years old. I love that anger. It has guided my life, my path, my parenting and my philosophy. You could almost say my philosophy of unconditional acceptance and love is based in anger. There's the meme for this piece! LoL What I have the opportunity to learn here is to notice that anger leaking out unintentionally. That is something I am continuously working on and learning. This is why I'm grateful for the double message. I would like to say both the people that offered me their feedback did so with great kindness and respect, which made it extremely palatable to receive. I was the recipient of the very treatment I advocate. Neither of them made me feel wrong. They saw me as a loving person and helped me to see myself more clearly. When I learn a lesson like this I take my time with it. I don't rush into making big changes. I let the feeling of the realization sink into my body and my nervous system. I listen for intuitions and insights. I hold the new ideas gently like a flower so that I don't put a lot of pressure on myself. The flower's scent is intoxicating and can also be overpowering. When I write my next comment I will make sure to pass it through the filter of this new level of awareness. It will be a conscious practice for a while until it becomes natural and integrated. To be clear I'm not acting out of fear of being criticized. I recognize criticism that's based in other people's projections. The experience I had on this post was not that. This is a beautiful example of the difference between the two approaches. Guiding with love and guiding with wrongness. I'm actually writing a whole other piece on that at this moment so keep an eye out for it. I share this experience with you in the hopes that you recognize it and the thought process is of some use or benefit in your life.

Almost daily I read a comment from someone saying "Young people today are too entitled. They have it too soft. They need to be toughened up" There are many variations to this theme, but they usually boil down to this. It is important to understand that entitlement comes from insecurity, from the fear that we are not worthy of love so we have to manipulate our environment in order to feel Worthy. Entitlement never comes from too much love and compassion. When we feel like we're not enough we have to try and make up for it by taking from others. This manifests as what we call entitlement. Not always, but often enough! When we feel we are enough, we don't have the need to take from others to lift ourselves up. In fact when kids are never punished they don't have the punishment mindset so they are naturally kind and generous. I've never understood the logic in thinking we're teaching kids to be kind by being unkind to them. The solution is never less kindness.

a Parenting is like Baseball a "Do you mean, if my parents say yes to me more often, I will feel like saying yes to them more often?" This was the question posed to me by an 8 year old girl during one of my very first parent coaching home visits. I had gone there to help her parents reach their kids because they were struggling every single day, in power struggles every single day. When I went into the home it seemed somewhat like a battle zone. It felt like it was adults vs kids! I started talking to the parents about shifting their patterns with the kids so they felt less like adversaries and more like they were on the same side. Part of this process of course is reducing how much we say NO to our kids. This was extremely hard for the parents to embrace, but this brilliant young mind understood the philosophy. So many aspects of mainstream parenting inevitably lead to this feeling of opposition and resistance. Recently I was talking about this experience with my spiritual teacher, Tulshi Sen. He said to me, "Vivek, parenting is like Baseball. When our kids go out into the world it's the same as when a batter goes up to bat. They are alone facing the opposition, but they know they have the support of their coach and team with them at all times." I wrote the following based on what he shared. This idea of seeing our family as a team is so powerful. In baseball when a player goes up to bat, they are alone facing 9 enemies. The whole team is focused on getting the batter OUT. The pitcher has only one thought, destruction. This is why baseball is a very apt analogy for life and parenting. In baseball, while it looks like it's just the batter against pitcher, on a good team the batter has the feeling of the support of all of their teammates. They have the memory of the work they've done together to get to this point. The player will also have the inspiration of the coach who has been refining their skill and boosting their confidence. As much as we try and take care of our kids, just like a player stepping up to the plate, there are going to be moments when our children will have to face obstacles on their own. This is why, as we send our kids out into the world (I'm talking even kindergarten here), we want them to know that the whole organization is behind them. Helping our kids feel like we are all on the same team is not the same as sheltering them from the reality of the world. So often parents will say if you don't give your kid punishment and consequences you're not preparing them for the real world. It does make sense to prepare our kids for the reality of life outside the home. We do our kids a favour when we give them a realistic understanding of the obstacles they may face. That doesn't mean we have to replicate those obstacles in our own environment and in our relationship with our kids! They will have enough challenges to face out in the world, let us instead be their refuge from it. All too often we become just another one of those obstacles for them to face. This is the inevitable result of a consequence and reward behavior management system. Instead we have the choice to be a wise and trusted guide, helping them learn how to navigate the complexity of their lives. Let's put our effort towards creating a family team that empowers our children such that when they are facing a challenging and frightening circumstance, and the way through isn't clear, they will never feel alone. They will feel the support of the team. They will feel confidence in their practice. They will feel the inspiration and empowerment they received from their coach (that's you!) The traditional, mainstream concept of parenting is that we are on opposing teams from our kids. It's a battle we need to win. We create an adversarial relationship. It doesn't take long for kids to get the message that we are not their coach. It is this mindset that leads to punishment and consequences. It is this mindset that leads to kids withdrawing and rebelling. The predictable responses to coercion are resistance, compliance and distance. None of which are deep human connection. None of which inspire the feeling of being on a team. I encourage you to think of your family in terms of a team. What kind of coach do you want to be? Does each member feel valued? Does the team feel like they can rely upon you for guidance and leadership? As a team we work together, we grow together, we support and encourage each other, we practice and learn skills together. We work as a family to overcome obstacles and create something beautiful together. In all of our interactions let us be thinking about what knowledge, attitudes and skills we can impart to build our children up. Focus all of our choices around what strength and inner resources can we leave them with, so they will feel a sense of empowerment and trust in their capacity. That way when they are up to bat facing someone trying to get them out, they will face it with confidence and courage. a

Teaching Values Non-Coercively We love doing jig saw puzzles in our house. Recently my kid bought the @[100064856793980:2048:Critical Role] puzzle. She's a HUGE FAN (if @[100064856793980:2048:Critical Role] sees this please connect with me. I'd love to surprise my kid with something <3). We have been noticing that each of us has our own way of working the puzzle. My wife uses colour flow. My daughter uses shape of the piece and colour cues. I focus in on the specific details, comparing to the picture. We all tend to be very dramatic about our puzzle game. Today she discovered that a few pieces I had put in were wrong and had made the whole thing impossible. She fixed it and we're back on track. As I walked by she pointed to the fix and my wife mentioned my strategy. I said: "I choose my strategy because I enjoy it. Not because it's flawless." This set off a wave of family laughter and we all felt the good energy. My daughter said: "That's JUST like me! My method isn't flawless either. I can't do the edges. But I like my way." She didn't resist it. There was nothing to resist. Self-Love in action. This moment will resonate in her nervous system and inform her in the future. It will inform her body awareness, her sense of optimism, her self-acceptance and realistic self-evaluation. If this were something that she wanted to get better at she now knows what to work on. If she's happy with her present level she has clarified for herself why she enjoys it. She also learns a lesson of accepting ourselves and others, even when there is difference. There was so much joy and laughter in the moment that we went farther than acceptance, we were celebrating! People always ask me how I teach values if I don't use punishment and consequences. Life has never ending opportunities to explore, guide and model the values you want to impart. Embrace the role of Guide in every moment, every interaction. I wasn't 'just making a joke'. I was revealing my process. I was sharing my wisdom. Hard earned wisdom. I did it in a way that was deeply received. This is what I call SMABO. Small Moments Affect Big Ones Small, every day, seemingly insignificant moments can hold great potential when we are present. Present with purpose. My purpose is to point my child to her own wisdom. I always focus on her inner journey. I look for the SMABO opportunities to point to self-acceptance, empathy or any number of values and mindsets I want to explore. What do you want to teach your kids? What do you want to explore with them? What mindsets do you think would be most helpful for them to navigate the world? What do you want them to know about relationships? About communication? About Emotions? About fear? Can you see how rich your co-learning relationship can be? Punishment fades away as we embrace the mindset of deep human relationship. We honour our roles as guides and use all of life to pass on our wisdom.

**There's no way in from the outside** There comes a time in every parenting journey where our kids might hold an opinion that we fundamentally disagree with. Perhaps we think that they are wrong, perhaps it is out of alignment with our values, perhaps we think they're going to hurt themselves with this opinion, or that they're going to hurt someone else! As kids grow they are continuously taking in the world and trying to process it. It's a very complex thing to make sense of. They have a growing body and brain, they have to. That journey is not always going to lead them where we want them to go. They are watching the way we respond very closely. They watch both consciously and unconsciously. They watch with their intellect and their emotions. They watch with their body and their nervous system. The choices we make around these moments informs them about how safe and reliable we are to engage with in the awkward process of learning. If we want to stay involved in their exploration of life for the long term, these moments in the developmental years are extremely important. They set a precedent that kids rely on later. They learn to rely on us to either be a stable place to lean on or place they need to hide themselves from. Realistically it's always going to be somewhat of both. The key is are we always making our efforts towards being that stable place? If we want to share an idea with our kids that may be different from how they think, doing it in a way that first connects deeply with their understanding is going to get us much further than trying to explain why they're wrong. When your kid says something that you disagree with and you have the impulse to correct them, or to "share your perspective", take a breath and pause. Shift your mindset to curiosity. Spend a few days or even weeks getting to know their perspective and really understand it. Ask them questions about it and explore their thinking. Of course this will help them understand it (and themselves) deeper as well. There's simply no route in from the outside. How DO I best explain challenging concepts to my child? By first going along with their perspective deeply and avoiding any sense of contradiction. The exercise of looking into the positive aspects of their thought process helps them, and US clarify our values. Once the values are clear it's much easier to talk about how those values apply in different systems and different situations. Now we're in a position to explore their thinking without it feeling like a threat or an interrogation. Trying to rush this emotional and relational trust building process by telling them they're wrong, that they should think and feel differently than they do is unlikely to produce long-lasting deeply integrated results. Focusing on nurturing the guide relationship will be the thing that allows us to impart our values in the deepest way. If we're not careful and we end up projecting our stuff onto our kids during their difficult times we can end up creating extra emotional and relational associations with the topic. Associations like: Power Autonomy Fear Defensiveness The need to belong To be seen To be valued These associations layer on top of the original conversation and now we're dealing with more than the subject matter. In order to have a relationship with our children where we can openly and safely discuss sensitive issues, we adults have the brunt of the responsibility in creating that safe space. Sometimes we can get caught in the right/wrong mindset when our kids think differently than we would like, when they hold opinions that don't align with our values. The right/wrong mindset carries within it the seed of judgement. Kids feel it. Their nervous systems respond to it. Kids quickly get into the habit of wondering whether their opinions are going to be accepted or criticized. Isn't it one of the most common stereotypes, the teen who responds defensively even when the parent isn't saying anything problematic? My kid says she sees that automatic reaction in the majority of her friends when they talk to their parents. Soon they are editing their words, thoughts and feelings, hoping not to share something that's going to get them criticized or questioned. So many kids feel they have to hide who they are from their parents. Much of the time when kids press back against us they are testing to see if we will turn away our acceptance. It's similar to the mainstream parenting idea about when kids push boundaries. The thinking is; children actually want us to hold the boundary stronger. This gives them a feeling of safety. (Ugh) The gentle parenting understanding is that they're seeking to meet an emotional need. They are testing to see if we will withdraw our acceptance of who they are. Will we stop seeing them? Will we reject a part of them? This is why, when communicating with our kids we will have the most profound impact if we pay attention to two main aspects of the interaction. Content and Relationship. It's important to nurture both at the same time. Often we get lost in the content, explaining, reasoning, asking questions and we lose sight of the relational/emotional experience. We will have a less effective impact overall if we look at any one moment as a single issue. Instead let's zoom out and see the wider arc. I talk about having a telescoping lens, where we are able to zoom all the way out to the broader context, and focus all the way in on the present. Framing this moment with our children in an overarching process of co-learning, life exploration and mutual guiding lasting 20+ years, gives us a different idea of time and scale. Then we can slow down and focus on making sure the connection/communication channel is open and stable. Work towards a relationship in which our kids WANT to hear our differing opinion, enjoy the experience, feel uplifted by it and look forward to more. This is possible when they feel no pressure to adopt our ideas, our values and opinions. It's not enough that we tell them, they have to feel it in their nervous systems. At this point instead of going the route that most people think of becoming entitled or resistant, what happens is kids reflect the same energy that they are treated with. This is why an attitude of curiosity is much more effective than control. Ask questions to explore their thoughts and feelings. Make sure you explore with the purpose of understanding, not convincing. Here's a phase you can use if you're I'm sure how to respond with curiosity when your kids say something challenging. You can of course change it up and make different versions, but the basic is: "That's interesting. Tell me more." This simple phrase can have the effect of deepening your relationship. It helps our children feel like we really care about their perspective. It also opens the door to exploring the subject matter in more depth. This also has the added benefit of helping them feel that you want to know what they think. In fact you could also say "I want to hear more." Asking follow-up questions to dig deeper helps them clarify their own understanding. At some point I will write a bit about how to ask questions in a way that deeply explores the topic, but doesn't have judgment attached to it. Once they trust you to partner with them in that exploration you can share your values with them without resistance. This is when you have the most profound and long-lasting guide relationship. In short, when your kids say something you disagree with, start by exploring their thought process before telling them they're wrong and letting them know what you think. Focus on relationship and keeping a mindset of curiosity. Guiding a human mind is a huge responsibility. Doing it with integrity and care, even more so! **

2020 09 22

If we want our kids not to lie to us, we have to make it safe for them to tell the truth. This means we have to make it safe for them to lie to us. . It can be very challenging when our children lie. It touches a deep place in us. We might feel hurt, betrayed or let down. We might feel like we failed and have a sense of urgency to fix the problem. . Usually our reactions don't inspire our kids to lie to us less. They may become better at it however, so they don't get caught! . Parents will often say to their kids that they don't have to lie to them, that they can always tell them the truth and they won't get in trouble. There is a subtle implication in this message that if they do lie they will get in trouble. . It's strange situation in which we're telling them anything they do we'll be there to support them, but they can never lie to us. . This means that any time if there's any component in what they are doing in which they've lied, they can't trust that we'll be there for them. They can't feel comfortable coming to us because we told them we never wanted them to lie. . it also means all the stuff we told them was safe to tell us actually isn't safe. If there's an exception for one thing, there could very easily be an exception to another. . When I talked to my daughter (now 23) about lying a number of years ago I told her that she never had to lie to me because I would always have her back in every situation. I told her that I was a safe place to share her victories and her mistakes. I told her that she would never receive a consequence or even my disapproval for anything she had done. . I ALSO told her that it would be a good idea for her to lie to me occasionally anyways! Sometimes it's good to keep things to yourself. . Kids lying to their parents is an ancient tradition. It happens all the time and I wouldn't want her to miss out on the experience! . I also told her if she ever did choose to keep something to herself, not to tell me the full story or even tell a direct lie, I would trust her judgment. I know that she had a good reason to do so and I would even be happy she did what she felt was right in that moment. . This way I made it safe for her to always tell me the truth and I made it safe for her to lie. . FREEDOM! . I am pretty sure that she doesn't lie to me very often and I also like to think that she is able to discern when it's appropriate to keep something to herself. . Life is more complicated than "Always tell the truth. Never lie." We don't tell the truth to everybody in every circumstance. It's not always the most effective, safe or even kind thing to do. . The study of when to tell the truth, how much truth to tell, what to keep to ourselves and how to communicate it, is a very delicate thing. It's not simple to understand and even less so to practice. I want my kid to feel safe exploring and learning this concept with me, rather than have me as an obstacle. . One of my one liners is: . "I didn't teach my kid not to lie, I taught her how to lie." . Because she never had to hide where she was going, what she was thinking, what she was feeling or what she was doing, we were always able to explore these things together. . Deep trust is one of the beautiful outcomes of freedom. . To this day I remain her guide. There aren't a lot of 23 year olds that actively seek out and value the wisdom and guidance of their parents without resistance. . This is what I mean in the meme when I say "we have to make it safe for kids to lie to us". We have to become so safe that they lose their fear of being vulnerable to us and lose their resistance to receiving our guidance. . In a safe relationship they'll never hear "I don't trust you because you lied." Those words make us feel judged and wrong. It's very difficult for kids to be vulnerable with their parents when they are afraid they might be made to feel wrong. . I feel that way to in all my relationships. Don't you? . When working with and guiding your kids, consider looking deeper into the idea of truth and falsehood. Examine your value around lying. Are you taking it personally? Are you reacting because of something in your past? Usually when there is tension there are underlying feelings and needs at play. . When we are honest with ourselves about our own stuff it makes it easier not to project it onto our kids. We can then be more present with them without making them feel judged. . The freedom, the choice and safety to tell the truth is something that comes from a connected, trusting relationship. It is a relational and emotional cause and therefore it needs relational and emotional work. . The behavior (the lie) is the effect not the cause. Therefore it doesn't work too try and get kids to change their behavior by telling them what to do and what not to do. Punishing them if they do the wrong thing and rewarding them if they do the right thing isn't appropriate, loving nor effective. . The impulse to tell the truth when there is risk involved does not come from being coerced to fall in line with expectation of an authority figure. Nor from avoiding the feeling that we've let down and disappointed our parents. Punishments and rewards do not inspire the courage that it takes. . Only love and connection inspire that courage. . Can you be that inspiration for your children? I believe you can. . Peace, Vivek d

When you read or hear something that you disagree with, before you express your disagreement re-actively - take a moment to think. Perhaps do some research into the concept. Ponder what is right and useful in the idea rather than what you might see as wrong in it. Consider making your first response a question rather than an argument. Ask for more information, for clarification, for definition. Seek to understand more about the idea and the perspective of the person who expressed/shared it. Taking this approach you will find a new freedom in your thinking and a deeper ability to learn and grow. -Vivek Edit to add: This post is more about my mind than it is about the effect I'm having on other people. I want to be a free thinker. I do not want to be controlled by the patterns of my past or external influences. I want to know my own values and align my thinking and choices with them. So when I respond with curiosity rather than an argument I am deepening my own thinking process. I am freeing myself from imposed automatic patterns.
