My daughter is so encouraging. After seeing one of my pics she replied: "A little more practice and you'll be a pro!" I appreciate how important it is to her to validate others. Actually as I write those words I question whether it's important to her, or has it become how she relates to the world because of how she's been raised? Maybe it's both. I have always been conscious of validating and encouraging my child. I focus on being unconditionally validating, which means I validate equally when she does something that is traditionally thought of as good or when she does something that is traditionally thought of as bad. As this text exchange indicates my now 23 year old young adult has taken on that quality quite naturally. She knows how good it feels and has a natural desire to want to offer it to others. An aspect of encouragement and validation that is important to focus on is nurturing a growth mindset. Growth mindset means that we recognize we are always in process... Growing! It has an understanding that the brain is not fixed, we can shift our patterns. Maybe not all of them, but certainly more than we might believe. Therefore, when I validate my kid I try not to make statements about fixed qualities or absolutes. For example I wouldn't say "You are very creative", I would say "I can see how much creativity this took." Or "Whoa! You really worked hard at this one." Instead of saying "That picture is quite beautiful", I might say "The water looks like it's really moving and I appreciate the shading around the trees. I almost feel like I'm in the forest." Or "You looked like you were really enjoying yourself while doing this." Instead of saying "I appreciate that you didn't hit and you spoke nicely when you expressed your feelings", I might say "I can see how much effort you put into that moment. I appreciated that you were thinking about the relationship and how you express yourself. I do that too, it's not easy. It's something that we can be learning about together our whole lives." When I read her response to me in this text I can see how she is putting an emphasis on the growth mindset. Encouraging me to practice without making me feel wrong for not having practiced 'enough'. In fact she says "a little more practice" which implies validation of the fact that I have practiced! Often when I post these kind of interactions with my kid people will comment that they feel I'm reading too much into it. I get accused of overthinking, they are just kids. I will occasionally respond by asking the person how much less they think I should be thinking about it! (I might be a little defensive about the whole thing, in case you couldn't tell) I do believe that parenting is one of the most important roles I will play in my life and it makes sense to me to think deeply about it. It makes sense to pay attention to and understand the millimetres. This is why a simple text exchange can have so much meaning. I often talk about not using praise and rewards to manipulate the behaviour of our children (you can find my article on that subject by searching the word 'rewards' on my Facebook page). How are encouragement and validation different? The difference is in the intent and implementation. Praise and rewards are problematic because they are conditional in nature. They are offered when our kids act in a way that we approve of, and withheld when they don't. The goal is to affect their behavior, choices, thoughts and feelings. Even with our best intentions, they can feel the underlying manipulation. The unconditional nature of encouragement and validation, combined with empathy, has a focus on inspiring kids to know themselves, love themselves and honour themselves. This is at heart, a relational process. One is an outside-in process, and the other is an inside-out process. When you are interacting with your children be on the lookout for ways you can validate and encourage them. Help them see that they are on a learning path and are always growing. Inspire them to feel you believe in them. Like my one liner says: "Children need us to believe them and believe IN them." Be that voice of validation and encouragement for your child, even in the hardest moments. They will in turn, learn to see it in themselves and offer it to others.

2020 08 07

Recently some parents asked how they could help their kids with their anger. They said they are teaching them to take deep breaths, getting them to punch a punching bag, giving them lots of empathy, and talking about different words he can use to express himself. Nothing seems to be working. What do we do? The following was my response which I really liked so I thought I would share it with you. The thing about helping kids work with their anger is we can very subtly give them the idea that their anger is wrong. . Even if you don't feel that way yourself, it still has an impact on their relationship with their anger that they have to take deep breaths, punch a punching bag and then we say "It didn't work." Implying that their natural emotional development is wrong. . I know you don't mean it that way, you sound like incredibly empathetic and gentle parents. I work with parents almost every day and I like to point out the millimetres in how we work with our kids because they can make a big difference when they add up. . In light of this I want to suggest something somewhat radical, try and give him the message that his anger isn't something to be fixed or controlled. I know this sounds like the opposite message, but we're taking a different approach here. Let him know that his anger has a real purpose and that you think it's beautiful. Help him feel a sense of deeper self-acceptance. . Self-awareness comes from self-acceptance. This is why radical acceptance has such power. . Maybe switch gears for a while and focus on the feeling of acceptance of his anger. Really embracing it as something beautiful about him. . I remember when I was working with this family a few years back, their kid expressed a lot of really big anger. I had encouraged them to tell him that his anger was beautiful, but every time they did he would get more upset. He actually hated it. . When I went over for a home visit one day I had a moment alone with him as we were walking through the woods. He was talking about his anger. He told me he hates it when people say that his anger is beautiful, because he had heard me say it. . I told him that I understood his feelings and that they were perfectly natural. I asked him if he knew why I thought his anger was beautiful? He shrugged his shoulders and said he didn't know. . I told him that he knew how he wanted to be treated as a human being. He knew he was a good person and that he deserves to be treated with respect. And I also believe that about him. . "So when you feel you are not being treated how you know you deserve to be treated, you get angry. I think that's beautiful because it means you love yourself." . He immediately stopped walking, paused and looked right at me. This wise 6 year old nodded his head, gave a little smile and said "Yeah, I get that." . In that moment he saw his anger as beautiful and understood the deeper meaning behind it. It was such a profound experience for both of us. . Everything I teach centres around working towards unconditional love and acceptance. I say 'working' because it is a journey, a lifelong journey of discovery. . After a certain amount of time of working towards this deep acceptance, you'll notice his relationship to anger shifting. At that point if you brainstorm with him about different ways he can relate to his anger it won't feel like you're trying to fix something that's broken. It will be more like how to work with something that's beautiful. . I hope this is a helpful perspective on how to work with children's anger.

2020 07 26

Recently I facilitated a workshop for young people to learn about anti-racism and social justice activism. The conversations we had were very deep and vulnerable. It took a little bit of time for the kids to trust me, but once they did they really opened up. I told them I remembered being 13 years old and feeling like nobody understood me. I could see that the adults around me weren't as smart as they thought they were. I felt they didn't value my wisdom, insight and perspective. I didn't want to forget what it felt like to be 13. That way when I was an adult I would never treat a 13 year old that way. I told them that I valued their insight, ideas and wisdom. I also told them that adults are guessing most of the time. We don't really know what we're doing any more than they do. We just act like we do. Don't take adults too seriously. The most important thing is to know yourself. What are YOUR values? What kind of person do you want to be? What kind of world do you want to contribute to? What kind of relationships and friendships do you want in your life? One of the kids parents was on the call and I was wondering what they might be thinking. dd I shared with them my favourite one liner: "I didn't teach my kid what to think. I taught her how to think." I would repeat that sentiment of empowerment in different ways throughout the talk. By the end the kids opened up to me so much because they could feel my deep respect and honouring of them as they are. It also opened the door for us to laugh, explore and imagine together. Next time you engage with a young person take a moment to observe yourself. Notice your mindset, notice any judgements or expectations that you are holding and try to release them. I say 'try' because it's not an instantaneous thing, it's more of a process. Releasing judgements and expectations is challenging because to a large degree they frame the way we see the world. They have a deep effect on our decision-making process. This is why it is so easy for us to project our reality on to other people. The problem with this is we miss out on sharing in their reality and having them share in ours. From a place of minimal expectation and judgment we can engage with the real wisdom of the young being in front of us. We can also remind them to tune in to their own wisdom and their own intuition. We can help them ask the self-reflective questions. I have yet to interact with a child that wasn't able to access their deep wisdom, their intuition, their ability to make sense of what's happening in their own way, and I always learn from it. When they notice me learning from them they become extremely willing to learn from me as well. This is how the relationship becomes mutual. These kids inspired me. They had such passion for change, wanting to make the world a better place. They give me hope for the future. I did my best to inspire them back. How can you inspire the children in your life? How can you be inspired by them? Peace, Vivek Patel

Give me everything you've got! Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel I tell people that I was a wild man as a parent when my now 23 year old daughter was young. Knowing who I am today it's hard for them to really understand. I was young and terribly idealistic (and I mean that in the kindest way). I was trying to do something radical in my relationship with my daughter. I wanted to turn the whole parenting paradigm upside down. I wanted to turn the whole world upside down! I wasn't content with doing mainstream parenting a little more gently. I wanted to rip it to shreds. My youth was spent rebelling and seeking trouble everywhere. I was aggressive, violent and self-destructive. When my daughter was born I channelled all that energy into rebelling against traditional thinking. I wanted a relationship where there was no coercion, no hierarchy, no force and no control. I wanted us to see each other's spirits deeply and continuously. I wanted to be one person in this world that always believed her and believed in her. That never criticized her for anything. Like my wise friend @[731895353:2048:Tanya Williams] once said, she could do no wrong. I treated everything as a learning and connecting experience. There was no reason to criticize or control. I was just telling a friend today that my daughter doesn't know what it feels like to get in trouble. She's never had that experience at home. I've refused to use my authority as an adult to say no to her. I've always honoured her decisions. One day a couple years ago I asked her how it would feel if I said no to her. We both sat in silence for a moment trying to imagine it. We couldn't picture it happening. If I have a different opinion than her about something I can share it for her consideration. I have no expectation that she'll follow my way. I will then fully support her in whatever decision she makes. This is deep respect and freedom. The benefit of this is I preserve and nourish the guide relationship I have with her. My opinion doesn't feel like force so she's free to let it in. She considers it without resistance. If we want our kids to listen to us, to let us guide them, they have to trust and desire that guidance. If there's any condemnation behind the guidance they'll feel it and hold it at arms length. They may even just resist on principle at that point. If they feel our respect and freedom they soften and protect themselves from us less. We cannot force someone to respect us. We can inspire it. This is the power of Non-Coercive parenting. In order to push so dramatically against my programming and parent in such a different way, I had to pour my rebellious spirit into fighting the system. Making my focus Relationship First. Setting my highest parenting priority to be connecting with my daughter. When I watch myself in this video I can see how intensely focused I was on shaking myself up. Focused on shifting my mindset. Creating my mindset. I'm hoping this will inspire you to release more and more control over your kids. Say an unreasonable YES on a regular basis. Don't be satisfied with where you're at. Dig deeper into the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset (NCCM). This video is from 2001 is a somewhat accurate representation of how our lives were in the early days. My kiddo would have been around 4 yrs old. She's holding the camera and I'm... well I'm doing my thing. This is the wild man Vivek, busting paradigms! In it I'm saying "give me everything you've got inside of and I'll give you everything I've got inside of me because I love y..." And it cuts out! LoL Please watch this and share your reflections with me. I'd appreciate it if you'd Follow @[100063717370269:2048:Meaningful Ideas] and share this around. If you would like more personal and consistent parenting support or if you would like to support what I do, I invite you to join my membership group https://www.meaningfulideas.com/courses/meaningful-ideas-membership ----

More thoughts on Consequences Imposing consequences is an ineffective and harmful way to attempt teaching values to children. It harms children's relationship with their parents and with themselves. The fundamental idea behind imposing consequences is to make our kids feel worse in the hopes that they will act better. It is to give them something that they are afraid of or that would cause them discomfort, pain or unhappiness so they'll want to avoid experiencing it again. If they don't want to suffer they will do the things we are telling them to do. When put this way it becomes clear that we are creating intentional and avoidable pain. This isn't a kind way to treat our children. It isn't a good model to set for them. I am sure you don't intend to make your kids suffer, you're just thinking that this is proper discipline. I totally get that the reason we may be tempted to use them is because we want our kids to learn responsibility and respect. The thing is that causing our children intentional and avoidable pain doesn't actually teach that. True respect and responsibility come from the feeling of caring for others, caring for the community, from empathy and fundamentally from LOVE! This is the deep and positive motivation that we want to impart to our children so they grow up into caring and compassionate individuals. Fear of losing something like a privilege or the fear of an unpleasant consequence are not positive motivations. Instead of fear, let's inspire self-love, self-knowledge and self-confidence. Let's help them heal the wounds that are holding them back. Let us help them believe in themselves and know that we believe in them! Let us make them feel an equal part of the family community so that they WANT to take care of it. Let us change our parenting so we can change the world! The prevalence of idea that consequences are the way to teach kids is a reflection of how parenting and human relations have been for millennia. Breaking out of that old paradigm is a hugely difficult task. It hurts just to think about it. The old paradigm that is based on control and focused on behaviour is so ingrained it seems impossible any other way can exist. But it does! That is why I am advocating for this parenting style. This a new paradigm based on relationship, communication, collaboration, connection and mutual benefit. Making the switch from one to the other is HAAAARRRRDDDD! Just look at any parenting post on Facebook and see all the controlling, aggressive and defensive responses. It's hard for most people to even begin to consider this way of relating to kids, let alone adopting the philosophy full on. It's the struggle and pain of that switch that can make these ideas so unpleasant and unreasonable to people. But I believe everyone has the potential to do this. It takes a lot of courage to shift perspectives like this. Do you have that courage? A way that has NO forcing or manipulation? A way that is all about communication and respect? A way that includes kids in every step, every decision? This new way is difficult, but it is also so beautiful. It is beautiful AND more effective in the long run.

An argument for imposing consequences I often hear is that they will have to deal with consequences in the real world so we have to prepare them now. There's an idea that if we don't start when they're 4 they'll be somehow disadvantaged when they're 18 or 20 and go to work.

A classic example is if they are at a job and they don't do their work well they have consequences, they can even be fired. Then what will they do? So how will they learn if we don't prepare them? I'd like to first make the point that I don't think modelling one's home after a corporate workplace is the best environment to emulate as a family. Let our homes be a refuge for our children from a world of coercion, violence and fear. If you're working somewhere that the reason you do your job well is because you don't want to get fired, that is a fear based motivation. It is not because you care about the company or your workmates. It's not because your boss or manager has your respect. This is not a very efficient or effective work environment. It doesn't inspire loyalty in employees. It doesn't make them want to go that extra mile. In fact it's more likely to have them work the minimum they can get away with, not care deeply about the quality of their work, cut corners when they can, lie to you if it's to their best interests and leave as soon as they can find something better. Many companies these days are changing their structure to one that is more horizontal, collaborative and systems aware. Employee review processes are shifting from a criticism of their work to a more empowering and supportive model, looking at successes, goals and areas of improvement. The idea is to help them feel they are doing meaningful work. They want their employees to feel cared for and relevant. Inspire them to feel they are part of a team rather than a cog in a machine. This leads to greater job satisfaction, performance and retention. This is how companies SHOULD be run and the more progressive ones do. They assist their employees rather than threaten them. They uplift them rather than punish. They take into consideration the whole being, including what's happening in their private lives, not just their input output. Even in the corporate world the old paradigm is starting to fade. It makes sense to prepare them for the hardships of the real world, I just don't agree that imposing consequences (intentional and avoidable pain) is the way to do it. If you want to help them navigate what they'll face, it's more effective to investigate what are the skills, attitudes and knowledge that people need in order to deal with the reality of society. To develop a clear understanding of the relationship with their own hearts and minds that gives them the motivation to do well in life. Then make a long term plan to consciously teach and inspire those skills in every facet of our parenting. Consequences don't do that. I teach martial arts. If i want to teach my students to defend against a punch I don't just start punching them in the face and hope they learn the most effective way to defend themselves. I slowly teach the skills they need first. How to recognize the attack How to move How to block How to counter strike Then when they have a good grounding in these skills we can test them out CONSENSUALLY and consciously in a way that feels supportive and safe. This is much more effective and the lessons are deep. In the same sense consequences aren't teaching the skills kids need to get along well in life. They only hurt and cause children to fear us and protect themselves. When we become unsafe they will lie to us and hide their truth from us. They turn to other sources for their life education. Peers, other adults, the internet and media. Now we've lost our opportunity to share our wisdom and teach them the important things in life. Can we think of our role as parents to be wise guides and learning partners who inspire, instead of authority figures with power and control? What wonderful relationships we will form with our little humans by taking this perspective and what a powerful gift we give them as they find their way in the world. Please share with others and subscribe to my page <3

A Lesson from sitting with my very sick Father - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel A Lesson from sitting with my dying Father My father seems like he's about to die. (Edit: he passed away Jan 29, 2020) I'm 51 years old, and I'm sitting at his bedside. He's got tubes everywhere. When I talked to him, he's not responding to me in any way. I don't know if he knows I'm there. Sometimes he squeezes my hand when I squeeze his. Mostly, it's hard to tell. I don't have a really close relationship with him, I never have. I mourn that loss, you know. Knowing myself, the kind of person I am and the way my life has gone, I don't think I could have made different decisions than I did. I don't regret any decision that I made, with respect to him. I actually regret a lot of my decisions, but not any with respect to him. He's a really nice guy, and he tries to be a really nice guy, but we've never really had a real relationship. I could never really be vulnerable in front of him. In a lot of ways I had to shut myself off emotionally, to be in relationship with him. It's taken me years and years to dig through all that and find myself and a sense of my authenticity again. Never mind getting hit and all that stuff. But you know, the gift that comes from all of that is that I've known all my life, since I was three years old that I was going to be a different kind of father. So when my kid came came along I put every other concern aside. I know that's hard in life to do, but I put every other concern aside. I didn't care about anything else and I just chose relationship. I know I talk about this all the time "Relationship First", but it's not just a philosophy, it's a whole life beingness. It's a deep, deep priority setting. It's a huge risk and it's a huge cost. It really is, because there's a big letting go that comes with it. I can't put relationship first and hold onto control. I can't do it and hold on to coercion. I can't punish or give consequences. I felt it in my bones, you know, it was never really a choice. When I talk about being three, I remember being over my dad's knee on the landing of the staircase. I had done something wrong, I don't know what, but he was hitting me for it. And I'm three right? Something in me was like self-aware at that moment and I suddenly knew I was a three year old human. I knew there was nothing I could possibly do that deserve to be hit. There's nothing I could possibly do to deserve being hit. I knew that right? So I'm over his knee and he's hitting me, and I have this like out of body experience where I'm kind of hovering over the scene and I'm watching it. I'm in it, because I'm feeling it, I'm getting spanked, but I'm also watching it. I teach a three part micro-practice to parents. One is micro-meditations, one is micro self-compassion, and one is micro self-observation. Those three go together. As part of the practice we do a couple of different meditations about observing ourselves. It occurs to me as I think of this story, that is what happened to me when I was three. I'm looking at the scene. I see from deep inside of me, the injustice, the indignity, the disconnection from humanity. I could see it, I could feel it, though I didn't have the words for it. Sitting here now at 51, I can still feel that moment. I said to myself: "One day, I'm going to be a dad and I'm not going to be like that. I'm going to do it differently." A resolve hit me in that moment, and I knew it was true. Now my daughter's 22 and the relationship we share is something I don't even understand, to be honest because I don't have a precedent for it. I've never experienced or known anyone who's experienced 22 years of non-coercion, 22 years of radical acceptance, 22 years of vulnerability. 22 years of being brought up in a home where she could do no wrong and never got told she was wrong. We never said No to her and she never got in trouble. In fact she doesn't even know what that feels like. Can you imagine not knowing what it feels like to be in trouble? I'm always looking over my shoulder thinking I'm in trouble! It's Deep in me from childhood. Not that she hasn't gotten in trouble at school or whatever, but it never touched her heart because she knew that she could never be in trouble. The relationship we share has this deep trust where nothing is held back. Not that she tells me everything. I encourage her not to. It's important for us to have some things to ourselves. This is part of the respect and honouring of her as a person. This is what develops that trust where they don't feel they have to protect themselves from us at all. Then I go and sit in my by my father's bedside as he is now, you know. in the latter years of his life he became such a gentle soul. Maybe he has been for a while and I just never got to know him again? In the last in the last few years I've done my best to let him know that I love him. I never said anything about forgiveness because I don't think he thought there was anything to forgive. I think he felt it. I think he's dying knowing that I love him and that's what I wanted. I'll probably spend a couple more decades working out my father issues and whatever, figuring out who I am. I'm crying as I write this. Thinking that soon his physical form will be gone. You know, I didn't expect to cry for him. I really didn't. But I'm glad I am. I mourn the loss of not having that deep connection with him, and that's okay. It made me who I am and it brought me to the insight of how I raised my daughter. That's worth everything to me. And now I have the honour to share the deep learning that I've done on this path. I get to help other parents have the kind of deep connection with their kids that I experience. This is a gift my father gave me in a way. I get messages every day from parents who say that they're closer to their kids than they ever imagined possible. Their kids are feeling more trust, joy and more connection with them than they ever thought would be possible. What a joy that is. I remember a couple of years ago, my kid and I were in the car together and I asked her: "Hey kiddo, how would you feel if I ever said no to you?" She's 18 or 19 years old at this point. In all these years the number of times I've said NO to her, really, is so rare. So the two of us had to sit there for a minute and try to picture it. We were trying to see it, you know, and it was hard for us to imagine. We were both kind of screwing up our faces and really trying to imagine me saying no to her. We laughed at this and then more seriously she said: "Well, you know, Dad, it's hard to imagine, because you never say no. So if you actually did say no, I would trust it. I would know you had a good reason. I trust you I was like: "Wow, thank you. I really appreciate that trust." And she says: "Well, that's just how it is." I like the two sides of that story. The one side being that we couldn't quite picture what it would feel like for me to exert authority over her. To act as if I had power over her. I never related to her as if I had power. We were equals. It's so foreign to most parents, this idea of letting go of that authority. That's why we do often hear the phrase "I'm your parent, not your friend." There's this level of connection with another person that you just can't get when you hold power over them in a hierarchical relationship. As parents we have systemic power over our children. We have access to resources power, we have emotional power and physical power over them. We also have the choice how we relate to these powers. I made a very conscious choice not to exert those powers and to voluntarily share them with her. She's always felt that deep respect from me. My daughter calls herself my guinea pig because the idea of unconditional acceptance, radical acceptance was so against what everyone else was doing. There are lots of objections people have, I've heard them all over the past 20+ years. I had prior telling me "Oh, there has to be a line. There has to come a point where you'll put your foot down." My foot never went down. I did it, I'm doing it and I'm teaching it. Thank you Dad. There are a growing number of parents are are learning to do without power and author, learning to collaboratively and non-coercively with their kids. The amazing thing is when we form a deep relationship with them, they are so much more open to our guidance, so much more open to our wisdom. The thing about systemic power is, unless we're actively working to dismantle it, and fight against it, we're benefiting from it. That's why even now that she's 22, I work tirelessly to watch my mind, my thoughts, feelings and perceptions. I watch my reactions, my responses and the stories that I have. That's a lot of damn watching! I do it so that I am relating to her in as deeply human way as possible. Deeply connected, respectful and equal. I call it having a "whole-being co-learning relationship of equals" So thanks dad. I appreciate you for that.

The Message of Empathy: "Your Feelings Are Valid - You're Not Alone" In this video I talk about giving empathy to my father who is in the hospital right now. Empathy is so powerful. I've always focused on creating a consistent experience of it with my daughter. When we do this our children know they can rely on our response to be one of empathy, acceptance, curiosity and exploration, in every possible circumstance. This creates a deeply trusting relationship that endures through any hardship. This is one of the gifts of Empathy.

2020 01 07

Micro Meditations The Micro-Meditation is one piece of a three part series of micro practices I teach to parents. They are: 1) Micro-Meditation 2) Micro-Compassion 3) Micro-Self-Observation I will be writing more and making more videos about them as they are so helpful. A Micro Meditation is taking One Conscious Breath. Do your best to block out the world and just take one breath. Let your shoulders relax. Feel the ground under your feet. Feel the infinite sky above your head. Just for one breath. Then go on about your day. When stress and overwhelm try and get their grips in you, that's a good time to connect with your centre. Much of life, as a conscious parent, is a search for balance amidst the chaos. This is where the Micro-Meditation is so powerful. People who practice it are finding greater awareness and calm in difficult moments. I try and practice Micro-Meditations throughout the day. In this video I demonstrate it live while I'm doing dishes. I was actually doing the meditation and was inspired to record the moment. I called my daughter to bring her phone. She loves helping me share these ideas! *Gentle Consistency* Sometimes people ask me for help when they have trouble meditating. I share the Micro-Meditation. The two main areas of struggle people have about meditation is either that they don't have time or they cannot concentrate. The Micro-Meditation addresses both of these concerns. With it being simply one breath, it's almost always the ideal time and place to meditate. We can even connect with our deep selves on the toilet! Take a momentary break from playing with your phone and use your toilet time to reach out to the spirit of the universe. (Then go right back to your phone like I do!) You can take that one breath pause when you are picking up a toy off the floor, when you are brushing your teeth, when you are putting your shoes on, or even tying your kids shoes. Take that one breath Micro-Meditation and value it, honour it and Oh, believe that you are worth it. There is an accessibility to meditation when you are not having to carve out blocks of time from your day. Take That Slow Conscious Breath In and out That's All. In and out. Practice being deeply with yourself for that breath. What does it mean to you to be deeply with yourself? This is something anyone can accomplish. The goal is not to have a quiet mind while you do it. The goal is simply to take the slow conscious breath. You can have your eyes open or closed, you can have your hands in any position and you can let any thoughts wander through your mind. *Honour the Micro* It is important to be gentle and soft with yourself in this practice. I find any discipline I engage in, I have a much higher chance of resiliency if I am gentle with myself as I practice. The reason for this and I've seen it time and time again is that people will feel they should take a second breath and then a third. Then the next day feel like they should also do three, and the pressure mounts. Maybe 3 will turn into 4 then the next day they can't concentrate for 4 and they get frustrated. They feel like a failure and give the whole thing up. I've seen it, and experienced it, many times. That's why I love the Micro. There Is No Rush In fact the success of this technique specifically relies upon you not rushing the process. If you practice every day you can build your capacity to do the Micro practices. You will be giving your mind the message that you really care about your development. If you do miss a day, don't beat yourself up for it. This is very important. Just get up the next day and keep going. It's life. Let's be kind to ourselves. The benefits will start to creep into your life. Gentle Consistency is a way of Tricking Resistance. Easing the obstacles to meditation. *Find Other Areas To Apply Gentle Consistency* See if you can find other things you want more of in your life, and that you are resisting, and apply this principle. Look for ways you can engage in things in a gentle and consistent manner. *The Micro Is Strong.* Gentle consistency may seem weak to some, but I have learned that it has great power. I myself have terrific resistance to growth and change. Gentle consistency helps me in building capacity, creating new patterns and accomplishing things that I otherwise never would. I hope this concept helps you in your journey of personal growth. Peace, Vivek Please share and subscribe <3

2020 01 06

It's never too late. The time is now - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel It's never too late. The time is now. One of the most common question I hear from parents who are thinking of transitioning from traditional parenting to non-coercive, conscious, gentle parenting is: "It's it too late for me to change parenting styles?" It's hard to imagine letting go of things like consequences, rewards and removing privileges. It's even harder to let go of authority and control over our kids. We can feel unsure and afraid of how things will go. Sometimes when parents become aware of how they are controlling and coercing their children they want to change. There is often a concern whether they can ever truly heal the disconnection in their relationships with their kids. Some parents are concerned that children will not be able to adapt to a new way of interacting. They are used to the old ways and it would just be confusing for them. In this video I talk about how regardless of what your situation is, it's always the right time and it's never too late to change. Your family will draw closer together, your kids will feel more trust and openness with you and real deep healing and connection can be nurtured.

2019 12 21

The Gratitude Response The Gratitude Response One of the most powerful secrets to increasing harmony and cooperation in your home. So many parents struggle with how to work with or discipline their kids in such a way that they learn proper values and their homes are places of harmony and cooperation. Often the strategies that we employ end up bringing us the opposite results. The system of thinking handed down to us is that strong boundaries and clear expectations, combined with rewards for positive behavior and consequences for undesirable behavior, will produce the kind of environment that we want in our homes. The thing is, that is rarely ever the case. Rewards and punishment are not effective strategies in producing long term harmony and cooperation or deep relationships where people care about each other's needs. In fact, when we engage with someone regularly from the coercive mindset, it degrades the relationship they have with us and degrades the relationship they have with themselves. The gratitude response is a way of responding to our children in difficult moments, and even in positive moments, so that they have a different experience of us. Throughout the day we engage with our children many, many times. Every time we do we inform them about the nature of our relationship, about our intentions, our desires, their worth/value, their boundaries and about how we see them. The gratitude response, when practiced regularly, creates for children an environment and relationship in which they can relax into us, trust our guidance and be open to learning from/with us. In this article we are going to look at the gratitude response in detail and how to respond to your children in different situations. As well as the theory behind how it works and what obstructs it. I will offer you some specific practices that you can take away. Implementing them you will see positive changes in the way that you and your kids interact. The gratitude response is a way of inspiring the feeling of appreciation, gratitude, compassion and the desire to care for each other's needs. I have found that the natural generosity of children can be awakened, sustained and nourished through practices like the gratitude response. The idea is to practice responding with gratitude to whatever situations arise with your kids. When I'm interacting with kids, I really try and make gratitude my first response. So when they say something, when they do something, I want them to feel that I see there's value in what they've done. Even if it is something we wish they weren't doing, when we start with gratitude, rather than with the correction or an explanation, it shifts how we are received by them. They become more open to hearing us. We are their guides and I take that role very seriously. We have lived many years and made many mistakes. It makes sense for us to share what we've learned with them, to talk about different way of thinking about things, looking at things or different strategies to get their needs met. Whatever it is that we want to share, if we start with gratitude we have a much better chance of having a good dialogue and avoid the eye rolls or defensiveness. When we receive gratitude it opens our hearts, makes us less defensive, it softens our thinking and deepens connection. Gratitude is powerful. It's also can be really challenging. When our children do something you don't want them to do, gratitude is likely not your first reaction! This is the challenge of the Gratitude Response, to find something that we can be grateful for in the difficult behaviours. A lot of the time I will say "Thank you for showing me your feelings". Sometimes it's hard to find anything else that we can be grateful for. At the very least we can be grateful that they're showing us their feelings, rather than keeping them inside, so we can help them. I'll actually say that to kids, "Thank you for showing me your feelings now I can help you. And I really want to help you." When kids know that you sincerely want to help them, and that's their consistent experience, they're more open to receiving that help. Another thing I say to kids is "Thank you for asserting your boundaries." So a kid might yell NO, or scream, "I hate this food", or "I'm not getting dressed." or "I am not going to put my shoes on!" and we're five minutes late already and we're in a rush. it would seem reasonable to think, "Well, this is not the time for me to use gratitude, Vivek, because we're trying to get out of the house." Yet if we continue to use the same stressful ways of dealing with those situations we will keep struggling with the same issues, in the same way. Coercion is NOT more efficient, but it is more familiar. That's one reason it's hard to let go of. The experience of slowing down for a moment and really being grateful creates a whole new way of relating to the moment and to each other. When your kids say NO, try using some version of "Thank you for asserting your boundaries. It's your body and you know your body best." When we tune in and acknowledge, "Wow, there was something powerful there" it lowers resistance in those moments. They feel like like we're seeing more than just a troublesome behavior. We see them as wonderful learning beings, we see their need for acceptance and belonging. The love goes in deep when we can consistently see these beautiful things in our children. This is why is worth practicing seeing beyond the troublesome behavior when they are clearly doing a troublesome behavior. Another supportive gratitude statement is, "Thank you for listening to your body." Let's say this is something about food, or about sleep, or hygiene. These are common areas for parents to encounter resistance. If we use the Gratitude Response we might say, "Thank you for listening to your body. I trust that you know your body and you have great body wisdom. I appreciate that about you." A little while ago I was talking to this four year old friend of mine at a dance festival. I'm a dancer and I often go to dance events. The parents asked me if I would hang out with the four year old for a while because they wanted to dance. While we playing he started talking about what he wanted to eat. I was naming all these different options and he would tell me is he looked them or not. I started talking about how well he knew his body. I appreciate how you are really listening to the messages of your body. He was so happy and said, "Yes, I really do know my body. And I learned to listen to my body when I was 2." He then proceeded to tell me all about the journey of listening to his body. He was really tuned in and excited with the idea. This is one of the benefits of gratitude, when we can recognize those things it inspires kids to know themselves more. It increases their self-awareness. It helps them become comfortable with their process. It helps to reduce fear. When they hear the gratitude messages consistently - Thank you for listening to your body. - Thank you for asserting your boundaries. - Thank you for showing me your feelings. - Then kids grow up thinking, Oh, I have the capacity to listen to my body. Oh, it's natural for me and acceptable for me to show my feelings. Oh, it's, it's reasonable for me to assert my boundaries. When they get these messages over and over again it lowers their resistance to learning with us and increases their trust in us. Granted it's not always our most natural response, especially if we didn't receive it growing up. Let's say you're on an important call and the come up and scream right at you on the phone. Immediately you might want to say, "Don't do that, I'm on the phone." But if we can instead dig deep and see the need beyond the behaviour we can say, "Thank you for screaming and getting my attention, because I see you really need me. I want to give you my attention because I love you. I thank you for giving me this information." Wow, what a difference that is. Here's an article video combo I created about working with kids who interrupt using these principles. If you're thinking that we are reinforcing the unwanted behaviour again, read the article and see if it answers any questions. www.bit.ly/kidsinterrupting The great thing about the gratitude response is that you can practice it in every day moments. You don't have to wait for big events. That's what my acronym SMABO is all about. Small Moments Affect Big Ones. SMABO So if you practice responding with gratitude first in small moments, then when the big moment comes, you'll be more prepared. +++++++++++++++++++++++++++ It helps when working with the Gratitude Response to develop a gratitude mindset. Practicing on ourselves is powerful. Practice trying to be aware of what we can be grateful for in our lives. One of my favorite times and one the hardest times to do it is when I make a mistake. To be sure there's no shortage of opportunities because it happens all the time. I'm human! I call myself a Mistake Making Machine. So what I do is I practice finding something to be grateful for in the mistake that I made. Sometimes what I'm grateful for is that I've learned I need to honor myself more. Sometimes it's that I see I see habit patterns I hadn't seen before. Often my mistake reveals something to me I didn't know about myself. Sometimes it's just an opportunity for me to be compassionate with myself when I've done something I wish I hadn't. I practice and practice giving myself validation and looking for what I can be grateful for in a situation. Being perfect at it is not the point. Practicing is the point. As I practice with myself I get better at being able to do that more consistently with children. Gratitude isn't only the words. Just like empathy isn't always the words. Even the feeling of gratitude is so powerful, right? Sometimes the phrase 'Thank You' doesn't even feel like gratitude, depending on what is the feeling behind it. This reminds me of a blog I wrote back in 2015. I was at a dance event and this one family had brought their three year old. Kids usually recognize me as a kindred so I wasn't surprised when the three year old wise teacher came over to me. I had a tennis ball I was using to massage my back. It was a bright pink tennis ball and she was so excited by it. She came over and said, "Ooooh that's so pretty." I said, "Oh, thank you. Do you want to play?" So we were rolling and tossing it back and forth, having a grand old time. I saw the look in her eyes about how much she was enjoying it. It was pure delight. It was her spirit, her unchanging consciousness shining through. I could feel the joy that was pouring through her for this beautiful pink tennis ball. At the end of two or three minutes playing I said, "Would you like this?" And she gasped, "Really?" And I said, "Yeah, yeah. Would you like it?" She really heard me and simply said "Okay." There wasn't the "I shouldn't take it" hesitation because we were so connected, in tune, playing together. She knew my offer was genuine, she could sense it was a gift to me to offer it to her. Right? She felt it so she took it. It was so natural for her to take it. I was honestly grateful to her for receiving it. In response she poured out this powerful gratitude to me. I was taken aback by the joy in her face. It lifted me so much my eyes lit up. When she saw my eyes light up, her eyes lit up even more. Suddenly we were caught in this gratitude cycle with each other. I was so thankful to her for accepting me and trusting me. She was so overjoyed that I was interacting and seeing her this way. We were to equal spirits appreciating the moment. It was beautiful... And then... Her dad comes over... He says "We gotta go Sweetie, give Vivek his tennis ball back." She got this sad look on her sweet little face as she was handing it back. She was also confused. I said, "No, no, no, I gave it to her. I gave it to her." He said "Oh, okay. Honey, Say Thank you now. Did you say thank you to Vivek?" At that moment, the two of us looked in each other's eyes and we knew he didn't understand. We felt it and both of our energies just fell. There was like this deep disconnection from the beautiful spirit of gratitude that we had. I said to dad "Oh, my friend, she said, thank you, to me more profoundly than you can imagine." or something like that. He said, Okay, good. Let's go. and off they went. Here's the link to that blog if you'd like to read the original. This young teacher showed how Gratitude is more than words. I will always remember that interaction. The gratitude response is about having that energy of really accepting and embracing our children. We're not just thankful for them behaving "well". We're thankful for them all the time. We're thankful for their struggles, we're thankful for their tendencies and patterns, we're thankful for their awkward learning processes, because they're no less awkward than ours. We accept them, we love them and we're grateful for them. It's amazing to me that when we offer kids appreciation and gratitude for who they are, how powerfully they respond.
