I recently got into a bit of a heated discussion with some guy on a post about "the 4 Problems with Punishment." He was making the case that if we don't control our kids they'll just do anything and chaos would ensue. I say that somewhat tongue in cheek, but that's essentially it. So we're going back and forth a bit when he writes a long response that had this line in it: "We are not good at heart, we are evil" That is the assumption he makes that prevents him from seeing a non-coercive possibility. I responded to him: "This is where we differ. As long as you believe that you'll never understand this philosophy. I prefer to believe that our essence is goodness and we're taken away from it by the very systems of thought you are defending. The philosophy I share points children to their inherent goodness and inspires compassion and empathy, not fear. I think at this point we both recognize an irreconcilable difference! I am struck by the assumption of evil. It's the direct effect (IMNSHO) of the traditional parenting paradigm. We are punished and made to feel wrong when we make mistakes or act out of alignment with the expectations adults hold for us. This gives us the repeated message that we're broken and need to be fixed. That we cannot be trusted. That we are not fundamentally good. Why else would this person who is my guide intentionally cause me pain, whether it's emotional, relational or physical pain, in order to modify my behaviour? There must be something wrong with me. Then we have adults who believe human beings, including themselves, are fundamentally broken and evil. This is one of the core principles of the parenting philosophy that I share... To do everything we can so children know they're unconditionally worthy of love, acceptance and connection. I do this because I believe that when children grow up feeling deeply valued and respected they will naturally reflect that mindset in all their relationships. Thank you for posting this Eric. It's given me pause to reflect. This work we are sharing with people is so vital. Every parent out there who is sweating with the effort of cycle breaking, I honour you. It's hard work to operate from a new paradigm. I thank you as well. You are helping the planet to heal and making the world a better place. p.s. I'm making this a separate post because it's come to my attention from some friends that when this is shared the piece I wrote above doesn't automatically accompany it. So I have to make a new post so this text can also be shared. I'm copying Eric's post below and also putting a link to his original post.

2019 09 05

This article is a detailed exploration of the Why and How of Empathy. Why is it important? How can we offer our kids empathy in a way that really has a powerful effect? Empathy is one of the most powerful parenting tools in the Conscious Parenting toolbox. There is a magic in empathy. I've seen it create incredible transformations in people. I've seen deep disconnects and seemingly inescapable pain shifted and eased with the experience of deep empathy. Every time I remember to put empathy into practice I see that magic. When I forget to use empathy, or I use it less effectively, I can always feel the effects. Less connection, less healing, less trust. There is something deep in being seen, in feeling we are not alone, not broken or warped. There is something that happens in the way we relate to our suffering when we feel connected to another human spirit. That connection is ALWAYS there, but life is such that we don't always feel it, we're not always aware of it. Life is so often hectic, stressful, painful and even frightening that it requires effort to open to that feeling of being connected to another. Empathy is a doorway to that connection, to that place where we feel a sense of acceptance and belonging. These are deep feelings. They help create a space to heal, a frame in which to hold the suffering. It also helps us see ourselves more clearly when we can have our experience reflected back to us we suddenly can see it with new eyes. An important point to note is that it's not necessary to have the right words or to guess the exact feeling to empathize with someone. It's really about the feeling of connection, receptivity and acceptance. Empathy also creates the ideal conditions for growth, learning and self-examination. The traditional parenting paradigm inhibits deep learning. It has at its centre the idea that mistakes are a problem. If mistakes are a problem, then learning is a problem. Learning is a messy process. It requires making lots of mistakes, examining them and making changes based on that analysis. Trying again and seeing what happens, then learning more. Repeat the cycle every day and you're a lifelong learner. This method of working together to learn from "what happens in life" (my replacement for the word mistake) is so wonderful. It really can be so exciting. It's like we're all on an adventure of learning together. That's why empathy is so important. It tells our kids that we see they are learning. This allows them to be much more open to our influence. When they feel we have a complaint about something that they honestly can't help, it feels like the complaint is about them, not just the behaviour. It says something deep about the nature of a child if we relate to them as if they CHOSE to hurt someone else or themselves. Instead let us see that kids are struggling when they act out. If they feel from us that we see they are doing their best, at their present level of development, with the tools they have, their hearts open to us and we become so much safer. When they can let go of self-protection in this environment, self-awareness and self-reflection bloom. From this deeply accepting mindset real collaborative problem solving can take place. Our emotions are such a big part of who we are that it makes sense to pay attention to and work with them in all our interactions. I have slowly realized over time that I used to ignore this important aspect of what makes us human. Emotions are deep and complex. They are integral to every experience we have. I used to be a fix-aholic. I would jump to what I thought was the obvious solution when someone expressed a problem. I thought it was a waste of time to bother with empathy when the answer to your suffering is right there. As I am growing in my understanding I am recognizing that I don't have to give up my identity as a fixer to offer empathy because empathy is actually the most direct and efficient route to finding a solution. Most often when empathy is sincere and sustained answers and insights arise on their own. These are always the most powerful solutions because they come from within. If kids feel bad about a mistake empathy is the most effective approach. Sometimes we try and rush kids out of their difficult feelings because we don't want to see them suffer. The fact is that emotions leave a residue if they are rushed through. The residue builds up layer after layer and it leaks out in other ways. I see that in myself every day. Reactions come out that aren't in alignment with my values. I know much of that comes from my residue. Instead of rescuing our kids from their pain if we can be with them in it, validate it and let them know their feelings are normal and that they're not alone, they soon find an emotional peace with themselves. This is a powerful way to teach emotional regulation. Kids become comfortable with their emotions and can find their way through them. This is why I stopped thinking "don't try to fix" and changed my mindset to "Empathy IS Fixing". Kids (and really all of us) are more prone to self-awareness and self-reflection when they are feeling seen and accepted for who they are.

EMPATHY BUT Sustained vs. Interrupted Empathy

So often when parents practice empathy with their kids they claim it doesn't work. It's frustrating that we're told empathy is supposed to help kids when they have big emotions, then when we are doing it and nothing changes it creates a lot of stress. Empathy is more than the words we say, it is the emotional connection and space we create for our kids. This space of acceptance feels really good. In order for children to experience and process their emotions they need time. It's not something that can be rushed, and yet we often do rush it. One way we do this is when expressing empathy we usually have the lesson not far behind. "I see that you're upset she took your toy. That's a natural feeling, BUT you can't swear at your sister when you're upset. You have to find a different way to express your feelings." This is what I call "EmpathyBut. The empathy is real. Those first few words are so helpful. The kid just starts feeling that sense of the weight being lifted (shared) and suddenly it's gone. The lesson is important too because we do want to teach kids to express in more appropriate ways. The issue is the timing is off. We lose a lot of effectiveness when we rush the lesson. The experience of connecting with the emotions needs to sit for a while before moving on. It takes time to process emotions. This is when our patience is important. We have to be willing to wait. Maybe an hour, maybe all day, maybe for a few days? We get in a rush to teach respect and change behaviours. This rush pushes us towards coercion. The problem is, coercion creates resistance which results in less self-awareness and self-examination. Organic opportunities for the lesson always arrive, it's not something we have to rush. Let the empathy sit. The process of examining emotions and learning from them requires a certain objectivity. This can't be achieved when we're at the height of our emotional intensity. We have to be able to look at our emotions from a distance in safety (relative safety). This is why the ability to move through our emotions to a place of being centered is important to develop. It is from this centered place that we are able to look at our emotions. To see more clearly their cause and the effect they have. By doing this we learn to choose different responses in the moment. This is the non-fear based way to learn and practice self-regulation. It is possible and it is practical. It is a far more resilient, stable and adaptive value system than one gained from force and fear. Trying to get kids to avoid wrongness is a fear based motivation. If we tell kids "This was wrong so don't do it." We place their attention on what is wrong. Focusing on avoiding the wrong is not the highest ethical standard we can pass on. Instead of thinking about what would be the least wrong, let's inspire kids to think/feel about what would be the most right. Thinking of the least wrong implies that I can seek to be the least cruel. Thinking of what feels most right is seeking to be the most loving. This difference is important. Wrongness is not a positive learning focus. When we work at transforming our patterns with our kids from EmpathyBut to Sustained Empathy it shifts everyone's mindset. Building new patterns is a daily struggle because it's not natural. We just have to keep practicing every day. It's only by tuning in will you know when your kid comes out of the intense emotions and be centered enough to self-reflect. Until then any lesson is just going to bounce off, or even worse, create resistance. Try expressing the empathy without the lesson. Sometimes we need the empathy to stand on its own for a while before we are ready to hear the lesson. EmpathyBut sounds like this. When we say: "I understand that your friend made you mad and it hurt you feelings they took your stuff. But it really hurt their feelings when you said mean things like that. You can have your feelings, but you have to learn to express them without hurting anyone." The empathy is interrupted as soon as we say "But". In this interaction the kid really gets about 3 seconds of empathy. They need to feel our acceptance and empathy longer for it to settle into the heart. When it is cut short too quickly kids learn not to trust it. They can't lean into it because they're never sure when it will disappear. This is how they learn to repress rather than process their emotions. Here's an example of empathy without the But: "Hey sweetie I see that you're mad they knocked down your tower." "Yes I'm mad. They're so mean." "Ya, it's so hard when someone wrecks our hard work. Of course you're upset about it. I can totally understand that. I get upset too when my friends aren't nice to me. Thank you for sharing your feelings with me. I love you." And that's it. No lesson. No But. The opposite of EmpathyBut is what I call "Sustained Empathy". I know it might feel like we're letting them get away with something if we don't add the lesson. The thing is that this sustained empathy helps kids be open to learning and exploring the issue together. This openness is more important than anything else. In fact they often end up coming to us to help them learn because we become such a safe place. Offering empathy is often more important than offering solutions, instructions and especially corrections. I love you, I accept you and I relate to you. Empathy is letting your children know you understand their feelings and that what they are feeling is natural and acceptable. It is letting them know they are not alone, that you have felt something similar in the past and therefore can relate in some way to what they're going through. When we rush kids through their big emotions they feel inhibited to express themselves in the future. It isn't safe for them to show their feelings so they repress them. If we deny our big feelings they do not disappear, they just get buried inside and can affect us for years and years. This is why it's important to face and embrace our feelings. Learning to regulate our emotions and choose better expressions does not effectively rest upon a foundation of repression. We cannot regulate something we have repressed. It has to be present for us to learn to manage it. If we get kids to repress their emotions because we don't find their expressions acceptable (justifiably or not) we are not teaching regulation. We also make it harder for them to learn to regulate in the future. Therefore if we are going help our kids learn emotional regulation and appropriate expression, we must support them in facing and embracing their feelings in all their fullness. Empathy is the doorway to change. It creates the ideal conditions for self-reflection and learning. Acceptance doesn't mean stagnation. When we offer empathy we open the mind to the possibility of change. Especially with young people who are so vulnerable, if they feel listened to, heard and accepted they are much more willing to learn and grow. This is because they feel safe. It's important to keep in mind that empathy isn't a quick fix. It isn't actually a fix or a strategy. It is sincere human connection. There is no timetable for this. If we are trying to reach a kid who is angry, sad, belligerent or apathetic, it will take time. It requires consistency and effort. When child has been hurt in some way or has put up an armour around their heart for some reason, it will take time and effort to pierce their shield and touch their spirits. This patient effort is so important because when they let us into their hearts we become the most effective guides. This is why EmpathyBut is so counterproductive and why sustained empathy is so important in order for us to get through to them. This is how we develop trust with our vulnerable young people. We truly touch their hearts when we continue offering empathy and acceptance past the point that they think is reasonable and even possible. This is why it is called sustained empathy. Transitions are Challenging. It may be that sustained empathy will be a new way of interacting for you. Perhaps you already practice empathy, but you have been doing some EmpathyBut. Now you want to commit to Sustained Empathy. If this is so be ready for a bit of a battle. They will fight you and resist you at first. Big emotions will come up. Emotions there may not have been space for before. It can resemble a tornado at times. In fact I call the transition period the "Test, Treat and Tornado phase. This applies to the whole of transitioning from traditional parenting to Gentle Parenting. I am writing an article about the "Test, Treat and Tornado phase so keep an eye out. This is when the Sustained Empathy becomes a practice. We have to tend to our inner garden very consciously so we can be in a guiding, supporting mindset with our kids. Once they see that we are not backing away from this new openness, they will let us in past the shield they have put up. Once your foot is in the door then you can do the work of healing, connecting and supporting them. This support that they so desperately want and need. Our Acceptance must be greater than their Resistance. The challenge here is to have our love, our empathy and our acceptance be stronger and more stable than the defenses they have built. If they feel that their armour is safer than we are they will not let us in. Sustained Empathy has transformational magic in it. I invite you to work with it in your family and see what unfolds. Here's a link to my video on EmpathyBut for more in depth info https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QX1RDvCped0&

I teach a system of empathy that is easy to remember and implement called "Use your EARS"

Empathize Affirm Relate Support There are so many families practicing EARS and they share with me how powerful this structure is when they consistently use it. Since we are now practicing Sustained Empathy the EAR of EARS is really the most important part. The problem solving will happen, but first let's focus on connection and emotional processing. One common situation where kids get frustrated is when they have to wait& for anything. They can get frustrated and super cranky. Often we try to distract them, sometimes that works. If it doesn't we try and explain why we're waiting hoping that will calm them down. Then we get upset and try to insist they behave differently. E - Oh my love I see that you are angry because you have to wait. A - It's perfectly natural to feel upset when that happens. R - I feel that way too sometimes when I have to wait. This kind of response, especially when repeated consistently over time, helps kids feel like their feelings are supported, accepted and even embraced. Life is hard sometimes, we all have to experience it. We can also be here for each other as we do. The feeling of being seen creates deep connection. That's empathy! I love EARS. It feels so loving. It's not a formula, even though it looks like one. It's more like a guided emotional journey. A journey we take together. The great thing about EARS is that it's easy to remember. Listening is so integral to empathy that it makes sense for us to use our ears! Let's look at each of the stages individually. Step 1 E - Empathize Empathy is connecting with another person on an emotional level. It's communicating that we hear and understand them. It's letting them know they are not alone. Empathy has many definitions. Just type "what is empathy" into Google and you'll see. Each of us has a different experience with empathy. We have different relationships with it and we also have different skill levels with it. It is a skill that is worth working hard at. One of my saying is, there is nothing you can practice that you won't get better at. Empathy is a skill we can practice and EARS helps give us something specific to work with as we do. It may feel awkward at first, but like all new skills eventually this becomes natural. E is first because starting with recognizing and reflecting a persons shows them we're tuning in. In the next sections we will explore how "Affirm/Acknowledge" helps to remove judgement. Followed by how "Relate" creates a feeling of being less alone, of belonging. Empathizing is a multi-layered relational experience. It includes the words we choose, the feelings we have and how we share them. It is affected by the mindset we hold, how we relate to suffering and joy as well as our comfort with emotions. Our ability to recognize and hold space for our own triggers and emotions is important. If we are managing them for ourselves during the empathy experience we aren't asking the other to do so. Emotional regulation doesn't mean we don't feel deep emotions. It's more about having a reliable and resilient relationship with them. This way when you are going through something I can be present for you. I can offer you empathy and care for your process. I am able to hold space for you because I'm able to care for my own needs while doing so. When we offer empathy to our kids we are teaching them this skill experientially. The more kids are able to rely on our empathy, the more they reflect it back in their own attitudes and behaviour. Here are some examples of Empathy statements: "I'm sorry you hurt your knee. It's looks painful. I see how upset you are. I'm sorry you're in pain" "You feel hopeless right now. I can see that. You lost your job. That is so hard. The future is unknown and scary." "It sucks you didn't get invited to that party. I can imagine you're feeling a bit rejected by your friends. That's a painful feeling." Notice in each of these examples I've avoided offering a solution. After offering empathy for the hurt knee I could have said: "Your knee will be better in no time. Don't worry about it." After "You feel hopeless right now. I can see that. You lost your job. That is so hard. The future is unknown and scary." I could have said: "Don't lose hope friend, things will work out." After "It sucks you didn't get invited to that party. I can imagine you're feeling a bit rejected by your friends. That's a painful feeling." I could have said: "What counts is how you feel about yourself in the end anyway. And I like you!" But I didn't. It's not that those things aren't true. It's not even that they aren't helpful. It's that they aren't helpful yet. This is why EARS is so important. The EAR, (Empathizing, Affirming, Relating) creates an environment conducive to the S which is Support. The S isn't so much suggesting or solving the problem. It is entering into a Co-Problem solving relationship with your child or whomever you're interacting with. I have noticed that when EAR is done really well, S seems to arise on its own. Meaning when someone feels heard and validated and when the relationship is connected and reliable, a solution that addresses deep needs usually shows up. Step 2 A - Affirm/Acknowledge This step is about softening the shame and wrongness that so often accompanies big feelings. It normalizes the experience. It acknowledges the journey and process the person is on. The basic message is: "What you're going through is natural. It makes sense for you to feel that way given what you're experiencing. A lot of people in the same situation would have a similar response." The traditional parenting model does not support a deep relationship with our emotions. The most prevalent message is that our emotions aren't acceptable if they disturb others, especially those we depend upon and those with power over us. This is why even happy emotions can feel unacceptable. Painful emotions often have so much judgement and shame attached to them that it can cloud our ability to feel deeply. This is why A is so important as a step. Letting someone know that you see this is a natural human experience, that they aren't broken because they're feeling these things helps people be more willing to sit with their feelings. This is how we foster integration instead of repression. Some examples: E Your blocks got knocked down. Oh No. I see you're so upset. A Of course you're upset about it. It's natural to feel sad when you worked so hard. E You got so mad at your brother for how he talked to you that you hit him. You are really angry right now. This sure is a hard moment for you. A If someone talks to you in a way you don't like it's normal to get angry. It's hard NOT to in fact. None of this is saying that you want them to do it again, but it does provide deep acceptance of where they are at. Step 3 R Relate Often when we're in pain, we can feel very alone. This feeling of isolation is a kind of an attack on our consciousness. It can make the pain feel much harder to handle. So when we are able to feel like there is someone else with us, really with us in our pain, it helps us to relax into it. It doesn't necessarily make the pain less, but as I mentioned before, the goal is to go into the pain and form a comfortable relationship with it. so we can move through it and come out the other side more integrated. So the R Relate section of EARS is how we connect human to human with each other. My past, my history, my experience. E is Empathize, it's really about offering my heart to the person in that moment. Seeing their pain and feeling it with them. A Affirm is about letting them know that it's totally natural what they're feeling. It's a normal natural human experience. The R Relate is more about you and I connecting as humans. Sharing my past, my feelings and experiences. It creates a feeling of belonging. The reason that the R is at the end of EARS is because if you say it too early, it puts the attention on you rather than on their process and experience. But after you've done E and A, they know you're listening, they feel you're listening. When you can feel that trust take root it is time for R. R can sound like: "Yeah, I get really upset when people talk to me that way too. ""When I when I got fired, it was really hard for me." I was scared and angry at the same time ""Last summer I built a sand castle" and then it got knocked down. I was really upset! Recently my niece who was afraid of cats had a scare when she was visiting. After I had given her some Empathy and Acknowledgement for her fear I said to her, ""You know kiddo, I'm afraid of bees." She looked at me and said ""You Uncle Vivek?" It was such a deeply validating moment for her. There was this relaxation that came over her. Later when we went back outside the cat was still there. Through our experience of EARS she felt much calmer and more empowered when she was trying to face her fear. So the R Relate is really important. Empathize Affirm/Acknowledge Relate Support E - Oh my love I see that you are angry because you have to wait. A - It's perfectly natural to feel upset when that happens. R - I feel that way too sometimes when I have to wait. If we put all three together, suddenly we have this incredibly powerful tool that allows us to really be with our children in their pain. This helps them move through it in a way where it's accepting and integrating. Repeated experience of this, especially with kids, really gives them a strong relationship with their own emotions. And this is something they carry with them rest of their lives. Here is my video on EARS for more info - https://youtu.be/fXGOGUrALEo Vivek Patel

EmpathyBut - Sustained vs Interrupted Empathy - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel EmpathyBut Sustained vs Interrupted Empathy

So often when parents practice empathy with their kids they claim it doesn't work. It's frustrating when we're told empathy is supposed to help kids when they have big emotions. When we are doing it and nothing's changing it creates a lot of stress. With empathy it is vital to understand how the process works, what's happening behind the scenes and how to implement it most effectively. This article combined with the video will give you a solid foundation to redesign your empathy skills! Empathy isn't the words we say so much as the emotional connection and space we create for our kids. This space feels really good. However it doesn't last long. When expressing empathy we usually have the lesson not far behind. "I see that you're upset she took your toy. That's a natural feeling, BUT you can't swear at your sister when you're upset. You have to find a different way to express your feelings." This is EmpathyBut. The empathy is real. Those first few words are so helpful. The lesson is important. We do want to teach kids to express in more appropriate ways. The issue is the timing is off. We lose a lot of effectiveness when we rush the lesson. The experience of connecting with the emotions needs to sit for a while before moving on. It takes time to process emotions. This is when our patience is important. We have to be willing to wait. Maybe an hour, maybe all day, maybe for a few days? We get in a rush to teach respect. This rush pushes us towards coercion. The problem is, coercion always leads to less safety which results in less self-examination. The process of examining emotions and learning from them requires a certain objectivity. This can't be achieved when we're at the height of our emotional intensity. We have to be able to look at our emotions from a distance in safety (relative safety). This is why the ability to move through our emotions to a place of being centered is important to develop. It is from this centered place that we are able to look at our emotions. To see more clearly their cause and the effect they have. By doing this we learn to choose different responses in the moment. This is the non-fear based way to learn and practice self-regulation. It is possible and it is practical. It is a far more resilient, stable and adaptive value system than one gained from force and fear. Avoiding wrongness always is the fear based motivation. If we tell kids "This was wrong so don't do it." We place their attention on what is wrong. In my opinion I do not think that focusing on avoiding the wrong is the highest ethical standard I want to pass on. I want my kid to think about what feels most right, not the least wrong. Thinking of the least wrong implies that I can seek to be the least cruel. Thinking of what feels most right is seeking to be the most loving. This difference is important. Wrongness is not a positive learning focus. This is why I work at transforming my relating from EmpathyBut to Sustained Empathy. It's a daily struggle because it's not natural. I'm better at it than I was. At the same time we don't want our kids to be ignorant of the world and how it works. We teach how the coercive systems in society operate. We point out that they won't receive this kind of acceptance in other systems. We learn and explore together how to navigate them most effectively. We learn about it, we just don't subscribe to it. It's only by tuning in will you know when your kid comes out of the intense emotions and be centered enough to self-reflect. Until then any lesson is just going to bounce off, or even worse, create resistance. Try expressing the empathy without the lesson. Sometimes we need the empathy to stand on its own for a while before we are ready to hear the lesson. EmpathyBut sounds like this. When we say: "I understand that your friend made you mad and it hurt you feelings they took your stuff. But it really hurt their feelings when you said mean things like that. You can have your feelings, but you have to learn to express them without hurting anyone." The empathy is interrupted as soon as we say "But". In this interaction the kid really gets about 10 seconds of empathy. They need to feel our acceptance of them for longer. The acceptance and empathy need time to settle into the heart. When it is cut short too quickly kids learn not to trust it. They can't lean into it because they're never sure when it will disappear. Imagine saying at that moment something like: "Hey sweetie I see that you're mad they took your toy." "Yes I'm mad. They're so mean." "Ya, it's so hard when someone wrecks our hard work. Of course you're upset about it. "I can totally understand that. I get upset too when my friends aren't nice to me. Thank you for sharing your feelings with me. I love you." And that's it. No lesson. No But. The opposite of EmpathyBut is what I call "Sustained Empathy". I know it might feel like we're letting them get away with something if we don't add the lesson. The thing is that this sustained empathy helps kids be open to learning and exploring the issue together. This openness is more important than anything else. In fact they often end up coming to us to help them learn because we become such a safe place. Offering empathy is often more important than offering solutions, instructions and especially corrections. I love you, I accept you and I relate to you. Empathy is letting your children know you understand their feelings and that what they are feeling is natural and acceptable. It is letting them know they are not alone. That you have felt something similar in the past and therefore can relate in some way to what they're going through. It is so important for kids to know that their feelings are natural, acceptable and that they're not alone. When we criticize kids for their big emotions they feel inhibited to express themselves in the future. It isn't safe for them to show their feelings so they repress them. If we repress or deny our big feelings they do not disappear. They just get buried inside and can affect us for years and years. This is why it's important to face and embrace our feelings. Learning to regulate our emotions and choose better expressions does not effectively rest upon a foundation of repression. We cannot regulate something we have repressed. It has to be present for us to learn to manage it. If we get kids to repress their emotions because we don't find their expressions acceptable (justifiably or not) we are not teaching regulation. We also make it harder for them to learn to regulate in the future. Often parents will point to how their kids don't act out as much as proof that the consequence or criticism worked. With this perspective we can see that what we've created is repression and not regulation. We haven't taught a skill. Therefore if we are going help our kids learn emotional regulation and appropriate expression, we must support them in facing and embracing their feelings in all their fullness. Empathy is the doorway to change. It creates the ideal conditions for self-reflection and learning. Acceptance doesn't mean stagnation. When we offer empathy we open the mind to the possibility of change. Especially with young people who are so vulnerable, if they feel listened to, heard and accepted they are much more willing to learn and grow. This is because they feel safe. It's important to keep in mind that empathy isn't a quick fix. It isn't actually a fix or a strategy. It is sincere human connection. There is no timetable for this. If we are trying to reach a kid who is angry, sad, belligerent or apathetic, it will take time. It requires consistency and effort. When child has been hurt in some way or has put up an armor around their heart for some reason, it will not be easy to pierce their shield and touch their spirits. This patient effort is so important because when we do touch their hearts we become the most effective guides. When you offer empathy and it is rejected by your child they are testing you. It's not that the empathy didn't work. They honestly do not know this is what they are doing, but they are testing to make sure our love and acceptance is stable. Intuitively they need to know that our love cannot be shaken regardless of how they behave. This is why EmpathyBut is so counterproductive and why sustained empathy is so important in order for us to get through to them. This is how we develop trust with our vulnerable young people. We truly touch their hearts when we continue offering empathy and acceptance past the point that they think is reasonable and even possible. This is why it is called sustained empathy. If you are able to stand in this space of acceptance, connecting and loving no matter how much effort your children put into pushing you away, eventually their hearts will open to you. Transitions are Challenging. It may be that sustained empathy will be a new way of interacting for them. Perhaps you already practice empathy, but you have been doing some EmpathyBut. Now you want to commit to Sustained Empathy. If this is so be ready for a bit of a battle. They will fight you and resist you at first. Big emotions will come up. Emotions there may not have been space for before. It can resemble a volcano at times. This is when the Sustained Empathy becomes a discipline. We have to tend to our inner garden very consciously so we can be in a guiding, supporting role. Once they see that we are not backing away from this new openness, they will let us in past the shield they have put up. Once your foot is in the door then you can do the work of healing, connecting and supporting them. This support that they so desperately want and need. Do they really want my support? It is natural to ask: "if they want and need it, why do they push it away? The fact is even though deep down they want and need unconditional love and support, they will not drop their armor to let it in unless they feel safe. They have built this armor over years so its layers are deep. It comes out of a need for safety and only a greater safety can break it down. The kids have come to depend on this armor. Persistence will be required. Our Acceptance must be greater than their Resistance. The challenge here is to have our love, our empathy and our acceptance be stronger and more stable than the defences they have built. If they feel that their armor is safer than we are they will not let us in. Sustained empathy has transformational magic in it and I invite you to work with it in your family and see what unfolds.

This is why the ability to move through our emotions to a place of being centered is important to develop. It is from this centered place that we are able to look at our emotions. To see more clearly their cause and the effect they have. By doing this we learn to choose different responses in the moment. This is the non-fear based way to learn and practice self-regulation. It is possible and it is practical. It is a far more resilient, stable and adaptive value system than one gained from force and fear. Avoiding wrongness always is the fear based motivation. If we tell kids "This was wrong so don't do it." We place their attention on what is wrong. In my opinion I do not think that focusing on avoiding the wrong is the highest ethical standard I want to pass on. I want my kid to think about what feels most right, not the least wrong. Thinking of the least wrong implies that I can seek to be the least cruel. Thinking of what feels most right is seeking to be the most loving. This difference is important. Wrongness is not a positive learning focus. This is why I work at transforming my relating from EmpathyBut to Sustained Empathy. It's a daily struggle because it's not natural. I'm better at it than I was. At the same time we don't want our kids to be ignorant of the world and how it works. We teach how the coercive systems in society operate. We point out that they won't receive this kind of acceptance in other systems. We learn and explore together how to navigate them most effectively. We learn about it, we just don't subscribe to it. It's only by tuning in will you know when your kid comes out of the intense emotions and be centered enough to self-reflect. Until then any lesson is just going to bounce off, or even worse, create resistance. Try expressing the empathy without the lesson. Sometimes we need the empathy to stand on its own for a while before we are ready to hear the lesson. EmpathyBut sounds like this. When we say: "I understand that your friend made you mad and it hurt you feelings they took your stuff. But it really hurt their feelings when you said mean things like that. You can have your feelings, but you have to learn to express them without hurting anyone." The empathy is interrupted as soon as we say "But". In this interaction the kid really gets about 10 seconds of empathy. They need to feel our acceptance of them for longer. The acceptance and empathy need time to settle into the heart. When it is cut short too quickly kids learn not to trust it. They can't lean into it because they're never sure when it will disappear. Imagine saying at that moment something like: "Hey sweetie I see that you're mad they took your toy." "Yes I'm mad. They're so mean." "Ya, it's so hard when someone wrecks our hard work. Of course you're upset about it. "I can totally understand that. I get upset too when my friends aren't nice to me. Thank you for sharing your feelings with me. I love you." And that's it. No lesson. No But. The opposite of EmpathyBut is what I call "Sustained Empathy". I know it might feel like we're letting them get away with something if we don't add the lesson. The thing is that this sustained empathy helps kids be open to learning and exploring the issue together. This openness is more important than anything else. In fact they often end up coming to us to help them learn because we become such a safe place. Offering empathy is often more important than offering solutions, instructions and especially corrections. I love you, I accept you and I relate to you. Empathy is letting your children know you understand their feelings and that what they are feeling is natural and acceptable. It is letting them know they are not alone. That you have felt something similar in the past and therefore can relate in some way to what they're going through. It is so important for kids to know that their feelings are natural, acceptable and that they're not alone. When we criticize kids for their big emotions they feel inhibited to express themselves in the future. It isn't safe for them to show their feelings so they repress them. If we repress or deny our big feelings they do not disappear. They just get buried inside and can affect us for years and years. This is why it's important to face and embrace our feelings. Learning to regulate our emotions and choose better expressions does not effectively rest upon a foundation of repression. We cannot regulate something we have repressed. It has to be present for us to learn to manage it. If we get kids to repress their emotions because we don't find their expressions acceptable (justifiably or not) we are not teaching regulation. We also make it harder for them to learn to regulate in the future. Often parents will point to how their kids don't act out as much as proof that the consequence or criticism worked. With this perspective we can see that what we've created is repression and not regulation. We haven't taught a skill. Therefore if we are going help our kids learn emotional regulation and appropriate expression, we must support them in facing and embracing their feelings in all their fullness. Empathy is the doorway to change. It creates the ideal conditions for self-reflection and learning. Acceptance doesn't mean stagnation. When we offer empathy we open the mind to the possibility of change. Especially with young people who are so vulnerable, if they feel listened to, heard and accepted they are much more willing to learn and grow. This is because they feel safe. It's important to keep in mind that empathy isn't a quick fix. It isn't actually a fix or a strategy. It is sincere human connection. There is no timetable for this. If we are trying to reach a kid who is angry, sad, belligerent or apathetic, it will take time. It requires consistency and effort. When child has been hurt in some way or has put up an armor around their heart for some reason, it will not be easy to pierce their shield and touch their spirits. This patient effort is so important because when we do touch their hearts we become the most effective guides. When you offer empathy and it is rejected by your child they are testing you. It's not that the empathy didn't work. They honestly do not know this is what they are doing, but they are testing to make sure our love and acceptance is stable. Intuitively they need to know that our love cannot be shaken regardless of how they behave. This is why EmpathyBut is so counterproductive and why sustained empathy is so important in order for us to get through to them. This is how we develop trust with our vulnerable young people. We truly touch their hearts when we continue offering empathy and acceptance past the point that they think is reasonable and even possible. This is why it is called sustained empathy. If you are able to stand in this space of acceptance, connecting and loving no matter how much effort your children put into pushing you away, eventually their hearts will open to you. Transitions are Challenging. It may be that sustained empathy will be a new way of interacting for them. Perhaps you already practice empathy, but you have been doing some EmpathyBut. Now you want to commit to Sustained Empathy. If this is so be ready for a bit of a battle. They will fight you and resist you at first. Big emotions will come up. Emotions there may not have been space for before. It can resemble a volcano at times. This is when the Sustained Empathy becomes a discipline. We have to tend to our inner garden very consciously so we can be in a guiding, supporting role. Once they see that we are not backing away from this new openness, they will let us in past the shield they have put up. Once your foot is in the door then you can do the work of healing, connecting and supporting them. This support that they so desperately want and need. Do they really want my support? It is natural to ask: "If they want and need it, why do they push it away? The fact is even though deep down they want and need unconditional love and support, they will not drop their armor to let it in unless they feel safe. They have built this armor over years so its layers are deep. It comes out of a need for safety and only a greater safety can break it down. The kids have come to depend on this armor. Persistence will be required. Our Acceptance must be greater than their Resistance. The challenge here is to have our love, our empathy and our acceptance be stronger and more stable than the defences they have built. If they feel that their armor is safer than we are they will not let us in. Sustained empathy has transformational magic in it and I invite you to work with it in your family and see what unfolds. Please watch the video for more info then let me know your thoughts on all this in the comments. Thank you. Vivek <3
