2019 07 03 I am not a nice person. Many people think I am a nice person because of the kinds of things that I share on Facebook, Instagram and YouTube. (By the way, you should follow me on Facebook, Instagram and YouTube @meaningfulideas)!! But the truth is, I'm not a nice person. I am hurt and wounded and angry. I am often filled with petty, judgemental and vengeful thoughts. It requires great effort for me to act in a way that is consistent with my values. The thing is, I ceaselessly and untiringly put that effort in, so it really does seem like I'm a nice person most of the time. But anyone who's seen me when I slip from that effort knows very well that I am not a nice person. I am not criticizing myself here. I work to accept all sides of myself, to honour and feel deeply all of my feelings. The reason I mention this is because so much of the parenting stuff I write feels out of reach and unattainable to many people. But the fact is, it's really honestly, continuous hard work. To be able to offer your kids a true unconditional space is hard work. I have to fight against the pain based reactions that I have. So that I can make different choices. I am not inclined naturally, or perhaps I should say habitually, to be gentle, accepting, and kind. It is a choice that I make and a choice that I work hard for, fight for. Yes, it is a fight. It is like I am daily in battle with myself. Some time ago, a friend of mine told me that they had an insight. The reason that I spent 30 years studying martial arts was so I could form the discipline needed to fight this inner battle. If you find yourself yelling at your kids, if you find yourself losing your temper, if you find yourself setting coercive limits, and you want to change, please know that it is possible. No matter how hurt you are, no matter how angry you are, no matter how much pain you have, it is possible. It is not a light switch that turns on. It's not like suddenly one day you wake up and decide you want to change and everything changes. It is a day by day effort. And you will slip back and you will make mistakes, just like me. The only thing really is to not give up. Today I spoke in a prison and I shared much of my past and much of the struggles with these guys because I know they can relate. They know the frustration and the trials of trying to deal with and overcome past pain and anger. They see that I am still fighting every day to change my patterns, to make different choices. I told them that as humans we have this amazing capacity to choose different from our reactions, to choose different from our instincts, habits and our patterns. We all close our eyes and just felt inside our brains this feeling of being able to choose. What a wonder it is to me that we have this power to choose. It is something I don't take for granted. It's something that I work on developing. Just today I was entering a construction zone near Dufferin and Eglinton and the lane two lanes merged into one. The guy behind me raced ahead and wouldn't let me in. I got really upset. I honked and gave him the finger. When I was 25 I would not have been able to let this go. I would have escalated the altercation and been angry all day. However 50 year old Vivek is very different from 25 year old Vivek so I pulled over and took a bunch of deep breaths. I relaxed my muscles, felt my butt on the seat connecting to the earth. I said to myself, "This is not who you are, Vivek, this is not who you want to be." I told the guys this today because I wanted them to know that even after so many years of daily work on myself, I still have to fight this battle. So please know that every millimeter of effort you put in has an effect. Every millimeter of growth you achieve makes a difference. Every mistake that you make is an opportunity for learning and self-evaluation. Even if we do give up at times, that's natural, even unavoidable. If we get depressed and sad, it's natural and unavoidable. If you're anxious and frightened at times, i's natural and unavoidable. All of these things are part of the human experience, especially when we are filled with pain and trauma in our lives. That doesn't mean that you're a failure. It doesn't mean there isn't another opportunity to try again and make a different choice. I said to the guys in the prison today, the wonderful thing about linear time is there's always another moment just after this one where we have a chance to make a different choice. Because the past, with all its pain, tries to control us. The future with its unknown and uncertainty tries to scare us. But in this moment, we have choice. Then we have another moment with another choice and another moment with another choice. This is the path. It's never ending. It's always evolving. Let's walk it together.

2019 06 26

Take the Pickle Out! 18 years ago when my daughter was in kindergarten I joined the school Council. I remember it was one of the very first meetings. One of the parents started going on and on about how the kids wear their pants down below their butts with the underwear showing. He was exclaiming with great authority "That is not how pants are worn. That's not what they're for. What is it about kids today?" Really, honestly, I got up in the middle of the meeting, I pointed my finger at this guy and I called him "Grandpa!" He wasn't older than me, right? I said, "Grandpa, have you forgotten what it's like to be young? Have you forgotten what it's like to be a teenager and live in this world?" I said "Get over yourself, man!" I was a lot less diplomatic and patient in those days! It was like a month later they voted me school council president and I was the president for the entire five years I was there. So let me tell you friends, the pickle is real. The pickle is real.

2019 06 09

Parenting and Intuition Workshop Parenting and Intuition Workshop This is a video I made of a talk I gave recently on the power of fostering your children's intuition. Most parenting info out there is about tantrums, sleep, hitting, food, screens, defiance, respect, setting limits and sibling conflict resolution. There isn't a lot of parenting information about deep things like intuition and relationship with self. When I think about my child going out into the world, and facing inevitable difficulties, obstacles and struggles, I think that having a strong connection to our intuition can be one of the most powerful things we can offer our children. There are so many aspects of life that are challenging. Much of the time the direction that we need to take isn't clear. We often struggle to make decisions or we make them based on fear, social pressure, insecurities, and trauma. When we have trouble setting boundaries, and tuning in to our deep needs and honoring who we are, so much of that comes from not having a deep relationship with ourselves nurtured from the early days of our lives. This is why I think it's so important for parents to pay attention to nurturing intuition. In fact this is powerful for anyone working with children. In this video, I go into detail about what intuition is. why it's important, and how we can best support our kids in forming that deep trusting relationship with themselves. I really want to encourage parents to look at the deeper aspects of relationship and the human experience as integral parts of their parenting. Their relationship with themselves is one of the primary things that we have the opportunity to help our children with. I would love it if you watch this video and let me know your thoughts and feelings on the ideas that I share.

2019 05 03

Join With Your Teens In What Is Meaningful To Them **Teens and Their Music** I remember when I was a teenager how important music was to me. In fact most of my peers identified themselves very strongly with the music they listened to. The groups of people sitting together in the cafeteria were most often bonded by their taste in music. There was a social order about things. **Parents Just Don't Understand** I remember the feeling of separation that came from not being understood. My parents and most adults didn't or couldn't appreciate the music I enjoy or understood how important it was to me. I'm sure it must have sounded like noise to them. I could feel that judgement and it separated me from them. I had to protect myself so I withdrew parts of who I was. It's not about the music, it's about feeling understood and accepted. This is why I always paid special attention to validating and joining in with my daughters taste in music. I encourage her to play her music whenever we are in the car together. I listen very closely and try to pick out things that I like. I share with her these observations of what I enjoy in her music. I know this has a profound effect upon how accepted she feels. My daughter also identifies very strongly with the music she listens to and the fact that I am able to be there with her enjoying it is tremendously meaningful to her. There are a few examples that stand out in my mind that demonstrate just how meaningful it has been. **Her Friends Were Stunned** I remember many years ago when my daughter was in grade 6 (she's 22 now!), I was driving her and some of her classmates home from a soccer game. I gave her the aux cord and she put on some screamo. If you don't know screamo search YouTube for - Bring Me The Horizon - "The House Of Wolves" and you'll get an idea. The other young people in the car whispered to her conspiratorially, ""Your dad lets you play this music in the car?" My parents would never let me play my music when they are around. She replied, "Not only does he let me play it, he actually enjoys it. Her friends said: "Nooo way! That's Awesome." She responded with a quiet, I know! I will never forget that moment. It was such a clear indication that the effort I had put into appreciating her music had not gone unnoticed. When I first heard the screamo I found it challenging. Instead of recoiling from it I took the time to listen very deeply. I sought what was interesting, pleasing or remarkable about it. I soon heard how complex the music was. The bass and drums were so intricate. And the passion of the singer moved me. Once I connected to these things she could feel my sincere enjoyment of the music. Earlier this year I was preparing for a parenting workshop I was delivering at a youth conference. I asked her if she had any thoughts about what I could share? Without hesitating she said that I should tell them how important it is to accept and enjoy your kids music. She said the fact that I enjoy her music means so much to her. She also expressed how difficult it is for most of her friends whose parents don't feel that way. They feel deeply misunderstood and undervalued because of this. Recently a friend of hers came over to hang out. As I was driving them somewhere the young man asked if he could play some music in the car. I said sure and he played some indie rock music. I was bobbing my head and enjoying it. I asked him some questions about the band and other music that he enjoyed. He was so moved by this unusual and unexpected show of interest from an adult that he actually texted my daughter the next day asking her to ask me what my favourite bands are. Then he sent over a list of recommended listening for me. I could feel him seeking that feeling of validation. It was like receiving a glass of water after crawling through the desert. Young people want to let us into their world. When we seek out as many opportunities to connect with them as possible they open up more and more. This kind of connecting experience is not only for music. This can be done with technology, food, movies and TV, books, humour and so much more. Young people make a deep connection between our opinion of their interests and how we value them as people. When we join with them in their joys and passions, when we inspire them to feel that we appreciate the things they value, they grow up with the inner foundation that they are fundamentally acceptable. This creates a foundation of self-acceptance that will help them navigate a challenging world. Rather than thinking of testing their strength, let's build their strength. Strength comes from drawing them closer and letting them know we see and value them. Life will give them many opportunities to be tested. They will encounter numerous, endless obstacles throughout their lives. Instead of being yet one more, let us aim to be the safest, most stable and loving place for them. A refuge from the onslaughts of the world. A message of unconditional love and acceptance. Giving a bit more attention to their interests is a good place to start. <3

2019 05 03

Supporting Teens through the Transition to Adulthood Teens live in a world of their own, at least it looks that way much of the time! They are between two phases of life. Neither fully autonomous grownups nor carefree children. They are expected to have the responsibility of an adult, but are given few of the freedoms or respect. It's a transition stage that is confusing and painful. Adults in general don't understand or appreciate the intensity of the teen experience. We don't give them enough validation for the struggles of teenage hood. The expectations that get placed on them by adults are most often artificial for them. They have to behave a certain way and achieve a certain standard in order to be acceptable. Young people often don't feel safe in their own homes. Never knowing when the next consequence or complaint will come. I call this "Reliable Unpleasantness". They develop coping and survival mechanisms and build up walls in order to manage all this. They are often dismissed and unheard. Rarely are they taken seriously. They are usually treated as if they are less than. We adults often do this without even realizing it. Young people get used to receiving a lower degree of respect than adults. They internalize this mindset and carry it into adulthood. If we can create an environment of freedom, support, validation and guidance, they will have the best chance to learn about themselves and life. This is why it's so important to show them we understand the struggles they are going through. To help them know that we are on their side during these challenging years. Rude and rebellious behaviour in teens comes from a desire for connection, validation, love and respect that is lacking in their lives. They have big feelings without a safe space to express and explore them. Young people experience struggles and pain that adults have forgotten about. We often think that our adult struggles are more valid. Yet teens Feel Very Deeply. The stress and pain of our young people is real. The journey from childhood to adulthood will be full of pain and challenges. We can serve them most effectively if we offer them conscious and loving guidance. Reacting to their outbursts only escalates things and creates more disconnection. Of course we have our own feelings as well and sometimes we do react. That is when we get to model forgiveness and apologizing. :) They need us to believe them and believe IN them. Even when they act out. The experience of someone accepting you and believing in you when you've screwed up is very profound. It is an example of unconditional love. This always has a transformative effect. Too many people think that returning to the strictness of the old ways will bring about more stability in youth. This is simply not the case. Children need powerful examples. They need love and acceptance. They need support and validation. They need gentle guidance. If you are wanting to reconnect or deepen your relationship with your teenager it's useful to remember that healing relationships and changing relational patterns takes time. There will be ups and downs as you change how you respond to your young person. Regaining connection and respect requires patience and persistence. It won't be an overnight job. We have the opportunity to show them they can trust us when they make mistakes. Part of this process is for us to admit, at least to ourselves, that we have treated our kids in ways we wish we hadn't and commit to change. If we can admit it to them so much the better. When they begin to see us treating them differently they will respond. I have seen it over and over. Teens open up to the adults in their lives and are even welcoming of their guidance and support, when they feel accepted for who they are. Here are some questions to think about when engaging with your teen. -Can we honour them for who they are rather than having expectations of who they should be? -Can we give them the freedom to make their own choices, even if we don't agree with them. -AND support them through whatever the consequences of those choices are? -Can we help them discover their own values instead of imposing our values upon them? -Can we accept them equally in their successes and their failures? -Can we demonstrate unconditional love and acceptance so they can begin feeling safe to be themselves around us? I can distinctly remember the feeling of not being seen and accepted as a teen. I acted out as a result. I could feel that none of the adults in my life understood what I was feeling. They were always minimizing the importance of my thoughts and the depth of my feelings. How healing it would have been to my conflicted mind and aching heart if someone had said I understand what you're going through. Your feelings are natural valid. I know you're doing your best. I accept and love you exactly as you are. How can I help you?" I hope for more adults to understand and embrace the struggle of teens, to respect the unique perspective of young people. Helping them feel understood and validating their struggles can make a huge difference in the quality of their transition. Let's create a relationship with them where they feel free to be themselves. Then we can be their guides and learning partners throughout their lives.

2019 04 22

When my kid was young I saw every interaction as a direct link to our relationship when she would be a teenager. I evaluated my decisions based on the emotional and relational residue they would leave. I did not pay as much attention to behavior as I did to these other elements. The result of this is all throughout her teenage years and even to this day as she approaches 22 the trust and connection between us is powerful and uncommon. It is not a foregone conclusion, nor is it the natural way of things that teenagers need to rebel against their parents. We set ourselves up as coercive authority figures that need to be rebelled against. We can choose another path however. We can choose to engage them in a way that helps them really feel we are their allies and not their adversaries.

2019 04 05

"What about the fact that kids crave boundaries?" This is a question/objection I receive often when talking about parenting from the "Non-Coercive, Collaborative Mindset" (NCCM). There is a misunderstanding about what it is that kids crave. They do want to know that the adults in their lives are reliable guides. They want to know that they can engage in the messy job of learning to be human and trust us to keep them safe as they do. It's not that Non-Coercive, Collaborative parenting doesn't include limits and boundaries. It's that there is a focus on setting collaborative ones instead of coercive ones. This means creating a relationship where everyone's needs are taken into account and no one exerts power over another. Collaborative limits feel good to the child. They inspire a feeling of safety. If the limits we set are met with resistance and require any force to impose, they aren't going to be helpful. In fact they are going to create disconnection and damage trust. These are coercive limits. When kids feel we respect their consent and autonomy, as well as their perspective and insight, they are much more open to working with us. This kind of connected trusting relationship is a solid foundation to build upon. Instead of thinking about boundaries it's more helpful to think about presence and guidance. Kids feel a certain safety in being able to rely on our stable presence. They feel free to trust our guidance when they sense we are deeply present with them. I can usher my child away from getting hit by some kid on the swing in the park and it's not coercive. I'm looking out for them. This might be what looks like boundaries from the old mindset, but I won't make a rule out of it. She won't get told that she shouldn't play by the swings. In fact I'm likely to encourage her to try and get as close to the swings as she can next time, but to keep her eyes on it! I think of boundaries as our loving arms encircling our children. Soft and stable at the same time. Not something they ever need to fight against. Something that feels at once empowering and loving. A support they can melt into as well as spring off from. They are ever flexible and by their very nature, mutual. By this I mean when we take this approach to boundaries, collaboration is the natural result. We live in a complicated, largely painful and unfriendly world. I know that my daughter relies upon me to guide her understanding of how to navigate it. Her trust in my capacity and dedication to collaboration is where she gains a lot of her sense of safety. I however have equally relied upon her for wisdom and guidance as well. I turned to her for her connection to the source. For her innocence and curiosity. For her ability to play with anything! I learned from her the power of unrestrained emotional expression. She also opened my heart to deeper levels of love than I knew existed. It was always an exchange. This is why it's most effective to hold non-coercive boundaries. The traditional boundaries create an adversarial relationship. Kids will either resist the imposition on their autonomy. This results in power struggles and lying, or as I like to call it "Creative Problem-Solving!" Or it results in compliance in which the child surrenders their personal truth for another's. Neither result in an authentic relationship with self or parent. Remember that "Coercive influence decreases over time. Relational influence increases over time." Collaborative boundaries are set together with common interests at heart. They involve communication, listening and vulnerability. The process feels loving and honest. We don't want to lose the connection and trust we have with our kids. Let's put effort into creating a collaborative relationship with them where they feel their freedom and input is respected. This will set up stable and resilient relationship and communication patterns that will last a lifetime. <3 @[593266790:2048:Vivek] "

2019 04 01

My Parenting Mantra - Relationship First - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel Recently I had a childhood memory come back to me. I remember I was around 8 yrs old and my dad was going to go to the pharmacy. He said, "Hey, Vivek, Why don't you come along with me?" He wanted me to come with him and I wanted to go with him. And yet something in me resisted. I didn't completely trust in his love and it made me hesitate. I wanted to push him a little bit. So I said no, I don't want to go. He tried again "Please Vivek, Please come with me." I remember this moment so clearly. I could hear his plea. Something in me just hardened, but also hopefully hardened. Wondering if he was going to see past my defense. I wanted him to see past my defense. I said no, I don't want to go. He said it a third time "Come on Vivek, I really want your company." I crossed my arms and said no, I'm not coming. It wasn't like I was just chill saying "No, I'm gonna play, I'm fine." It wasn't like that. It was "NO! I'm not coming!" You know, I was testing, I was pushing. So after he asked me three times, with real pleading for me to join him, he said, "Okay, I'll take your sister." I'm sure it was very frustrating for him. It seemed like the only option to him. I was being inflexible. Then I started to cry. No, no, no, I want to come. And he said no. I guess it was some kind of lesson about teaching me not to manipulate or not to cry wolf, or maybe standing by my agreements? Focusing on standing by agreements is only looking at the surface of what is going on. It's not perceiving what is happening under the surface. My heart was breaking at that moment, really my heart was breaking, because I didn't feel loved or worthy of love. When this memory came back to me and I thought about what I REALLY wanted from my dad, I started to cry. I had not thought of it before. I wanted him to see me, I wanted him to soften, I wanted him to embrace me. I've spent my lifetime trying to give my daughter the opposite experience in every interaction. That's why "Relationship First" is my mantra, right? "Relationship First" Vivek! If you have any question of what to do, "Relationship First". What's going to preserve the trust? What's going to preserve the feeling of acceptance and love? What I wanted from my dad was for him to stop everything, to sit down with me, hold me and say: "Little Vivek, I see you, I see you're struggling. I want to be here for you. I'm not going to go to the pharmacy until we figure this out. Because I care about your happiness. I care about your well-being, I care about your heart more than anything else. Let's sit down and work this out. What's happening for you? I love you so much." But he didn't say that and something broke in me that moment. I work hard to avoid giving my kid the same experience. I'm also working to give myself healing for that memory. Relationship First I know to the adult mind it's illogical to have wanted that, but I was crushed and still feel that pain to this day. Kids are much deeper than we realize. Your kid is NOT being stubborn. They are expressing deep needs in the only way they know how. The idea of teaching our kids lessons through natural consequences is dangerous. When only look at behaviour and not at the heart, natural consequences turn into punishment. Punishment is not determined by the intent of the parent, but by the emotional, relational experience of the child. I know it was beyond his capacity, but as I sit here weeping with 8 year old Vivek, I so wish he had made a different choice, a deeper choice. It put a deep message in me about my worth. I'm reclaiming it, for my daughter's sake if nothing else! It's decades of work I've had to put in. Decades. So don't give up, it's not hopeless, you are not hopeless! You are powerful and Worthy. You have great love in you to offer. All the blood sweat and tears that I have put into my journey over the years is geared towards saving her from the deep sense of my lack of worth. Something I carry with me everywhere I go and colors all of my experiences. This is why my highest priority is focusing on... "Relationship First" I go into more detail about all this in the video. Please watch it and let me know what you think? <3 @[593266790:2048:Vivek Patel]

2019 03 25

There is a common idea that we can get kids to behave better if we let them know we feel disappointed in them when they do something wrong. . This will make them not want to disappoint us so they avoid doing the thing, whatever it is. This mindset comes from wanting to teach values to our kids. The problem is this method produces the opposite outcome. . When we want to help kids with a particular behavior it makes sense for us to understand what leads to the behavior and also what conditions would lead them to make different choices. . If the kid hits another kid or if they steal something or perhaps they get swept away by peer pressure and engage in something like bullying, we want to address those choices and help them learn different ways. . I understand the concept behind expressing disappointment to our kids. Our hope is if we express our disappointment they will feel they have let us down and will want to avoid that in the future. This will hopefully encourage them to make different choices. . The reason the gentle or conscience parenting philosophy tends to avoid working with our kids through things like disappointment is because it places the focus of their ethical sense outside of themselves. . What this means is they will be looking for what is right and wrong based on trying to avoid making us feel disappointed. When our parents feel disappointed in us it reflects directly on the kind of person we think we are. We become afraid to make mistakes because we don't want to experience the loss of that approval. . The reason this is ineffective is because we are not teaching our kids to tune into other people from a place of caring about them. We are teaching them to make their decisions based on trying to not make mistakes so they don't lose the connection with their parents. . Even though your child might only be four years old you are still training them with every interaction how to be in relationship with other people when they are older. . Once this pattern is set, as they grow older, the focus of their attention won't be you anymore, it will shift to other important people in their lives. Peers, teachers, lovers, bosses etc. Now it will be those people they're afraid to disappoint. . I don't want my kids to go out in the world thinking that they have to please other people in order to be acceptable. . There are three main problems that come with this mindset. The first one is that if they're in a situation where saying no makes sense and someone will be (or says they will be) disappointed by that choice, they never developed the skill to set a boundary under those conditions. . For example, let's say they are on a date, and the person they're on the date with wants to have some kind of sexual experience that your child doesn't want to. . If the person tells them, "You'll hurt my feelings if you don't do it" they will be more likely to deny their own feelings because that's what they have learned. . They base their understanding of how to make decisions on not wanting to disappoint the person who is the source of their love and connection. This can lead them to do something sexual that they don't want to do. . This is a real big problem that so many young people face. This is why I use sexuality as an example. Teaching consent is so important. Both to honour someone else's consent and their own. . Certainly making decisions based on trying not to have someone feel disappointed in us, doesn't lead us to honoring our own consent. . The second problem with this is that when the reason to avoid doing something is to not disappoint the other person, if we can find some way to get away with it without the other person knowing there's no reason to avoid it. . This is one of the causes of children lying to their parents. They're not only trying to save themselves from the traditional type of consequences, but they are saving themselves from the relational consequence which is deeply painful. . If I actually care for the experience of the other person, and respect them deeply, I'll make caring decisions even if no one knows or sees me do it. . Which is different than trying to avoid the other feeling disappointed because it makes the kid feel bad. . It's about protecting their own feelings at this point. It is not about tuning into the other. So they will find ways to do the thing without you finding out. This is how we teach our kids to lie to us. . We teach them not to open themselves to us and that we are not a safe place for them to make mistakes. . This is another thing that we teach kids, it's not safe to make mistakes. If the person they love and rely on the most is disappointed in them when they make a mistake, there must be something fundamentally wrong with who they are. . Mistakes aren't learning opportunities anymore, they feel like a threat to our acceptance and safety. No matter how many times we tell kids with our words that mistakes are learning opportunities, if they don't experience it in our relationship they won't feel it. In fact, their relationship with learning itself gets damaged. . This is why it's so important for us not to have that attitude of disappointment when they make a mistake, but instead have an attitude of embracing them and loving them, so that they feel open to learning about the issue with us. Otherwise they close themselves off and have to protect themselves from us emotionally. . I hope this makes sense. We're trying to break an age old cycle of modifying behavior through causing some kind of pain. Emotional pain and relational pain are just as damaging as physical pain or taking away privileges. . In fact taking away privileges, grounding, timeouts, yelling and all of the things that are in the traditional parenting toolbox, are designed to make a person feel worse in order to get them to behave better. There is an inherent contradiction in this thinking. . The real pain of those things is not that they can't watch TV. The real pain is the relationship. The there is a deep lack of connection and respect in those moments. Disappointment falls into the same category because it's relational pain that they feel. . Any motivation that comes from pain rather than love is never going to be as sustainable, resilient and stable and the lessons we teach therefore are not as effective. . The most effective thing we can do for our kids is to let them know they are unconditionally accepted and loved. Then they will open their hearts to us and become our learning Partners about life for life. @[593266790:2048:Vivek Patel]

2019 03 25

I don't want to teach my kid to respect boundaries. I want to teach my kid to want to respect boundaries. I want to inspire them to have an enthusiastic desire to respect boundaries. I want my kid to feel like respecting boundaries is a natural part of life and the most enjoyable way we can treat each other. I don't want to teach my kid to respect boundaries. I want to teach my kids to want to respect boundaries. The reason I mention this is the two approaches can be radically different at times, because wanting to respect boundaries cannot come from a coercive, outside in demand that they do so. This may give rise to the appearance of respect, but not the feeling. The feeling comes from nurturing the mindset, the relationship-set, the environment-set and the emotion-set that give rise to the desire to respect boundaries.

I don't really know what to say about the massacre in New Zealand. My heart aches for everybody there and really all of us. It seems like anger and hate are consuming our world. In the face of this it is challenging to keep believing in the work I do. It also feels more important than ever. I am fortunate to have powerful friends and colleagues who inspire me. They are my family of ideology. If anything this whole thing re-affirms my conviction that is it vital we change the way we raise our children. The whole idea that one person is less worthy than another for whatever reason is always going to cause division, coercion and violence. Sharing the message with our children that we are all worthy and all deserving of love and compassion is so important. It's important for us to do so. Not just with our words, but with every aspect of our lives. It's important to start modelling this message for them from the earliest age possible. If our kids truly believe that they are acceptable as they are, they will see others through the same lens and we will heal the painful divisions that create and sustain the violence that we live in. I have done my best to inspire my daughter to think for herself, to question her beliefs and make sure they are hers and not imposed upon her. When she agrees with me I always ask her if she's sure. Does she have any further thoughts about it? I wanted to be clear that I did not desire agreement, I want her truth. Her sense of integrity is profound because she has developed it from within. Her values are hers. She will not be swayed into hate by any external force because she knows herself. This is her favourite shirt. It represents her powerful personality. It represents a hope for me that a new generation raised respectfully will challenge the corruption of the world and transform it.

2019 03 08 The Four Problems with Punishment and Consequences Punishment and consequences don't stop kids from doing what they want. They are however excellent at making them focus on not getting caught. I was a kid and I remember this very well. When my parents would spank or punish me for doing something, it made me want to do it even more. It certainly didn't kill the urge, which ended up expressing itself in more and more dangerous ways. That's how it goes quite predictably when we use force. I still remember the day I realized I could take any punishment my parents could dish out, and I would still do whatever I wanted. That was the day they lost influence over me and in a way our relationship as well. We want to teach our kids right from wrong and pass on solid values. That's a great thing. The key is to make sure we don't lose our kid's trust in the process, so they stop listening to us. Be their safe space to talk about difficult things and you will be able to guide them throughout their lives. Force them, scare them, control them or push them away and you'll lose your influence and your relationship. It's a lot harder to communicate than to use force, but in the long run we all come out ahead. This is why I always advocate for never using any kind of punishment or consequences to discipline children. They always produce far more problems than they solve. It's a challenge to transition away from things like consequences, removal of privileges and timeouts. However when we do we create a whole new relationship with our kids. Here are a few of the reasons why it's not effective, and even damaging, to use punishment and consequences to modify our children's behaviour. ***1) Punishment gives kids the message that we love them conditionally and not unconditionally. While it may be true that we don't love our kids less when we are punishing them, the fact is in their experience they do not feel like they are being loved when they are being punished. Regardless of the intent, the impact on the child is to feel a withdrawal of acceptance. Therefore from their perspective they are more worthy of love when they meet the expectations of the authority figures in their lives. What they hear is we love them more when they behave like this, and less when they behave like that. If the pattern is set that love and acceptance come from the external, that will be something they have to deal with all their lives. Right now it's the parents that are that external source, but as they grow the source will shift from us to other people. Friends, intimate relationships, media and entertainment role models etc. Learning to re-tune into our own inner voice of wisdom as an adult is so challenging. There are so many adults working to trust themselves and believe in themselves again. How can we guide our kids to start out believing in themselves? Encourage them to develop their own values from within? How can we help them to trust in their value and in their values? We want to send our kids out into the world with the strongest foundation possible. The mindset of seeking our worth in the acceptance and approval of others is in direct opposition to that. We do not want them to spend their lives seeking acceptance from other people. ***2) Punishment teaches kids that the reason to do good is to avoid pain. It does not teach the idea of doing good for its own sake. It does not teach the mindset to care for the best outcome for everyone in the community. It does not produce a mindset focused on working towards mutual benefit. In essence we are teaching kids to modify their behaviour and make choices based on avoiding pain for themselves. This is a Fear based, self-centered, self-protective motivation. It also means that when there is no threat of punishment there is no reason to continue the expected behaviour. When kids learn to make choices from their own values, they will make them even when no one is watching. In fact when kids are given the guidance to choose their values consciously and freely, they will often give up their own immediate pleasure in order to honour these values. This is very different from imposed consequences where we are trying to get them to behave better by making them feel worse. There is an inherent contradiction in that idea. On the surface it seems like we're teaching kids to do right by making them want to avoid the unpleasant effect of doing wrong. This creates a world where adults only do good on the surface so they can avoid punishment. Not because they have empathy and care about the experience of others. Let's instead work towards a world where people do what is kind, just and loving For Its Own Sake, because they FEEL it. This cannot be taught with fear. Let's foster the qualities in children that we want them to have as adults. Help them to be happy, healthy, self-loving, self-confident, caring, creative and powerful young people so that they will be caring and powerful adults. Let's use collaboration, communication and connection. Let's lead by example and empower them. *** 3) Punishment and consequences erode the bond of trust and love between parent and child Every time we punish our children they trust us a little bit less. They believe in our love a little bit less. They believe in our good intentions a little bit less. Punishment produces the condition in which kids are forced to lie to us. They may not even know they are lying at times because it's self-preservation. This is the mindset that is formed when kids have to navigate a course of system. They learn early that they cannot simply be themselves if they want to be loved and accepted by their parents. (ouch) This means they have to put on a false mask so that they do not receive unpleasantness at the hands of the people who are supposed to love them unconditionally. If we put ourselves in the mind of a child looking at its parent while receiving the punishment, we can get an idea of how it feels for them, understand their perspective. ""My parent is supposed to be my support," my foundation, my inspiration and my protection. And yet I can never be sure of when they will also turn into my tormentor. This doesn't only affect our kid's sense of love and trust with us, but it changes their relationship with love and trust itself. The effects of this last a lifetime. ***4) Punishment teaches kids how to treat others when they have power over them The only reason a parent can punish their child is because they have power over them. We have economic, housing, physical and emotional power over our children. The way we use that power demonstrates to them how to treat others. One of the primary causes of bullying is the model kids have for how to treat others from their parents. Imposing consequences is telling our kids that there are appropriate times for them to cause other people pain in order to get their way. If they have power over someone else it's okay to use it. It is teaching them that they do not have to consider the feelings of other people to be as valid and important as their own. Kindness comes from empathy and true empathy comes from Love not from Fear. Our greatest influence when teaching respect is the example we set. If we want our kids to be respectful when they're upset instead of lashing out, we must model the same behaviour. If we cannot be respectful in the midst of chaos and big feelings, how can we expect our kids to? This learning is experiential and goes deeper than any lecture or explanation we can offer. When I say deeper I mean it's beyond the intellect. It goes into the subconscious patterning and the nervous system of the body itself. One way to decide how to react/respond to your child in difficult moments is to try and imagine how you'd like to be treated in a similar situation. Imagine that you've made some big mistake and the person who's responding to you is your dearest friend. The friend who knows you the most. They know your dark and light sides and still loves you as you are. Imagine how you'd like that friend to react... and offer the same reaction to your kid. Thinking of responding this way there can't be anything punitive nor even judgmental. We just accept each other as human and learn about life together. If you don't have a friend like that then this is your chance to be one. It's such a gift to offer our kids, to be someone that believes in them no matter what. Treating them with respect in difficult moments teaches them to do the same. As you decrease your use of consequences as a means of altering behaviour you will see a profound effect upon the emotional, mental and relational experience of your children. You'll experience a transformation on the relationship you have with them and on the overall energy in your home. If you can increase that percentage a little at a time you can completely transition to a relationship and interaction based on cooperation, mutual respect, connection and communication, rather than power and control. It's hard work. It's also the most beautiful gift you can offer your family, and yourself. It's one that you all will value for the rest of your lives. Peace, Vivek

2019 03 08

A few words about the damaging effect of using rewards Rewards tend to back fire relatively quickly. They do seem like great motivators at first because we're using something our kids like to get them on board. What is wrong with getting kids excited over receiving a treat? The problem comes when kids realize (consciously or unconsciously) that we're using rewards to manipulate their behaviour. We are trying to get them to do things that they don't want to do. As soon as this of being manipulated the motivation is lost because the need for autonomy is so strong. Kids have an innate understanding that effective community living requires collaboration, not control or manipulation. They desire harmony and cooperation as much as we do. They also recognize that the true reward of contributing to the home is about the relationships. This is why they resist manipulation and the appeal of rewards diminishes quickly. One of the most common problems parents share with me is "The reward chart isn't working anymore. Now what do I do? Another thing about rewards is they focus on a self-centered source for cooperation. We clean because we're going to get something out of it, instead of cleaning because we have learned to value the family community. Rather than trying to get kids to do things for an external reward, it will be more effective in the long term to instil the feelings and attitudes that give rise to the cooperation we seek. Trying to force a habit pattern from the outside in will eventually create resistance and resentment. It is much more stable and resilient when motivation arises from within, from connection, from caring about the experience of others as well as ourselves. When we take this approach kids will often help out even when it's unpleasant to them because they access a deeper emotional/relational reward. The sense that it feels good to help because& it feels good to help. The third reason to avoid rewards as motivators is they diminish connection between parents and children in a very similar way that punishments do. Rewards teach our kids to trust us less. This may be hard to see that at first. In fact when I first heard this idea years ago I totally balked at it! It seemed nonsensical to me until I gave it some serious thought. Once I realized how alike are the effect of punishment and rewards, I had to change my parenting style. The reason rewards damage the connection between parent and child is rewards foster a feeling of conditional love and acceptance. Kids hear the message that they are more worthy of our love and acceptance when they act like this and less worthy of it when they act like that. When our kids don't do what we want them to and we deny them the reward, it's emotionally exactly the same as taking away a privilege or sending them to their room. It's a way of saying - because you didn't live up to my expectations I'm going to use the power I have to make you less happy. Oh, that stings! This is why the longer and deeper route of communication, collaboration, cooperation and connection is always more effective. It creates trust and connection. It establishes relational patterns that are stable and resilient. It requires a LOT more patience and self-regulation too. When we abandon rewards and focus on engaging in a deep learning process with our kids we give them the message that we love them unconditionally no matter what they do. We teach them that mistakes are opportunities for learning and growth. They are to be embraced rather than avoided. We inspire them to know that they are fundamentally worthy of Love and acceptance. This sense of unshakable self-esteem is one of the greatest gifts we can give our children as we send them out into the world. It helps them ask the question: Do I care about my family and my home enough to do the dishes? Instead of Do I want the reward enough to do the dishes? It's hard to let go of these strategies as theyve been the only way we have worked with kids for centuries. Working from the outside in, modifying behaviour through coercion. Changing a deeply set pattern like this takes a lot of work. That is why Gentle Parenting is so powerful, it transforms us as we transform our parenting. Our children call us to be our most conscious, to identify and change our patterns daily, to offer ourselves compassion for our mistakes and to learn deeply from them. Always learning! I wish 22 years ago when my daughter was born that I understood more about how ineffective rewards can be. When I learned about this and stopped using them I saw an immediate change in the flow of our home. I didn't want my kid to get the message that they were doing things for external approval. It's the other side of the coin of punishment and consequences. Letting go of Rewards (and consequences) help our kids make good choices without the desire for reward or the fear of punishment. Their choices will instead come from a deep sense of caring for themselves, the family and the home environment. <3 @[593266790:2048:Vivek Patel]

"And I try to laugh At whatever life brings Cause when I look down I just miss all the good stuff When I look up I just trip over things" -Ani Difranco - As is I love Ani Difranco. I took my daughter to see her when she was like 10 years old At one point Ani forgot the words to her own song. She was so cool about it. She asked the audience to remind her and we all sang together. It was such a beautiful moment. It felt like a unity in that concert hall. Her profound acceptance of herself drew us all in. We became one. The kid and I talked about it for quite a while afterward. It made an impression on us both. I always like to follow up any experience we have. The follow up is a great way to establish a fun co-exploring co-learning relationship. "Remember when Ani forgot the lyrics the other day. I loved that moment. I want to feel that comfortable with who I am and with my mistakes." "Ya me too!" We are together. Neither of us look up or down at each other. There is no hierarchy between us. This is still an uncommon thing, to relate to kids with no hierarchy, but it is a growing awareness. We don't have to be above our kids to guide them. Part of our role as guides is to help them learn (I say help learn instead of teach) deep values, life skills, communication and relationship skills, emotional regulation and expression skills... and the list goes on. We can help them learn these important things and still hold them as our equals. We can work with them non-coercively. Engage with them collaboratively and cooperatively. The thing about having a hierarchy between us is we teach them one human is above another. It doesn't matter what the reason is. If one person is above another then one person is below. We almost force them into looking up and down at people. Not up as in admiring a positive role model. This is up as in, I'm not as good. I'm not worthy. I'll never be successful. I'm not enough. Looking down, thinking that someone else is on a lower level than you is such a dangerous thought. The reason for the lower status starts out because of the parent child dynamic, but it often manifests later judgment based on race, social status, gender, sexual preference and so on. Once the mindset is set we are prone to looking for the up and down. The up and the down come together. That means we ourselves can never be okay. We'll always be down because someone where out there someone is up. Someone is always above us. My Spiritual teacher Tulshi Sen says "Don't look up at anyone and don't look down on anyone. Either way you get a neck ache" How often do you see someone putting another person down (most often a child, but could be anyone) and it's so clear they're compensating for their own lack of self-worth and self-love. I see it every time I leave the house. I DO IT every time I leave the house. Help me Divine one I'm trying, but I was raised in a traditional manner so I have been contaminated with the up down mindset. This is the source of so many of my insecurities. I want to spare my kid from that fate. She knows in her bones we are equals. Recently I asked her what it would feel like if I ever said "No" to her. We both paused and there was a silence as we tried to imagine it. Neither of us could. We both shook our heads! She then said that if I ever did say no to her that she'd trust it because I never say no to her and if I did say no to her I would have to have a really good reason. I want to clarify that what I mean by "I don't say no" is I don't say no from a place of authority. Like I'm the parent and I'm saying No you can't have a second bowl of ice cream before dinner. That can only happen if one person has power over another. I worked very hard to not have authority over my daughter. The concepts of authority and equals do not dance together very well. Even now at 22 I still pay close attention to how we relate to each other. After over 2 decades of practice I still have to be vigilant. Even though I don't say no, sometimes I will say "I can't" when it's honest, which is very different from no. However it's true that most of the time I make an effort to say yes. In the early days my parenting I used to always practice "10 yeses for every no". I remember when my kid got too heavy for me to spin around. I used to have a bad back. I had a collection of back braces. Those who knew me in the early days of my dancing know how broken I was physically. Fortunately now I'm much healthier and stronger. In those days however there came a point I just couldn't lift her and spin her around. I had to say "I Can't". We both felt the grief of the loss. We both were upset I had to say I can't. We felt it together, I empathized and spoke it out loud. Once we had traveled along the emotional journey together then we were able to think of fun replacements for that activity. We experienced it as equals. The experience brought us closer together and she learned about how to deal with loss and grief. She had a lived experience of moving through her emotions without having to run from them. She was safe because she felt me with her so she could really be with her feelings. This usually brings us out the other side into more self-understanding and integration. When parents ask about how to teach emotional regulation, this is the type of thing that does it on a deep level. I would love to hear what you think about all this. I believe it is important for us as parents and as people to move beyond the "up down mindset" to a "collaborative relationship of equals" mindset. This is where we become lifelong Learning Partners. This is where harmony and community are born. Peace, @[593266790:2048:Vivek] "
