2019 02 15

Learning is a subtle and complex thing. It is more than information in/information out. Learning happens along multiple dimensions. It deepens with repeated experiences. There are unending layers to learning. There are leaps, plateaus and many apparent regressions. With a strong awareness and practice of these subtleties, we can inspire a resilient, courageous and endlessly fulfilling learning mindset in our kids. I remember telling my grandfather years ago (when he was still alive) that I learn something every day. He challenged me, "Oh ya! What did you learn today?" It so happens earlier that afternoon someone I'm close to had said something that hurt me. I was upset and angry. I reflected on my feelings and realized that I didn't have to buy into the reality the other person was creating. In that moment I relaxed and was able to look more objectively at the issue. It helped me in moving through my feelings and communicating with the other person. I didn't tell him all this, I just said that I learned not to take things so personally and I'll be more free. He said, somewhat derisively "Didn't you already know that?" I explained that I learned it in a new way, a deeper and more embodied way. He wouldn't hear it. "If you knew it already you didn't learn it." And yet that is a lesson I learn and re-learn because we learn in layers. The lesson went in deeper as a result of my reflection. That is one of the flaws of the memorize and regurgitate education system. It doesn't account for the layers. Being able to sense and work with these layers is such a valuable skill as a guide/teacher/learner. I have been teaching in one form or another for about 30 years now. I've worked with adults, teens, youth and kids. People often tell me they love my classes. I believe one of the main reasons for my effectiveness as a teacher is that I see myself as a lifelong learner.

2019 02 12

Toys are a very deep thing for children. They are tied into their emotions, their perception of the world, their joy and pain, their sense of wonder, order, meaning and their self-image. Adults who tune into this perspective have a much easier time navigating all things toy related with their children. Adults who see toys as trivial playthings will struggle. A common thing for parents to do is criticize a child's desire if it doesn't make sense to them. For example imagine you're shopping and pass by the toy aisle. Your kid starts asking for the blue Gamagamagon. They HAVE to have it, it's the coolest thing and everyone has one. They get home all excited and play with it for 10 minutes. They end up playing with the box more than the toy. A week goes by and it's in the same spot it was after that first day, on the floor beside the couch. We're back in the store a week later and this time they ask for the RED Gamagamagon. You remind them that they already have a Gamagamagon. It's blue, it's new and it's under the couch. They insist that they need the red one too. They are quite sure their life depends on it. This is when most adults miss the opportunity to enter the world of the child. It really is so illogical, unnecessary and frustrating when kids do this type of thing. It feel wasteful and shallow. While we may or may not say such harsh things as we say NO, they feel it from us. Often when we express our usually invalidating adult perspective it makes them dig their heels deeper into the desire. This is because when they first expressed it, the desire came spontaneously. After the initial resistance it became about autonomy and power (or any other number of issues). Whether you buy the thing or not isn't the point. Being truly with them in their experience is. I'm not saying you have to buy it if you can't afford it or if you really don't have space for it. But don't avoid buying it to teach them a lesson. Be transparent about it. Honour their desire, their perspective and let them know you embrace it. At the same time let them know that circumstances are such that you can't get it. You really want to because you see how much it means to them. You feel the same remorse at not being able to get it. Being honest about this means that if you can afford it you'll buy it for them. It's what I call the difference between saying NO and saying "I can't". Saying NO from the mindset that their relationship to toys is less valid than the adult one, or in an effort to teach them something, guaranteed you'll end up teaching them the opposite of whatever positive lesson you had in mind. This post is more than just about buying toys though. It's about kids whole relationship with toys. One of the reasons so many parents struggle with getting their kids to clean up their toys is that they don't see what their kids see. Their sense of order is specific and unique. I remember as a kid walking into a messy room with my toys all over and feeling a deep satisfaction. It was familiar, safe, ordered and mine. I also remember feeling overwhelmed by it sometimes and being grateful for my mom's help. This is why discernment is so important. If we have a preconceived agenda around how our kids should relate to toys we miss the opportunity to tune into how they ARE relating to their toys. This deeper awareness allows us to be more effective in helping them and guiding them when they need it. The other benefit of tuning into their relationship with toys is that they feel we are with them rather than above them. When they know we are with them where they are, they are much more open to being with us where we are. When I interact with a kid and their toy I tune into how they relate to it. Is it special, is it sacred, is it wild, is it pretty, is it aggressive. Whatever it is I join in that energy with them. Sometimes I can feel I get it a bit off, but I'm watching and adjusting so they feel me feeling them. It usually only takes seconds before children open up and tell me all about the toy and their experience with it. I have found even the youngest children have these complicated and rich lives with their toys. See if you can increase your awareness of your kid's relationship to their toys and belongings in general. Take it more seriously than you did before and watch what arises. If you do play with this idea I would love to hear how it goes.

2019 02 12

Workshop Title: Honouring a child's essential right to freedom contributes to maximizing their learning potential I was originally going to write "maximizes their learning potential", but changed it to "contributes to maximizing". I did this because there are many elements that all combine to create ideal learning experiences. This one I feel is quite fundamental so I will be focusing on it for this hour long talk. Description: In this workshop we will be looking at what enhances learning and what obstructs it? What mind-set/emotion-set/environment and relationship are ideal for learning to take place? We will be looking at this from a parent/primary caregiver perspective. One area I want to focus on specifically is respecting children's autonomy and how that relates to education. Honouring a child's essential right to freedom contributes to maximizing their learning potential. It creates a space where they are truly safe to think right to their edges. This is where deep learning happens. Usually we shy away from the edges because we exist in a system of controlled expectations. Kids especially have a lot of expectations on how they behave. Our minds become restricted. We lose touch with our potential. This is what the system of memorization and recall fails to take into account. When those expectations are removed and children are honoured for who they are, they no longer have to restrict how they think in order to gain love and acceptance. If we want to teach our kids to learn from their mistakes we have to create an environment and repeated experience where making mistakes and learning from them feels good. The moment it feels like a drag we've lost the point. I asked an 8 year old recently, "Do you know what mistakes are for?" She hung her head and sighed, "To learn from..." She replied in a defeated voice. I asked further "Do you know how to learn from mistakes or what that really means?" She just shook her head. The question hadn't occurred to her. When my kid makes a mistake they're always excited to tell me about it. Even if it has some dire, real-world consequence, she never hesitates. She knows my learning mindset is stable and reliable. This makes it safe for her to process anything. A true learning partner relationship is created.

2019 02 07

The other day I had some work on the computer that I wanted my kid to do for me. It was going to take a couple hours. I felt a little bad asking her so when I did I offered to pay her something for her time. She looked at me with an offended expression on her face. Her voice was almost uncomprehending as she repeated my words back to me: "Pay me?" Her face looked pained. It was like I had asked her to drink a brussel sprout smoothie! I shook my head and apologized. I said to her: "Sometimes the world gets to me too kiddo." From her perspective we don't help each other for money. We help each other because that's how it is! That is love, respect and collaboration. We are together in this. This is how she's been raised. My wife and I always treat her as an equal. She never had an allowance, but we also never said no to her if she wanted something, if it was financially feasible. Actually we did give her an allowance at first. Largely because we just thought that's what you're supposed to do. 21+ years ago we didn't know how we were going to put this radical, non-coercive, non-authority based parenting into action. We did things and then evaluated and tried again. So we gave her an allowance, but it was meaningless because if she wanted something and didn't have the money we just bought it. After a while we stopped giving it to her and no one noticed. When I talk this way someone will bring up the question of teaching value for money and hard work. I ask them why they work hard for money? They usually say they have to. I ask why? Because otherwise my family would starve. Who cares if they starve? I do, I love them. So is that why you work then, because you care for them? Are you really working for money or because you care about other human beings? The value of work is love. This is why artificial scarcity doesn't teach respect for money. The reason to make money isn't because we don't have money. The reason to make money is to care for those we love (incl ourselves). This is an important distinction because the method of teaching will change DRAMATICALLY depending on which mindset we are operating from. Notice that with never having restriction on money she wanted to help me because of our relationship, not because she would get something for it. This is the opposite of entitled. The fact that I never said NO to her doesn't mean we were able to buy everything she wanted. If we couldn't afford something we wouldn't say "NO", we say "I can't". The difference between these two is profound. It has to be honest though, that's why I said if it was financially feasible for me to buy something that we did. Most of the time for us it hasn't been and we've had to say "I can't" a lot more than yes. There have been years through her childhood where friends were buying us groceries weekly because we were struggling. My daughter's experience hasn't been that she gets whatever she wants. It's something that does break my heart, but it's our reality. The reason I bring this up is one objection I often hear is "Not everyone is so privileged as to buy anything their kids want." This is a significant misunderstanding of the point. This philosophy creates unity and cooperation in lean times more than any coercive approach. It creates a feeling of being together. Kids are so willing to go without and even help to make money when they feel sincerely included. The releasing of NO and being true to "I can't" means there's no authority, coercion or power in the relationship. Removing money as a power point between us made it so all our interactions were about our relationship and not about getting anything. We work together as a family community to ensure everyone's needs are met the best we can, given our circumstances. This freedom and trust in relationship has resulted in her having a profound understanding and feeling of cooperation, collaboration and giving. This is why she scowled at me when I suggested I'd pay her for helping me. Haha! She is my teacher. <3 Vivek Edit to Add: A little more about collaborative exploration Setting a budget for what to spend on different things each month can be done as a family, taking everyone's ideas into consideration. That's the essence of a collaborative relationship. It's not giving kids total power, and it's also not taking power for ourselves. It's about thinking of money relationally. If you're saving for a vacation or paying off debt, then that money isn't available for other things. The thing is that applies to everyone the same. After those kind of expenses are taken into consideration, what's left over is family money and everyone decides together how to manage it. This is where real learning takes place. Working together to manage the money means we have to learn all about how money works, what it's for, different ways of relating to it... there's lots to explore. Saying NO from an authoritative position is always going to degrade the relationship and cause disconnection. When this happens money becomes related to power and autonomy. In fact any issue we deal with goes that way with authority and coercion.

2019 02 05

How to respond when one kid hits another or How to teach the skill of self-motivated self-regulation (SMSR) When one kid hits another it's always a tricky moment. On the one hand we want to protect the one who's been or about to be or IS BEING hit! Protect them physically and emotionally. In most cases it makes sense to intervene when hitting is taking place. We want them to know they didn't deserve to be hit, that no one does and that it's not their fault. Their emotional reaction is natural, whatever it is. We are here for them and we are continuing to work as a family to change that dynamic. On the other hand we want to help the one who's hitting as much as possible. Hitting people is not an effective or sustainable emotional communication strategy. It will be to their benefit (and everyone else's) for them to learn other ways to express themselves. It's important to note that I didn't say we have to make them stop hitting. The make/stop mindset is adversarial in nature and not effective in creating lasting change. Learning something as subtle and deep as self-motivated self-regulation (SMSR) takes guidance and practice. Practice is another word for making lots of mistakes. When we can accept this process we relax into it. The skill of self-motivated self-regulation (SMSR) involves many aspects. Paying attention to our emotions, noticing when we're upset, then noticing in an instant how our body wants to react before it does, then having the capacity to interrupt that impulse and choose another without repressing the actual feelings or they'll leave residue and leak out in other ways. Whew. That is no small feat. Learning that takes time. We must be with them on that learning journey. That's why I always say we are Learning Partners. The opposite of SMSR is FMSR which is Fear-Motivated Self-Regulation. The motivation of fear is less stable and resilient. It is destined to fall because it's not built on a solid inner foundation. When the motivation for an action or choice arises from our own consciously chosen value system, as opposed to an imposed value system, the foundation is strong. This requires being able to tune into our authentic values rather than trying to fit into the value system of an authority figure who holds power over us. This cannot be taught in a context of wrongness. When we focus on the idea that something is wrong and we have to avoid it we are not coming from that sincere inner compass. We are no longer practicing the above mentioned SMSR skills. Remember that practicing includes making lots of mistakes. Part of the stress we parents often feel is the desire for kids to learn quicker than they are. This expectation creates tension that causes us to see them as wrong. The wrong mindset practically forces us to use coercion because that's its root. This of course causes them to learn even slower which confirms our original stress point! This is why so many parents say that their kids know better so they don't understand why they keep doing the same thing. Instead I try and encourage parents to anticipate the behaviour so that their emotional reaction is chosen rather than reactionary. For example if one kid hits another out of frustration I might tell them that their feelings are valid and I want to help them express their emotions without hitting or hurting someone else. We discuss alternatives and role play them to practice. I ask them to call on me if they're struggling so I can help them. They say they understand and we hug it out. Lovely interaction. As soon as I turn around in my mind I adjust my mindset to anticipate the next hit. I know it's coming. I won't be surprised. I know it takes time to learn. I know I may have to repeat the empathy and connection many times. I'm ready to engage in a long term learning process with my kids so I'm not upset when they hit again just 5 minutes later. If instead I react and see them as wrong they will feel judged. When this happens kids just can't hear us and really can't hear themselves. It's really not necessary to make anyone feel wrong in order to handle a hitting situation. We are so programmed to think it is necessary that it feels like we're not being responsible if we don't do it. We must project at least a little bit of wrongness or how will we demonstrate our values? In fact wrongness is always less productive in teaching compassion, empathy and SMSR. Instead we can practice holding everyone in their learning process (including ourselves). We can see and trust in their deep intelligence (a term I've adopted from my friend @[731895353:2048:Tanya Williams]). We can have compassion for their struggle and offer them that compassion through empathy. When one kid hits another they both deserve our empathy for they are both struggling and learning. We can let them both know that we see their struggle and their pain. I call it ping pong empathy. Reflecting and naming feelings honestly and non-judgmentally can help everyone learn. "I'm sorry you're hurt. It's no fun to be hit (or yelled at or whatever the behaviour we're addressing is). I can see you're upset. It's natural to be upset and cry if someone hits you. I get upset and cry too. I'm here for you." Then to the other kid. "You were so upset they knocked down your blocks. I'm so sorry that happened to you. It's totally natural to feel upset and to express it. I know that's why you hit your sibling. I get upset sometimes too. Thank you for sharing your feelings with me. I'm here for you." No need to point out anybody's wrongness. Yes we want them to learn not to hit. That is not the most effective moment to bring it up. We want our kids to feel safe in those moments so they continue to turn to us. Telling the kid who hit that you feel their pain does not diminish the validity of the other kid's experience. Any time people interact it's never going to be perfect, because learning is messy, emotions are messy and humans are messy! The key isn't to avoid the mess, but to get right into the mess with our kids so they feel us with them. We are figuring life out together. Learning is a lifelong process. When we are process focused rather than behaviour focused, we see quite a difference in how our kids relate to us. When our relationship is based on collaboration and co-learning instead of competition and control they feel safe with us in a whole new way. It takes practice to learning to adopt a no wrongness mindset. Especially when one's kid is being hurt. We want to jump in and put a stop to it. In these moments it's most effective if we can keep our centre and remember the power of empathy. Of course we'll forget. That's what practice is for. See... We have to practice just as much as our kids do. When we recognize that we realize we really are on a learning path together. It's not just a philosophy. Since it is challenging to at times it is useful to practice seeing other situations this way as well. It helps to drive the perspective home. See where else you can apply this radical acceptance, no wrongness, sustained empathy mindset in your interactions. Does your kid leave a mess? Get huffy when you them to do something? Complain about things they really doesn't need to? Refuse to do homework? Act ungrateful? There are so many possibilities, really the list is endless, as are the opportunities for practice! :D Peace, @[593266790:2048:Vivek Patel]

2019 02 03

Compassion cannot be taught through Coercion. The most effective way to guide children as they grow and learn is to continually point them inward to their own ethical/value compass. Learning to hear, trust and follow its direction is one of the most powerful abilities we can help our kids develop. If we tell them "This is right and this is wrong" We aren't guiding them towards inner listening. We are putting their focus on external sources of values. The problem with this is that right now that external source is us so we think it's okay. If the pattern is set that values come from external, especially as a condition of acceptance and approval, then as they grow the source will shift from you to other people. Friends, intimate relationships, media and entertainment role models etc. Learning to re-tune into our own inner voice of wisdom as an adult is so challenging. Just about every adult I know is working to trust themselves and believe in themselves. How can we guide our kids to develop their own values from within? How can we help them to trust in them and honour them? How can we inspire them to always be open to examining and adjusting their values as they learn and grow? This is what integrity is I believe. These are the kind of deep life and self-knowledge skills that create a high quality of relationships and life experiences. You can't spell Compass without Compassion.

2019 01 06

Cooperation - Inspire the Desire (2 of 2) - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel Cooperation - Inspire the Desire - Conscious Parenting with Vivek Patel This is part 2 from the video of my recent workshop in San Diego on Cooperation. Cooperation is a beautiful thing to experience. It creates a relationship of collaboration. It meets so many deep needs. It gives us a sense of our contribution being valued, of mattering to another and a sense of belonging. Cooperation arises from the feeling of caring for the experience of others. This is something that cannot be forced. It can only be inspired. It's the same as respect, love, and gratitude. This is why I say "Inspire the Desire. I love posting full workshops because I go into a lot of detail. I also love my 5 minute videos, but there's something about going through one idea for a full hour that's very satisfying. The video is in 2 parts so make sure to watch both. I hope you enjoy it and I would love to know what you think.

2018 12 30

I turned FIFTY years old 3 days ago on Dec 27, 2018. When I held the birthday card from my wife and daughter in my hand, the big "50" jumped out at me. I remembered being 19 or 20 and picking up a 50th b-day card and thinking that was so old. I couldn't imagine myself there. Most of the adults I knew seemed to be missing something. I remember that feeling very clearly. I was aware of this difference from very young. I think most kids are. I didn't have a name for it, but I knew I didn't want to lose it. Partly because it seemed like a big loss to me. Every time an adult would assert authority of any kind I would see the loss in them. They thought they were above me. On the one hand I ended up internalizing this mindset. Surrounded by it in my formative years I took it on as my own. That is why I have so many insecurities. Why it's so hard for me to believe people like me. Even my closest of friends have to remind me that they like me and love me (Thank you for your patience!). At the same time there was a part of me that saw the false hierarchical separation of value and worth that authority creates. The thing about believing one is above others is that there will always be someone above you. You are destined to be less than. So much of life is compensating for this "less than/greater than" mindset. My desire to not lose this thing that I saw the adults had lost was also fuelled by my thoughts of parenting. I didn't want my kids to look at me and see that separation. I wanted them to feel me with them. To know that I know. Or more accurately to know that I know that they know. This seemed so important to me, to maintain that feeling of deep equality with children. It has been one of the principle areas of my personal development efforts. It is also a central theme in my parenting philosophy and practice. When I'm with kids I hold no authority over them. It is an attitude that creates trust very quickly. When I was 20 and held that card in my hand I realized I didn't want to inhabit the authority mindset that seemed inherent to being 50. I was determined not to let it get me! My mother had a stroke last week and I've been feeling her mortality more clearly since. It's pushing me. I was going to say "It's pushing me to..." but then so many things came to mind that I'm being pushed on, I realized it's just pushing me. Push. My 75 year old mom, @[666241384:2048:Shivani Patel] has been teaching weekly self-empowerment workshops in a men's prison for the past 6 years. In that time her 6 week program has become the most popular and sought after course in the institution. There is always a waiting list to take her course. The institution psychologists and counsellors recommend her workshops. Some even mandate the residents in their units to take the course. They have never audited her course. They are responding purely to the effect they see when the residents complete it. They leave there wanting a better life for themselves. They are self-motivated to find what is meaningful to them and pursue it. They believe in their own potential and are propelled by it. Often when they walk in to the room they are sceptical. They slump down in their chairs with arms crossed or grabbing their crotch. Staring at my sweet little mother in silent challenge. Sometimes not so silent. Almost without fail, after the first 20 minutes of listening to her talk, they are all sitting straight, leaning forward, engaged and interested. By the end of 2 hours they're in love. After the 6 weeks are over they would do anything for her. Many of these guys have been in and out of prisons for years. They have been through a lot of courses. They always say they've never experienced anything like her. My nickname for my mom is "Little body, Big Spirit!" When she sits in front of those men she holds no authority over them. She is one with them and they feel it. She sees through their layers to the light within. My mother has more trauma in her life than pretty much anyone I know. She's quite weak right now due to the stroke so I'm staying over tonight to care for her. We just spent about 90 minutes talking and all these memories from her past came up. She told me story after story. Things I'd never heard before. We were both in sort of a story telling trance. She has witnessed and experienced more pain than I can conceive. Somehow she has avoided getting jaded. I don't know how she did it. Even with her painful past she sees the men in front of her as whole and good, fully worthy of love, no matter what they've done. They feel it and it awakens something in them. I go in as a guest speaker on week four. I see these guys fumbling over themselves to be respectful to Shivani, to demonstrate their gratitude, to show their love. It's like they've never been seen before. And some of them argue with her. They assure her that they really are bad. She refuses to entertain it. She empathizes with them for feeling so, but her mindset doesn't waver. My mother teaches me about love through her example. Growing up she parented me often in a traditional manner. Yet she kept fighting it. She kept learning and growing. Even to this day she's learning about life and about herself. One story she told me was when she was recently in the hospital (she's been in the hospital a lot in 2018), one nurse was thanking her for being so nice (cause that's my mom!). The nurse told her she's so tired of being treated badly by people that she just shuts off. No matter how much care and empathy she gives, some people are just mean to her. Now she starts out nice and if she's not treated well she just does her job, but doesn't connect. My mom said she understood. It's hard to be treated that way. It hurts the heart. She then told her about her volunteer work: "I do these prison workshops. 6 years every week. I've worked with hundreds of prisoners, as well as the security guards and staff... and in all that time I've never met a bad person." She says it, and she means it. This is the foundation of her course. It is what creates such a dramatic effect on the prisoners. The power of unconditional love and acceptance. She does not tell them that they are bad. She does not tell them that they're wrong. She doesn't make them feel like they're broken and they need to be fixed. She sees them whole. She also sees the layers of pain and fear covering their wholeness. Seeing both she can point out the layers by pointing TO their wholeness. This is so different from pointing to the layers themselves. From this place they feel safe and are willing to hear her, to try what she teaches and to be challenged by her. Even when she challenges them they feel loved for it. The conscious parenting philosophy I teach is the exact same one she operates from in prison. We share the same mindset and philosophy. We discuss it every day. If the non-punitive, non-wrongness, non-coercive, non-authoritative, collaborative, process focused, relationship focused, equal power-sharing and learning partner mindset works so well with prisoners that it's the most recommended workshop by clinical professionals - it's reasonable to think that it would likely be effective with children. My mom often says that the Conscious Parenting principles I share will hopefully one day make her program obsolete. When my daughter was born in 1997, just over 21 years ago, everyone I knew was parenting authoritatively. I had no models to follow. Even every family on TV parented from a hierarchical power structure. I wanted no part of it. From the beginning I worked hard to treat my daughter as an equal. I saw her wisdom as equal to mine. I always felt she had so much to teach me. She truly has been my teacher. I learned many profound lessons from her when she was a child. I learned play, curiosity, exploration and finding wonder and joy in the simplest of things. I wanted her to feel seen like I rarely did as a child. I wanted to meet her where she was. Kids live in their own universes. So often parents try to drag, coerce or convince kids to operate from the adult universe. I wanted to be in her universe. I knew in order to do that I had to really open my heart to my child like energy. This is one of the greatest gifts I have received as a parent. It stays with me to this day. Just this afternoon as I entered the lobby of my mom's building there were three kids with their dad by the elevators. They were yelling and laughing. They were trying to guess which elevator would open. Without a moments hesitation I jumped in with them and proclaimed that I thought it would be the middle one. The youngest kid was with me and she yelled "YA! the middle one!" I was so excited to be in on the game that the kids accepted me as one of their own. We waited in anticipation and the older brother's elevator on the right won. The rest of us were groaning and moaning and laughing as we piled into the elevator. The young sister had a big happy face ball. She said she won it. She bounced it and I kicked it back to her. It went all over the elevator and everyone laughed again. They got off at the third floor all saying "bye bye bye!" The dad had such a smile on his face as he exited the elevator. He was a bit confused, but in a connected happy way. The whole interaction from beginning to end was probably not 5 minutes, but it was so full of joy and play. At that moment I felt grateful to my kid for that gift and I felt quite happy to be 50 and be me. When I think about 20 year old Vivek holding that birthday card, he didn't want to get old because he so wanted to believe in the Magic of Play and Love. As I settle into my 50th year I can confidently tell him that both are real and worth chasing! Happy birthday to me! Thank you for reading <3

2018 12 13

I've just arrived home from San Diego where I was teaching a Conscious Parenting workshop on cooperation. The workshop was fantastic and the video will be released soon. I hope you'll watch it. I spent the evening chatting with my family who missed me very much these past two weeks. We got caught up, listened to music and danced around. After my wife went to bed my daughter and I played Magic the Gathering (a card game) for a couple of hours before she finally went to sleep. She's been wanting to teach me and I said I was ready, so the two of us got right deep into it. It was such a connecting time. Laughing and learning together. Sharing things from the past two weeks. Spending this beautiful time with her reaffirms for me why I teach the philosophy that I do. I know what I share seems extreme. To be honest I wish that weren't true. And yet it is. When I post an article about consequences or power struggles and I write about relating in non-coercive manner, many people get quite upset. To some it actually seems irresponsible! When I witness the beauty of a relationship that has been primarily non-coercive for a couple of decades, I want to share it with everybody. What I mean by "primarily non-coercive" is that I did my best to never impose my will upon my child. This meant what she ate, when she slept, how she related to school, how is she related to the physical environment like caring for her toys or whatever, like cleaning, like saying please and thank you or sorry... I always did my best to never impose any of this he's things on her. I was her guide, but I chose never to have any authority over her. I saw her as my guide as well. I treated her as an equal. She has almost never been in trouble, she's almost never been punished, never been told she was wrong for any decision she's made. I say almost because I am always making mistakes and learning myself. Of course there are times that life demands we have to insist and strap a screaming toddler into a car seat. I have found that these times are far far fewer than we realize. This kind of consistent effort towards being partners in loving, learning and living creates a profound relationship. I don't know what my daughter's experience feels like because I grew up traditional. In my formative years my main experience was the consequence and punishment model of discipline. That meant I was always less than my authority figures. I internalized that self-image and it's followed me most of my life. Cracking that lie, so I don't pass it on is a full time occupation! I look at her and wonder what it's like to have never been in trouble? To know experientially that she's equally worthy in her "success" and her "mistakes". Quotes because all experiences are learning opportunities on the road of life. Everyone says and everyone knows that mistakes are for learning, but how do we really know how to learn from our mistakes? Do we know how to pass that skill on? Recently I was spending time with an 8 year old friend of mine. We were playing in the playground and during a moment of stillness I asked her if she was ever punished. She said "not too much, sometimes grounded, sometimes a timeout. But I do get in trouble a lot." I empathized with her. I didn't offer her any solutions or try to make her feel better at the time. I could feel that she was really happy to have someone that understood and could just be with her in her feelings. Oh, I'm crying as I write this and remember it. A little later we were in the kitchen with my wife and daughter and she spilled some juice on the floor. Suddenly she got a worried expression on her face and looked up at us. We all just stared for a moment because we didn't get what was happening. In our family we have made it a principle and a practice that no matter how big the spill or how terrible the mistake we respond with empathy and support. When I saw the look in her eye, it clicked. She started to go and get some paper towel to clean up the juice. I said "Hey kiddo I'll do that for you." Cause I always do. She paused, thought for a moment and said "No, it's okay, I'm used to it. It's like the time out." That hit me hard. This 8 year old made a profound connection. Being put in a time out was the same as her parents making her clean up. They were both based on force, not learning, not relationship. I asked her "Do you know what mistakes are for?" In a sad voice she replied "To learn from." It really felt like she was repeating something she'd been told. I followed up, "Do you learn from your mistakes? Do you know how?" She just shrugged and said No. We cleaned up the juice together and were soon laughing and playing. My kid doesn't have this consequence based mindset. She generally doesn't do things or avoid doing things because of the consequences. She makes her choices based on her values, on her deep thinking, on her intuition and her trust in her intelligence. Her values have come to her from her own investigation of life because they were never imposed upon her. It's like my saying "Respect comes from caring about someone, not from being afraid of what will happen if we don't." The most common question about this topic is "How do we teach kids to face consequences in the real world if we don't give them consequences at home? It has always made sense to me to prepare my kid for the systems of consequences and rewards that she will be facing when she goes out of the house. It never made sense to me that in order for her to learn about coercive systems she had to live in a coercive system. We related to each other with respect and freedom as equals. We co-created a relationship of learning partners. It was through that safe relationship I taught about what the world outside was like. "Hey kiddo, did you know that there are consequences in the world for not doing what people think you should do? Yes, it's true. "Not everyone out there treats each other with the same respect and love we do. I'm telling you this because when you go out into the world you'll have to face many things that you don't at home." That explanation has been part of our daily lives since the beginning. This is about having a deep relationship of continuous learning. My kid is 21 and that conversation is still ongoing. A much deeper understanding, integrating and living of values occurs with this kind of years long profound interaction. An interaction based on freedom. This of course forces us to think deeply about pretty much everything so we can explore that wisdom with our kids. Using consequences seems so ineffective, when compared to the deep and elegant relationship of learning partners. When my daughter went to school, visited other people's homes or pretty much anywhere outside our home, she had to face some sort of punishments, consequences and rewards. Once we notice the millimeters of the coercive mindset we can really see it everywhere. Because of her experience at home she doesn't take it personally. She sees it as a system to manage when necessary. It is not a reflection on her worth. This way she can make intelligent and informed decisions, taking into account the potential risk, the potential gain, her values and her intuition. This kind of decision making that involves so many aspects of the self, cannot be taught through consequences. It is something learned through living and investigating life. Choosing this as the basis for your relationship with your kids is radical! This kind of Parenting (and relating) isn't for everyone. I know there will always be people who think I'm wrong, unrealistic or at worst idealistic. I share it not because it's nice, which it is, but because I see it as the most practical and effective approach.

2018 11 16

This positive cycle is hard work. Practicing loving myself goes against the overwhelming messages of society. I do believe it's one of the greatest gifts we can offer our children.

2018 10 23

The WAR of Priorities I'm sitting at my computer and typing something that I think is quite brilliant about parenting. My daughter is sitting next to me engaging with me and asking me questions. I'm also chatting with a parent who is asking for help. I'm deep in with them and so I'm only giving my kid about 1/2 my attention or less. She's used to a lot more, so it doesn't faze her when I'm distracted. She knows it's not about her. She knows she's worthy. So she just walked away and started getting ready for bed. Still I felt that she felt that I wasn't present. I was writing about parenting and helping a parent all the while disconnecting from my child as I did so! I was mid-sentence when I knew I had to get up and go be with her. But I wanted to finish that sentence. My fingers quivered. People were depending on me. I might lose the flow. I don't want to be rude. She won't mind anyway. I started to scream and yell internally: "GET UP VIVEK!! GET UP!!" It wasn't gentle. It wasn't quiet. I was screaming and yelling and grabbing myself by the neck and dragging myself away from the computer. "GO GO GO GO GO" Why so much resistance? I don't know. The old priorities still have a hold of me even after over 2 decades of conscious work. Still I fought and fought... and I got up. Suddenly we were brushing our teeth together and she was chatting about these shoes she loves and how she'd love me to have a pair. She runs to her phone to show me a picture. 1/2 hr later we're still chatting and connecting so deeply. My heart is full. This is what I value. Of course I'm composing this piece as we're doing so because my mind is just like that :) When Dr. Shefali was here in Toronto she said that The Conscious Parenting path is a death. Many deaths! I felt a death today. I felt a killing too. It feels liberating. One acronym I share is SMABO Small Moments Affect Big Ones This was just me stopping typing a sentence and going to hang out with my daughter. From the outside it's really not a big deal. And yet I felt the challenge of my deepest parenting priorities. Opportunities to face this challenge arise daily. The effort we put into small moments affects everything. There is a great beauty in the war we fight with ourselves and the love we make with ourselves.

2018 10 22

Power Struggles - A Conscious Parenting Approach with Vivek Patel A Conscious Parenting Approach to Power Struggles This is the video of a talk I gave to parents at a youth empowerment event called @[100068327562212:2048:G Day Toronto]. I would love to hear what you think. Power struggles, like much of life, are largely a matter of perspective. When kids are acting out, there is always an unmet need being expressed. When we shift our awareness from their behavior to what is underneath, we create a growth and learning opportunity. This mindset change increases the trust and connection you have with your child. Neither engaging in the struggle nor tightening control creates connection and harmony. Instead we can use difficult moments to deepen the relationship. We find a greater freedom and connection with our kids when we let go of the struggle and seek to understand them. If we look at the situation through a different lens we can trust the learning path of our kids and partner with them on their journey.

2018 10 02

The lens through which we choose to see our children's behaviour has a profound impact on how effectively we are able to work with it. By work with I mean deepen connection and trust. With us as their parents and with themselves. How do you remind yourself to look deeper when you notice you're getting caught up in the behaviour?

Here is an excerpt from my chapter:

I often get asked why I didn't want obedience from my kid. The thing about obedience is it comes from the external. The way I use the word obedience is following the commands, rules and expectations of an authority figure without analyzing and making a conscious choice. It's different from cooperation, it's different from compassion, it's different from thinking of the mutual benefit of everyone involved in fact it's not thinking at all. The world is very complex. It's not easy to deal with so many aspects of life. As parents we want to give our kids the best chance at success that we can. Obedience is not the most sophisticated mindset we can impart to our children. It doesn't have the depth necessary to navigate this ever changing world. I wanted to foster a more effective decision making mindset in my daughter. I wanted her to independently evaluate every situation, to think with her mind and her heart in balance, to take into account her own value system (a value system that she chose for herself from the inside out, not one that was imposed upon her) as well as respecting that she's part of a community and taking everyone's needs and feelings into account. This is complex thinking! Complexity cannot be adapted to with strict rules. It is best responded to with guidelines, principles, deep feeling, deep thinking and connection. Obedience is the opposite of these qualities. Let's change our thinking to educating and inspiring deep qualities.

---------------

2018 09 24 A free mind finds beauty and value in the simplest moment I am still joyfully reeling from something my daughter told me recently. She came to me full of enthusiasm - "Dad, I want to share a dream I had last night. You and I were in a bakery buying some bread. As you were paying you saw a homeless person in the store. You gave the cashier extra money and told them to let the person buy whatever they wanted. They bought the last loaf of pretzel bread, which is what I wanted, but I didn't mind. Then we just walked out together." I was so moved that she had such a dream about us. I've never told her to be kind and generous. I've just done my best to live that way myself, to share my own experiences, my successes and my challenges with her. Including her in my process AND always seeing that spirit in her has made it so natural that she dreams of us walking through the world together living like this. People always ask me how will you teach her daughter values and to have an ethical sense if you don't tell her she's wrong when she makes a mistake? I felt a sense of deep fulfillment for the blood, sweat and tears I've shed over the years to parent the way I have. The path of parenting without control, shame, wrongness and authority is deeply challenging. These qualities are deep in us from 10,000 years of history. I fight the battle daily because I am steeped in the old paradigm. I have to be always aware. It is a constant discipline to choose acceptance. I do my best because I believe that love and connection are always stronger, more effective and more enjoyable than any coercion. About an hour later she comes to me and says, "Oh, I just remembered another dream. You came home with new shoes. They were really nice runners! I was so excited that you bought those shoes! Then I helped you pick out an outfit to go with the shoes and we went out together to show them off." Now to understand the significance of this dream you have to realize that my daughter loves shoes! I mean she really loves shoes. She knows all the best and latest styles and it's something that excites her very much. In her dream my enthusiasm for her passion and my joining in with her joy seemed so natural to her. I've always made it a point to express excitement and enthusiasm about anything that she was interested in. I know that has made a difference in how she perceives herself and the closeness of our relationship. I remember many years ago when she was in grade 7 or 8 I was driving her and a few friends to a neighbouring school where they were going to play soccer. At one point my daughter put on some thrashy, loud metal music with screaming and lightning bolts coming out of the stereo! Her friends immediately got nervous and whispered to her "Are you sure it's okay with your dad to play this kind of music?" She replied "Yes! He lets me play whatever I want." They said "My dad would neeeever let me listen to this music in the car." "Not only that but he actually likes it!" They exclaimed "That's awesome!" and with a quiet confidence she said "I know." They all really thought I couldn't hear them as they were whispering in the backseat. That honestly was one of the best moments of my life! The dream she had so many years later shows she still feels my celebration of her. The next day she had a third dream. I've been drawing a lot lately. In her dream she spilled water all over one of my best drawings. I asked her what happened? She said, "You just shrugged it off... Like you always do." I share these dream stories because I myself amazed when these things happen. Even though I practice and teach these principles I still am in awe at their depth and effectiveness. I can see the profound results of the priority my partner and I set early on - relationship first. Such a hard priority to follow in society. Hard enough at home, but in a restaurant? Like really hard! Many years ago when I started writing about our parenting journey I asked my daughter if she was okay with me writing about her. She gave her consent because she wanted to help people. Every six months or so I ask her again how she feels about it and she renews her consent. An arbitrary timespan, but it's something. Even with the consent if I feel something might be more personal I will double check. Recently one of my double checks resulted in her asking me not to share and feeling grateful for the inquiry. I felt something similar about sharing her dreams so I asked her how she felt about it? She said she liked the idea because it showed the naturalness of our relationship. What she valued about the dreams was that they were every day moments. Not some big, dramatic thing. She asked me to make sure I emphasize that. There is something unreasonable about choosing relationship first. Imagine you're in a restaurant, like I mentioned above. Your kid is eating spaghetti and throwing it on the table and floor. If your priority is solidly on building your relationship with your kid, on deepening the connection and trust above (almost) all else, how do you respond? It's not a comfortable question. What if they lie or steal? When I think of these dreams my daughter had and how she sees our relationship I feel so fortunate. I feel grateful for all the "unreasonable" choices I made over the years in my pursuit of putting relationship first. I encourage you to look at every moment you have of struggle with your kids and see how things might change if your priority shifted. It's a challenging proposition! The benefits, both short term and long term, are worth the leap. I would love to hear your thoughts on all this. Peace, Vivek

2018 09 21

My 21 year old daughter is watching Bob's burgers on TV. It's an adult animated show. One of the characters was pretending to be sick so they could skip school. She paused the show and turned to me to say: "Dad, I'm glad you never forced me to go to school." I said, "Me too kiddo." She told me about the show and said she was thinking about it and wanted to express her gratitude. From the beginning we let our daughter choose how she wanted to do school. We took her to visit a public school, an alternative school and we talked about what homeschooling might be like. All the way along she chose to go to public school and we honoured her choice. We had a standing principle that she could stay home from school anytime she wanted without having to give us a reason. She never had to do any homework she didn't want to do, she never had to study for or take any tests she didn't want. She never had to achieve any particular grade for us to be more proud or accepting of her. We did explore together what her personal goals were and made plans of action to achieve them. We did all her projects together, studied for all of her tests together and basically school was a family affair. Sometimes I wonder what her memories are and today I got a little glimpse. It's gratifying to know that at 21 she's grateful for the freedom and respect that she was shown in her younger years. A common question I receive is "Did she ever take advantage of it." I have two responses. First of all: No. She used it when she really needed it. Right from the beginning. She never had to manipulate so her requests were always from sincere need. Secondly: In a way the phrase "Take advantage" has no real meaning in our relationship. She could only take advantage if I had an expectation of how she should use that freedom. The thing is, if I have that expectation, it's not true freedom to begin with. My focus is on developing her relationship with herself. It's not about how often she goes to school or what grades she gets. According to the school board rules, when she turned 14 she was allowed to leave school grounds if she had a note from a parent. The day she turned 14 I walked into the office with a letter saying that my daughter could leave school at any time for any reason and I didn't have to be notified. I specified that she was to be given no consequence for not attending class. I also acknowledged that she was responsible for her performance. Of course if she ever wanted to skip she would always text me and tell me. Hey dad I'm skipping and going to get a slice of pizza with some friends. Honestly could anything make me happier? Because of this deep respect for her freedom she understands consent in a profound way. She knows how precious it is and feels grateful for the efforts my partner and I made to honour hers from the beginning. It's hard to go against the grain of society. Little moments like we shared today remind me that's it's all been worth it. ---------- Edit to add: I've received the two questions: "Did you do this from the beginning?" and "What about the work, grades, teachers etc.?" Here is how I responded to someone who asked this on my blog: Yes we honoured her freedom right from the beginning. Of course there were times she couldn't come home for logistical reasons. That's different. That is just life. When that happened we empathized with each other about how hard it was. But most of the time if she didn't want to go to school she didn't have to. There are a couple benefits to this approach. One is that she never used that freedom irresponsibly. She would make mistakes, like we all do, but she learned from them. It's an amazing thing how much respect is earned in a relationship when deep trust is shown. By giving her that freedom she had a self-motivated desire to use it with integrity. She had to look within to see what really made sense to her because she knew I would support her no matter what. When she wasn't sure she would come to me to discuss it. We would weigh the pros and cons of missing that day. What was on the agenda? What info would she miss? Was anyone depending on her for anything that day? Those kind of questions. Like maybe she was tired and didn't want to go, but she realized through our discussion that a friend was hoping to get their book back. I might ask her to think about how her friend might feel not getting it back? Now when I ask this question it's not with the undercurrent of ""She would feel betrayed" or let down so you have to go. It's a sincere question for her to consider in freedom. Each friend is different. Each loan situation is different. I give her something to consider and allow her to make sense of it with her own intuition. This is how continuous guidance happens. This is how a relationship of learning is created. If she missed work she learned from it. If teachers were upset she learned from it. Everything is about learning together. Today my daughter said to me: ""Dad did you ever notice that we have our deepest conversations at night?" Even at 21 she values our co-explorations and co-learning.

Adding a bit more due to some great questions about the challenges and logistics of this choice.

I'll be honest with you in my mid to late twenties I didn't think things through quite as carefully as I do now! And even now I don't think things through quite as carefully as perhaps I ought to! I knew in my heart the damage forcing would do and we organized our lives around it as much as possible. I recognized there were risks and I did my best to manage them as intelligently as possible. Or I should say we knew the risks and we worked together to manage them as intelligently as possible. We treated the whole school experience as a family journey. I will admit I was not above writing a fake sick note! Imagine how deeply supported she felt to have her desire to stay home taken so seriously. Recognizing that we were managing this terribly designed system together meant she felt a natural responsibility to play her part. We Knew in our hearts that every time she received a consequence at school, it was only because the system was broken and didn't understand the true nature of love and human relationships. With continuous support and guidance this kind of Freedom never turns into a free-for-all. We think it will because we're not used to deeply trusting the sense-making ability of our kids. There is always an adjustment period when increasing freedom. I call it the test, treat and tornado phase. When we tell our kids that they have more freedom at first they will want to test it to see if it's real. For a time it may appear as if they are abusing the freedom, but in fact they are testing to see if this thing that has never existed before could possibly be real. The treat phase is a natural revelling in the joy of the New Freedom. This is something I love to see even though it throws life out of balance for a Time. The tornado comes when they finally have the freedom to express all the repressed feelings they have been hiding from us. What they need is consistent support for their freedom and consistently giving them the message that we believe in their ability to manage that freedom. The whole family can work together to find a personal balance which works for them. Can you trust your kid enough to get through the test, treat and tornado phase to a place of self-motivated, self-regulated responsibility? It's a big leap of faith! Even at the youngest age, if my daughter took a day off school one week and really needed one the next week she might choose to go to school anyways recognizing the effect that it had on the system. When this would happen I would always be amazed. And I have to mention very clearly here, it's not that my kid is special in any way. As a father of course I think my daughter is special! However the philosophy of non-coercive relating, of treating our kids with respect and love and dignity, always increases trust and connection. There were times we could not take her out of school. Logistics might demand it. In this case if she has to stay at school when she doesn't want to it's not because an authority figure is telling her she has to because it's good for her in some way. Sometimes parents force their kids to go to school because of their fear of the system. This can make kids feel like we are choosing the system over them in some way. Deep connection comes when it's all of us in the family community recognizing the difficulty of the situation and holding it together. You would be amazed at the difference this makes when the kid can't get their way. Thank you for reading these thoughts. I would love to hear what you think.

2018 09 17

Teaching Kids to Deal with Consequences in the Real World When my daughter was getting ready to go to school for senior kindergarten I talked to her about how the school culture was very different from our home culture. I told her that some adults have this idea that they have authority over children. Authority means that they can tell you something and you have to do it. This concept was quite foreign to her as my partner and I worked hard to never hold authority over her. For many people it's hard to imagine how this can be. When people saw us interact though, it became obvious. Even now at 21 people have trouble believing that we're parent and child when they see us together. In preparing her for the outside world I also told her that if she doesn't do what some adults say they might do something called "Giving her a Consequence." At this point I had the difficult and painful task of explaining that concept to her as well. Adults don't like it when they want you to do something or to not do something and you don't obey, or even worse, won't obey. Because people are in a lot of pain they think it makes sense to force the children to do these things. In an effort to do so they will make you do something that causes you pain. The thinking is that you'll want to avoid the pain in the future so you'll make different choices. The idea quite reasonably upset her. I told her that even if that happens it's never about her. It's just something that comes with living in the world. That she can always make conscious choices knowing how the system works. I also told her that no matter what happens, no matter what the situation I will always have her back. As a result of this she has always related to the system of consequences and power from an outsider perspective. She knows it's not how it's supposed to be, not how we're really supposed to treat each other. It's not theoretical either. It's how she's grown up. Her consistent experience is that we don't punish or make others feel bad to get what we want. She knows that her needs are important, and so are everyone else's. Everyone told me... Over and over... She'll be selfish, she'll only think of herself, she'll be entitled and rude. You have to tell her no sometimes. You have to let her know she's wrong. How else will she learn? I remember going to school for the Grade 5 teacher student meeting. She said "Your kid is the most patient person. If someone buds in front of her in line she just shrugs it off. It isn't from fear, but of honestly not wanting to bother. "She isn't a push over either. There is a line that no one can cross. She knows that line and when someone crossed it she just says: "No." She stands firm and nothing can move her. She knows herself." This is the exact middle ground between being a push over and being aggressive or entitled. It's the quiet confidence of knowing yourself, of knowing your boundaries and knowing your worth. My 21 year old daughter (who is supposed to be entitled and selfish) told me a story yesterday about an interaction with her mom. They were both sitting and relaxing and they got thirsty at the same time. Neither wanted to get up so they played rock paper scissors. The loser would get up. So they got serious, gave each other the "It's On!" eyes. 2 out of 3 and my daughter won. My wife had to get the drinks. They were laughing and having fun. After telling me the story she left the room. She told me one last detail as she walked away, almost as an afterthought to complete the story. "I got the drinks anyway. I like doing things for her." It wasn't showing off. It was just a statement of how things went down. This is the mindset that is created with non-coercive relating. She never needed a consequence to learn that. Consequences cannot teach that. Growing up with being deeply embraced produces a particularly free state of mind. When we receive kids with gratitude, regardless of how they behave, it fosters a spontaneous expression of love because there's no consequence for not showing it. My father used to say: "In conclusion I have this to say about that." In his honour I'll say... In conclusion I have written all this to make the point that it's not necessary to give kids consequences in order to teach them to effectively deal with consequences.

2018 09 17

Power Struggles are the worst. They sap our energy, deplete our relationships and make communication next to impossible. Everyone leaves feeling upset, drained and unsafe. Something in us knows this is not how things were supposed to be. We feel that more harmony and connection with our kids is possible. Yet it seems like there's no way out. So many families live this way for years. The disconnection builds over the decades and when the kids are young adults they can't wait to get away from their parents. One of my daughters friends told me a power struggle story from when he was 17. If his parents told him to get out the shower and he was already getting out, he would climb back in for 10 minutes just so that he wasn't getting out when they told him to. This isn't unusual. There is an urge in us that wants to protect our autonomy when it is threatened. Power struggles, like much of life, are largely a matter of perspective. We can shift our awareness from their behavior to what is underneath. There is always a need being expressed, there is always a growth and learning opportunity and there is always a way to increase the trust and connection you have with your child. Believing this, it makes sense to focus on what will actually reach our kids. Engaging in the struggle never does. Even when we KNOW we're right. ESPECIALLY when we know we're right. That's when the greatest disconnection can occur. It can also be a moment of deepening the relationship. We can find a greater freedom and connection with our kids when we let go of the struggle and seek to understand instead. Often we have a pre-conceived idea of exactly HOW they should behave. Oh those expectations. We're bound to be disappointed! If we look at the situation through a different lens we can let go of all those expectations. We can trust the learning path of our kids and partner with them on their journey.

When I'm interacting with my daughter I can feel how open she is to me. If I want to offer her some feedback, something for her to consider, I pay close attention to this openness. It's like an art form almost, or a dance. I can push so far and then I'll feel the edge of where it feels like an imposition.

I'm careful to stay on this side of the line because I want to keep the line of influence open. I want to keep the relationship of trust solid. I want her to feel free to think about my suggestions. It's most effective for me and it's most effective for her. Plus it feels better for us both. She wants me to give her my perspective. She never rolls her eyes. Actually she does when I'm not coming from my centre. Because she knows me. But when I offer my perspective on something she is grateful. She thinks about it and comes back to me saying. "This is what I've decided." What do you think? I treasure that she takes my opinion into account and I also value that she seeks her inner wisdom as her primary source. I'm 3 months shy of 50 as I write this and I clearly remember being a teenager. In fact all throughout my teenage years I made a conscious effort to remember my state of mind. I knew none of the adults in my life really saw me. My mom did a little, but not enough. I didn't want to forget, so I kind of spoke to my future self. I still remember those conversations. The clearest is when I was 13. I had this moment of deep frustration. I cried out: "No" one understands me. No one understands young people in general. We are so much more than you realize. We deserve more respect. That moment is etched in my memory. I remember also from the youngest age if an adult tried to take my freedom away I would do anything I could to take it back. I instinctively valued my power and independence. Sometimes Id lose hope or the force would be more than I could stand. I might give in for a time. Soon I would find my way back to myself and the struggle would start again. Then if the adult tried to clamp down further to take hold of the situation, we would end up in a battle for power and control that NO ONE is going to win! Eventually we cannot force them. They grow up and find their power. At that point all we have left is our relationship. When force is gone, trust and influence is all we have. If we start focusing on influence from the start there is no dramatic transition. As they find their power we are right there beside them. They use their power to push against the obstacles of the world, but we are not one of those obstacles.

What kids need is to be connected with, to be accepted and validated for their feelings. They need to believe they are understood. They need to believe they are not being judged or shamed so they can trust. In this atmosphere it's safe to actually examine the impact of their choices. They can learn to make different choices that are more in alignment with their values. I believe even a 1 or 2 year old can understand this when given the chance.

If they are acting out as a call for attention or because of low self-esteem, making them feel worse, even a little, won't help the situation. They need unconditional love and acceptance so that they can be open to our guidance. If they feel any judgment they will close down their hearts to protect themselves. That precious path of influence is closed. When kids of all ages act out, there is a feeling of power. That is hard to give up. Part of our guidance is to show them that they have a deeper power. We can show them that their needs can be met in a more complete way through other means. This is so different than making them not repeat the behavior because they want to avoid a consequence, even an unintentional emotional consequence. We can now redefine the power struggle as an opportunity to show our kids their own true power rather than trying to diminish or control their power. When my kid born I kept one eye on her being 16. I wanted to think deeply about what kind of relationship I was building. I knew every choice I made would impact how she would trust me and be open to me. If I wanted her to be open to my guidance all along the journey, I had to establish myself as a safe place from the start. This is why I did everything I could to relate to my kid in a way that didn't create power struggles. Of course it happens, but my efforts were to always minimize the struggle and maximize the joy. This mindset was often inconvenient when bumping up against the real world. I dedicated myself to it because I knew in my heart that it would create the deepest relationship of trust and connection with my child.

One thing that can be useful as parents wanting to move beyond power struggles (notice I didn't write avoid power struggles), is to examine the power structure that does exist in our homes. As parents we have unavoidable systemic power over our children. We have economic power, physical power, emotional power and housing power over our kids.

As they grow we lose our hold on these powers. If we have relied upon them for controlling or even influencing our kids, very soon we lose that influence. The image of the rebellious and distant teen is common and expected. It doesn't have to be this way. We don't have a choice whether or not to have these systemic powers over our kids when they're young. We do have the choice how we use them, how we relate to them and how we share them. When we consistently treat our kids with a high degree of respect and autonomy, they reflect that in the respect they show us. I have made so many mistakes in my life, hurt so many people and hopefully learned something along the way. I want to share those lessons with my kid. I want her to know her power lies within so she doesn't spend a lifetime chasing it externally like I have. I don't want her to find out in her forties (like her old man) that the source of her power is closer to her ""than her hands and feet" (Tennyson) and it is inexhaustible. Throughout most of her life I held this as one of my dearest parenting priorities: That my kid would know her worth and power. That she would know herself, love herself and honour herself. This mindset guided how I related to all of these systemic powers (economic power, physical power, emotional power, housing power and maybe more). I chose to share them all equally with her. I chose not to have authority over her. Our lives were guided by principles, not rules. Rules have consequences attached to breaking them. Only an authority can implement a consequence. Principles are something we are always striving for together. They are flexible and mutually beneficial.

Changing from a mindset of authority and control to one of collaboration and connection is hard. Really Hard. The differences between the two inner states are significant. The behaviours that flow from them are also vastly different. One predisposes us to unconsciously think of our kids as problems to be fixed. The other inspires us to engage in co-problem solving so each of us feels our needs are addressed.

Much of society is steeped in the dualistic mindset of right/wrong good/bad. This thinking leads to the natural idea that parents have power over their kids. Letting go of this can be quite a challenge, and quite liberating. We can achieve a deeper peace when we adopt a mindset of seeing everything as a process and a journey. Our kids are always learning, even in the most difficult of moments. We can also be always learning if we so choose. Seeing the learning path and being on it with them is so different from seeing them as defiant, rude, or manipulative.

In Conscious Parenting what would normally be seen as a power struggle is instead a foundation building opportunity. The purpose of a power struggle is to teach our kids to own their power. When a moment like that comes up between myself and a young person I get so excited. There is so much potential. I also get very concentrated because I know what a wonderful opportunity there is for growth and connection and I want to be my best.

When this approach is taken we will almost never fail to connect with young people. They feel us, feel our sincerity and they respond in kind. A conscious approach to power struggle moments will also to teach our children how to responsibly use power. Isn't that an important lesson to send young people out into the world with? Certainly the way we wield/share our own power demonstrates more than any words we can say. In moments where big emotions arise, our example becomes amplified and they learn what we SHOW them. They take the information in experientially. We want to teach them that they have personal power and choice. We want to inspire them to use that power and choice as responsibly as possible. We do this by creating a relationship that is safe, by processing the situation with them in an accepting and non-judgmental atmosphere, by helping them listen to their inner wisdom, by giving them courage to follow their wisdom and by being a powerful model with our own power. When we see through the lens of using power struggle moments to empower our children, we never want to win. Vivek Patel

2018 08 23

My wife is notorious for not checking her texts. Yesterday I texted her something romantic and she didn't respond till this morning. I called her and thanked her for the response. It was a nice moment and I said: "I would text you romantic things more often if you checked your text more." Her response was a slightly defensive: "I see them eventually." Right away I could feel that I had been complaining. I was blaming her for my not sending her more texts. Like she put restraints on my thumbs or something! I didn't say anything right away. I wanted to sit with the feelings and the awareness for a while. After some reflection I came to realize that my true intention was to celebrate the nice exchange and express my desire for more of the same. What came out of my mouth was very different. It had a different intent and a different tone. I was protecting myself, projecting an intent of lack of interest on her part and generally spiralling into my patterns of pain and fear. It was only one sentence, but the disconnection it created was real. I called her back after about 15 minutes and told her what I noticed. "When I said to you earlier that I would send you more texts if you were checking them more often, I realized that I was blaming you. I am sure that could not have felt very good. I am sorry for that. What I really wanted to say was I enjoyed that text exchange we had and I want more of the same because I enjoy you. At first she she said "Oh! That feels so good. I want that too." She could feel my genuine excitement and celebration in that moment with no complaint to be seen. She then thought deeply about it and said that she could feel the complaint and the disconnection that happened in that moment. She said she was grateful for my pointing it out and she would like to watch for that in her own interactions with me as well. It's not such a bad thing that I criticized her the way I did because I noticed it, I loved myself for it, I exposed it to her and we bonded as a result.
