2018 06 18

Happy Father's Day 2018 I want to celebrate all the conscious dads out there. We are making a choice to do things differently. We are breaking a cycle of generations. It's hard work and it's rewarding. Gentle parenting as a father isn't easy. There are a lot of obstacles in society. As a staunch feminist ally of almost 30 years I do not usually talk much about the struggles of being a male. They are real, but not as intense or pervasive in comparison to what non-male folk have to deal with in this patriarchal, misogynistic world. And yet it's Father's day so I think it is appropriate today! A gentle man is still seen as weak. I cannot tell you the number of people who criticized me, looked down on me and even ridiculed me because of how I treated my daughter when she was young. I did not control her at all. I did not tell her what to do. I didn't tell her no. I didn't punish her or criticize her. I celebrated everything! How will she learn? She has you wrapped around her little finger. She'll be disrespectful and selfish if you don't tell her NO. How will she handle criticism if you never criticize her? How will she handle consequences in life if you never give her consequences? She doesn't need you to be always soft and loving, she needs a firm hand, she needs to know you are the parent first. Now keep in mind, I'm a martial artist so we played hard. She did not have a "gentle" childhood! But I was always (almost always) as gentle as I could be. The picture of the gentle, connected and child led relationship for a man... it just doesn't fit with how we (mainstream) see masculinity. The message is reflected in so many areas of society. The media being one of the biggest influences. Men with deep feelings and gentle natures aren't "real men". I am a martial artist. In the martial arts world embodied gentleness is often seen as a weakness. When I go to seminars or martial arts events I'm often looked down upon at first because of how I carry myself. Especially when I was younger. I often had to break someone's nose before people would start to show any respect! Yet I wouldn't sacrifice my integrity to avoid the criticism. That's why I celebrate Conscious Parenting dads. We go against the grain. We see a different way and a deeper strength and we work towards it. -When we choose not to yell and not to punish we are making a difference. -When we communicate and connect instead of control and correct we are breaking the cycle. -When we want our kids to honour themselves more than we want them to obey us we build them up in ways previous generations never experienced. -We inspire peace when we model a more well-rounded, integrated and confident masculinity than the world is used to. Thank you Fathers for all the love, courage and growth that you commit to every day. Love, Vivek

2018 05 18

Today is my daughter's 21st birthday. I can remember the moment she popped out (Thank you to mom!). I looked her in the eyes and repeated over and over... I love you I love you I love you I love you for about 30 seconds before the doctors shooed me away! That was her first interaction in the world. I remember we looked into each other's souls. Deeper than language, deeper than ideas, maybe deeper than love? She spoke to me so clearly. Gave me a warning: "If you treat me like most parents treat their kids I'm going to hate you when I'm a teenager!" I heard this as clear as day, I'm not even kidding. I just said "Noted. Thank you." Thus began my conscious parenting journey. It has been an exploration, of myself mostly! I remember when she was just a couple years old someone asking me what the hardest part of her development was? I replied, the hardest part of her development is MY development. I recognized early that most, if not all friction and tension in our relationship was my doing. I have many less functional and effective patterns. They come from my past, my pain. Every time I would see myself react harshly or lack patience I found another spot in myself to love and heal. My wife and I decided that we would never punish or use consequences with our daughter. We never had any rules. To enforce rules one needs consequences. We also never said NO to her. Never? Hardly ever. We never told her we were disappointed in her for "this choice" or that she was wrong for making "that choice". Every choice had its effects and we learned from them together. This atmosphere of acceptance is quite empowering. Acceptance of mistakes, of process, of the messy job of learning. She knew when she did something "wrong" she was not going to be judged. She knew I would see her as wonderful and beautiful including whatever thing she did, not separate from it. I celebrate her humanness I celebrate her vulnerability I celebrate her messy learning Learning IS messy. When we try and avoid that mess, when we judge it rather than work with it, we can never get into the deep stuff. Parenting is deep stuff. Growing up is deep stuff. Deep stuff is messy. For her being treated with that kind of respect was just life. It wasn't until she started to see other families interact that she noticed something different. When her friends would come over they often were in shock at first because of how we all treat each other. There's no authority, no fight for independence. Her independence was honoured from birth! Each day I feel more blessed and fortunate for the relationship we have. There is a deep trust and knowing. We have this 18 year, ongoing game of punch buggy. One of our traditions is if we see one at the same time, we break the tie with ROCK-PAPER-SCISSORS. This happened yesterday morning as we were driving somewhere together. First game - Tie - rock rock Second game - Tie - scissors scissors Third game - Tie - scissors scissors We started to laugh because we just kept tying. We tied 12 times before she bailed and decided to just keep doing rock over and over till one of us lost!! We were amazed how similar our minds work. It was a moment of celebration for us. She values our relationship as much as I do. I know she's getting ready to spread her wings and fly from the nest. I am soaking up every moment I have with her. Continuing the practice of opening my heart. I do believe that is the greatest gift I can offer her. Happy Birthday Kiddo. I love you!

2018 01 12

Teaching Kids to Think for Themselves Recently a friend asked if they could stay the night at my place. I mentioned that I would have to ask the rest of the family. When I asked my 20 yr old daughter, she paused for a full 30 seconds before answering. After the silence she said "Sure." Now the thing that amazes me is that she really loves this friend of mine. She enjoys interacting with her. She also knows I'd enjoy the visit very much and she likes to support my happiness. With all that she still took the time to look within and see how she really felt. Sometimes she knows right away and sometimes she doesn't. This time she didn't so she waited till she was sure. She also knew that her feelings would be respected so she was able to make the decision in freedom. All her life I've encouraged her to make decisions by listening to her inner knowing. If her inner knowing told her something that was in opposition to what I wanted to do, I tried to go with her direction as much as possible. As a result she grew up believing she could trust her intuition. This creates a quiet, loving and generous confidence. I remind myself Trust their path Trust their process Trust their wisdom For we are deep mirrors for them as they discover themselves and shape themselves. If they see that trust in us they will reflect it in themselves. Then when they're 20 and someone asks them to do something they'll listen to and trust their inner wisdom. Now some people object that this creates a self-centered personality. Selfishness is the inevitable result. Here's the thing, my daughter didn't want to interact with anyone. She pretty much stayed in her room. She was feeling like having her own space. She balanced that feeling against the joy she perceived I would experience and decided that the cost was worth it. The opposite of selfish. She also knows if she said she'd prefer not, that I would celebrate her honesty and feel joy. It happens often. That's our relationship. So she wasn't doing it for fear I'd be upset or sad. I remind myself Trust their path Trust their process Trust their wisdom

2017 12 16

Fostering a Positive Body Image My daughter and I spent the day together yesterday. It was a lovely time. She got a tattoo and we went to a thrift store. She bought a shirt that she liked, but didn't try it on. She just had a good feeling about it. I supported her intuition of course! Today she tries it on and we are all commenting on how nice it looks. She said: "Well it makes my boobs look nice. At least from my angle and that's the one that counts!" AHHH... I felt so full of joy! THAT is the result of a body positive, sex positive, gender positive upbringing. She knows her perspective is the one that counts. We didn't teach her that by TELLING her that! We taught her that by 1) Seeing her beauty unconditionally 2) Modelling (practicing) seeing our own beauty unconditionally 3) Modelling (practicing) seeing everyone's beauty unconditionally Especially #1! #2 and #3 are harder because of our own conditioning. It goes deep. It is a daily challenge for me to dig my way out of the mindset of conditional and comparative beauty. As I do I am more able to say "That's the angle that counts." I never never criticized her body or her body choices. She always felt my support, acceptance and celebration of who she is. She can see I see her as perfectly beautiful in every moment. As her style has emerged over the years she has felt my joy. I am thrilled by watching her path unfold. The relationship she has with herself was my main concern. When she says "That's the angle that counts" I feel like it was all worth it. It's hard work to not criticize. It goes against so much of how society is. Unconditional acceptance is hard to imagine. Someone recently said they could see I loved my daughter unconditionally. I said in fact I DIDN'T love her unconditionally. I love her "Minimally-Conditionally". I am too wounded myself to believe I'm loving truly unconditionally. I just keep working hard to reach that goal. Seeing this inner and relational work reflected in her now is quite gratifying. Stay true to the path dear conscious parents! Peace, ~ @[593266790:2048:Vivek Patel]

2017 12 11

Letting kids discover their own value system from the inside out is such a challenging journey. We are so used to teaching right from wrong by telling them what is right and wrong. Supporting them to feel it by themselves is much deeper. It's full of many unknowns. It requires us to trust our children. It also requires us to see them on their path, rather than rush them into a destination! When we use punishments to try and stop kids from doing "wrong" we are making them feel worse, hoping that will inspire them to behave better. This never works because it teaches that it's okay to disregard a person's feelings if one feels justified in doing so. I remember when my daughter was like 7 years old. She stole $20 from her uncle's place while we were visiting. It clearly didn't sit right with her because she came to me shortly after we got home and told me. "Dad I stole $20 from uncle, now I'm sure what to do." Oh can you imagine how my heart sang in that moment!!?? That trust, that innocence, that openness, it's what I've always strove to nourish. So we processed it together. I didn't ever tell her how to feel. I didn't tell her stealing was wrong. I asked her how she felt about it. I said that I would love and accept her regardless of what she felt. She said she wasn't sure, but it didn't feel good. She asked me what she should do. We looked at a bunch of different solutions, ranging from "keeping the money and forgetting about it" to "giving it back and apologizing face to face", and everything in between. I told her that she can think about it and decide what feels right to her. That I trust her, I accept her and I love her regardless of which option she chooses. Here's the thing, the hardest part of all this, I meant it. I genuinely would have felt the same pride and love if she kept the money as if she gave it back. Because even a mistake is a learning process. I trust her heart to guide her. She doesn't have to be afraid to make mistakes with me because I see her just as powerful and beautiful when she makes them. In the end she decided that we would go for a visit. I'd distract him and she would return the money. We did this and the feeling of joy, connection and rightness was so present. She felt good about herself. She's also made the opposite sort of decision at other times. Receiving the same support from me. Her value system is truly hers. She mined it from her own depths. When I need ethical guidance I often go to her. Now she's 20 and we're the best of friends. There's a deep respect and trust between us. It's the best thing in my life. Definitely worth all the work (inner work primarily). The blood, sweat and tears of compassionate and honest self-reflection! Peace, Vivek Patel

2017 09 15

Children can be very difficult. This is a long one. I appreciate you taking the time to read it. I promise it'll be worth it! Children can be very difficult. They can tire us to our core. Tire us more than we knew it was possible to be tired! It can really be tough when our little ones are so challenging. We give them all of our time, love and energy and when we feel disrespect and a lack of gratitude from them, it hurts so much. To exist with our children in a relationship with constant Defiance and disagreement is exhausting. If there is throwing, swearing or hitting involved that compounds the challenge. The longer it goes on the more disconnected we end up feeling from our kids and the more disconnected they end up feeling from us. The traditional approach to misbehaviour and disrespect is to clamp down and try to regain control. This can appear to be working for a time, it's not hard to be fooled at first. If you yell at a kid and they do what you say it seems like the yelling worked. However there is significant damage to your relationship being done. When they're old enough to start rebelling, trying to stay in control will end up being a full time job. To be honest I'm quite sure we're never really in control anyway. We can certainly feel like it sometimes though. Feeling out of control can be terrifying. What will happen? We try and avoid it at all costs. And yet when we let go and trust our process and trust the path and process of our children, we can find more ease in life. Ease and joy amidst the chaos. There is effort involved to connect and reconnect to our little ones. It's not quick nor is it easy. We are complex and deep beings after all. You don't have to be perfect. No one is! Just making the effort to be connected and gentle consistently can have a significant effect. It will improve your relationship with your children and the environment of your home. It is a challenge to change the relational patterns we have developed in our families. They run deep. Often they started generations ago and are lodged in our subconsciousness. We cannot (ought not?) rely upon our kids to change. In order to make change in our families we have to change ourselves... significantly. Changing ourselves is extremely hard. It is important to give ourselves recognition and empathy for that hard work (even if no one else does). It is challenging to change and at the same time it's much easier than trying to FORCE a change upon our kids. I have found that the more I change and am willing to change, the more my kid is open to change. In fact this holds true in all my relationships. In life one of the things that guides our decisions, actions and reactions are the priorities that we set. Parenting priorities are super important. If we can create powerful parenting priorities, then we create a solid Foundation from which to operate. The problem is usually these priorities are unconscious in us. I wrote a beautiful blog about parenting priorities and I will post a link to it for further reading. In the traditional model of parenting, priorities tend to be focused around the behavior of the child. This results in a mindset focused on how to modify and alter our kid's Behaviour. When we are focused on this we see our children as a collection of behaviors that are either: good or bad respectful or disrespectful in line or not in line with our expectations. If they fall out of line suddenly they are a problem to be fixed. This is different than seeing them as human beings with Deep Emotions, a spirit and soul (if you're into that type of thing), having powerful wisdom and an equally valid perspective on life. This is where the conscious/gentle parenting philosophy differs. It revolves around a whole different set of priorities. In this parenting style our priorities are more concerned with what our kids are feeling and learning than how they're behaving. We recognize that behaviour is communication of their needs and linked to their stage of learning and development. When my daughter was born I spent a long time thinking about what I wanted my parenting priorities to be and I review them on a regular basis. The thing is I knew that in practice the priorities that I would naturally react with were the ones that were programmed into my consciousness by my past experiences. They are so deep that any unconscious moment and they come out. I certainly didn't want to repeat the same cycle of control, authority and punishment that I grew up with. It has been repeated for so many generations it's time to put it to an end. I should mention here that my mother actually started breaking the cycle. Against mountainous odds she did her best to parent us gently and with uncommon respect. She went against the grain and suffered for it from her environment. It is because of her efforts and sacrifice that I was able to shake off even more of the old paradigm and discover a new way. I wanted to do things differently so I decided to override my unconscious priorities with conscious ones. I made my relationship with my daughter my number one priority. In all our interactions and whenever I have a decision to make I would ask myself if the choice I'm making is going to bring us closer together: as father daughter, as friends, as learning partners and as souls traveling along the path of life together. I know there is a common idea in the traditional parenting mindset that we have to be parents first and Friends second or maybe even friends never. Personally I can't stand this idea! I wanted to be my daughter's friend from the beginning. I don't think the problem is with being our children's friend. I think the problem is that most people who think this way have a poor definition of friendship. A good friend is always there for you. A good friend loves you unconditionally. A good friend has your best interest at heart. A good friend will tell you the truth when you need to hear it and will offer you compassion when you need healing. By placing relationship first on my list of priorities, all of my reactions changed because a lot of things were taken off the table. If I was going to focus on building a connected and trusting relationship with a deep foundation of mutual respect then I couldn't do things like: Spank Punish Yell Give consequences or Timeouts Those were the obvious ones that I recognized had no place in a relationship between equals who have deep respect for and care about each other. For example if my daughter wants to do something and I say no and she does it anyways, I can choose to react to her in that moment with the old paradigm or the new one. I can treat her as an equal or I can treat her as if I have power over her. How I treat her informs her about how she should be reacting to me and to other people in her life, because I am her primary model for Human Relationships. In order for me to punish her, give her a consequence or yell at her, I need to set myself up as someone with power over her and I use that power to cause her pain. The reason I mention pain here is that is the goal of all punishment and reward techniques. Without causing pain there would be no motivation to change or obey in the traditional way of looking at things. We think that they will want to avoid that pain in the future (or avoid losing the reward) so they behave how we want them to. We don't usually like to face the fact that we're trying to cause our kids pain so we soften that fact. I did not want to relate to my daughter that way because of the distance that creates between us. Instead of trying to force the issue, I prefer to work in a gentle and guiding way. Granted it can take longer, but the results are deeper and create a more connected relationship between us. As my daughter's guide through life I recognize that if I create a relationship with this kind of distance she would not be open to my wisdom or influence. She would not feel safe to come to me with difficult or vulnerable emotions. She might not call me if she was in trouble for fear of how I might react. I know of young people who choose to get a ride with a drunk driver rather than face the disappointment of their parents. I did NOT want that between us. Then I'd lose the ability to help her gain the skills she needs in order to become successful in life. Another parenting priority I consider fundamental is developing and Inspiring her to have a powerful and loving relationship with herself. I wanted to give her the strongest inner foundation that I could. I want her to know herself, to love herself and to honour herself in every moment. I want my daughter to know that I believe in her. I believe in her wisdom, I believe in her process and I believe in her path. Partially through the reflection of my faith in her, she has developed a tremendous faith in herself. None of this is permissive Parenting by the way, just to be clear. Permissiveness is letting kids do whatever they want from a place of being disengaged. This is something different. This is going with the direction of the child and trusting their wisdom around most things, except dangerous moments like running into the street of course (or touching a hot stove, eating poison, jumping off the balcony or any of the usual extreme objections I hear!). "Going with" means that you are with them, you are connected and you are guiding them through the whole process of learning and life. Your love and acceptance are reliable and secure through all the ups and downs, through every mistake and resistance. Definitely not permissive! It is actually much more involved than imposing rules, punishments and consequences or even something as subtle as expressing disapproval. "I'm not mad. I'm just... Disappointed." Ouch. In my experience and observation that type of manipulation, whether conscious or unconscious, never works out well in the long run. Creating an environment of harmony and mutual respect allows for natural cooperation to arise. There's a common perception that taking this approach will produce kids that rule the household, be disrespectful, entitled and think only of themselves. In fact the opposite is true. All of those negative behaviors and attitudes actually come from feeling a lack of connection and love. Disrespect and entitlement are protective reactions. We are trying to protect from feeling unworthy of unconditional love. The solution to a lack of love is always more love! No matter where you are in your parenting journey you can change. It's never too late. The Gentle Parenting philosophy starts in your heart! Consider letting go of all punishments and consequences. This alone is a huge first step. Even if you try and yell, punish and give consequences a little less it will have an effect. Drop them altogether if you can. You will look back upon that decision years from now and feel such gratitude to yourself. You will say: "Wow! I'm so glad I stopped punishing. I could have wasted all those years locked in power struggles, hoping to make my kid a good person." Instead you can choose to see that your kid IS a good person. When you see them as already good your job becomes helping them be who they truly are. This is a very different perspective on parenting. It places emphasis on creating that deeper relationship filled with a sense of love, respect and joy. Having a foundation of unconditional love and acceptance. Letting Go of all the moments throughout the day where we habitually create power struggles. We create them by wanting things done in a certain way, at a certain time, or at the very least we want it done! Letting that go and trying to place equal importance and validity on your child's perspective of things as your own. My Approach is always to go with the direction of children if possible instead of trying to force them to follow my direction. I have found that the times I need them to follow, they are more willing to do so from having had that very experience so consistently. This makes them feel much more connected and open to us because they sense that we are on their side and we understand them. There is a lot of work to be done. It's OUR reactions that need working on more than theirs. When kids feel us with them, deeply with them, their need to act out diminishes. One of my sayings is: "Kids are not acting out, they're reaching out." When my kid reaches out to me I want to be there. When they lash out and I don't flinch they learn quick that I'm safe. Of course I fail every day. Like seriously! It's not even funny. I do however make the effort to forgive myself so I don't carry that baggage around. Now forgiveness... that's a whole other topic! I hope this perspective helps. Feel free to ask any questions you may have.

2017 09 10

I would like to share my response to the idea that logical consequences teach responsibility. Here's how logical consequences work. For example the child breaks a window. They learn about how to fix a window. They fix, or help fix the window. They work to earn some money to pay for the window. Of course we're not punishing, we're just giving a realistic experience. We are not angry. We also talk to them about why we're doing this. Why what they did was wrong and why it's important to fix it. This teaches them responsibility for their mistakes. In life they will have to deal with consequences, like if they hit someone's car, they'll have to deal with the police and insurance and everything. So this type of consequence prepares them for that experience. Whew! That is the philosophy as I have seen it explained. Here is what I wrote:

---------------

In my opinion the only way this isn't punitive is if the child comes up with the plan themselves (or in non-forced cooperation with parent) and is self-motivated to follow through. If it is forced against their will it is punitive and I simply cannot see how it will teach the skills required to actually deal with the life situations mentioned above. For example if I hit someone's car the skills I need are -Empathy so I can be present and kind during the interaction that follows -Communication so I can share information and listen effectively. -Feeling of caring for other human beings so that I want to make things right. So that it makes sense for me to take responsibility. These type of skills are what need to be taught to deal with these life situations and it's 100% possible to teach those skills in a non-punitive fashion. It just takes looking at the whole system in a different way. I'll add to the skills, -Being calm and confident talking to authority figures -Knowing how to ask questions - of the police - of the insurance company etc. Personally I love making these lists because they show me how very involved and engaged I have to be to teach and inspire such amazing qualities!! This is the relationship I want with my kid. I want her to think of me as the person who inspires her to be herself!! To own who she is and to love the best way she knows how. If I force her to do something to rectify a situation I automatically damage the inspirational relationship. I'm not willing to do that, the cost is too high. It means I don't trust her to do the right thing. It means I don't trust her heart, her sense of what's good, her conscience. And because I don't trust that in you I have to force it into you. That is what forcing is. This is why forcing amends backfires in such a fundamental way. On the other hand (my dad would always say "4 fingers and a thumb!" and we would all grooaaannn! On the other hand I have found that when I approach kids with the IDEA of making amends, and when I do so from a deeply accepting and NON-Judgmental place, They are very willing to make amends and can get quite creative themselves. This may not happen the first time you try this Maybe not the second With repeated experiences however I have seen kids' natural compassion come out. In fact when I SEE it in them they are very motivated to let it shine through. The amends that come from this process are deep because they spring from within the child's own heart. YES! This is something worth the patience to teach. Even if it takes years (which realistically it does!!) it is worth it. For this is how we put our kids in touch with their true conscience. That deep inner guide that tells us what is right, compassionate, strong and loving. I don't want her to figure this out when she's 40 like I had to do. I want her to know from her earliest development that she can trust her inner voice. That she is worthy of respect because she is a human being. I trust that if she knows herself, loves herself and honours herself her conscience will guide her well throughout her life. I would very much enjoy hearing your thoughts and feelings about what I've written, whether you agree or not! Thank you,

2017 09 07

How to teach kids value for work, financial responsibility and a respect for money. It's not what you might think, unless you know me then it's exactly what you might think! From the day my daughter was born I never considered my money as MY money. I gave her equal share in every dollar. I decided that she had exactly the same right to every cent as I. We are life journey partners. 100%! My only responsibility was to keep us all healthy and safe. But even that was really all our responsibility. So how does this play out? If I could afford it I would buy her anything she wanted. I asked her to listen to her intuition and not her media influenced excitement (if it was something expensive) But if she said she wanted it I got it for her. Even if her reason was that she was media excited and she wanted to go with that I embraced her decision. One thing this did was create an environment where she never had to manipulate me for anything. Nor did she feel the need to use getting stuff as a way to assert herself. I always said yes. If I couldn't afford it I made sure she knew that the ONLY reason I can't get it is because I can't afford it. Then when she was upset, I was also upset. It was true empathy. I was still saying yes. I just couldn't do it. We tried giving her an allowance at the beginning, but it didn't make sense. There was no separation of money with us so it was redundant. We forgot about it after just a few months!! I'm laughing about this now as I write it. I don't know how the hell I knew this back then!! I'm so glad this inspiration came to me. An interesting effect of this type of relationship is that my kid is extremely generous. She LOVES buying things for others. She LOVES paying for her own stuff. The moment she had any money she wanted to give back. Now she has a job and she loves to contribute. She has learned responsibility without pressure. She also enjoys buying herself the things she loves. She doesn't hesitate to be good to herself because she knows she's worthy. Such natural balance. People looking in from the outside over the years could never understand how this approach would teach her responsibility! How will she learn if you always say yes? There's a subtle (and sometimes not so subtle) idea that there must be some pushing, some pain, some struggle, some distance in order to teach responsibility. Ugh I hate that!! Haha. I've always believed that the strongest motivation/foundation is love. I believe in love. It's corny and simplistic and idealistic I know!! That's me. I believe that if I can always frame things from a place of love and connection, even when I have to say no, we grow closer to each other and SHE grows closer to herself. This type of freedom and equality is how I endeavour to embody in every area of my relationship with my daughter. It's rarely easy or convenient. I'm much better at it now than I was. In the early days I was really fumbling and bumbling around trying to figure this out. The struggle is worth it because the joy of our pure and deep connection is the best thing in my life. One thing I often hear from parents is that they get frustrated when they buy something their kids really wanted and they're bored of it in 2 days. It seems like a waste of money. Personally I refused to judge how she used things when we got home. When I was a kid I hated it when adults would do that to me. Why the heck are my parents judging the way I relate to happiness? I knew myself. How could my feelings be wrong? So if I bought something and she was done with it in 20 minutes I would thank her for her honesty and tell her that I appreciate how well she knows herself. I might make an effort to make that toy more exciting. Maybe find new and interesting uses for it. Maybe get obsessed with it myself for a couple days without specifically inviting her to join me. But embracing her if she showed interest. Combining it with other toys in unexpected ways. Fun stuff like that. I ended up having fun with the damn toy anyway and she almost always wanted to join in. If she didn't... I embraced and celebrate that. Of course, of course I make many mistakes!! Of course the traditional parenting paradigm rears its ugly head once in a while and I have to claw my way back to my centre. Or sometimes something else in my life takes up more of my energy than usual and I'm less connected at home. I just keep re-focusing myself on my goal Unconditional love and acceptance. I want to share something about my past to give context to where I'm coming from. We have always lived just from pay check to pay check. There were years where friends bought us groceries because we couldn't afford them. Because of this I would say that 70% of the time when she wanted something more than at the dollar store we HAD to say no. This experience was not foreign to her. She learned to flow with that experience because of the relationship we built over time. It was also never really no. It was Oh goodness! Yes Yes Yes! I want to buy you that thing. Your joy is my joy!! I just don't have the money right now, but the moment I do let's go get it. Maybe we can create a plan to earn and save that money so we can get it sooner? Then we're engaged in some creativity together. I share this because there can be the thought that this type of relationship with money doesn't work if you don't have much and have to say no all the time. It's not so much about buying them stuff as it is the relationship you have to them and to the stuff! They learn about relating to stuff by how we relate to stuff. Also by how we relate to them relating to stuff! The other day she wanted to buy something. She didn't have enough money and asked me if I could lend her some. I said yes, would it be possible to get it back in the next couple weeks. She said "Yes. I'm getting paid on Friday." (Did I mention that she's 20 and working?) Saturday morning I received an e-transfer from her. Simple, straight forward, punctual, responsible, relaxed and enjoyable. The title of this piece is: "How to teach kids value for work, financial responsibility and a respect for money." The answer is with total freedom and love with no conditions. It's a tough sell, but it works!

The idea is that if they want to do a thing and we tell them not to it sets up an adversarial relationship. If we instead accept their urges and desires and then partner with them in learning appropriate ways to express them we are on the same side working together. Teaching discernment and awareness rather than trying to put a hard stop on the behaviour will have more lasting effects. It also sets up a dynamic between us and our kids where they don't feel we're their critics and judges, but instead they deeply feel that we see them, we understand them and we want the best for them. This way they are more inclined to come to us for guidance as they grow up. When I talked to my daughter about lying a number of years ago I told her that she never had to lie to me because I would always have her back in every situation. I told her that I was a safe place to share her victories and her mistakes. I told her that she would never receive a consequence or even my disapproval for anything that she had done. I ALSO told her that it would be a good idea for her to lie to me occasionally anyways. That's sometimes it's good to keep things to yourself. That kids lying to their parents is an ancient tradition. It happens all the time and I wouldn't want her to miss out on the experience! This way I made it safe for her to always tell me the truth and I made it safe for her to lie. FREEDOM! I am pretty sure that she doesn't lie to me very often and I also like to think that she is able to discern when it's appropriate for her to keep something to herself. The idea is that if they want to do a thing and we tell them not to it sets up an adversarial relationship. If we instead accept their urges and desires and then partner with them in learning appropriate ways to express them we are on the same side working together. Teaching discernment and awareness rather than trying to put a hard stop on the behaviour will have more lasting effects. It also sets up a dynamic between us and our kids where they don't feel we're their critics and judges, but instead they deeply feel that we see them, we understand them and we want the best for them. This way they are more inclined to come to us for guidance as they grow up. Teaching discernment rather than enforcing rules may be more challenging, but the results are deeper and longer lasting. The idea is that if they want to do a thing and we tell them not to, it sets up an adversarial relationship. If we instead accept their urges and desires and then partner with them in learning appropriate ways to express them, we are on the same side working together. Teaching discernment and awareness rather than trying to put a hard stop on the behaviour will have more lasting effects. It also sets up a dynamic between us and our kids where they don't feel we're their critics and judges, but instead they deeply feel that we see them, we understand them and we want the best for them. This way they are more inclined to come to us for guidance as they grow up. When my kid came home with a swear word in her mouth, I jumped for joy. We talked about all the ways swear words are used. I shared a list of them and we explored each one. When parents make it a thing, it becomes a thing. But it doesn't have to be a thing! Same with arguing (aka back talk) and lying. I embraced these and all their expressions. My kid never felt the need to hide themselves from me. They recognized me as a safe place, a fellow explorer, someone learning alongside them. When we avoid setting up an adversarial relationship, guidance becomes a joy.

Today my daughter and I went for a walk in High Park to see the cherry blossoms. There were hundreds of people all around taking pictures and enjoying the outdoors. At one point we were nearby a father and his 2 year old son. The little guy was yelling and screaming in Joy at the top of his lungs. His father kept shushing him, not in a really harsh way or anything, but kind of feeling embarrassed and wanting him to be quiet. I turned to the dad, looked him in the eye and said: "This is really the right place for him to scream." I gestured to the open-air and the sky all around us. He paused for a moment and looked at me, then he looked at his son and looked around and replied: "You're right this IS the place for that!" I smiled and reflected back - yes if there's any place that it's appropriate for him to scream this is it. I could see the father visibly relax and join with his son in his vibrant energy. I am always so grateful when the universe conspires to have me in the right place at the right moment to share something like that. I think of the potential ripples. Perhaps that family will have a much more relaxed and pleasant day? Hopefully this awareness will continue to grow in the father and he will think about what are appropriate places for different behaviors so that he's not always shushing out of habit. There are so many habits that we can easily fall into and yet with a little bit of self and context awareness we are able to make different choices, more informed and conscious choices.

2017 05 14

A few words about the damaging effect of using rewards Rewards tend to back fire relatively quickly. They do seem like great motivators at first because we're using something our kids like to get them on board!! The problem comes when kids realize (consciously or unconsciously) that we're using them to get them to do things that they don't want to do. It feels manipulative. As soon as that feeling creeps in the motivation is lost because the need for autonomy is so strong! Another thing about rewards is they focus on a selfish source for cooperation. We clean because we're going to get something instead of cleaning because we have learned to value the family community. It will be more effective in the long term to instil the feelings and attitudes that give rise to cooperation. Trying to force a habit pattern from the outside in will eventually create resistance and resentment. The third thing is that rewards diminish connection between parents and children in a very similar way that punishments do. It's hard to see that at first. In fact when I first heard this idea I totally balked at it! It seemed ridiculous to me until I gave it some serious thought. Once I realized how alike are the effect of punishment and rewards, I had to change my parenting style (again!). I do my best to be open and learn continuously. Learning continuously also means changing continuously. The reason rewards damage the connection between parent and child is that it's based on conditional love and acceptance. We are in essence sending them the message that they are more worthy of our love and acceptance when they act like this and less worthy of it when they act like that. When our kids don't do what we want them to and we deny them the reward, it's emotionally exactly the same as taking away a privilege or sending them to their room. It's a way of saying - because you didn't live up to my expectations I'm going to use the power I have to make you less happy. Oh man that stings!! This is why the longer and deeper route of communication, collaboration, cooperation and connection is always more effective. Requires a LOT more patience and self-regulation too. When we abandon rewards and punishments and focus on engaging in a deep learning process with our kids we give them the message that we love them unconditionally no matter what they do. We teach them that mistakes are opportunities for learning and growth. They are to be embraced rather than avoided. We inspire them to know that they are fundamentally worthy of Love and acceptance. This sense of unshakable self-esteem is one of the greatest gifts we can give our children as we send them out into the world.

I wrote the following for a parent who has parented in an authoritative and punitive manner for many years and now wants to change. They want to repair the damage done to their relationship with their kids. Now that they see the damage that punishment and control create they feel shame for having done so for so long. This is causing them great pain. I didn't want them to be too hard on themselves (a little is okay). I wanted them to have hope, to believe they had the strength to make real and lasting change. I wanted to give them something that was philosophical and practical at the same time. Here's what I wrote. I'd love to hear what you think? ----

My dear friend I would like to offer you a sincere plea to not feel ashamed.

The fact that you are opening your heart now and the fact that your heart is breaking shows what a deeply loving person you are. The only way to truly make the change and repair the damage is one step at a time. It feels to me like you are really ready to make this change and I believe in you. It is natural to feel lost when such a big realization comes upon us. I feel that way frequently! Try your best to work daily on forgiving yourself and loving yourself because one of the greatest gifts you can offer your children is your own self-forgiveness. And I don't mean that in a philosophical, wishy-washy way. I mean it in a very serious and practical way. When we hold on to our self-judgement it actually interferes with our ability to be a channel for unconditional love for our children. This is why it is so important for us to work on forgiving ourselves. Forgiveness is a process though, it is not an on-off switch. Recognize that it will take time. You will have to chip away at the pain little by little. At the same time the feeling of your heart breaking is actually a very positive thing. If you allow yourself to feel it, it can drive you to be deeply focused and powerful on this new path that you're taking. Once you start working on forgiving yourself you can also start adopting new relational patterns with your kids. Here are some basic ideas to focus on and practice: Look for opportunities to offer your children empathy where at other times you would have criticized, minimized or avoided their feelings. For example if your child feels angry and throws a dish on the floor and it breaks, instead of saying "why did you do that?" or "we don't throw dishes." or "clean it up right now young man." or "I'm removing your privileges." or anything like that, You could instead say something like: "My dear love, I see that you are angry and I'm sorry that you're feeling that way. I care about you and I want to help you through this. It's natural to feel angry. Sometimes when I'm angry I want to throw things as well." Ahhh, how deeply accepting and connecting that is. They are longing to be loved that way. I know I myself long for that kind of acceptance. That's why I work to offer it to my kiddo. And then depending on the moment take some sort of action. Try feeling into what would make your kid feel loved and supported. You can ask them what is wrong and let them know that you're there to help. Often when kids can tell their story in a safe environment there is great emotional processing and healing that take place. You could offer them a hug or a cuddle. They might really need a physical reminder that they are loved. My daughter is 20 so often it's something like I'll put my hand on her shoulder if I feel she's down. Sometimes I will gently punch her in the arm. Often it's just a fist bump! Perhaps they just need to vent and you can be a safe space for them to express their emotions. Remember to start with empathy for their emotions and their experience. Once they feel you connected with them emotionally and if they are able to find their centre again, you can do some problem-solving. Another thing to start working on is removing all punishments and consequences for any Behavior. Once we as parents recognize that behavior is actually our children's way of communicating with us things that they can't communicate otherwise, it allows us to look for the information between the lines, to look for the cause underlying the behavior and address that. Addressing the cause of things is always better than addressing the effects - and behavior is an effect. It's not easy to give those things up when we have used them for a long time. However once you get used to doing things with communication, connection and collaboration, you will NOT want to go back! The closeness that you will develop with your kids will be something like you've never experienced before. Even though some damage has been done I believe your kids are longing for a closer relationship with you, just as you are with them. I'm am confident that if you put forth sincere effort you will be able to bond deeper with them once again. Just don't give up. It might take a little while, maybe a couple more years of consistent work on your part, before they open completely. Healing takes time. But even so just starting you will notice some differences and that is wonderful. I would also like to give you the heads-up that often when parents make a switch from a more authoritative style to a more collaborative, cooperative style, sometimes kids can actually seem to regress because they don't quite believe what's happening is authentic. You might experience a period of time where they are testing to see if this new found respect is actually real. Truly the only thing you can do is persist. One of my sayings is: "Your acceptance must be greater than their resistance." Much love to you friend You can do this! I wish you all the best, Vivek

Yesterday my 20 year old daughter went out to a club with her 29 year old cousin and the two of them had a great time. When they were getting ready to come home I suggested they take an Uber because the subway was closed. My daughter texted me to say that she wasn't sure exactly how to call the Uber. Immediately I started composing a text explaining to her the procedure. Make sure your location is on. Type in your destination. Pick the kind of uber you want Etc. I was just about to press send when something stopped me. I suddenly realized I was offering her advice that she may not want. So I deleted the text, well actually I copied it and then deleted it just in case, and instead I simply asked her "Do you want any help?" She said that she was cool and that was the end of it. They figured it out and got a ride home with no problem. This is one of the most difficult and most important parts of conscious parenting, being conscious! Of course there are times when we need to jump in and help our kids at every age, this wasn't one of them! By asking if she needed help rather than jumping in with it I was respecting her ability to manage the situation. I was demonstrating trust and also making it known that I was there for her if she needed me. I am glad that I was able to interrupt myself before I reacted with the desire to rescue and instead was able to make a conscious choice. The interruption gave me a chance to listen closely to my intuition which I believe guides me unerringly when I tune into it.

My daughter and I are profound friends. The quality of our relationship has developed and deepened over the years. One of the main reasons we are so close is because I have always worked hard to not hold any authority over her. We relate to each other with no hierarchical separation between us. I Refused to be an Authority Figure in her life. I chose to be a friend, a guide, a willing student& an equal. In our interactions she feels she can really be herself. She knows she doesn't have to act a certain way to gain my approval. This is one of the main messages I have always worked at making sure she knew I accepted her unconditionally. I accept all of who she is. The light and the dark. I did my best to be a good friend to her. Though I focused on friendship based parenting I am still her dad. Being a friend does not mean I abandoned my role as a father. I am a source of wisdom and comfort for her. I am a foundation of safety and strength that she knows she can rely on. She comes to me for counsel when she is unsure about a big decision. I don't make the decision for her. Instead I offer her things to think about when making the decision. I also stand by her regardless of what choice she makes. The beautiful thing is that, in her way she does all these things for me as well. We are learning partners.

My daughter is 20.5 years old. Her time to leave the house and spread her wings is approaching faster every day. I can feel her living with one foot out the door already! It is an amazing thing to watch her independence blossom. Her confidence grows every day. She herself can feel those wings spreading. I was talking about this with my good friend @[1602607417:2048:Scott] today. I was saying I am preparing myself for the letting go that could happen any day now!! He mentioned that once a few years ago he asked me how I felt about her impending departure. I answered: "Scott why are you trying to hurt me? You are wounding my heart. I'm a very emotional and deeply attached father! I have been working hard at accepting the transition though because I want her to feel my confidence. I want her to know that I know that she will be okay. The thing about her independence is I never pushed her to be independent. I saw her as independent. I saw her as whole. I trusted that her path would lead her to herself... To self-knowledge and self-love (which create self-confidence). When we as parents feel the need to push our kids they sense that we don't trust them. Pushing is different from encouragement. Encouragement goes with the flow of our children. It sees them as whole and joins in their evolution. Pushing sees the child as broken and needing to be fixed in some way. I do not want my daughter to feel that I see her as broken and needing to be fixed. So I didn't push. I chose uncommon trust instead. My saying is: Trust their Path Trust their Process Trust their Wisdom Sooooooo hard to do when things don't look like what we want them to look like. When they don't behave how we want them to behave. At least be reasonable kid, come on! Hard to trust. In stressful moments my unconscious takes over so often. I react instead of respond. Still, when I am conscious (and I work hard at being so) I err on the side of unconditional acceptance. Just this afternoon I was crying thinking about the loss of not having received that kind of acceptance in my childhood. And crying with gratitude that I've been able to give that to my daughter. Ask your kid what feels right to them. Tell them that you trust their intuition about their own lives. Tell them that what you want most of all is that they: Know themselves Love themselves And Honour themselves And you will support them along whatever path that leads. Let them know that you will: Trust their Path Trust their Process Trust their Wisdom My daughter didn't work until she was 19. One day she was watching YouTube and suddenly she said: "I'm bored. I want a job." 3 weeks later she was working in a retail store in the mall downtown. In an instant her learning and maturing process accelerated! Now she's talking about studying overseas! (Sigh...) Every single moment she was watching YouTube she KNEW that I KNEW that she was doing what she believed was best for her and I trusted that. As a result she has learned to hear and trust her own inner voice. She truly: Knows herself Loves herself And Honours herself What better gift could I possibly give to my child? Vivek

My daughter has never felt from me the desire for her to be anything other than what she is. I've never thought that the solution to any problem was that she should change. What if our homes were places where it was safe to expose one's mistakes? What if we didn't have to fear receiving a consequence? What if we knew from deep inside that the whole community will help support mine and each other's learning and healing? What a wonderful family environment in which to grow up. What a beautiful world we would create. People often ask "Why would a person avoid doing a bad thing if there was no consequence?" I ask "Why would a person ever admit to doing something that hurt someone else, if they knew they were going to be punished? Why would they willingly enter into a healing and restoration process if they know they'll be made to feel badly about themselves?" Likely they won't. If we want to teach kids about integrity, if we want to teach them about seeing mistakes as opportunities and to always be learning in life and if we want them to be honest and open with us... we can most effectively achieve those goals by fostering an environment that is going to support them. We have to create a relationship in which they feel safe enough to be vulnerable at open. Every time We punish our kids, every time we give them any kind of consequence and even when we show them disapproval or disappointment, we become that much more unsafe and they withdraw their Hearts from us. At this point we have no hope of influencing them in a positive way. Let us instead focus on developing the skill of unconditional acceptance and unconditional love. It is not something that's automatic. It is a lifetime discipline. And yet if we can respond to our kids with love and acceptance regardless of what they do, regardless of what they say then they will be more open to our influence.

We are doing a family jigsaw puzzle right now. It's one of our traditions. As you can see from the picture we are closing in on the end and I just mentioned this to my daughter. She said to me This Time I haven't contributed the puzzle at all, I haven't put a single piece in! I said to her Well maybe you can put the last piece in that would be fun. She thought for a moment and then replied I think I'd like to put the third last piece in that way you and Mom can have the satisfaction of finishing the puzzle since you've being the ones that have been doing all the work. It wasn't coming from a place of feeling bad of not having contributed to the puzzle. It was coming from a place of genuinely thinking of our experience. The reason I'm bringing up this example is because I want to share how the idea of thinking of others was worked with in our parenting strategy. I have never told my kid to think of others. I have never told her to be generous or to make choices with the welfare of others in mind. I know from experience that lectures are not the most effective way of inspiring deep qualities in a person. When we tell a person what they're doing is wrong it makes them FEEL wrong and they cannot see you, they cannot hear you because they enter a self-protective mode. What we focused on was giving her a consistent experience of what it felt like to be care for this way. In every circumstance her feelings were important. When she threw food on the floor - her feelings were important When she would say no and stomp away - her feelings were important When she would scream and yell and hit me - her feelings were important She grew up with the feeling that we treat each other as if our feelings are important. That's natural. That's life. It's not a sacrifice, not an effort. It flows from her so naturally. I have noticed that even the most aggressive kids, when I treat them this way even for just an hour or two their whole demeanor changes. A weekend and real inner transformation can be seen. Even though it's predictable it amazes me every time. Of course is not easy to respond with love, acceptance and kindness in difficult moments. It is a constant challenge. It requires a lot of practice, dedication, discipline and patience in myself because I make mistakes all the time. I want to give myself the same Grace for my mistakes that I want to give her so that we can recognize that we are on a lifelong learning path together. As she was growing up everyone who saw my parenting style or at least most people who saw my parenting Style told me that she was going to grow up selfish and entitled because I never said no to her. At least it seemed like I never said no to her! I think those years of criticism make me extra special sensitive to small moments of natural generosity and kindness like this.

2018 12 11 All difficult behavior with children is communication of their unmet needs. Whether it is an emotional need, or a physical need, a mental need or a relational need. Our most effective approach is to help them meet their needs rather than try and punish the need out of them. Marji Zintz says "You cannot punish away a need." Even if a consequence makes them unhappy enough to avoid the behaviour, the unmet need or unprocessed emotion will still be in their consciousness and will come out another way. The main thing consequences teach kids is if they make mistakes they cannot trust us to be there with them and help them through it. Instead they learn to hide their mistakes, to hide their learning process and essentially their humanity from us. Only with unconditional love, acceptance and understanding can children find their way to their Center again so that they can be free and open to be themselves. It's perfectly reasonable to be triggered by rudeness and disrespect from our children because we ourselves did not learn the emotional capacity stay centered and at peace in those moments. Our parents did not model deep acceptance of our learning process. Our basic understanding of ourselves and the world was created in our formative years. Through consequences (including the painful "I'm not angry, just disappointed") we learned it was not safe to make mistakes and that our big emotions were not acceptable, even dangerous. We had to protect ourselves so we learned to either comply or resist. Neither was about caring for the relationship. This is why it's so important for us to model a very different way to our children The only reason consequences work is because they make children feel bad. The reason we can make children feel bad is because we have power over them. We have physical, emotional, economic and housing power. When we use that power to control them we diminish their trust in us. We also teach them an unhealthy use of power. When we use consequences we are modeling and teaching the opposite lesson we usually want to impart. We want to teach kindness, respect and caring for the mutual needs of everyone in the family community. Instead the lesson we teach is that if we think we are right about something we can use our power to force the other person to think, feel and act how we want. If we want to teach them how to manage consequences in the real world it makes more sense to engage with them in a lifelong Co-learning process. Do you know what are the skills, knowledge and attitudes necessary to effectively manage the consequences of the real world? It's worth thinking about them deeply. When I made my list I found they are in fact quite deep and profound. There are things like discernment, empathy, research, knowledge of our own values, compassion, an understanding of which consequences we are willing to suffer and which ones we aren't... The list goes on. If we spend our time teaching these things, rather than using consequences, we will give them a much stronger foundation with which to go into the world. When a kid is disobedient, rude or even destructive, they are genuinely doing their best to express themselves in the way that they think will get their needs met. The problem is they have not yet learned effective need meeting strategies. Part of the gift we can give them is to teach them strategies that are more effective, elegant and enjoyable. This kind of education and inspiration is the opposite of imposing consequences. It is a longer process because teaching a deep skill takes time. It might take weeks, months or even years! Are you willing to spend a year or more working deeply with your kid on how to regulate their emotions? Let's work with our children in a deep learning process so that they feel safe to make lots of mistakes as they grow. After all, isn't learning the process of making mistakes, analyzing them and then trying again? Making more mistakes and more and more and learning and trying again? We inhibit this process by giving them the repeated experience that if they make mistakes, even big mistakes, they're going to receive some sort of pain or disconnection from us. We teach them the opposite of learning from mistakes. Let's be our kids learning Partners shall we? Give them the kind of support that we never had. Give them the confidence that their parents will be there emotionally, relationally, physically and materially regardless of what they do. This is the kind of relationship Foundation that lasts a lifetime!

2019 01 03

When teaching respect our greatest influence is with the example we set. If we want our kids to be respectful when they're upset, instead of lashing out, we must model the same behaviour. If we cannot be respectful in the midst of chaos and big feelings, how can we expect our kids to? If we punish them when they do something wrong, if when the chips are down they cannot count on our deep respect, this is what they learn about life. This learning is experiential and goes deeper than any lecture or explanation we can offer. When you have a moment of choice on how to react/respond to your child, try and imagine how you'd like to be treated in a similar situation. Imagine that you've made some big mistake and the person who's responding to you is your dearest friend. The friend who knows you, your dark and light sides and still loves you. Imagine how you'd like that friend to react... and offer the same reaction to your kid. Thinking of this person there can't be anything punitive nor even judgemental. We just accept each other as human and learning about life together. If you don't have a friend like that then this is your chance to be one. It's such a gift to offer our kids, to be someone that believes in them no matter what. Treating them with respect in difficult moments teaches them to do the same. d Vivek

2020 01 24

One of the benefits of committing to the non-coercive, collaborative parenting path, is having a deep relationship with your kids. Today was prison day. My wise and loving mother teaches weekly self-empowerment workshops in a prison. I drive her every week and I go in as a guest speaker once every six weeks. The whole trip usually takes me about 6 or 7 hours. It's a long day. More often than not my daughter, who's 22, comes along and hangs out with me while we wait for Granny to finish her workshop. This week her back was a bit sore. She woke up tired and didn't really feel like going out. She also wanted to spend time with me, and chose not to let all that stop her. We didn't do anything special. We bought a few groceries from Walmart and then just hung out at Starbucks for an hour. We chatted a bit, but mostly we were doing our own thing. It is a relationship of deep comfort and safety. It didn't have to be anything fancy, we enjoy being in each other's company. This is not me showing off (maybe a little). I am sharing this because the principles of non-coercive, collaborative parenting allow for the opportunity of a deeper relationship than mainstream parenting ever can. I apologize if that sounds harsh. It's just how things are. Coercion and authority create disconnection and damage trust, every time. Most older kids are really looking forward to getting out of the house. It's not common for 20 year olds to have this strong desire to spend long hours with their parents, just enjoying each other's presence. Even as I type those words I can feel how rare of a condition that is. Yet it is available to you. It's not easy. Parenting from a different paradigm is powerful and challenging work. Letting go of control and authority with children goes against all of the ways we deal with children in society. Going against the grain is hard and it is a lifelong journey. It requires effort and continuous self-evaluation. People often think that I'm permissive and uninvolved because I never punished my child, I do not tell her what to do, I do not tell her she's wrong and I don't say no to her. I can adhere to those principles and still be involved. In fact conscious/gentle parenting is much more involved. Here's an example. This afternoon as my kid and I were spending time together waiting for Granny, she was in a withdrawn mood and short with her speech. Many thoughts went through my mind, many feelings rushed through my body. Feelings like: Offense, anger, confusion, relief, joy, acceptance. A full range. Thoughts like: What have I done? Is she upset at me? What can I do to make her feel better? Should I say something? Should I ask her a question? Give her space? The first thing I had to do was separate my own feelings and fears, from my parenting priorities, values and principles. My feelings of fear and offense were my responsibility to deal with and take ownership for. My child is not responsible for my feelings. Once I am firmly set in that understanding I can mostly avoid projecting my issues on to her and I can be present as support and guide. Without some kind of self-awareness practice we inevitably will project our past and our wounds on to our children. Taking responsibility for my own feelings allowed space for my heart to open. I was able to see that she was offering me the gift of her truth. She was honouring me by feeling comfortable enough to be herself. I tuned into her energy. Her non-verbals, her tone, her responses. Then I intuit whether to engage, what kind of engagement or to give space. It's not really a parenting method. It's a connected and tuned in relationship. Today I chose to give her lots of space and hold a very gentle response when she was harsh. I could feel that she made a sacrifice to be with me today. I loved her for it. I could have said "Hey, I was hoping we'd have a nice afternoon together. I can see you're not feeling that great, but perhaps you could try not taking it out on me and we could enjoy each other's company." I could have said that, but I'm glad I didn't! That would have given her the message that I don't accept her and I'm not a safe place for her feelings. At that point she's going to have to repress what she feels and adjust herself to something inauthentic in order to gain my approval and acceptance. This is not a very effective way to create a deep and trusting relationship with somebody. It certainly is not going to make me a safe place for her to process her challenging emotions and experiences. Holding space for her also meant that I needed to trust in our relationship. I needed to trust in the communication patterns we have built over the years. I needed to trust in the love and understanding we have between us so that I didn't take her reactions personally. After a long day we finally got home. She went to her room and spent a half hour by herself, probably watching YouTube. I think she was really happy to be home because when she came out her whole energy had changed. Suddenly we are talking about all sorts of things. She told me of a book she loves. I love hearing about it. She knows I love what she loves and she loves it. I could also feel an unspoken gratitude for letting her be herself today. For seeing her heart and not the surface behavior. This is hard work! Later that evening my wife came home from work. I'm fortunate that my wife and I have had very similar ideologies around parenting from the very beginning. My daughter's relationship with her mother is something amazing and magical. When my daughter hears my wife's key in the door, she drops whatever she's doing and heads to the door to greet her. The two of them then follow each other around the apartment for a half hour just talking. It's part of my wife's arrival ritual. I delight in the relationship between them. Hearing them chatting like girlfriends in the kitchen makes my heart sing. They are making food together and talking about their day. The result of 22 years of non-coercive, deeply connected, relating, shows itself in their ease and comfort with each other. It's truly one of the greatest gifts of non-coercive, collaborative parenting. I know that there are so many things that feel important when we are raising kids. Sleep, food, chores, manners, obedience, homework, hygiene, social skills.... The list is never ending. Having our attention pulled in many directions like this can make us forget our deep priorities, principles and values. I want to encourage you to put relationship first in all your interactions with your children. Preserve the trust and connection between you. Help them to create a powerful relationship with themselves. You will create a powerful foundation that will grow and deepen throughout the years. Peace Vivek

One of the most profound tragedies of the traditional, authoritative parenting style, is that your children never get to know the beautiful being that you are. This is a thought I'm steeped in as I contemplate life, after coming home from my father's funeral today. The damage to the trusting relationship feels like too big a cost for me. Especially if I have the choice. I don't want to make any choice that distances me from my child. Or worded in the positive, I want to always make the choices that bring my child and I closer.
