Peace Vivek ------------ Edited to add: I chose the word Authoritative on purpose, knowing the three commonly defined styles of Authoritative, Authoritarian and Permissive. I was even going to originally mention that in the piece, but I didn't want to interrupt the flow. In the mainstream "Authoritative" is supposed to be the good one. It's warm and affectionate with loving limits and discipline. This traditional idea of authoritative parenting doesn't go far enough for me. I have always worked hard to not hold any authority over my kid. Authoritative parenting has the word authority right in it! Granted the intent is to use that authority benevolently. It still sets up a hierarchical power structure that necessarily limits trust and vulnerability. All three of the mainstream parenting styles - authoritative, authoritarian and permissive - are operating from the same power paradigm. The difference between them is how they engage with that power. What I practice and teach moves away from this paradigm altogether. It's about forming a relationship of equals where no one has authority. I used the word authoritative to demonstrate my desire to step away from that whole way of thinking. Yes this is as radical as it sounds :)

2023 07 10

The QUESTIONS As non-coercive collaborative parents, we are always trying to dig deeper into our mindset, into our thinking, into our choices. We are always trying to uncover deeper layers of our coercive patterns so that we can shift them. Rather than imagine we aren't being coercive, we accept that we probably are and are always on the lookout. This of course is very challenging, to try and be conscious all the time. I have developed a number of tools to make it easier, and one of them is something I call the questions. I ask these questions of myself all the time when I'm interacting with my kid and it helps me be clear in my mindset. The Questions: 1) Am I oppressing or empowering? 2) Am I imposing my values or supporting their self-knowledge? 3) Am I violating their consent or respecting their autonomy? 4) Am I controlling or collaborating? 5) Does this decision make me feel less safe or more safe to them? When we let these questions guide our thinking and our decisions, we soon find many things we need to change. As challenging as that can be, it is also something to celebrate. I invite you to start asking these questions in your interactions with your kids.

August 10 2025

There are people who think children are inherently bad and need to be fixed. This is where the idea of punishment, consequences, rewards, and corrections come from. The thing about people who believe children are a problem needing to be fixed, is that deep down they feel that about themselves as well. Letting go of that core belief is not easy. That's why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting (NCCP) there is a high emphasis placed on the parent's relationship with themselves. Self-compassion, self-reflection, self-care, No-Wrongness, inner child healing, all that stuff. This is the beauty of NCCP, it forces us to humanize ourselves in ways that we never got as children. Because the more we humanize ourselves, the more effective we are at humanizing our children. This is how we break the cycle and don't pass on the deep unworthiness that conditional parenting creates. Consider letting go a little bit more of control. Look for places where you habitually control, and interrupt those patterns. Notice the times that you think your kids are a problem to be fixed. And when you notice it, interrupt that pattern as well. Remind yourself that a kind and loving approach is always going to be more effective. Even if all the influences in the world, inner and outer, are trying to convince you that force is necessary. You will find that as you soften your heart towards your kids, you will soften your heart towards yourself as well. The deeper you believe that your children deserve to be raised without any form of power or violence, the more you will believe that about your own self. What a beautiful model this sets for our kids. Even as we're going through the process we are modeling going through the process! They see us learning to love ourselves, and it gives them more permission to love themselves. Because even with all our best efforts, they will encounter a lot of non-loving messages in the world. Our modelling is one of our main areas of influence in combating those negative messages. So you can see that NCCP is a Win-Win-Win! -----

Punishment Produces Selfishness

When we use punishment, consequences, or any form of wrongness to alter our children's behavior, we actually inspire a selfish motivation. If the kids get a consequence because they didn't clean up, they might clean up next time to avoid the consequence. But they're not cleaning up because they care about the family community, they're not cleaning up with a sense of joy or even a sense of genuine responsibility. They are not cleaning up feeling connected to their parents, they're cleaning up to avoid experiencing the pain that they've been promised by their parents. The focus is on how they can avoid feeling pain, and experiencing the disconnection that comes with it. Their focus is not on caring about their impact, or on working together in a cooperative spirit with the family community. And I want to be very clear about this, you can't have both. If you are punishing and giving consequences to your kids, it is not creating a sense of family community. It is creating a division of hierarchy. A relationship of power over. Necessarily. This is why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting we don't use any of those techniques, including enforcing limits and boundaries. We try to do everything collaboratively, through connection, collaboration, exploration, learning, play, and the understanding that this process takes time. The difference in result however, is that the kids really own their values. They make their decisions based on an exploration of the kind of person they want to be, the kind of relationships they want to have, the impact they want to have on those relationships, the impact they want to have on their communities, etc. They are not making their decisions based on a fear of consequences. Doesn't that seem like a much more shallow motivation now? Let's teach our kids a deeper and broader understanding of decision making. Will you join me in leaving behind the old ways of hierarchy and control?

---------------

I love discussing Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting with ai. They always suggest that a balance of consequences is necessary and I convince them otherwise. This convo is with an ai dedicated to debunking myths and inaccurate info. I gave it a shot It's not really a conspiracy theory, though most parents would profoundly disagree. I stated that children should never receive consequences or punishments as part of parenting. All our guidance should be loving and collaborative, honoring their consent and autonomy. I've been doing this for a while so I am confident my my reasoning. the ai argued at first, but agreed with me in the end. ------------- ai: I appreciate your commitment to nurturing children with respect and empathy, and your emphasis on making discipline a loving and collaborative process. You've made some powerful observations based on your experience, and it's clear you're invested in the well-being of the children and families you work with. On the subject of children never receiving consequences or punishments, it's valuable to consider the distinction between punitive measures and natural, logical consequences that can help children learn from their actions. While punitive punishments often focus on making a child suffer for wrongdoing, which can indeed be counterproductive, natural consequences are the outcomes that naturally flow from a child's actions. For example, if a child refuses to wear a coat on a cold day, the natural consequence is feeling chilly, leading them to understand why dressing warmly is beneficial. Logical consequences are similar but involve an element of discussion and understanding. For instance, if the screen time is too excessive, a logical consequence could be agreeing that it will be limited the following day to ensure balance. This isn't a punishment but an agreed-upon result of their actions that helps them understand cause and effect. Incorporating children into the decision-making process regarding their behavior is indeed important and respects their autonomy. But recognizing that consequences natural or logical are not inherently punitive allows for teaching accountability in ways that align with loving, collaborative discipline. Children benefit from understanding that all actions have consequences, which is a vital life skill. This understanding doesn't take away from their autonomy; rather, it helps them to mature into individuals who can anticipate and consider the results of their decisions. It's about guiding, not coercing. The balance lies in ensuring the child feels heard and involved while also comprehending that their choices lead to outcomes that can be positive or negative, depending on the situation. Considering cultural, social, and psychological research, it's evident that children learn to navigate the world through the structures and limits provided to them. Not all limits are coercive; some are essential for safety and teaching. If we frame limits as part of our guidance and a natural part of life, rather than imposing them without explanation, children can learn to trust them and understand their purpose. It's also about finding a balance. Collaboration and discussion should be at the forefront of parenting, but children also need to develop the coping skills to deal with situations where they can't make their own choices. Well-thought-out consequences and limits can help children learn to deal with the realities they'll face growing up, fostering responsibility and personal growth within the safe, loving framework you advocate for. ------------- Vivek: the way you described both logical and natural consequences still rely on the child experiencing discomfort and therefore wanting to avoid it in the future. It does not teach discernment, it does not impart values. for example if the child goes out without a jacket and feels cold, it's not automatically correct that they need to wear a jacket next time. every time they go out, I want kids to use their discernment to decide whether or not it makes sense to wear a jacket. Perhaps they want to play and the jacquard would be cumbersome, therefore it would be worth the cold in order to be free. Perhaps they're going on a long walk and the jacket would be necessary that day. I didn't want to teach my kids to respect boundaries, I wanted to teach my kid to watch to respect boundaries. This is one of my favorite one liners of mine! And it very accurately portrays how I was with her as a guide. The way I figured, if I really wanted to teach my kid to respect boundaries, the experience of boundaries in our home had to feel very positive to her. The moment it felt oppressive, the moment it felt like a sacrifice, the moment it felt like it was against her will, she was not going to have a positive association with the idea of boundaries. If we think about the way a person learns, the more strict we are with boundaries, the less a kid is actually going to care about respecting boundaries. Strictness feels oppressive. It doesnt teach kids to want to respect boundaries. Nor does it teach them the discernment to think about which boundaries make sense, and question the ones that dont. The moment we become the authority, we are no longer the trusted guide. This is the central problem with the authoritative approach. We can easily teach kids about the boundaries in society without ever imposing a boundary on them against their will. In fact, well be much more effective, because our kids wont have to put up a protective barrier between us and them. But the moment we violate their consent and autonomy by imposing our will, they have to protect themselves from us. We are no longer their partners. We are now the obstacle. We are now the adversary. Parenting approaches rarely take into account the emotional/relational associations children form based on how we treat them. The moment we take the tablet out of their hands, the moment we stop them from eating the cookie, the moment we tell them they are wrong, learning shuts down. They move into survival mode. It is so much better to treat our kids in ways that keep their learning minds open, enthusiastic, vulnerable, and trusting. From this place, we can guide them far more effectively. -------------

The family is a system. What we put into the system profoundly affects how the system operates. In Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting We strive to input love, peace, collaboration, connection, respect into the family system. The times we input something more harsh, or controlling, perhaps we're triggered or overwhelmed, when that happens we don't excuse it. We take accountability, apologize and repair. This deepens our relationship with our kids, because they know that we are actively working to treat them with respect. The thing about authoritarian parenting, and authoritative parenting, is that by design they input peace at times, and violence at times, into the family system. This produces an imbalance that creates disconnection, on all levels of relationship. Even in gentle parenting, we are still advised to hold a boundary that the kid doesn't like, and then when they protest and cry, we empathize with their feelings. We say, it's hard not to get what you want, it's natural to feel frustrated. And yet the reason we are doing this is because we are using a power over technique to control our kids. Emphasizing might soften the blow, but it is still a blow. Authoritative parenting is a wonderful step away from authoritarian. It makes parents and kids so much closer than authoritarian does because at least we remove the harsh punishments. Kids feel a lot safer with authoritative parents than authoritarian ones. It is a great step away, but it is only a step. There are many more steps to go as we evolve in our understanding of how we want to treat each other as human beings. Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting Is the next logical step in that progression. Away from the hierarchical, power over, and violent authoritarian. We recognize how dehumanizing it is and we strive to be deeply humanizing instead. This is why we choose not to use consequences, rules, limits and boundaries. All things that kids resist and we do against their will, or things that we have to enforce. Instead we work at creating collaborative relationships where our kids feel deeply heard and involved in all aspects of our lives. We recognize that the family is a system, and we nourish every part of that system. It really is a very different way of approaching the parent child dynamic. Children soon learn that they don't have to fear their parents, that they can be their true selves and they won't get in trouble, they won't be disapproved of, they will be accepted as they are. This inspires kids to be so open and connected with their parents, that cooperation and collaboration tend to flow much easier. If you think you might be ready to take a step further along the journey of non-coercion, I might recommend checking out and subscribing to my YouTube channel. I have over 200 videos there, that go into so many details, full of so many stories! I really love my YouTube channel. See if right here, right now, you can think of a rule or a limit that you can let go of. You don't even have to tell your kids necessarily, just stop enforcing it. Then replace the time you would have spent on the rule or limit, with something connecting, appreciating, admiring, fun, or something along those lines. With every little bit of hierarchy we let go, a deeper connection arises, a deeper trust is possible. -------------

Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting Is distinctly non-hierarchical. That means we don't hold power over our kids, we don't think of ourselves as above them, we treat them as equals. This is different from authoritative parenting, which is quite specifically hierarchical. Authoritative parenting is gentler than authoritarian of course, but still operates from a similar power structure and relationship structure. So in NCCP, we focus on nurturing the following three new parenting relationships that replace the old school authoritative hierarchical. They are: Model, Guide, and Friend. With all three being mutual relationships. Bringing conscious attention to nurturing the Model Guide Friend Mutual Relationships, creates such a deep dynamic between parent and child. I have been living those relationships for decades, and this morning I went to brunch with my 28-year-old daughter. The easy, joyous, deeply respectful relationship we share is so precious. Because I never placed myself above her, she feels very little need to protect any part of herself from me. She knows that I accept all of her. Not only do I accept all of her, I delight in who she is! And that is also mutual. After I dropped her back at her apartment I went to see my friend Tanya, and she asked me how was brunch? I put my hands on my chest and said, "I'm so in love!" I think little red hearts were pouring out of my ears! LoL. Part of my joy comes from how much I enjoy being with this amazing human. And another part of my joy comes from reflecting on the 28 years of constant intense work to foster and nourish this non-hierarchical, deeply connected relationship. In a safe relationship like this, kids are so much more willing to collaborate and cooperate. When kids don't feel like they are going to get in trouble, they don't need to lie or hide things from us. When They can trust that we are not going to exert our power, they can listen to our point of view and take it into account. There are so many wonderful effects That come from working with the Model Guide Friend relationships, and releasing our attachment to power and control. -------------

Honoring our children's consent and autonomy is a vital ingredient in keeping them in touch with their humanity. Traditional parenting is designed to separate us from our relationship with ourselves. It is designed to break the connection to our deep wisdom. This is why giving kids the message that their autonomy and consent are valid and valuable is so important to their sense of self. Honoring children's autonomy is not creating entitlement, as we hear so often. Entitlement is a reaction to a disconnection from self. When we feel disconnected from our essence, we try to make up for it through the external. And this often manifests as what people call entitlement. But it is in fact a response to an insecurity. This is why in Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting, we put in great efforts to honor our children's autonomy, (physical, mental, emotional, and spiritual autonomy). We want our kids to have a deep and stable relationship with themselves. We want them to know their worth. Most of the world doesn't think twice about violating kids autonomy and consent. Anytime I post about autonomy & consent people always respond saying, Oh, of course you can't honor their autonomy, they're kids. The brainstem, and the brain development, and they're immature, and we know more. I don't think that kids being more vulnerable is a justification for honoring their consent and autonomy less. In fact, given the immense power we have over them, we should act with more integrity not to use that power to control them. It's also important for us to be aware of the model we are setting. We are teaching them experience by experience, layer by layer, their actual worth. Is their autonomy worth protecting and honoring? Is their consent worth protecting and honoring? Then of course, they learn that about others too, because if we use our power to consistently violate their autonomy and consent, they're going to learn that when they have more power, they can do the same to others. This is why I say - you cannot take the tablet out of your child's hand without violating their consent. Yes, even if you empathize. When we do this it hurts and they can't trust us. We are not a safe, wise guide at that point. He became the adversary. This adversarial relationship makes it much more difficult for us to guide them into learning about self-regulation, about setting intelligent and self-care limits for themselves, and about caring for their impact on others. We can't guide them to those things because they shut us out. And rightly so! Anything that we do that has force, that violates their consent and autonomy, they know it's a violation, they feel it. I remember as a kid feeling as if I were less than, don't you? Let's not do that to our kids. We have the opportunity to write a new story, to create a new pattern of human interaction based on true respect, love, and compassion. And an amazing side effect is we also heal ourselves in the process. Every time we fight against the urge to control we heal our inner child a little bit too. So I encourage you to think about how you can more deeply honor your kids' consent, even when it's inconvenient. Honor it a little bit more every day, and you'll see huge changes happen. ------

Be On A Healing Path An old guy in a donut shop was going on to his friends about "kids today always talking about mental health, back in my day&" I heard them, so I butt my nose into their conversation. As I often do! I gave them all my card and introduced myself. They were very welcoming. I talked for just a moment about treating kids like full human beings with respect for their experience, when one of the other people in the party, (another old guy) stood up and said, "Actually you know what, it's important for us not to minimize the fact that a lot of young people are talking about this. It's a serious problem and we have to think deeply about it." I was like "Who are you?". In that moment he knew that I saw him, so he came over and said "You know, I just like to think deeply about these things. What do we need for us all to thrive together?" That guy knew how important it is to be on a healing path. We all have things from our past that it would be useful to heal from, to help us shift our patterns, our reactions, our perceptions. It is interesting that we are more effective at loving our kids as we deepen our capacity to love and accept ourselves. Every one of us has experienced pain and trauma in our past, to different degrees and in different ways. Those experiences get wired into our nervous systems and into our neural pathways. They affect how we see the world, and how we see our kids. They affect the patterns, and the reactions that we have. Being on a conscious healing path means we are continuously working at rewiring those pain patterns. That way we don't pass that stuff on to our kids. Of course, we're going to pass it on to our kids. There's no way to avoid it. But what we can do is try our best to minimize it. And minimizing it means being consciously healing ourselves all the time. The actual work is different for everybody, depending on what you've been through, depending on how your brain is wired, how your body is wired, your personality, and your temperament. Depending on your relative privilege, marginalization, and your access to resources. It will be different for all of us, it will never be perfect, and yet in order to do this radical parenting, we need to do what we can. Can you be on a conscious healing path? It's not about perfection, it's about constant evolution. I always say It doesn't matter if you make a million mistakes. It's being on the path that counts. There's tons of information out there and there's so many different healing modalities. I'm not advocating for one over the other. Try different things and find what works for you. I have a video on my YouTube channel called processing challenging emotions. It's for people who don't have access to therapy and don't have a lot of tools, resources and time. How can you still do that processing? It is a full workshop packed with a couple information. I will put the link to that in the comments. Whatever you do, do something! In the long run, it's going to make a huge difference for how you are with your kids. Your children also get the benefit of seeing you on that healing path. It's a powerful and beautiful model to set. Ps I've been making a bunch of pretty memes lately. I've been doing so that you can print them out and put them all around your house. At some point I'm going to be selling high res versions preformatted as printable pdfs.

In my experience we need to say no to kids 90% less than adults normally think we do. Whenever we have more systemic power in a relationship we have an increased responsibility to care for the consent & autonomy of the other. Kids are profoundly dependent on us, physically, mentally, emotionally, relationally. That is a huge responsibility for the adult to treat with integrity. I encourage parents to avoid saying no at all costs unless absolutely necessary. And those absolutely necessary times, as I said before, are much more rare and we think. I am also aware that I am an outlier in the parenting world. The majority of folks who talk about how to treat kids are operating with one foot still in the old mindset. I advocate for treating kids radically Non-Coercively. To change the old, authoritative, hierarchical paradigm that we have operated from for centuries with children. This is why I call the parenting style I teach Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting. How we treat our young people has to be based in values and principles, not convenience and practicality. Of course convenience and practicality play into it because we're human, but if we're going to give our kids our deepest (and I believe they deserve our deepest), the foundation needs to be based on profound values. Non-coercion is a fundamental principle I operate from. Here are a couple of videos that talk about my philosophy of YES if you are interested in understanding the Non-Coercive, Collaborative Parenting mindset more deeply. Say yes as much as possible -------------

Obedience and Respect are Opposites! We and the respect of our kids so much more by modeling it rather than demanding obedience. The traditional mindset thinks we have to demand respect, demand obedience, and then use punishment and reward to create those conditions. It really is a dehumanizing way to treat other people. Especially our children. To respect is formed from a deep, trusting, connected relationship. It comes from going through hard times together, good times together, and developing trust over the long term. There is a realization that occurs where we recognize that control and authority do not create a respectful relationship, that punishment, consequences, and rewards, actually work against our interests as parents. When you're on this side of that realization, it seems obvious that when you demand obedience from your kids, you actually lose respect. But before you have the realization, it seems impossible to let go of control and authority. Because if you release that grip, the kids are going to run wild and you won't be able to control them. This is a very stressful thought. This thought makes us force and push our kids, then they resist, and power struggles are not far behind. You slowly grow apart and they're off with their friends, they don't listen to your advice, they roll their eyes at you, and eventually we lose the relationship. It doesn't have to be this way though. If we parent from a mindset of respect and deep connection, the relationship is preserved. The other benefit of this is our kids learn to trust our guidance and wisdom. No one wants to trust the wisdom of someone who punishes them, criticizes them, and controls them. But it's easy to trust the guidance of someone whom we feel has our best interests at heart. And when I say feel, I mean in our nervous system, and our subconscious. So the next time you are tempted to demand obedience, or when you feel frustrated that your kids aren't listening, take a breath, step back, and try a different approach. Obedience and Respect are Opposites! -------------
